# Valid Pullback in Trading — 3-Step Guide, Wick Grab vs Closing Break, Bullish/Bearish Identification

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback/)

![Valid pullback in trading — bearish pullback candle inside a bullish leg that grabs the low of the highest bullish candle and is followed by the break of its high](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/valid-pullback.png)

Valid pullback in trading is the specific retracement candle (or candle cluster) that confirms the leg is structurally valid — and once you can identify it, every downstream ICT concept (inducement, order block, order flow, BOS) snaps into place.

Pullback is a retracement inside an impulsive move, but a valid pullback has some specific identifications. In this guide I walk you through the valid pullback concept in 3 simple steps — the meaning, the bullish and bearish identification rules, the wick-vs-close distinction, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: What is Pullback in Trading?
content:
#### What is Pullback in Trading?

Pullback in trading is a retracement of an impulse move, which can be a single candle or a number of candlesticks.

Bearish candlesticks in a bullish move and bullish candlesticks in a bearish move are simply called pullbacks.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: What is Valid Pullback in Trading?
content:
#### What is Valid Pullback in Trading?

As discussed earlier, a pullback is a retracement move — but every retracement is not a valid pullback.

A valid pullback has a specific structure: the pullback candle has to grab the low (or high) of the most extreme opposite-color candle in the impulse, and the impulse leg has to then resume by breaking the high (or low) of that candle.

I will divide valid pullback into two types — bullish and bearish.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Valid Pullback in Bullish Market
content:
#### Valid Pullback in Bullish Market

When price moves higher it is called a bullish market — so in a bullish market the bearish candles are the pullbacks.

But to identify a valid pullback in a bullish market you have to check the following.

**(I)** Mark the highest bullish candlestick before the pullback candlestick.

**(II)** Mark the low of that highest bullish candlestick.

**(III)** Check if the low of that highest bullish candlestick is grabbed by the pullback candlesticks.

**(IV)** Check that after the low (of the highest bullish candlestick) is grabbed, the high (of the highest bullish candlestick) is broken.

**For grabbing the low, you just have to check if price went below the low — no matter whether by just a wick or by a candlestick closing.**

**But for breaking the high, the closing of the candlestick above the high is compulsory.**

A real market example is shown below.

![Bullish valid pullback example — bearish pullback wick grabs the low of the highest bullish candle, then the next candle closes above the high of that bullish candle](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/valid-pullback.png)

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Valid Pullback in Bearish Market
content:
#### Valid Pullback in Bearish Market

When price moves lower it is called a bearish market — so in a bearish market the bullish candles are the pullbacks.

But to identify a valid pullback in a bearish market you have to check the following.

**(I)** Mark the lowest bearish candlestick before the pullback candlestick.

**(II)** Mark the high of that lowest bearish candlestick.

**(III)** Check if the high (of that lowest bearish candlestick) is grabbed by the pullback candlesticks.

**(IV)** Check that after the high (of that lowest bearish candlestick) is grabbed, the low (of that lowest bearish candlestick) is broken.

**For grabbing the high, you just have to check if price went above the high — no matter whether by just a wick or by a candlestick closing.**

**But for breaking the low, the closing of the candlestick below the low is compulsory.**

A real market example is shown below.

![Bearish valid pullback example — bullish pullback wick grabs the high of the lowest bearish candle, then the next candle closes below the low of that bearish candle](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/valid-pullback-1.png)

**Note:** This entire phenomenon of valid pullback may happen with a single candlestick or a number of candlesticks.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Wick Grab vs Closing Break — The Asymmetry Rule
content:
#### Wick Grab vs Closing Break — The Asymmetry Rule

The asymmetric rule for valid pullback is what separates a real institutional retracement from a stop-hunt or fake-out.

For the GRAB side (the low in a bullish leg, or the high in a bearish leg) — a wick is enough. Smart money frequently sweeps the level with a wick to trigger stops, and that wick alone qualifies as the grab.

For the BREAK side (the high in a bullish leg, or the low in a bearish leg) — a wick is not enough. The candle has to close beyond the level. A wick that does not close is a stop hunt against the new direction, not a confirmed continuation.

This single asymmetry is why valid pullback works so well — it filters out the stop-hunt pullbacks that have grabs but no follow-through.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Why Valid Pullback Matters for Every Other ICT Concept
content:
#### Why Valid Pullback Matters for Every Other ICT Concept

Valid pullback is the building block of the rest of the framework.

The first valid pullback inside a leg before a [BOS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>) is the [Inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>).

The last bullish (or bearish) candle before the displacement that produced the BOS — that is, the candle whose break confirms the valid pullback — is the candidate [Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>).

Every pullback inside the leg becomes a [ICT Order Flow](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-order-flow-explained/>) re-entry zone.

So mastering valid pullback is the prerequisite for everything that follows.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Step-by-Step Valid Pullback Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Valid Pullback Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading from a valid pullback.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — bullish, bearish or neutral structure.
  2. **Identify the impulse leg.** A clean directional move on the analysis timeframe.
  3. **Mark the most extreme opposite-color candle.** Bullish leg — the highest bullish candle. Bearish leg — the lowest bearish candle.
  4. **Mark the GRAB level.** Bullish — the low of the highest bullish candle. Bearish — the high of the lowest bearish candle.
  5. **Wait for the pullback to grab the level.** A wick is enough. The grab can be by a single candle or a cluster.
  6. **Wait for the BREAK in the original direction.** Bullish — a candle closes above the high of the highest bullish candle. Bearish — a candle closes below the low of the lowest bearish candle.
  7. **Confirm the valid pullback is now valid.** Both grab and break conditions are satisfied — the pullback is structurally complete.
  8. **Use the valid pullback as inducement / order flow / order block.** Wait for price to retrace back to the valid pullback zone.
  9. **Enter on the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation.** At the valid pullback zone, in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  10. **Set the stop.** Beyond the valid pullback extreme, with a small buffer.
  11. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Best Timeframe for Valid Pullback
content:
#### Best Timeframe for Valid Pullback

Valid pullback works on every timeframe. For day trading, mark valid pullbacks on the 15-minute or 1-hour and use the 1-day and 4-hour for the directional context. For swing trading, use the 4-hour and daily for the pullback marking and the daily / weekly for the bias.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Best Pairs for Valid Pullback Analysis
content:
#### Best Pairs for Valid Pullback Analysis

Valid pullback is timeframe-agnostic and instrument-agnostic — it works on every major pair (GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD), metals (XAU/USD, XAG/USD) and indices.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the valid pullback framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for valid pullbacks because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: Common Mistakes Around Valid Pullback
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Valid Pullback

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start identifying valid pullbacks.

  1. **Treating every retracement as a valid pullback.** A retracement is just a counter-color candle. A valid pullback requires both the grab AND the break to occur in sequence.
  2. **Marking the wrong reference candle.** Use the MOST EXTREME opposite-color candle — the highest bullish candle in a bullish leg, the lowest bearish candle in a bearish leg. Not the most recent one.
  3. **Requiring a closing break for the grab.** The grab side accepts a wick. Requiring a closing break disqualifies real institutional sweeps.
  4. **Accepting a wick for the break.** The break side requires a close. A wick above the high (in a bullish leg) without a close is a stop hunt against the new direction — not a valid pullback confirmation.
  5. **Entering at the valid pullback before the break confirms.** The valid pullback is only valid AFTER the break candle closes. Entering at the grab and waiting for the break exposes you to the failed-pullback scenario.
  6. **Skipping the higher-timeframe bias.** Valid pullbacks work best in the direction of the higher-timeframe trend. Counter-trend valid pullbacks have a much lower hit rate.

title: 3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback
section: FAQs about Valid Pullback
content:
#### FAQs about Valid Pullback

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about valid pullback.

**What is a valid pullback in trading?**

Valid pullback is a retracement that grabs the low (in a bullish leg) or the high (in a bearish leg) of the most extreme opposite-color candle, AND is followed by a candle that closes beyond the high (or low) of that reference candle. Both conditions are required.

**How is a valid pullback different from a regular pullback?**

A regular pullback is just any counter-color candle. A valid pullback adds the grab + break confirmation — it tells you the pullback is structurally complete and the impulse leg has resumed.

**Can a valid pullback be a single candle or multiple candles?**

Both. The grab and break can happen with a single candle (one wick that grabs the level and then closes through the opposite extreme) or with multiple candles (one cluster grabs, another cluster breaks).

**Why does the grab accept a wick but the break require a close?**

Because smart money frequently sweeps levels with wicks to trigger retail stops — that wick is the institutional accumulation. But for the impulse to be confirmed as resumed, the next candle has to close beyond the structure, not just wick through it.

**How does valid pullback relate to inducement?**

The first valid pullback inside a leg before a BOS is the inducement. Smart money sweeps the inducement before delivering the real direction.

**How does valid pullback relate to the order block?**

The reference candle (the highest bullish candle in a bullish leg, the lowest bearish candle in a bearish leg) is often the candidate order block. Once the break candle closes through, that reference candle is the OB.

**How does valid pullback relate to ICT Order Flow?**

Every valid pullback inside a leg is a candidate order flow re-entry zone. After the BOS, price typically returns to one of the valid pullbacks before continuing.

**What timeframe is best for spotting valid pullbacks?**

Valid pullback works on every timeframe. For day trading, the 15-minute and 1-hour are the natural marking timeframes. For swing trading, use the 4-hour and daily.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the valid pullback extreme — below the bullish valid pullback low or above the bearish valid pullback high, with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw on liquidity — old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

**Does valid pullback work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook valid pullbacks, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if the grab happens but the break never comes?**

Then the pullback never becomes valid, and the impulse leg has effectively reversed. Mark the new structure and look for the opposite-direction setup.

# Bear Flag Pattern Explained — Pole, Flag, Breakout-Retest & Measured-Move Target

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bear-flag-pattern-explained/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bear-flag-pattern-explained/)

![Bear Flag Pattern — bearish continuation pattern formed by an energetic vertical down-pole and an upward-sloping or horizontal flag retracement](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-flag-pattern-1.png)

Bear Flag is one of the most reliable bearish continuation patterns — an energetic vertical “pole” (a strong sell-off) followed by a slower retracement “flag” that, when broken to the downside, signals the next leg lower. Master the breakout-and-retest entry and you have a clean trend-following short setup.

This guide walks you through the bear flag pattern from formation to identification to execution with real market examples. By thoroughly studying it and dedicating yourself to practice, you will gain the ability to identify a bear flag pattern and execute trading opportunities with the skill of a professional trader. For the bullish mirror see my [Bull Flag Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy/>) guide.

In this guide I walk you through the bear flag concept — the formation, the identification rule, the breakout-and-retest entry, the stop and target rules, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

Table of Contents

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: What is Bear Flag Pattern?
content:
#### What is Bear Flag Pattern?

The bear flag pattern is one of the most reliable bearish continuation patterns. Often seen in downtrends, it is formed when there is a strong sell-off followed by a period of consolidation.

The objective of trading this pattern is to catch the next leg down in the trend.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Bear Flag Pattern Formation
content:
#### Bear Flag Pattern Formation

Bear flag pattern is formed when price has moved down significantly with an energetic move, and at some point it slows down seeking retracement.

The retracement can be due to profit taking of initial sellers.

During the retracement, price may move in the form of a rectangle sloping upward — or it may consolidate between two price levels, making a horizontal rectangle.

So the initial bearish move looks like a vertical pole, and the retracement in the form of a rectangle joined with the pole looks like a flag — which is termed the bear flag pattern.

![Bear flag pattern formation example — energetic vertical bearish pole followed by an upward-sloping flag rectangle, marking the pre-breakout consolidation higher](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-flag-pattern.png)

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: How to Identify Bear Flag Pattern
content:
#### How to Identify Bear Flag Pattern

**(I)** To identify a bear flag pattern, first look for a bearish trend in the market.

**(II)** Now identify the energetic bearish move (the pole).

**(III)** After identifying the trend and a strong bearish move, look for a less energetic retracement move (the flag).

During the retracement, price may make higher highs and higher lows — or equal highs and equal lows by consolidating between two price levels.

Draw a trendline by joining the highs and another trendline by joining the lows. The retracement will form a rising rectangle / wedge shape or a horizontal rectangle shape.

Now join the rectangle with the energetic bearish move by drawing a vertical line. The vertical line indicates the pole and the rectangle indicates the flag — you have a complete bear flag pattern.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: How to Trade Bear Flag Pattern
content:
#### How to Trade Bear Flag Pattern

To trade a bear flag pattern, after identifying the bear flag, wait for price to break the lower trendline of the bear flag.

When price breaks the lower trendline, wait for a retest of the trendline.

![Bear flag breakout example — bearish candle breaks below the lower trendline of the flag rectangle, signaling the continuation of the original bearish trend](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bear-flag.png)

When price retraces back and retests the lower trendline of the bear flag after breakout, look for some bearish signs — for example a bearish candlestick pattern formation or strong price rejection — as a confirmation.

After the confirmation, you can execute a sell trade.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Stop Loss and Take Profit
content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

While trading a bear flag, your stop loss will be above the lower trendline of the bear flag — or as a safety measure, you can set the stop above the upper trendline of the flag, depending on your risk-to-reward ratio.

![Bear flag breakout-and-retest trade example — price breaks the lower trendline, retraces to retest it, and confirms with a bearish rejection candle for the sell entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bear-flag-trading.png)

For take profit, measure the pole length of the bear flag and set your target at the length of the pole, measured from the lower trendline of the flag.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Bear Flag in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Bear Flag in the ICT Framework

Although the bear flag is a classic technical analysis pattern, it sits perfectly inside the ICT framework as a visualization of a bearish [break of structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>) followed by a [valid pullback](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback/>).

The pole is the displacement leg that produced the bearish BOS. The flag is the valid pullback inside that leg. The first valid pullback inside the flag becomes the [inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>). The breakout-and-retest entry is the bearish continuation play after the inducement is taken.

If you trade with ICT, treat the bear flag as a visual shortcut for the BOS-plus-inducement setup and add a lower-timeframe [MSS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) confirmation to filter false breakouts.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Step-by-Step Bear Flag Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Bear Flag Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a bear flag.

  1. **Confirm bearish trend.** Higher-timeframe structure must be bearish — lower highs and lower lows.
  2. **Identify the pole.** An energetic bearish move with large-body candles and clear displacement.
  3. **Mark the flag.** Draw two trendlines connecting the highs and lows of the retracement — either upward-sloping or horizontal rectangle.
  4. **Wait for the breakout.** Price must close below the lower trendline of the flag.
  5. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to the lower trendline after the breakout.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** Bearish candlestick pattern, strong rejection wick, or lower-timeframe MSS at the retested trendline.
  7. **Enter the sell.** On the confirmation candle close.
  8. **Set the stop.** Above the lower trendline (tighter) or above the upper trendline (safer).
  9. **Set the target.** Measure the pole length and project it from the breakout point.
  10. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1 risk-reward, trail to the full pole-projection target.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Best Pairs for Bear Flag Trading
content:
#### Best Pairs for Bear Flag Trading

The bear flag works on every major instrument that produces trending moves — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD, and indices like NQ and ES.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the bear flag framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for bear flag breakouts.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: Common Mistakes Around Bear Flag
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Bear Flag

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading bear flags.

  1. **Trading a bear flag against the trend.** The pattern only works in a bearish trend. A bear flag inside a bullish trend is just a bull retracement waiting to fail.
  2. **Entering at the breakout without retest.** Many breakouts are fakeouts. Wait for the retest of the lower trendline plus a confirmation candle before entering.
  3. **Marking the flag too early.** The flag needs at least 3 to 5 candles of retracement. Treating a single pullback candle as a flag produces noise.
  4. **Wide flags (50%+ retracement of the pole).** A valid flag retraces 30%–50% of the pole. Beyond 50%, the pattern is no longer a flag — it is a reversal candidate.
  5. **Tight stops below the lower trendline.** Stops at the boundary get hunted on the second test. Place the stop above the lower trendline with a buffer, or above the upper trendline for safer trades.
  6. **Ignoring the pole-height target.** The measured-move target is the disciplined way to take profit. Holding for longer than the pole projection breaks the model.

title: bear-flag-pattern-explained
section: FAQs about Bear Flag Pattern
content:
#### FAQs about Bear Flag Pattern

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the bear flag pattern.

**What is a bear flag pattern?**

A bearish continuation pattern formed by an energetic vertical “pole” (initial bearish move) followed by a slower retracement “flag” (upward-sloping or horizontal rectangle). Breakout below the flag’s lower trendline signals continuation lower.

**How do I identify a bear flag?**

Find a bearish trend, identify the energetic bearish move (pole), then draw two trendlines joining the highs and lows of the retracement that follows. The retracement should form a rising rectangle or horizontal rectangle shape (flag).

**What is the difference between a bear flag and a bear pennant?**

Bear flag has parallel trendlines (rectangle). Bear pennant has converging trendlines (triangle). Both are bearish continuation patterns with the same trade rules — measure the pole and project from the breakout.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After price breaks below the lower trendline and retests it, enter on the bearish confirmation candle (rejection wick, bearish engulfing, or lower-timeframe MSS).

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Above the lower trendline (tighter) or above the upper trendline (safer) of the flag, with a small buffer.

**How do I set the take profit?**

Measure the pole height and project it from the breakout point of the lower trendline. This is the measured-move target.

**What timeframe works best for bear flag?**

Bear flag appears on every timeframe. For day trading use 15-minute and 1-hour. For swing trading use 4-hour and daily. Higher timeframes produce more reliable bear flags.

**How does bear flag fit in the ICT framework?**

The pole is the bearish BOS displacement leg. The flag is the valid pullback inside that leg. The breakout-and-retest entry is the post-inducement continuation play. Add a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest for filter.

**Does the bear flag work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook bear flags, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if the breakout fails?**

If price breaks above the upper trendline of the flag instead of breaking down, the pattern is invalidated. The trend may be reversing — switch to looking for long setups.

**What is the success rate of the bear flag?**

In a confirmed bearish trend with a clean pole and tight flag, the bear flag historically has a 65–75% breakout-success rate. The success rate drops significantly when traded against the higher-timeframe trend.

**Do bear flag patterns fail?**

Yes — bear flag patterns can fail too. That is why you should look for confirmation like a clear breakout and retest before taking a trade.

**Can I trade the bear flag with no other indicators?**

Yes — the bear flag is self-contained. But pairing it with the higher-timeframe ICT bias and a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest produces a much higher hit rate than the pattern alone.

# Break of Structure (BOS) in Forex — Bullish/Bearish, Major vs Minor & BOS vs MSS vs CHOCH

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/)

![Break of Structure \(BOS\) in trading — smart money concept showing bullish BOS as a higher high above the previous structure after the inducement is grabbed](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/break-of-structure.png)

Break of Structure (BOS) is the smart-money concept that confirms a trend is continuing — price breaks its previous structure in the direction of the existing trend, after the inducement has been taken. BOS is the level that lets you mark the order flow, the order block and the next valid pullback inside the leg.

In this guide I walk you through the break of structure concept — the meaning, the bullish and bearish variants, the major-vs-minor distinction, the BOS vs MSS comparison, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

Before going in-depth into break of structure you should also know about [Inducement](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>) — the inducement is what defines the difference between a major and a minor BOS.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: What is Break of Structure in Trading?
content:
#### What is Break of Structure in Trading?

Break of structure is the continuation of the market trend by breaking its previous structure.

Break of structure helps us catch continuation trades and identify the market trend.

A bullish break of structure indicates higher prices in the future, while a bearish break of structure indicates lower prices in the future.

You can see the example of BOS in the picture given below.

![Break of structure example — clean break above the previous swing high after price grabbed the inducement, confirming continuation of the bullish trend](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Break-of-structure-BOS.png)

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: How to Identify Break of Structure
content:
#### How to Identify Break of Structure

Before identifying break of structure you should know about [Inducement](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>), because the break of previous structure after taking the inducement is the valid break of structure.

On the basis of market trend, break of structure can be divided into two types — bullish and bearish.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: (I) Bullish Break of Structure
content:
#### (I) Bullish Break of Structure

When price is in a bullish trend it makes higher highs — meaning it always breaks its previous high making a new high — and this is called a bullish break of structure.

But break of structure is incomplete without inducement, so a break of structure in a bullish trend happens when price grabs the inducement and breaks the previous high making a higher high.

You can see the real market example of bullish break of structure in the picture given below.

![Bullish break of structure real market example — price grabs the inducement low, then breaks the previous swing high to confirm a higher high BOS](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bullish-break-of-structure.png)

If price breaks the previous high without grabbing the inducement, it is called a minor break of structure — a new high is found but the previous low remains intact.

You can see the example of bullish minor BOS in the picture given below.

![Bullish minor BOS example — price breaks the previous swing high without first grabbing the inducement, shifting only the high while the low remains intact](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bullish-Minor-Bos.png)

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: (II) Bearish Break of Structure
content:
#### (II) Bearish Break of Structure

When price is in a bearish trend it makes lower lows — meaning it always breaks its previous low making a new low — and this is known as a bearish break of structure.

But break of structure is incomplete without inducement, so a break of structure in a bearish trend happens when price grabs the inducement and breaks the previous low making a lower low.

You can see the example of bearish break of structure in the picture given below.

![Bearish break of structure real market example — price grabs the inducement high, then breaks the previous swing low to confirm a lower low BOS](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/bearish-break-of-structure.png)

If price breaks the previous low without taking out the inducement it is called a minor break of structure — a new lower low is formed but the previous lower high remains the same.

You can see the example of bearish minor BOS in the picture given below.

![Bearish minor BOS example — price breaks the previous swing low without first grabbing the inducement, shifting only the low while the high remains intact](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bearish-Minor-BOS.png)

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: Major vs Minor Break of Structure
content:
#### Major vs Minor Break of Structure

The single rule that separates a major BOS from a minor BOS is whether the inducement was taken before the break.

Major BOS — price grabbed the inducement first, then broke the structure. This is the high-conviction continuation signal that confirms the structural shift.

Minor BOS — price broke the structure WITHOUT first taking the inducement. The high (or low) shifts, but the rest of the market structure remains intact, and a new inducement has to be marked. See my [Inducement After Break of Structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/inducement-after-break-of-structure/>) guide for the full breakdown.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: Best Timeframe to Identify Break of Structure
content:
#### Best Timeframe to Identify Break of Structure

Market structure appears across all timeframes, and different timeframes often display different market structures.

So you can identify break of structure on any timeframe by marking the previous structure.

The best approach is to have a clear understanding of the market as a whole — this includes low timeframe, medium timeframe and high timeframe structure. Think about each timeframe and align the market structure as a top-down analysis.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: How to Trade Break of Structure in Forex
content:
#### How to Trade Break of Structure in Forex

**In a bullish market** , when price breaks the structure you should mark the inducement and wait for price to retrace back and take the inducement.

When price grabs the inducement you can look for buy trades with confirmations like a [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) or trend reversal on the lower timeframe.

**In a bearish market** , when the market breaks the structure you should mark the inducement and wait for price to retrace back and take the inducement.

When price grabs the inducement you can look for sell trades with confirmations like a market structure shift or trend reversal on the lower timeframe.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: Step-by-Step BOS Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step BOS Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a break of structure.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — bullish, bearish or neutral structure.
  2. **Identify the previous structure.** The most recent swing high (bullish) or swing low (bearish) on the analysis timeframe.
  3. **Wait for the BOS to print.** A clean break above the previous swing high (bullish) or below the previous swing low (bearish).
  4. **Mark the inducement inside the leg.** The first valid pullback inside the leg that produced the BOS — this is what defines a major BOS once swept.
  5. **Wait for price to retrace and grab the inducement.** Bullish — price dips below the inducement low. Bearish — price spikes above the inducement high.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** A lower-timeframe MSS, fair value gap or order block formed after the inducement sweep.
  7. **Enter on the retest.** Take the trade in the higher-timeframe direction at the post-sweep PD array.
  8. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept inducement extreme, with a small buffer.
  9. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: ICT MSS vs BOS
content:
#### ICT MSS vs BOS

Break of structure indicates the break of previous structure (high or low) AFTER taking out the inducement.

ICT market structure shift indicates the break of a [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>) or [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>).

So the difference between break of structure and market structure shift is just inducement.

Break of structure indicates the larger shift in the price trend, while market structure shift indicates the initial shift in the structure.

You can see the picture below explaining BOS vs MSS.

![ICT MSS vs BOS comparison — MSS breaks a swing high or low to signal initial reversal, while BOS breaks the previous structure after the inducement is taken to confirm continuation](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/MSS-vs-BOS-1.png)

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: BOS vs CHOCH
content:
#### BOS vs CHOCH

Break of structure (BOS) confirms the continuation of the existing trend. [Change of character (CHOCH)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>) confirms the reversal of the existing trend.

In a bullish trend, BOS is the break above the previous swing high. CHOCH is the break below the most recent higher low.

In a bearish trend, BOS is the break below the previous swing low. CHOCH is the break above the most recent lower high.

BOS = continuation. CHOCH = reversal.

Break of structure works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD. The cleanest BOS prints come from instruments that produce strong displacement legs.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the BOS framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for BOS trades because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: Common Mistakes Around Break of Structure
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Break of Structure

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the break of structure concept.

  1. **Treating every wick as a BOS.** A BOS requires a clean close beyond the previous swing high or low — not just a wick. Wicks above the high without a close are stop hunts, not BOS prints.
  2. **Ignoring the inducement.** A BOS without an inducement sweep is a minor BOS at best. The full directional confirmation requires inducement to be taken.
  3. **Confusing BOS with CHOCH.** BOS is continuation. CHOCH is reversal. Mixing them up flips the trade direction entirely.
  4. **Trading the BOS without higher-timeframe alignment.** A BOS on the 15-minute against the daily bias has a much lower hit rate than a BOS aligned with the daily.
  5. **Entering at the BOS level itself.** The BOS is the structural confirmation. The entry is the post-inducement-sweep retest at a PD array — not the BOS candle.
  6. **Chasing the BOS after the move has already extended.** If price has already moved several ATRs past the BOS without retracing, the trade is gone. Wait for the next setup rather than chasing.

title: break-of-structure-bos
section: FAQs about Break of Structure
content:
#### FAQs about Break of Structure

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about BOS.

**What is break of structure in trading?**

Break of structure is the smart-money concept that confirms a trend is continuing — price breaks its previous swing high (bullish) or swing low (bearish) after taking out the inducement. BOS is what lets you mark the order flow and the order block inside the leg.

**What is the difference between BOS and MSS?**

BOS = break of previous structure AFTER taking inducement (continuation). MSS = break of a swing high or swing low (initial reversal signal). The single difference is whether the inducement was taken first.

**What is the difference between BOS and CHOCH?**

BOS confirms the continuation of the existing trend. CHOCH confirms the reversal. In a bullish trend, BOS is a higher high; CHOCH is the break of the most recent higher low.

**What is a minor break of structure?**

Minor BOS is when price breaks the previous structure WITHOUT first grabbing the inducement. The high (or low) shifts, but the rest of the structure remains intact, and a new inducement has to be marked.

**How do I trade a break of structure?**

Wait for the BOS to print, mark the inducement inside the leg, wait for price to retrace and grab the inducement, then enter on the lower-timeframe MSS or order block confirmation. Stop beyond the swept inducement extreme; target the next draw on liquidity.

**What timeframe is best for spotting BOS?**

BOS works on every timeframe. For day trading, mark the BOS on the 15-minute or 1-hour and use the 1-day and 4-hour for the directional context.

**Where do I place the stop loss on a BOS trade?**

Beyond the swept inducement extreme — below the inducement low for buy trades, above the inducement high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw on liquidity — old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

**Does BOS work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook BOS prints, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if price breaks the structure with a wick but no close?**

A wick without a close beyond the previous swing is not a valid BOS — that is a stop hunt. Wait for the candle to close beyond the structure for the BOS to be confirmed.

**Is the inducement required for every BOS?**

For a major BOS — yes. For a minor BOS — no. The minor BOS is the structural shift without the inducement; a major BOS requires the inducement to be swept first.

# BOS vs CHOCH — Continuation vs Reversal, BOS vs CHOCH vs MSS & Combined Trade Flow

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character/)

![BOS vs CHOCH — Break of Structure confirms continuation while Change of Character confirms reversal, with the only difference being the direction of the structural break](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/BOS-vs-CHOCH-ICT.png)

Break of Structure (BOS) and Change of Character (CHOCH) are the two opposite-direction structural breaks that drive every smart-money trade decision — BOS confirms continuation, CHOCH confirms reversal, and the single difference between them is the direction of the break relative to the existing trend.

Break of structure in trading refers to the break of the previous high in a bullish trend and the break of the previous low in a bearish trend, which indicates continuation of the trend.

Change of character in trading refers to the break of the previous low in a bullish trend and the break of the previous high in a bearish trend — and CHOCH indicates reversal of the trend.

In this guide I walk you through the BOS vs CHOCH comparison — the definition of each, the key differences, the reliability question, the role of candle close, the step-by-step trade flow that uses both, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: What is Break of Structure (BOS)?
content:
#### What is Break of Structure (BOS)?

When price breaks its structure in the direction of the previous trend, it is called a Break of Structure (BOS) — a trend continuation pattern.

In a bullish trend price makes higher highs. Each time price breaks a previous high and marks a new high, it is known as a bullish break of structure.

In a bearish trend price makes lower lows. Each time price breaks a previous low and makes a new low, it is called a bearish break of structure.

Traders utilize break of structure to identify the current trend of the market.

You can see the example of break of structure (BOS) in the picture given below.

![Break of Structure \(BOS\) example — bullish trend producing a clean break above the previous swing high to confirm continuation of the bullish trend](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Break-of-Structure-BOS.png)

For the deep-dive on BOS — major vs minor BOS, the inducement requirement and the trade flow — see my dedicated [Break of Structure (BOS) guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>).

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: What is Change of Character (CHOCH)?
content:
#### What is Change of Character (CHOCH)?

Change of Character refers to the reversal of market trend — either from bullish to bearish or bearish to bullish.

CHOCH is also a break of market structure, but in the opposite direction.

If price is in a bullish trend but breaks its previous low (higher low) and makes a lower low, it is termed a “bearish change of character” because price has changed its trend from bullish to bearish.

Likewise, if price is in a bearish trend and breaks its previous high (lower high) making a higher high, it is marked as a “bullish change of character” because price has changed its trend from bearish to bullish.

Traders utilize change of character (CHOCH) to identify the reversal of market trend.

You can see the example of CHOCH in the picture given below.

![Change of Character \(CHOCH\) example — bullish trend ending with a break below the previous higher low to confirm the reversal from bullish to bearish](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/CHANGE-OF-CHARACTER-CHOCH.png)

For the deep-dive on CHOCH — bullish and bearish variants, the inducement after CHOCH, and the trade flow — see my dedicated [Change of Character (CHOCH) guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>).

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: BOS vs CHOCH — Side-by-Side
content:
#### BOS vs CHOCH — Side-by-Side

The single difference between BOS and CHOCH is the direction of the structural break relative to the existing trend.

**Direction.** BOS = same direction as the existing trend. CHOCH = opposite direction.

**Signal type.** BOS = continuation. CHOCH = reversal.

**What gets broken.** Bullish trend BOS breaks the previous swing HIGH; bullish trend CHOCH breaks the most recent higher LOW. Bearish trend BOS breaks the previous swing LOW; bearish trend CHOCH breaks the most recent lower HIGH.

**What it confirms.** BOS confirms the trend is intact. CHOCH confirms the trend has flipped.

**What you do with the bias.** After BOS, keep trading the existing trend. After CHOCH, flip the bias and start looking for setups in the new direction.

**The structural extreme.** BOS = swing extreme of the dominant direction. CHOCH = counter-trend swing extreme inside the dominant leg.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: BOS vs CHOCH vs MSS
content:
#### BOS vs CHOCH vs MSS

A third concept lives in the same family — the [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>).

**BOS** — break of the previous structural extreme in the trend direction (continuation, after inducement).

**CHOCH** — break of the most recent counter-trend structural extreme (reversal).

**MSS** — break of any swing high or low (initial reversal trigger). MSS often precedes a CHOCH but does not always become one.

For the full MSS-vs-CHOCH breakdown see my [MSS vs CHOCH guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/mss-vs-choch/>).

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: Which is More Reliable — BOS or CHOCH?
content:
#### Which is More Reliable — BOS or CHOCH?

Both BOS and CHOCH are breaks of structure — their directions are opposite, and both have the same structural reliability.

The difference is what each one offers. BOS offers the continuation of the trend with high probability and shorter targets (the next continuation level). CHOCH offers the reversal of price with more pips of potential, because the new trend has to travel through the entire prior leg before the next reversal.

In practice — BOS for safer continuation, CHOCH for higher-reward reversals.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: Can We Trade on the Basis of BOS Alone?
content:
#### Can We Trade on the Basis of BOS Alone?

Yes — you can trade on the basis of break of structure once you have identified the market trend correctly.

But for executing a trade you should look for extra confirmation — for example a lower-timeframe MSS at the post-BOS PD array, or a fair value gap formed after the inducement sweep. The BOS is the structural confirmation; the MSS or FVG is the entry trigger.

section: Does the Candle Need to Close for BOS and CHOCH?
content:
#### Does the Candle Need to Close for BOS and CHOCH?

Yes — after the close of the candlestick, both break of structure and change of character are confirmed.

Without the closing of the candlestick we cannot mark a BOS or CHOCH. A wick that pokes above the level without a close is a stop hunt, not a confirmed structural break.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: Step-by-Step Trade Flow Using BOS and CHOCH
content:
#### Step-by-Step Trade Flow Using BOS and CHOCH

This is the exact sequence I run when using both concepts together.

  1. **Set the higher-timeframe bias.** 1-day and 4-hour structure — has there been a recent CHOCH? If yes, the bias has flipped. If no, the existing trend is intact (BOS country).
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe PD array.** Order block, FVG or breaker that price is drawn to inside the bias-aligned zone.
  3. **Wait for the structural confirmation.** Continuation play — wait for BOS in the trend direction. Reversal play — wait for CHOCH at the higher-timeframe extreme.
  4. **Mark the inducement inside the BOS or CHOCH leg.** The first valid pullback inside the leg.
  5. **Wait for the inducement sweep.** Bullish — price dips below the inducement low. Bearish — price spikes above the inducement high.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe (5-minute or 15-minute).** For the entry trigger.
  7. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS at the swept inducement.** A clean break of the most recent counter-trend swing point in the bias direction.
  8. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the post-sweep PD array.
  9. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept inducement extreme, with a small buffer.
  10. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG. Reversal trades target the entire prior leg.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: Common Mistakes Around BOS vs CHOCH
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around BOS vs CHOCH

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using both concepts.

  1. **Confusing BOS and CHOCH.** BOS = continuation. CHOCH = reversal. Mixing them up flips the trade direction entirely.
  2. **Trading the BOS without inducement.** A BOS without an inducement sweep is a minor BOS at best. The full directional confirmation requires inducement to be taken first.
  3. **Trading the CHOCH without a higher-timeframe key level.** A CHOCH at a random place is unreliable. CHOCH at a higher-timeframe support, resistance, FVG or order block is high-conviction.
  4. **Treating wicks as structural breaks.** Both BOS and CHOCH require a candle to close beyond the structure — a wick alone is a stop hunt.
  5. **Entering at the BOS or CHOCH level itself.** The structural break is the confirmation. The entry is the post-inducement-sweep retest at a lower-timeframe PD array.
  6. **Trading every CHOCH against the higher-timeframe bias.** A CHOCH that flips the lower timeframe but contradicts the daily is a weaker setup than a CHOCH aligned with the daily reversal.

title: break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character
section: FAQs about BOS vs CHOCH
content:
#### FAQs about BOS vs CHOCH

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about BOS vs CHOCH.

**What is the difference between BOS and CHOCH?**

BOS = break of structure in the direction of the existing trend (continuation). CHOCH = break of structure in the opposite direction (reversal). Same structural break, opposite signal.

**Is BOS the same as CHOCH?**

No — BOS continues the trend, CHOCH reverses it. The directional difference is what makes them opposite signals.

**Which is more reliable, BOS or CHOCH?**

Both have the same structural reliability. BOS offers higher win rate on continuation; CHOCH offers larger reward on reversal because the new leg has to travel the entire prior leg before the next reversal.

**Can I trade on the basis of BOS alone?**

Yes, once the trend is correctly identified — but always wait for an extra confirmation (MSS, FVG, OB) inside the post-BOS PD array before entering.

**Does the candle need to close for BOS or CHOCH?**

Yes — both BOS and CHOCH are only confirmed after the candle closes beyond the level. A wick alone is a stop hunt, not a confirmed structural break.

**How does CHOCH relate to MSS?**

MSS breaks any swing high or low; CHOCH breaks the structural extreme. Every CHOCH involves an MSS, but not every MSS becomes a CHOCH. See my [MSS vs CHOCH guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/mss-vs-choch/>) for the deep-dive.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the swept inducement extreme — below the inducement low for buy trades, above the inducement high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

For BOS continuation — the next draw on liquidity in the trend direction. For CHOCH reversal — the start of the prior leg, plus relative equal levels and higher-timeframe FVGs along the way.

**What timeframe is best for spotting BOS and CHOCH?**

Both appear on every timeframe. For day trading, mark them on the 15-minute or 1-hour and use the 1-day and 4-hour for the directional context.

**Do BOS and CHOCH work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook BOS and CHOCH prints, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if a CHOCH happens but no inducement is created?**

Then it is a minor CHOCH and the next CHOCH inside the new leg becomes the confirmation. Wait for the inducement to print before committing to the reversal trade.

# Bull Flag Pattern Trading Strategy — Pole, Flag, Breakout-Retest & Measured-Move Target

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy/)

![Bull Flag Pattern trading strategy — bullish continuation pattern formed by an energetic vertical pole and a downward-sloping or horizontal flag retracement](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bull-flag-pattern-1.png)

Bull Flag Pattern is one of the cleanest bullish continuation patterns on the chart — an energetic vertical “pole” followed by a slower retracement “flag” that, when broken to the upside, signals the next leg higher. Master the formation and breakout-retest entry and you have a reliable trend-following setup.

This guide walks you through the bull flag pattern from identification to execution with real market examples. By thoroughly studying it and dedicating yourself to practice, you will gain the ability to identify a bull flag pattern and execute trading opportunities with the skill of a professional trader.

In this guide I walk you through the bull flag concept — the formation, the identification rule, the breakout-and-retest entry, the stop and target rules, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: What is Bull Flag Pattern?
content:
#### What is Bull Flag Pattern?

Bull Flag — also known as Bullish Flag — is a bullish chart pattern that indicates higher prices for an asset in the coming days.

Bull Flag is a bullish continuation pattern formed in between a bullish trend, and it signals the continuation of the trend.

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: Bull Flag Pattern Formation
content:
#### Bull Flag Pattern Formation

Bull flag is formed when price has moved up significantly with an energetic move, and at some point it slows down seeking retracement.

The retracement can be due to profit taking of initial buyers.

During the retracement, price may move in the form of a rectangle sloping downward — or it may consolidate between two price levels, making a horizontal rectangle.

So the initial bullish move looks like a vertical pole, and the retracement in the form of a rectangle joined with the pole looks like a flag — which is termed the bull flag pattern.

![Bull flag pattern formation example — energetic vertical bullish pole followed by a downward-sloping flag rectangle, marking the pre-breakout consolidation](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/BULL-FLAG-PATTERN.png)

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: How to Identify Bull Flag Pattern
content:
#### How to Identify Bull Flag Pattern

**(I)** To identify a bull flag pattern, first look for a bullish trend in the market.

**(II)** Now identify the energetic bullish move (the pole).

**(III)** After identifying the trend and a strong bullish move, look for a less energetic retracement move (the flag).

During the retracement, price may make lower highs and lower lows — or equal highs and equal lows by consolidating between two price levels.

Draw a trendline by joining the highs and another trendline by joining the lows. The retracement will form a falling rectangle / wedge shape or a horizontal rectangle shape.

Now join the rectangle with the energetic bullish move by drawing a vertical line. The vertical line indicates the pole and the rectangle indicates the flag — you have a complete bull flag pattern.

![Bull flag identification example — vertical pole drawn from start of bullish move, two trendlines joining highs and lows of the retracement flag rectangle](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/BULLISH-FLAG-PATTERN.png)

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: How to Trade Bull Flag Pattern
content:
#### How to Trade Bull Flag Pattern

To trade a bull flag pattern, after identifying the pattern you have to wait for price to break the upper trendline of the flag.

![Bull flag breakout example — bullish candle breaks above the upper trendline of the flag rectangle, signaling the continuation of the original bullish trend](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/breakout-of-flag.png)

When price breaks the upper trendline, wait for a retest of the trendline.

When price retraces back and retests the upper trendline of the bull flag after breakout, look for some bullish signs — for example a bullish candlestick pattern formation or strong price rejection — as a confirmation.

![Bull flag breakout-and-retest trade example — price breaks the upper trendline, retraces to retest it, and confirms with a bullish rejection candle for the buy entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bullish-flag-trading.png)

After the confirmation, you can execute a buy trade.

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: Stop Loss and Take Profit
content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

While trading a bull flag, your stop loss will be below the upper trendline of the bull flag — or as a safety measure you can set the stop below the lower trendline of the flag, depending on your risk-to-reward ratio.

For take profit, measure the pole length of the bull flag and set your target at the height of the pole, measured from the upper trendline of the flag.

![Bull flag pattern target measurement example — pole height measured from the start of the bullish move to the high of the pole, then projected from the breakout point](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bull-flag-pattern-strategy-1.png)

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: Bull Flag in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Bull Flag in the ICT Framework

Although the bull flag is a classic technical analysis pattern, it sits perfectly inside the ICT framework as a visualization of a [break of structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>) followed by a [valid pullback](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/3-step-guide-to-master-valid-pullback/>).

The pole is the displacement leg that produced the BOS. The flag is the valid pullback inside that leg. The first valid pullback inside the flag becomes the [inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>). The breakout-and-retest entry is the bullish continuation play after the inducement is taken.

If you trade with ICT, treat the bull flag as a visual shortcut for the BOS-plus-inducement setup and add a lower-timeframe [MSS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) confirmation to filter false breakouts.

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: Step-by-Step Bull Flag Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Bull Flag Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a bull flag.

  1. **Confirm bullish trend.** Higher-timeframe structure must be bullish — higher highs and higher lows.
  2. **Identify the pole.** An energetic bullish move with large-body candles and clear displacement.
  3. **Mark the flag.** Draw two trendlines connecting the highs and lows of the retracement — either downward-sloping or horizontal rectangle.
  4. **Wait for the breakout.** Price must close above the upper trendline of the flag.
  5. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to the upper trendline after the breakout.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** Bullish candlestick pattern, strong rejection wick, or lower-timeframe MSS at the retested trendline.
  7. **Enter the buy.** On the confirmation candle close.
  8. **Set the stop.** Below the upper trendline (tighter) or below the lower trendline (safer).
  9. **Set the target.** Measure the pole height and project it from the breakout point.
  10. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1 risk-reward, trail to the full pole-projection target.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the bull flag framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: Common Mistakes Around Bull Flag
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Bull Flag

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading bull flags.

  1. **Trading a bull flag against the trend.** The pattern only works in a bullish trend. A bull flag inside a bearish trend is just a bear retracement waiting to fail.
  2. **Entering at the breakout without retest.** Many breakouts are fakeouts. Wait for the retest of the upper trendline plus a confirmation candle before entering.
  3. **Marking the flag too early.** The flag needs at least 3 to 5 candles of retracement. Treating a single pullback candle as a flag produces noise.
  4. **Wide flags (50%+ retracement of the pole).** A valid flag retraces 30%–50% of the pole. Beyond 50%, the pattern is no longer a flag — it is a reversal candidate.
  5. **Tight stops above the upper trendline.** Stops at the boundary get hunted on the second test. Place the stop below the upper trendline with a buffer, or below the lower trendline for safer trades.
  6. **Ignoring the pole-height target.** The measured-move target is the disciplined way to take profit. Holding for longer than the pole projection breaks the model.

title: bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy
section: FAQs about Bull Flag Pattern
content:
#### FAQs about Bull Flag Pattern

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the bull flag pattern.

**What is a bull flag pattern?**

A bullish continuation pattern formed by an energetic vertical “pole” (initial bullish move) followed by a slower retracement “flag” (downward-sloping or horizontal rectangle). Breakout above the flag’s upper trendline signals continuation higher.

**How do I identify a bull flag?**

Find a bullish trend, identify the energetic bullish move (pole), then draw two trendlines joining the highs and lows of the retracement that follows. The retracement should form a falling rectangle or horizontal rectangle shape (flag).

**What is the difference between a bull flag and a bull pennant?**

Bull flag has parallel trendlines (rectangle). Bull pennant has converging trendlines (triangle). Both are bullish continuation patterns with the same trade rules — measure the pole and project from the breakout.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After price breaks above the upper trendline and retests it, enter on the bullish confirmation candle (rejection wick, bullish engulfing, or lower-timeframe MSS).

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Below the upper trendline (tighter) or below the lower trendline (safer) of the flag, with a small buffer.

**How do I set the take profit?**

Measure the pole height and project it from the breakout point of the upper trendline. This is the measured-move target.

**What timeframe works best for bull flag?**

Bull flag appears on every timeframe. For day trading use 15-minute and 1-hour. For swing trading use 4-hour and daily. Higher timeframes produce more reliable bull flags.

**How does bull flag fit in the ICT framework?**

The pole is the BOS displacement leg. The flag is the valid pullback inside that leg. The breakout-and-retest entry is the post-inducement continuation play. Add a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest for filter.

**Does the bull flag work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook bull flags, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if the breakout fails?**

If price breaks below the lower trendline of the flag instead of breaking up, the pattern is invalidated. The trend may be reversing — switch to looking for short setups.

**What is the success rate of the bull flag?**

In a confirmed bullish trend with a clean pole and tight flag, the bull flag historically has a 65–75% breakout-success rate. The success rate drops significantly when traded against the higher-timeframe trend.

**Can I trade the bull flag with no other indicators?**

Yes — the bull flag is self-contained. But pairing it with the higher-timeframe ICT bias and a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest produces a much higher hit rate than the pattern alone.

# Bullish Pennant Pattern — Flag Pole, Symmetrical Triangle & Measured-Move Target

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bullish-pennant-pattern/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bullish-pennant-pattern/)

![Bullish Pennant Pattern — bullish continuation chart pattern with strong flag pole followed by converging trendlines forming a symmetrical triangle pennant](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/pennant-pattern.png)

Bullish Pennant is a bullish continuation pattern — a strong bullish “flag pole” followed by a tight consolidation between two converging trendlines that forms a symmetrical triangle (the “pennant”). When price breaks out of the pennant in the original trend direction, it signals the next leg higher. It is the converging-triangle cousin of the [Bull Flag Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy/>).

In this guide I walk you through the bullish pennant — the formation, the 5-step identification rule, the breakout-and-retest entry, the measured-move target, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: What is Bullish Pennant Pattern?
content:
#### What is Bullish Pennant Pattern?

It is a type of [bullish flag pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/bull-flag-pattern-trading-strategy/>), with only one difference — a pennant has converging trendlines forming a symmetrical triangle, whereas a flag has parallel trendlines forming a rectangle.

The bullish pennant is a bullish continuation pattern that indicates the extension of the uptrend after a period of consolidation.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: Bullish Pennant Pattern Formation
content:
#### Bullish Pennant Pattern Formation

It starts with a strong bullish move termed the flag pole.

After a strong move up, price tends to consolidate between two converging trendlines, making a pennant.

During the consolidation phase, volume is marked lower.

The formation of the pattern suggests that market participants are taking a temporary break and consolidating their positions.

![Bullish pennant pattern formation example — strong bullish flag pole followed by converging trendlines forming the symmetrical triangle pennant consolidation](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bull-pennant.png)

This indicates a period of indecision and balance between buyers and sellers.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: How to Identify Bullish Pennant Pattern
content:
#### How to Identify Bullish Pennant Pattern

**(I)** Look for a bullish market structure and a strong move up. Without a strong bullish move, it is just a symmetrical triangle.

**(II)** After identifying the trend and strong bullish move, look for a less energetic retracement move.

**(III)** During the retracement move, identify “lower highs” and “higher lows”.

**(IV)** Now draw a trendline by joining the lower highs and another trendline by joining the higher lows. It will form a symmetrical triangle shape because the trendlines are converging.

**(V)** Now join the top of the symmetrical triangle with the previous bullish move (the flag pole) by a vertical line. It will form a complete bullish pennant pattern with flag pole and pennant.

![Bullish pennant identification example — vertical flag pole, two converging trendlines connecting lower highs and higher lows, forming the symmetrical triangle pennant](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bullish-pennant.png)

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: How to Trade Bullish Pennant Pattern
content:
#### How to Trade Bullish Pennant Pattern

To trade a bullish pennant, be patient and wait for the breakout of the pennant to the upside.

After the breakout of the pennant, wait for price to retrace back and retest the upper trendline of the pennant.

At the moment when price approaches the pennant and retests the upper trendline, look for some confirmations like a bullish candlestick pattern or a strong price rejection to the upside.

After the confirmation, you can execute a buy trade.

![Bullish pennant breakout-and-retest trade example — price breaks above the upper trendline of the pennant, retraces to retest it, confirms with bullish rejection for the buy entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bullish-pennant-trading.png)

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: Stop Loss and Take Profit
content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

While executing a buy trade using the bullish pennant pattern, your stop loss will be below the upper trendline of the pennant — or for safety, set your stop loss below the lower trendline of the pennant, depending on your risk appetite.

For take profit, measure the length of the flag pole and target that height from the pennant breakout point to the upside.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: Bullish Pennant vs Bull Flag
content:
#### Bullish Pennant vs Bull Flag

Both are bullish continuation patterns and both use the same flag-pole + measured-move logic. The structural difference is in the consolidation:

**Bull Flag** — parallel trendlines, rectangle shape, sloping downward or horizontal.

**Bullish Pennant** — converging trendlines, symmetrical triangle shape, narrowing toward the apex.

In practice, the pennant suggests slightly tighter consolidation and often resolves faster than the flag. Both have the same trade rules — wait for breakout, retest, confirmation, then enter with measured-move target.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: Common Mistakes Around Bullish Pennant
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Bullish Pennant

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading bullish pennants.

  1. **Trading a pennant without a flag pole.** Without the strong bullish move before, it is just a symmetrical triangle — not a pennant. The flag pole is mandatory.
  2. **Trading a pennant against the trend.** The pattern only works in a bullish trend. A bullish pennant in a bearish trend is just a bear retracement waiting to fail.
  3. **Entering at the breakout without retest.** Many breakouts are fakeouts. Wait for the retest of the upper trendline plus a confirmation candle.
  4. **Marking the pennant too early.** The pennant needs at least 4 to 6 candles of consolidation with clear converging trendlines. Forcing the shape too soon produces fakes.
  5. **Tight stops above the upper trendline.** Stops at the boundary get hunted on the second test. Place the stop with a buffer below the upper trendline, or below the lower trendline for safer trades.
  6. **Ignoring the flag-pole-height target.** The measured-move target is the disciplined way to take profit. Holding for longer than the flag-pole projection breaks the model.

title: bullish-pennant-pattern
section: FAQs about Bullish Pennant Pattern
content:
#### FAQs about Bullish Pennant Pattern

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the bullish pennant pattern.

**What is a bullish pennant pattern?**

A bullish continuation pattern formed by a strong bullish “flag pole” followed by a tight consolidation between converging trendlines that forms a symmetrical triangle (the “pennant”). Breakout above the upper trendline signals continuation higher.

**How do I identify a bullish pennant?**

Find a bullish trend, identify the strong bullish move (flag pole), then draw two converging trendlines joining the lower highs and higher lows of the retracement. The result should be a symmetrical triangle attached to the top of the flag pole.

**What is the difference between a bullish pennant and a bull flag?**

Bull flag has parallel trendlines (rectangle shape). Bullish pennant has converging trendlines (symmetrical triangle shape). Both are bullish continuation patterns with the same flag-pole + measured-move trade rules.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After price breaks above the upper trendline and retests it, enter on the bullish confirmation candle (rejection wick, bullish engulfing, or lower-timeframe MSS).

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Below the upper trendline (tighter) or below the lower trendline (safer) of the pennant, with a small buffer.

**How do I set the take profit?**

Measure the length of the flag pole and project it from the breakout point of the upper trendline. This is the measured-move target.

**What timeframe works best for bullish pennant?**

Bullish pennant appears on every timeframe. For day trading use 15-minute and 1-hour. For swing trading use 4-hour and daily. Higher timeframes produce more reliable pennants.

**How does the bullish pennant fit in the ICT framework?**

The flag pole is the bullish BOS displacement leg. The pennant is the valid pullback consolidation that contains the inducement. The breakout-and-retest entry is the post-inducement continuation play.

**Does the bullish pennant work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook bullish pennants, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if the breakout fails?**

If price breaks below the lower trendline of the pennant instead of breaking up, the pattern is invalidated. The trend may be reversing — switch to looking for short setups.

**What is the success rate of the bullish pennant?**

In a confirmed bullish trend with a clean flag pole and tight pennant, the bullish pennant historically has a 60–70% breakout-success rate. The success rate drops significantly when traded against the higher-timeframe trend.

**Can I trade the bullish pennant with no other indicators?**

Yes — the bullish pennant is self-contained. But pairing it with the higher-timeframe ICT bias and a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest produces a much higher hit rate than the pattern alone.

# Candle Range Theory (CRT) — Bullish & Bearish Models, MSS Entry & Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/candle-range-theory-crt/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/candle-range-theory-crt/)

![Candle Range Theory \(CRT\) — bullish and bearish CRT models showing the higher-timeframe candle range and the liquidity raid that triggers the entry on the lower timeframe](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/WhatsApp-Image-2024-10-01-at-04.29.16.jpeg)

Candle Range Theory (CRT) is a viral trading concept that maps a higher-timeframe candle as a range on the lower timeframe and uses the liquidity raid of that range as the trigger for the trade.

Being an ICT trader I know that price moves because of liquidity and inefficiency. CRT is also based on liquidity, which is why it slots so cleanly into the ICT methodology.

Before going forward I want to give a short disclaimer that the candle range theory is not an ICT concept but it is derived from the ICT trading concepts like the [ICT Liquidity Sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>), [ICT Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>) and [ICT Session High/Low Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-asian-range/>).

This article walks you through the bullish and bearish CRT models, the exact 3-candle sequence, the entry triggers, the stop placement, the best pairs, common mistakes and the free PDF download.
