title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: What is Candle Range?
content:
#### What is Candle Range?

Before understanding the candle range you should have a basic knowledge of the [candlestick](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/all-candlestick-patterns-explained-with-visuals/>).

Every candlestick on a higher timeframe represents a range on the lower timeframe.

So the high of a candlestick represents the high of a range on the lower timeframe — which is called the CRT-High — while the low of the candlestick represents the low of the range on the lower timeframe — which is called the CRT-Low. ICT himself has explained this principle in his earlier mentorships.

![Higher-timeframe H4 candle defining the CRT range — the candle high becomes the CRT-High and the candle low becomes the CRT-Low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/CRT-H4.png)

![Lower-timeframe 15-minute view of the same H4 candle showing the price action that built the CRT range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/CRT-15-MINUTE.png)

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: What is Candle Range Theory (CRT)?
content:
#### What is Candle Range Theory (CRT)?

Candle Range Theory is based on the liquidity raid of the previous candle range and then a run to the next liquidity level.

If price grabs the liquidity of the previous candle’s low we can expect price to run toward the high of the candle range, and vice versa for a sweep of the high.

That single mechanic — sweep one side of the range, then deliver to the other side — is the entire CRT model.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Bullish CRT Model
content:
#### Bullish CRT Model

If price is at a key support level on a higher timeframe then you can look for a bullish CRT model.

For a bullish CRT model you mark the high and low of the candlestick that closed at support. Now wait for the next candlestick to grab the low of the previous candle and close above the low.

After that, wait for another candlestick to close above the high of the candlestick that raided the low — or simply look for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on the lower timeframe and then execute a buy trade on the retest.

This entire phenomenon can happen with only 3 candlesticks, but sometimes price may accumulate after raiding the low so the setup can involve more than 3 candlesticks.

![Bullish CRT model on a 2-hour chart — sweep of the prior candle low at support followed by a higher close](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Bullish-CRT-2H.png)

![Bullish CRT entry on the 5-minute chart — MSS confirmation and retest entry inside the prior candle range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Bullish-CRT-05M.png)

In this case your stop-loss sits below the low of the candlestick that raided the liquidity or below the MSS-low. For take profit you target the CRT-High or the next liquidity level above.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Bearish CRT Model
content:
#### Bearish CRT Model

When price is at a key resistance level on a higher timeframe, you can look for a bearish CRT model.

For a bearish CRT model, begin by marking the high and low of the candlestick that closed at the resistance level. Then wait for the next candlestick to grab the high of the previous candle and close below that high.

After this setup, you can wait for the following candlestick to close below the low of the candlestick that took out the high. Alternatively, you can look for an ICT Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe and then enter a sell trade on the retest.

This entire scenario can unfold within just three candlesticks, but sometimes price may consolidate after grabbing the high, so it could involve more than three candlesticks.

![Bearish CRT model on a 4-hour chart — sweep of the prior candle high at resistance followed by a lower close](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Bearish-CRT-4H.png)

![Bearish CRT entry on the 5-minute chart — MSS confirmation and retest entry below the swept high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Bearish-CRT-5-minute.png)

For risk management, your stop-loss should be placed above the high of the candlestick that grabbed liquidity or above the MSS-high. For take profit, target the CRT-Low or the next liquidity level below.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Step-by-Step CRT Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step CRT Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run before placing a CRT trade — from higher-timeframe context to lower-timeframe execution.

  1. **Anchor on a higher timeframe.** Identify the H4, H1 or daily candle that has just closed at a key support or resistance.
  2. **Mark the CRT-High and CRT-Low.** The high and low of that anchor candle define the entire range.
  3. **Wait for the raid.** The next candle must take out either the CRT-High (for a bearish setup) or the CRT-Low (for a bullish setup).
  4. **Confirm the close.** The raiding candle must close back inside the range — above the CRT-Low for a bullish setup, below the CRT-High for a bearish setup.
  5. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** Move to the 15-minute or 5-minute chart to look for the entry trigger.
  6. **Look for an MSS.** A market structure shift on the lower timeframe confirms the change in delivery direction.
  7. **Enter on retest.** Enter on the retest of the MSS — typically into a fair value gap or order block left behind by displacement.
  8. **Set the stop.** Stop-loss below the candle that raided liquidity (bullish) or above it (bearish), or simply at the MSS swing.
  9. **Take profit at the opposite side of the range.** Target the CRT-High for bullish trades and CRT-Low for bearish trades, with extension to the next external liquidity pool.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: High Probability CRT Setups
content:
#### High Probability CRT Setups

High-probability CRT setups can be found during the [ICT Kill Zones](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-kill-zones/>) or [ICT Sessions Raid](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-asian-range/>).

I personally trade CRT setups most often when the higher-timeframe candle that anchors the range closes inside a London or NY-AM kill zone, because that is where the algorithm tends to deliver the strongest displacement after the sweep.

The CRT-High and CRT-Low also tend to coincide with prior session high/low and prior day high/low — which adds a second layer of confluence to the model.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Best Pairs and Markets for CRT
content:
#### Best Pairs and Markets for CRT

CRT works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to — major forex pairs, indices and metals.

I have personally taken CRT setups on GBP/USD, EUR/USD, NQ (NASDAQ futures), ES (S&P 500 futures) and XAU/USD with consistent results. The model is timeframe-agnostic, but the daily, H4 and H1 candles produce the cleanest CRT ranges in my own log.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, CRT is particularly natural on NQ and ES futures (CME Group) because there is no short-selling restriction on index futures. Many of my US-based readers trade CRT on the daily candle as a swing setup and on the H1 candle inside the 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>).

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: ICT Power of 3 vs CRT
content:
#### ICT Power of 3 vs CRT

Candle range theory is basically the application of the [ICT Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>).

ICT PO3 states that price will first accumulate, then manipulate by moving in one direction and taking short-term liquidity, then distribute by moving in the opposite direction.

According to CRT, price accumulates inside the range and takes the liquidity of either the CRT-High or the CRT-Low, then moves toward the opposite side.

The CRT-High/Low can also be the ICT previous day high/low or previous session high/low — which is why CRT setups are so often telegraphed by the higher-timeframe [PD array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>).

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Common Mistakes When Trading CRT
content:
#### Common Mistakes When Trading CRT

These are the mistakes I see most often from traders who first start trading the CRT model.

  1. **Trading CRT in the middle of the range.** The model only works when the anchor candle closes at a meaningful support or resistance — not in the middle of nowhere.
  2. **Skipping the close confirmation.** The raiding candle must close back inside the range. A wick that pokes the level and continues without a close-back is not a CRT, it is just a continuation.
  3. **Entering without an MSS.** The lower-timeframe market structure shift is the trigger. Entering on the raid alone front-runs the setup.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked exactly at the MSS swing get hunted on the wick. A small buffer (a few pips on forex, a few ticks on indices) is required.
  5. **Targeting only the CRT-High/Low.** The opposite side of the range is the first target — not the only one. The next external liquidity pool is often a higher-quality target on a strong day.
  6. **Ignoring the kill zone.** CRT setups outside of the London or NY-AM kill zones (and outside of the Asian-range raid window) deliver less reliably.

title: candle-range-theory-crt
section: Conclusion
content:
#### Conclusion

Candle range theory is nothing new — this is what ICT taught us years ago and people just renamed it and packed it into their label claiming a new trading strategy. The model is sound, the mechanics are clean and the alignment with PO3, liquidity sweep and the kill zones makes it one of the more accessible ICT-derived setups for traders who are still building their core read of the market.

**What is Candle Range Theory in trading?**

Candle Range Theory is a model in which the high and low of a higher-timeframe candle define a range on the lower timeframe, and a sweep of one side of that range is followed by a delivery to the opposite side.

**Is CRT an ICT concept?**

CRT is not an original ICT concept, but it is derived from ICT trading concepts including liquidity sweep, Power of 3 and session high/low liquidity.

**What is the CRT-High and CRT-Low?**

The CRT-High is the high of the higher-timeframe anchor candle and the CRT-Low is the low of the same candle. Both levels mark the boundary of the range on the lower timeframe.

**How many candles does a CRT setup take?**

The classic CRT can complete in 3 candles, but sometimes price may accumulate after the raid, so the setup can involve more than 3 candles.

**Where do I place the stop loss on a CRT trade?**

For a bullish CRT, place the stop below the low of the candle that raided the liquidity or below the MSS-low. For a bearish CRT, place the stop above the high of the candle that raided the liquidity or above the MSS-high.

**What is the take profit on a CRT trade?**

The first target is the opposite side of the range — CRT-High for bullish trades and CRT-Low for bearish trades. The next external liquidity pool is the secondary target.

**Which timeframe is best for CRT?**

The daily, H4 and H1 candles produce the cleanest CRT ranges. The 5-minute and 15-minute timeframes are used for the entry trigger and MSS confirmation.

**Does CRT work on forex pairs?**

Yes — CRT works on major forex pairs like GBP/USD and EUR/USD, on index futures like NQ and ES, and on metals like XAU/USD.

**Is CRT the same as ICT Power of 3?**

CRT is a direct application of the ICT Power of 3. The accumulate-manipulate-distribute sequence is the engine that drives the CRT range.

**Can beginners trade CRT?**

Yes — CRT is one of the more accessible ICT-derived models for beginners because it requires only 3 things: a higher-timeframe close at support or resistance, a sweep of one side of the range, and an MSS for the entry.

# Change of Character (CHOCH) in Trading — Bullish/Bearish Reversal & CHOCH vs BOS vs MSS

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/)

![Change of Character \(CHOCH\) in trading — break of the previous market structure in the opposite direction signaling a trend reversal from bullish to bearish or vice versa](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/CHANGE-OF-CHARACTER.png)

Change of Character (CHOCH) is the first structural confirmation that the trend has reversed — the break of the most recent higher low (in a bullish trend) or lower high (in a bearish trend) that ends the existing series and opens a new one in the opposite direction.

Change of Character in trading is the first indication of trend reversal in the financial markets, and it helps you catch good reversal trades early.

In this guide I walk you through the change of character concept — the meaning, the bullish and bearish variants, the CHOCH vs BOS vs MSS distinctions, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

Table of Contents

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: What is Change of Character in Trading?
content:
#### What is Change of Character in Trading?

As obvious from the term, change of character signals a possible change in the trend of the market — either from bullish to bearish or bearish to bullish.

It is a break of structure, but in the opposite direction of the previous trend, which indicates the change of market trend.

On the basis of market trend, change of character can be divided into two types — bullish and bearish.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: (I) Bullish Change of Character
content:
#### (I) Bullish Change of Character

Bullish change of character is the reversal of market trend from bearish to bullish, and it happens at the end of a bearish trend.

In a bearish trend price makes lower lows and lower highs. At the time when price changes its trend, it breaks its structure in the opposite direction making a higher high.

Previously price was making lower highs — but at the time of change of character, price breaks the lower high and makes a higher high.

In this way the series of lower highs comes to an end and a new series of higher highs starts — meaning the trend has reversed from bearish to bullish.

![Bullish CHOCH example — bearish trend ends with a break above the most recent lower high, confirming the change of character to bullish and the start of higher highs](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bullish-CHOCH.png)

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: (II) Bearish Change of Character
content:
#### (II) Bearish Change of Character

Bearish change of character is the reversal of market trend from bullish to bearish, and it happens at the end of a bullish trend.

In a bullish trend price makes higher highs and higher lows. At the time when price changes its trend, it breaks its structure in the opposite direction making a lower low.

Previously price was making higher lows — but at the time of change of character, price breaks the higher low and makes a lower low.

In this way the series of higher lows comes to an end and a new series of lower lows starts — meaning the trend has reversed from bullish to bearish.

![Bearish CHOCH example — bullish trend ends with a break below the most recent higher low, confirming the change of character to bearish and the start of lower lows](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/bearish-choch.png)

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: CHOCH vs BOS vs MSS
content:
#### CHOCH vs BOS vs MSS

These three concepts overlap but they are not the same — and confusing them flips the trade direction.

**BOS ([Break of Structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>))** — continuation. In a bullish trend, BOS is the break of the previous swing high. In a bearish trend, BOS is the break of the previous swing low. BOS confirms the existing trend is still intact.

**CHOCH (Change of Character)** — reversal. In a bullish trend, CHOCH is the break of the most recent higher low. In a bearish trend, CHOCH is the break of the most recent lower high. CHOCH confirms the existing trend has flipped.

**MSS ([Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>))** — initial reversal signal. MSS breaks any swing high or swing low — a short-term shift in delivery that may or may not become a full CHOCH. See my dedicated [MSS vs CHOCH guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/mss-vs-choch/>) and [BOS vs CHOCH guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-vs-change-of-character/>) for the deep-dive.

The shortest version: BOS = continuation, CHOCH = reversal, MSS = early reversal trigger.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: Best Timeframe to Identify Change of Character
content:
#### Best Timeframe to Identify Change of Character

Market structure appears across all timeframes, and different timeframes often display different market structures.

So you can identify change of character on any timeframe by marking the previous structure.

The best approach is to have a clear understanding of the market as a whole. This includes lower timeframe, medium timeframe and higher timeframe structure. Think about each timeframe and align the market structure as a top-down analysis.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: How to Trade Change of Character
content:
#### How to Trade Change of Character

**In a bullish CHOCH** , when the market changes its character from bearish to bullish, you should mark the inducement and wait for price to retrace back and take the inducement.

When price grabs the inducement, you can look for buying opportunities with confirmations like a market structure shift or trend reversal on the lower timeframe.

**In a bearish CHOCH** , when the market changes its character from bullish to bearish, you should mark the inducement and wait for price to retrace back and take the inducement.

When price grabs the inducement, you can look for selling opportunities with confirmations like a market structure shift or trend reversal on the lower timeframe.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: Step-by-Step CHOCH Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step CHOCH Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a change of character.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — identify the existing trend and the higher-timeframe key level price is approaching.
  2. **Wait for price to reach a higher-timeframe PD array.** Order block, FVG or breaker at the extreme of the existing trend.
  3. **Watch for the CHOCH on the analysis timeframe.** Bullish CHOCH — clean break above the most recent lower high. Bearish CHOCH — clean break below the most recent higher low.
  4. **Mark the inducement inside the CHOCH leg.** The first valid pullback inside the leg that produced the CHOCH.
  5. **Wait for the inducement sweep.** Bullish — price dips below the inducement low. Bearish — price spikes above the inducement high.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** A lower-timeframe MSS, fair value gap or order block formed after the sweep.
  7. **Enter on the retest.** In the new (post-CHOCH) direction at the post-sweep PD array.
  8. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept inducement extreme, with a small buffer.
  9. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe FVG.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: Best Pairs for CHOCH Trading
content:
#### Best Pairs for CHOCH Trading

CHOCH works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD. The cleanest CHOCH prints come from instruments that produce strong reversal legs at higher-timeframe key levels.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the CHOCH framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for CHOCH reversals because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: Common Mistakes Around the Change of Character
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the Change of Character

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the change of character concept.

  1. **Treating every counter-trend break as a CHOCH.** CHOCH requires the break of the most recent STRUCTURAL higher low or lower high — not just any swing point. Random swing breaks are MSS, not CHOCH.
  2. **Ignoring the higher-timeframe key level.** A CHOCH at random place is unreliable. CHOCH at a higher-timeframe support, resistance, FVG or order block is high-conviction.
  3. **Entering before the CHOCH inducement is swept.** Pre-positioning into the CHOCH zone almost always ends with a stopped trade. Wait for the inducement sweep.
  4. **Confusing CHOCH with BOS.** BOS = continuation. CHOCH = reversal. Mixing them up flips the trade direction entirely.
  5. **Stop too tight after the CHOCH.** Stop must sit beyond the swept inducement extreme — not at the CHOCH level itself. Tight stops at the level get hunted on the second test.
  6. **Trading every CHOCH against the higher-timeframe.** A CHOCH on the 15-minute against a daily trend is a weaker setup than a CHOCH that aligns with the daily reversal.

title: change-of-character-choch-in-trading
section: FAQs about Change of Character
content:
#### FAQs about Change of Character

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about CHOCH.

**What is change of character in trading?**

Change of character is the first structural confirmation that the trend has reversed — the break of the most recent higher low (bullish trend) or lower high (bearish trend) that ends the existing series and opens a new one in the opposite direction.

**What is the difference between CHOCH and BOS?**

CHOCH is reversal. BOS is continuation. In a bullish trend, BOS is the break of the previous swing high; CHOCH is the break of the most recent higher low. They sit at opposite extremes of the same structure.

**What is the difference between CHOCH and MSS?**

MSS breaks any swing high or low — a short-term reversal signal. CHOCH breaks the structural extreme — a confirmed long-term reversal. Every CHOCH involves an MSS, but not every MSS becomes a CHOCH.

**How do I identify a bullish CHOCH?**

In a bearish trend, watch for price to break above the most recent lower high after reaching a higher-timeframe support or demand level. That break confirms the bullish CHOCH.

**How do I identify a bearish CHOCH?**

In a bullish trend, watch for price to break below the most recent higher low after reaching a higher-timeframe resistance or supply level. That break confirms the bearish CHOCH.

**What timeframe is best for CHOCH trading?**

CHOCH appears on every timeframe. For day trading, mark the CHOCH on the 15-minute or 1-hour and use the 1-day and 4-hour for the directional context.

**Where do I place the stop loss on a CHOCH trade?**

Beyond the swept inducement extreme — below the inducement low for buy trades, above the inducement high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw on liquidity — old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe PD array in the new direction.

**Does CHOCH always result in a change of trend?**

No — trading is the game of probabilities. CHOCH gives a high probability of trend change but may fail. Its success ratio is greater than its failure ratio.

**What if CHOCH fires but the trend does not actually reverse?**

Then the move was a deep retracement that reclaimed the structural extreme. The fix is to wait for the post-CHOCH inducement sweep before entering — that filters out the failed CHOCHs.

**Does CHOCH work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook CHOCH reversals at higher-timeframe key levels, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**How does CHOCH relate to QML?**

QML is structurally similar to CHOCH but can form at any non-structural higher low or lower high — earlier than the full CHOCH. Every CHOCH is a QML, but not every QML is a CHOCH.

# Complete ICT Trading Strategy 2022 — The 2022 Mentorship Model + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022/)

![ICT 2022 trading strategy diagram showing London open liquidity sweep, market structure shift, and PD Array entry flow](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-trading-strategy.png)

The complete ICT trading strategy I cover here was introduced by Michael Huddleston in his 2022 mentorship and it changed how a generation of retail traders read price action.

It is an algorithmic strategy built on time and price — as Huddleston puts it, price is nothing without the time. The 2022 model gives you a clear daily bias, two well-defined session entry windows (London open and New York open), and a precise execution framework on the lower timeframes.

When followed strictly, this is a complete intraday strategy that can deliver 50 pips or more on a single setup at a 1:3 risk-reward ratio or better. I trade it on indexes and on the major USD pairs, and I have walked hundreds of these setups on live charts since I started teaching the method.

This guide is the full breakdown — what the 2022 model is, how I execute it on London and New York opens, the exact times and timeframes I use, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

Use the table of contents to jump to any section.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: What is the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy?
content:
#### What is the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy?

The ICT 2022 trading strategy is the algorithmic intraday model Michael Huddleston taught in his 2022 mentorship. It treats price as a delivery mechanism that institutions move through specific time windows in pursuit of [Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>) and the rebalancing of imbalances.

The strategy is built on three pillars: a higher-timeframe daily bias to anchor direction, a session liquidity sweep to mark the inflection, and a lower-timeframe entry trigger off a refined ICT PD Array. When all three line up, the trade is high probability. When even one is missing, I stand aside.

It is a complete intraday strategy that can yield 50 pips or more at a 1:3 risk-reward ratio when paired with a correct [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>).

**How the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy Works**

To trade the 2022 model successfully, I follow this sequence on every setup. The daily bias comes first — without it, the rest of the model is guesswork.

Once the bias is set, I wait for the London session to open at 03:00 AM New York local time and I let the model unfold from there.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: Step-by-Step Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Trade Flow

This is the exact ten-step execution checklist I run before every 2022-model trade. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Establish daily bias** on the daily and 4-hour charts before the session opens.
  2. **Mark the price range** from NY-midnight (00:00 NY local) to the London open (03:00 NY local). The high and low of this range are your reference levels.
  3. **Wait for London open** at 03:00 AM NY local time. Do not pre-position.
  4. **Look for a liquidity sweep** of the previous range high or low in the direction opposite to your bias (a typical Judas move).
  5. **Watch for an ICT Market Structure Shift** on the lower timeframes (5-minute, 3-minute, or 1-minute) in the direction that aligns with your bias. See the dedicated [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) guide.
  6. **Confirm displacement** on the MSS leg. The candle that breaks the prior swing should close decisively, ideally leaving an imbalance behind. See [Displacement Move](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/>).
  7. **Mark the ICT PD Array** created during the displacement leg — fair value gap, order block, inverse fair value gap, or breaker block — using the [ICT PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>) framework.
  8. **Validate that the PD Array sits in the correct premium or discount zone** relative to the swept range, using the [premium and discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) framework.
  9. **Wait for price to retrace** back into the PD Array. Do not chase.
  10. **Execute the trade** at the PD Array tap, with stop loss beyond the swept extreme and take profit at the opposite end of the swept range or beyond.

The same ten-step flow applies at the New York open, with the New York range substituted for the London range when London has been quiet.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: London-Session Trading Strategy
content:
#### London-Session Trading Strategy

Before the London open, I always mark the high and low of the price range that has formed from NY-midnight (00:00 NY local) to London open (03:00 NY local). These two levels are the reference for every London setup.

When the London session opens, I look for price to take the high or low of that previous price range in line with my bias — that is the [Liquidity Sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>).

After the liquidity sweep of the previous price range, I look for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) with a clean [Displacement Move](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/>) on the lower timeframes (5-minute or 3-minute, or even 1-minute when I have the experience to read it cleanly), on the opposite side of the sweep — aligning with the daily bias.

After the ICT market structure shift, I mark the [ICT PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>) — fair value gap, order block, inverse fair value gap, or breaker block — using the ICT premium and discount tool.

I then wait for price to trade back to the ICT PD Array sitting in the correct premium or discount zone.

When price tests the ICT PD Array, I execute the trade as shown in the example below.

![London session trade example — NY-midnight to London open price range high and low marked on EURUSD chart](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ict-london-trading-strategy-1.png)

In the picture above the price range high and low are marked before the London open.

![London open liquidity sweep followed by ICT market structure shift to the sell side and FVG entry execution](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ict-london-trading-strategy-2.png)

Price moves up after London open to raid the liquidity of the range high and right after the liquidity sweep, price returns and shifts the structure to the sell side.

After the MSS, price retraces back to the FVG and the sell trade is executed inside the FVG with the stop loss above the London high and take profit at the range low.

The trade successfully raided the low of the range and delivered 70 pips at a 1:3 risk-reward ratio.

**The London open is highly volatile and can yield strong moves because it overlaps with the ICT London Open Kill Zone time.**

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: New York Session Trading Strategy
content:
#### New York Session Trading Strategy

The New York session opens at 08:00 AM New York local time. There are two scenarios I plan for, depending on what London did.

**Scenario I — London already swept liquidity and moved away.** The New York session typically delivers a retracement followed by continuation in London’s direction.

In this scenario I draw a Fibonacci from the London session low to the high reached prior to the New York retracement (or the inverse, depending on the direction of the move).

I then wait for price to tap the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) levels and execute in the direction of the London delivery, after a confirmation like an ICT MSS on the 1-minute timeframe.

![New York session continuation example — range high and low marked before London open](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-NewYork-trading-strategy-1.png)

In the picture above, the range high and low are marked before the London open. Price runs above the range high after the London session open.

![Price reverses after London sweep, retraces into ICT Optimal Trade Entry zone at New York open, sell trade executed](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-NewYork-trading-strategy-2.png)

After sweeping the liquidity of the range high, price reverses to the downside and slows down. Meanwhile the New York session opens at 08:00 AM and price retraces back into the London range to tap the ICT Optimal Trade Entry levels.

A sell trade is executed at the ICT Optimal Trade Entry with stop loss above the London high and take profit at the range low. Price grabs the range low and successfully hits the target.

**Scenario II — London ranged and did not sweep liquidity.** If London remained range-bound, I mark the high and low of the price range from NY-midnight to the New York open and wait.

When the New York session opens, I look for the liquidity sweep on either the high or the low side, in line with my daily bias.

After the liquidity sweep, I look for an ICT market structure shift with displacement on the lower timeframes (5-minute or 3-minute, or 1-minute with experience) on the opposite side of the sweep — aligning with the daily bias.

After the ICT market structure shift, I mark the ICT PD Array — fair value gap, order block, inverse fair value gap, or breaker block — using the ICT premium and discount tool.

I then wait for price to trade back to the ICT PD Array sitting in the correct premium or discount zone.

When price tests the ICT PD Array, I execute the trade as shown in the example below.

![New York session example — range high and low marked, London session ranged without sweeping](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-trading-strategy-1.png)

In the picture above the range high and low are marked. The London session remained quiet and did not grab the high or low of the range.

![New York open sweeps the range low, taking sell-side liquidity](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-trading-strategy-2-1.png)

After the New York session opens, price grabs the low of the range.

![Market structure shift after sweep, retracement into breaker block, buy trade execution with stop below order block](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-trading-strategy-3.png)

While grabbing the low of the range, price reverses to the upside and shifts the market structure. After the MSS, price retraces back to the Breaker Block where a buy trade is executed with stop loss below the low of the order block and take profit at the range high.

Price ran up cleanly and hit the target, delivering 70 pips.

content:
#### Key Time-Frames for the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy

The 2022 model uses a clean timeframe ladder. I read each of these every session, in this order:

  * **Daily timeframe** — to set the ICT daily bias.
  * **1-hour timeframe** — for the higher-timeframe perspective and key levels.
  * **15-minute timeframe** — to identify the liquidity pools and price imbalances.
  * **5-minute, 3-minute, and 1-minute timeframes** — for the trade confirmation (MSS) and execution.

The 1-minute is the sharpest entry tool, but it is also the easiest to misread. I do not recommend it until you have at least a hundred logged 5-minute setups behind you.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: Types of Liquidity for the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy
content:
#### Types of Liquidity for the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy

These are the six liquidity references I work with on every 2022-model session, in order of priority:

  1. Previous day high / low draw on liquidity.
  2. Previous session high / low draw on liquidity.
  3. Previous week high / low draw on liquidity.
  4. Established high / low on the 15-minute timeframe.
  5. Return to current or old week opening gap.
  6. Return to current or old day opening gap.

The first three carry the most weight because the orders sitting at those levels are the largest. The lower three are intraday refinements.

The volatility is high, the news flow concentrates here, and most of the day’s range is delivered in this window.

For US-based traders, this is also the cleanest window to trade because it lines up with morning hours in the New York and Eastern time zones — no late-night sessions required.

content:
#### Best Pairs to Trade Using the ICT 2022 Model

The ICT trading strategy works across markets, but the indices Huddleston favours are **NASDAQ 100 (NQ Futures)** and the **E-mini S &P 500 (ES Futures)**. These two are tracked in every 2022-mentorship lecture for a reason — the time-of-day delivery is cleanest on the US index futures.

For forex, the major USD pairs work very well: **GBP/USD** , **EUR/USD** , and **XAU/USD** (Gold). The 2022 model on these pairs respects the same kill-zone logic and the same liquidity types.

US futures traders should note that ES and NQ are CFTC-regulated futures and execute through a US futures broker (NinjaTrader, AMP, Tradovate, or a prop firm such as Topstep). TradingView is for chart analysis only — order placement happens at the broker.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the 2022 Model
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the 2022 Model

Five mistakes show up in nearly every comment I receive on this strategy. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading without a daily bias.** The 2022 model is a directional strategy. Without a higher-timeframe bias, the liquidity sweep and the MSS are just noise. Set the bias on the daily before the session opens, then trade only in that direction.
  2. **Entering before the market structure shift confirms.** A liquidity sweep alone is not a signal. Price has to break the most recent counter-trend swing on the lower timeframe before I act. A wick poke into the PD Array without an MSS first is a setup that fails far more often than it works.
  3. **Stop loss too tight on the sweep.** The sweep candle often takes out a few pips beyond the prior extreme before reversing. If your stop sits one pip beyond the swing high or low, you are trading on the wrong side of the algorithm. Place stops beyond the wick of the sweep candle, with a small buffer.
  4. **Ignoring the kill-zone time window.** Setups that print outside the London Open or New York Open kill zones are generally lower quality. The 2022 model is built around specific times. If the chart pattern looks right but the clock says 11:30 AM NY, I usually skip.
  5. **Oversizing the position.** A 1:3 risk-reward target is realistic on this model, but only when stops are honoured. Risking 2% per trade is the upper bound I would suggest for anyone still in the first six months on this method. The discipline matters more than the entry technique.

title: complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022
section: FAQs About the ICT Trading Strategy
content:
#### FAQs About the ICT Trading Strategy

**What is the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy?**

The ICT 2022 Trading Strategy is the algorithmic intraday approach introduced by Michael Huddleston in his 2022 mentorship. It focuses on liquidity sweeps and price imbalances, with time and price as the two anchoring inputs that guide every trade.

**How does the ICT 2022 Trading Strategy work?**

The strategy revolves around identifying the correct daily bias, waiting for a session liquidity sweep at the London or New York open, confirming with a market structure shift on the lower timeframe, and executing on a refined PD Array entry in the right premium or discount zone.

**What is an ICT Daily Bias?**

ICT Daily Bias is the directional read of the market for the day — bullish or bearish — drawn from higher-timeframe price action and the next significant draw on liquidity. It is the first input in the 2022 model and the rest of the model relies on it being correct.

**What is a liquidity sweep in ICT trading?**

A liquidity sweep is when price takes out the stops sitting above a previous high or below a previous low, then reverses or accelerates. The sweep is the trigger event that opens the entry window for the 2022 model.

**What are the key timeframes for the ICT 2022 strategy?**

Daily timeframe for bias, 1-hour for higher-timeframe perspective, 15-minute for liquidity and imbalances, and 5-minute / 3-minute / 1-minute for confirmation and execution. The same ladder applies to indices and forex pairs alike.

**When should I trade using the ICT 2022 Trading Model?**

The two highest-probability windows are the London open at 03:00 AM New York time and the New York open at 08:00 AM New York time. Both overlap with kill zones and carry the volatility that the 2022 model needs.

**How is Fibonacci used in the ICT 2022 strategy?**

Fibonacci is used to mark Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) levels during retracements after major price moves, particularly after liquidity sweeps. The OTE zone identifies the discount or premium price levels for trade entries.

**What are the best currency pairs to trade using the ICT 2022 model?**

The model works well on US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) and on the major USD pairs — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, and XAU/USD. The cleaner the time-of-day delivery on the instrument, the better the model performs.

**Why does time matter so much in the ICT 2022 strategy?**

Price moves only when liquidity is available and volatility is concentrated. Both of these align with specific session windows — London open and New York open. Outside those windows, the model gives fewer high-probability setups.

**Can I trade the ICT 2022 model on a 1-minute chart?**

Yes, but the 1-minute timeframe demands experience. It magnifies wicks, false breaks, and noise. I recommend running at least a hundred logged 5-minute setups before moving down to the 1-minute for execution.

**What should I do if the London session is range-bound?**

If London remains range-bound, wait for the New York open. Mark the NY-midnight to NY-open range, then look for the New York session to sweep one side of the range and shift structure on the lower timeframe before entering.

**Is the ICT 2022 model profitable for beginners?**

The model is profitable when the rules are followed strictly. It is not easy, but it gives a clear bias and clear triggers. Beginners should expect six to twelve months of demo work before risking real capital. There is no shortcut.

I hope this guide helps you master the ICT 2022 trading strategy. You may also want to read my guides on [ICT Optimal Trade Entry Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) and [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>) before you put the model on charts.

# Dragonfly Doji Candlestick — Bullish Reversal at Support with Long Lower Wick

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/dragonfly-doji-candlestick/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/dragonfly-doji-candlestick/)

![Dragonfly Doji Candlestick — bullish reversal pattern with long lower wick and almost no real body, open high and close at the same price level](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Dragonfly-Doji-Candlestick-2.png)

Dragonfly Doji is one of the cleanest bullish reversal candlesticks on the chart — a single candle with a long lower wick and virtually no real body, signaling that sellers pushed price down but were forcefully overwhelmed by buyers who drove it back to the open. When it prints at a strong support area, it is one of the highest-conviction reversal triggers in candlestick analysis.

In this guide I walk you through the Dragonfly Doji — the definition, how to use it, stop and target rules, the limitations, comparisons with the hammer and gravestone doji, other bullish reversal candles, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: What is Dragonfly Doji?
content:
#### What is Dragonfly Doji?

A doji candlestick is one which has a small body range — almost 5% to 10% of its wick.

A Dragonfly Doji candlestick has its open, high and close price at the same level, with a long wick at the bottom.

It signals potential reversal of price to the upside. As the candlestick opens, price initially goes down — but when buyers enter the market, they push price up, resulting in the close of the candlestick near its open price.

![Dragonfly doji candlestick anatomy — open, high and close at the same level, with a long lower wick showing buyer rejection of the lows](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/dragonfly-doji.png)

It is named because its shape resembles a dragonfly — having a long tail and a small body at the top.

Most traders wait for the follow-up candlestick to close above the high of the dragonfly candlestick as a confirmation of the dragonfly doji.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: How to Use Dragonfly Doji
content:
#### How to Use Dragonfly Doji

To trade using dragonfly doji, look for a bearish market trend approaching a strong support area.

When price approaches the support zone, it gets strong rejection as buyers enter the market. Wait for the candlestick to close.

When you see a dragonfly doji candlestick forming at the support zone, wait for the next candlestick to close above the high of the dragonfly doji — it will confirm the reversal of price from the support zone.

After the confirmation of the dragonfly doji, wait for price to retrace back and test the dragonfly doji candlestick’s body or wick.

When price approaches the dragonfly doji candlestick, you can execute a buy trade.

![Dragonfly doji trade example — bearish trend tests support, dragonfly doji forms with confirmation candle, then retraces back to the doji body for the buy entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/dragonfly-trading.png)

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Stop Loss and Take Profit
content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

When you buy at the support using a dragonfly doji, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the low of the dragonfly doji.

For profit target, set your take profit at the next resistance level — keeping in view your risk-reward ratio.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: What Does Dragonfly Doji Tell Us?
content:
#### What Does Dragonfly Doji Tell Us?

Dragonfly doji informs about the losing control of sellers and the entrance of buyers in the market — which indicates the potential reversal of price.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Limitations of Dragonfly Doji
content:
#### Limitations of Dragonfly Doji

Dragonfly doji sometimes may fail as an indicator of reversal — price may go down below the low of the dragonfly doji.

Sometimes the follow-up candlestick may close much higher and price may not retrace back, so traders may not get into a buy position because of the larger stop loss disturbing the risk-reward ratio.

Dragonfly doji candlestick does not define the profit target — so you have to use other strategies to find a safe exit.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Dragonfly Doji vs Hammer Candlestick
content:
#### Dragonfly Doji vs Hammer Candlestick

Both dragonfly doji and hammer are bullish reversal candlesticks formed at the end of a downtrend.

But dragonfly doji has no real body — its open, high and close price are almost the same. The hammer candlestick has a small real body, either bullish or bearish.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Can We Use Dragonfly Doji for Scalping?
content:
#### Can We Use Dragonfly Doji for Scalping?

Yes — dragonfly doji can be used for scalping on lower timeframes like 15-minute or 5-minute.

But keep in mind that lower timeframes have less reliability as compared to higher timeframes, and they offer low risk-to-reward as well.

section: Dragonfly Doji vs Gravestone Doji
content:
#### Dragonfly Doji vs Gravestone Doji

Both are doji candlesticks with almost no real bodies, and both candlesticks indicate reversal of price.

The main difference between dragonfly doji and gravestone doji is the direction of price.

![Dragonfly doji vs gravestone doji comparison — dragonfly has long lower wick \(bullish reversal\) while gravestone has long upper wick \(bearish reversal\)](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/gravestonedoji-VS-dragonfly-doji.png)

[Gravestone doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/gravestone-doji-candlestick/>) has a long upper wick — and its formation at a resistance level indicates lower prices in the future. Dragonfly doji, as discussed earlier, indicates bullish reversal.

section: Dragonfly Doji in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Dragonfly Doji in the ICT Framework

In ICT terms, the dragonfly doji is the single-candle signature of an [inducement sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) followed by a strong rejection.

The long lower wick is the sweep — sellers grab the liquidity below support. The close at the open is the candle-level [change in state of delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>) — sellers exhausted, buyers in control.

For the highest-conviction setup, look for dragonfly doji at a higher-timeframe demand zone or bullish PD array, then drop to the 15-minute for the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation before entering.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Step-by-Step Dragonfly Doji Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Dragonfly Doji Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for a dragonfly doji trade.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Bearish — making lower highs and lower lows.
  2. **Mark the support zone.** Strong horizontal support, ideally aligned with a higher-timeframe PD array.
  3. **Wait for price to test support.** Patience is mandatory.
  4. **Watch for the dragonfly doji to print.** Open, high and close at the same level with a long lower wick.
  5. **Wait for the candle to close.** Only the closed candle counts.
  6. **Wait for the confirmation candle.** Next candle must close above the dragonfly’s high.
  7. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to test the dragonfly’s body or wick.
  8. **Enter the buy.** On the retest, with bullish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.
  9. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips below the low of the dragonfly doji.
  10. **Set the target.** Next resistance level, keeping the risk-reward ratio in view.

content:

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: Common Mistakes Around Dragonfly Doji
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Dragonfly Doji

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the dragonfly doji.

  1. **Trading every dragonfly doji.** Without a support level under the wick, the dragonfly is just noise. The level is mandatory.
  2. **Skipping the confirmation candle.** The follow-up candle must close above the dragonfly’s high. Without it, the doji may fail.
  3. **Trading dragonfly doji on low timeframes.** 5-minute and 15-minute produce many fake dragonflies. Higher timeframes (4-hour, daily) are far more reliable.
  4. **Stops too tight.** The 10-20 pip buffer below the low is mandatory — wicks often spike just past the doji low on the second test.
  5. **Confusing dragonfly with hammer.** Hammer has a small real body; dragonfly has no body. Treating them as identical is wrong — the no-body version is stronger.
  6. **Entering before retest.** The clean entry is on the retest of the doji body or wick, not on the confirmation candle close.

title: dragonfly-doji-candlestick
section: FAQs about Dragonfly Doji Candlestick
content:
#### FAQs about Dragonfly Doji Candlestick

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the dragonfly doji.

**What is a dragonfly doji?**

A single candlestick where open, high and close are at the same level, with a long lower wick. It signals strong bullish rejection from a low and potential reversal upward.

**What does dragonfly doji tell us?**

It signals the losing control of sellers and the entrance of buyers, indicating potential reversal of price from a downtrend to an uptrend.

**Where does a dragonfly doji form?**

Most reliably at strong horizontal support after a bearish trend. Dragonflies in the middle of a range or against the trend have a much lower hit rate.

**How do I confirm a dragonfly doji?**

Wait for the next candle to close above the high of the dragonfly doji. That close confirms buyers have taken control.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After the confirmation candle, wait for price to retrace back to the dragonfly’s body or wick. Enter on the retest with bullish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips below the low of the dragonfly doji.

**Where do I take profit?**

Next resistance level, with risk-reward ratio kept in mind. For extended targets, use the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What is the difference between dragonfly doji and hammer?**

Both are bullish reversal candles with long lower wicks. Hammer has a small real body; dragonfly has virtually no real body (open and close at the same level). Dragonfly is the stronger signal.

**What is the difference between dragonfly doji and gravestone doji?**

Dragonfly doji has a long LOWER wick and signals bullish reversal at support. Gravestone doji has a long UPPER wick and signals bearish reversal at resistance. They are direct opposites.

**Can I use dragonfly doji for scalping?**

Yes — on 15-minute or 5-minute timeframes. But lower timeframes are less reliable and offer lower risk-to-reward ratios than 4-hour or daily dragonflies.

**Can a dragonfly doji fail?**

Yes — sometimes price continues lower below the dragonfly low. That is why confirmation candle, support level alignment, and trend context are all required filters.

**How does dragonfly doji fit in the ICT framework?**

It is a single-candle signature of an inducement sweep at a bullish PD array, with the close at the open functioning as a candle-level CISD. The strongest setup is dragonfly doji at a higher-timeframe demand zone with lower-timeframe MSS confirmation.

**Does dragonfly doji work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook dragonfly dojis at higher-timeframe support and demand zones, especially during the New York AM session.

# Elliott Wave Theory — 5-Wave Motive + 3-Wave Corrective Sequence with Trade Rules

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/elliot-wave-theory/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/elliot-wave-theory/)

![Elliott Wave Theory — 5-wave motive sequence followed by 3-wave corrective sequence with impulse and diagonal motive variants and the three unbreakable rules](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Elliot-wave.png)

In 1938, after 9 years of research, American financier Ralph Nelson Elliott formulated the Elliott Wave Theory. He stated that financial markets follow some random and disorderly but repetitive patterns — which he named waves. He observed the fractal nature of markets: price patterns repeat themselves over and over again on all timeframes.

In this guide I walk you through Elliott Wave Theory — the motive and corrective waves, the impulse vs diagonal motive variants, the 3 unbreakable rules, the 5-wave and ABC sequences, advantages and disadvantages, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: What is Elliott Wave Theory?
content:
#### What is Elliott Wave Theory?

The Elliott Wave Theory is a type of technical analysis that seeks out repeating long-term price patterns associated with continuing shifts in investor sentiment and psychology.

This theory states that there are two types of price movements in the market.

**(I) Motive Waves:** Aligned with the large trend.

**(II) Corrective Waves:** Contrary to the large trend.

![Elliott Wave Theory illustration — motive 5-wave sequence \(1,2,3,4,5\) aligned with the trend, followed by 3-wave corrective sequence \(A,B,C\) against the trend](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ELLIOT-WAVE.png)

The Elliott wave sequence contains 5 waves (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) that make up the motive wave, and 3 waves (A, B, C) that make up the corrective wave.

After the completion of wave 5, the market will develop into a 3-wave (A, B, C) retracement move contrary to the motive wave.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Motive Wave
content:
#### Motive Wave

Motive wave is further classified into two waves depending on the form and location within the overall market structure.

**(I) Impulse Waves** are the most common form of motive wave and are easiest to spot in the market.

These waves look flat-vertical or zigzag in shape and are quite heavy movements in one direction. In this wave, price travels a great distance in a short period of time.

**(II) Diagonal Waves** look like a wedge — either expanding or contracting.

This form of price movement is less energetic than an impulse wave, and hence it moves in one direction taking retracements, creating a wedge pattern.

![Elliott motive wave types — impulse wave \(flat vertical or zigzag with strong directional move\) vs diagonal wave \(expanding or contracting wedge shape\)](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/impulse-wave.png)

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Corrective Wave
content:
#### Corrective Wave

Corrective waves are basically the retracement moves which are contrary to the large trend of market, and hence are less energetic than the motive waves.

Corrective waves can be in the form of triangles, flag or a zigzag move.

![Elliott corrective wave variants — triangle, flag and zigzag corrective patterns retracing against the motive wave direction](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Corrective-Wave.png)

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: The 3 Unbreakable Rules of Elliott Wave
content:
#### The 3 Unbreakable Rules of Elliott Wave

To identify an Elliott wave structure, you should first know about the 3 unbreakable rules of Elliott Wave Theory.

If one of these rules is violated, the structure is not an Elliott wave.

**(I)** Wave 2 cannot retrace more than 100% of wave 1.

**(II)** Wave 4 cannot move into the territory of wave 1.

**(III)** Wave 3 cannot be the shortest wave.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave 1 in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave 1 in Bullish Market

Wave 1 begins the impulse sequence. During this wave, price begins to bounce higher after a long sustained downtrend.

The sentiment in the market is very bearish at the start of wave 1.

It is generally the least predictive wave within the entire Elliott wave structure — there is really no way to know how long the wave will last.

However, at some point it will clearly become apparent that wave 1 has ended as a significant swing high is breached and price begins to move lower in a bearish direction.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave 2 in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave 2 in Bullish Market

Wave 2 is a corrective wave — it will move counter to wave 1 and will retrace a larger portion of wave 1.

Often it will retrace wave 1 by either 50%, 61% or even 78%.

Remember the unbreakable rule that wave 2 cannot go beyond the low of wave 1.

Informed traders will start to recognize this pattern and will start to position on the long side.

![Elliott Wave 1-5 motive sequence example — wave 1 initial bounce, wave 2 retracement \(50-78% of wave 1\), wave 3 strongest leg, wave 4 shallow correction, wave 5 final push](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Elliot-wave-12345.png)

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave 3 in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave 3 in Bullish Market

Wave 3 offers the largest potential for profit, as it is usually the largest and most powerful wave in the Elliott wave structure.

After the break of the swing high of wave 1, price will begin to accelerate upward as more and more traders recognize the bullish sentiment and start taking long positions.

Many sellers will have their stops triggered at the wave 1 high, which adds fuel to the upside price movement.

If you identify the 3rd wave, you need to join the trend as quickly as possible in order to take advantage of the explosive price movement.

Those waiting for a pullback will miss the entire move as wave 3 offers very little pullback.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave 4 in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave 4 in Bullish Market

Wave 4 is also a corrective wave — it will retrace a portion of wave 3.

Typically wave 4 will be a shallower retracement and will often terminate at 38% or 50% of wave 3.

Wave 4 will be less aggressive in comparison to wave 2.

Keep in mind the core rule of Elliott Wave Theory: wave 4 should not overlap the territory of wave 1.

Wave 4 is also seen as a profit-taking wave for traders who bought early in wave 3 — and it creates sideways movement, so wave 4 often takes the form of a triangle.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave 5 in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave 5 in Bullish Market

Wave 5 is the final leg within the Elliott wave impulse sequence. It moves in the direction of the overall trend just like wave 1 and wave 3.

Wave 5 is often considered the retail wave because during its progression almost everyone is bullish — and mostly retail traders drive prices higher.

The momentum behind the bullish activity in wave 5 will be less dynamic than wave 3 and wave 1.

During the last stages of wave 5, you will also see technical divergence between price and momentum indicators like [RSI (Relative Strength Index)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence/>), MACD and Stochastic.

These divergences signal that the velocity of price movement higher is diminishing — and you should expect the upside trend to reverse.

Along with momentum divergences, wave 5 will often register lower volume compared to wave 3. This is another indication of trend weakness — profits should be locked in as a potential reversal is imminent.

The end of wave 5 brings the completion of the impulse sequence — so you can expect the corrective 3-wave pattern A, B, C.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave A in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave A in Bullish Market

Wave A starts the corrective sequence. During this wave, most traders are still very bullish and consider wave A just a pullback — a minor retracement.

However, some experienced traders begin to recognize the overbought market conditions during wave 5.

Wave A is often a sharp move and may subdivide as either a 5-wave pattern or 3-wave pattern.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave B in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave B in Bullish Market

Wave B is the second leg of the corrective sequence structure. It follows wave A in the contrary direction, retracing either 50%, 61% or 78%.

Wave B will be short-lived and will fail to surpass the wave 5 swing high.

Wave B will often create a double-top formation as it tries to test the wave 5 swing high.

Wave B is mostly seen as a zigzag pattern but sometimes forms as a triangle.

![Elliott Wave ABC corrective sequence example — wave A sharp drop, wave B counter-retracement \(50-78% retrace, fails to surpass wave 5 high\), wave C powerful final leg](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Elliot-wave-ABC.png)

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: How to Identify Wave C in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Wave C in Bullish Market

Wave C marks the final leg within the corrective structure.

When the swing low of wave B is broken, it marks the turning point where more and more traders will be convinced that the uptrend has ended and the market is poised for lower prices.

Wave C has the same characteristics as wave 3. Both tend to be relatively long waves and can be quite powerful from a momentum point of view.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Elliott Wave in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Elliott Wave in the ICT Framework

Elliott Wave and ICT are not competing frameworks — they read the same chart from different angles.

Wave 1 is the displacement leg that produces the first [BOS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>). Wave 2 is the retracement that sweeps the inducement. Wave 3 is the high-conviction continuation after the inducement sweep. Wave 4 is a smaller retracement that respects the wave 1 territory. Wave 5 is the final extension with weakening momentum (often with RSI divergence and a [CISD](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>) at the top).

The ABC correction maps onto the bearish reversal sequence — wave A breaks the wave-5 high, wave B is the retracement to a premium PD array, wave C is the post-[CHOCH](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>) bearish leg targeting the wave-4 low or below.

Use Elliott Wave for the macro narrative; use ICT for the entry trigger inside each wave.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Advantages of Elliott Wave
content:
#### Advantages of Elliott Wave

**Understanding Market Cycles:** The Elliott Wave Theory offers a structured approach to comprehending market cycles, illustrating how they fluctuate in waves of sentiment. Through the examination of wave patterns, traders can identify potential trends and reversals within the market.

**Entry and Exit:** By pinpointing crucial levels of support and resistance, the Elliott Wave Theory can offer precise entry and exit points for trades. This approach aids in risk management and the optimization of profits by strategically timing trades.

**Conjunction with Other Tools:** The Elliott Wave Theory can be integrated with other technical and fundamental analysis tools to validate trading decisions. This collaborative approach enhances the accuracy of assessments and ensures a more comprehensive understanding of market dynamics.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Disadvantages of Elliott Wave
content:
#### Disadvantages of Elliott Wave

**Complexity:** Mastering the Elliott Wave Theory needs a substantial investment of time and effort due to its complexity, requiring dedicated learning and practical application to utilize effectively.

**Subjective Interpretation:** The interpretation of wave patterns within the Elliott Wave Theory can be subjective, as different analysts may perceive and interpret these patterns differently based on their individual perspectives and analytical techniques.

**Not a 100% Accurate Approach:** Although the Elliott Wave Theory can be valuable for detecting potential trends and reversals, its accuracy is not guaranteed, and it can sometimes produce false signals.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Step-by-Step Elliott Wave Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Elliott Wave Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading using Elliott Wave.

  1. **Identify the macro trend.** Higher highs and higher lows (bullish) or lower highs and lower lows (bearish).
  2. **Mark wave 1.** The first impulsive leg in the new direction after a sustained counter-trend.
  3. **Wait for wave 2.** Corrective retracement (50%–78% of wave 1) that does not exceed the wave 1 start.
  4. **Identify wave 3.** The strongest extension — enter on the BOS of the wave 1 swing high (bullish) or low (bearish).
  5. **Wait for wave 4.** Shallow retracement (38%–50% of wave 3) — never into wave 1 territory.
  6. **Trade wave 5 cautiously.** Look for RSI divergence and weakening volume — this is the last leg before reversal.
  7. **Watch for wave A.** First sharp counter-trend leg after wave 5 completes.
  8. **Identify wave B.** Failed retracement that double-tops near the wave 5 high.
  9. **Trade wave C aggressively.** Same characteristics as wave 3 — powerful, sustained, low-risk entry after wave B failure.
  10. **Apply the 3 unbreakable rules at every step.** Wave 2 < 100% of wave 1, wave 4 outside wave 1 territory, wave 3 never the shortest.

content:
#### Best Pairs for Elliott Wave

Elliott Wave works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD, and indices like NQ and ES.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the Elliott Wave framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. Higher-timeframe Elliott Wave (daily, 4-hour) is more reliable than lower-timeframe wave counts.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: Common Mistakes Around Elliott Wave
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Elliott Wave

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start with Elliott Wave.

  1. **Forcing wave counts on every chart.** Not every move is an Elliott Wave. If the structure does not respect the three rules, do not label it.
  2. **Trading wave 1 too aggressively.** Wave 1 is the least predictable. Wait for wave 2 retracement to confirm before committing capital.
  3. **Missing wave 3 by waiting for a pullback.** Wave 3 offers very little pullback. Aggressive entry on the wave-1-high break is often the only realistic option.
  4. **Violating the wave-4 / wave-1 territory rule.** If wave 4 overlaps wave 1, the count is invalid. Re-label and start again.
  5. **Trading wave 5 without divergence confirmation.** Wave 5 is the retail wave — without RSI / MACD divergence, you may catch a sustained continuation instead of the topping move.
  6. **Treating wave B as a new trend.** Wave B is a retracement that fails to break wave 5. Trading it as a new bullish leg flips the direction of the ABC correction.

title: elliot-wave-theory
section: FAQs about Elliott Wave Theory
content:
#### FAQs about Elliott Wave Theory

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about Elliott Wave Theory.

**What is Elliott Wave Theory?**

A technical analysis framework formulated by Ralph Nelson Elliott in 1938. It states that financial markets move in repetitive wave patterns — 5 motive waves aligned with the trend, followed by 3 corrective waves against the trend (the 5-3 sequence).

**What are the two types of waves?**

(1) Motive waves — aligned with the large trend, 5 waves labeled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. (2) Corrective waves — against the trend, 3 waves labeled A, B, C.

**What are the three unbreakable rules of Elliott Wave?**

(1) Wave 2 cannot retrace more than 100% of wave 1. (2) Wave 4 cannot move into the territory of wave 1. (3) Wave 3 cannot be the shortest wave.

**What is an impulse wave?**

The most common motive wave — flat-vertical or zigzag in shape, with strong directional movement and minimal retracement.

**What is a diagonal wave?**

A motive wave shaped like an expanding or contracting wedge — less energetic than an impulse wave, with directional retracements that form the wedge.

**Which wave is the most profitable?**

Wave 3 — usually the largest and most powerful wave in the motive sequence. It offers the most pip potential and the cleanest momentum.

**How do I identify the end of wave 5?**

Look for RSI / MACD / Stochastic divergence between price and the momentum indicator, plus reduced volume compared to wave 3. Both signal that the trend is exhausting.

**How does Elliott Wave relate to ICT?**

Wave 1 = displacement BOS. Wave 2 = inducement sweep. Wave 3 = high-conviction continuation. Wave 4 = shallow retracement. Wave 5 = exhaustion with divergence and CISD. The ABC correction maps onto the post-CHOCH bearish leg.

**What timeframe works best for Elliott Wave?**

Higher timeframes (daily, weekly) produce the most reliable wave counts. Lower timeframes are subject to noise and false wave-count interpretations.

**Can I trade Elliott Wave alone?**

You can — but combining it with ICT structure (BOS, MSS, inducement sweep) and momentum filters (RSI divergence) significantly improves the hit rate.

**Does Elliott Wave work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all respect Elliott Wave structures on the higher timeframes (daily and weekly).

**What are the disadvantages of Elliott Wave?**

(1) Complexity — requires significant study and practice. (2) Subjectivity — different analysts may label the same chart differently. (3) Not 100% accurate — false signals do occur, especially in choppy markets.

ICT FVG, known as the Fair Value Gap, is a three-candle formation with an un-retraced area between the high and low of the 1st and 3rd candlesticks. The fair value gap is the cleanest single concept ICT teaches — once you can spot one, you can build inducement, order block, displacement and order flow on top of it.

A fair value gap is indicated by an imbalance and acts as a level of support and resistance on the price chart.

In this guide I walk you through the FVG concept end to end — the meaning, the bullish and bearish variants, the 6-step identification method, the step-by-step trade flow, the FVG family (regular, inversion, implied, balanced, breakaway, NWOG, NDOG), common mistakes and the FAQ.
