title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: What is ICT FVG (Fair Value Gap)?
content:
#### What is ICT FVG (Fair Value Gap)?

ICT fair value gap is a three-candle structure indicating a gap between the high and low of the 1st and 3rd candlesticks.

The gap between the three candles is created because price does not retrace into that area and leaves it open.

You can see the example of an ICT FVG in the picture below.

![ICT FVG example — three-candle pattern with a clean gap between the high of the 1st candle and the low of the 3rd candle marked as the unmitigated fair value gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/ICT-FVG-1.png)

ICT FVG acts as a magnet for price — price retraces back to the fair value gap to balance the price delivery. After retracing to the FVG, price then reverses and continues its trend.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: How to Identify an ICT Fair Value Gap
content:
#### How to Identify an ICT Fair Value Gap

To identify an ICT FVG you need to look for a large candlestick with most body range.

After identifying the large candlestick, mark the high of the candlestick prior to the large candle and the low of the subsequent candlestick.

There will be a visible gap between the high and low of the two candlesticks — that gap is the ICT fair value gap.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: Types of ICT FVG
content:
#### Types of ICT FVG

On the basis of price move, the ICT FVG has two main types — bullish and bearish.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: (I) Bullish Fair Value Gap
content:
#### (I) Bullish Fair Value Gap

A bullish fair value gap in ICT terms appears during an uptrend with a three-candle pattern.

It happens when the middle candle has a large body, leaving a gap between the high of the first candle and the low of the third candle.

In an uptrend, a fair value gap can serve as strong support, with price often retracing to fill the gap before moving higher.

You can see the example of a bullish fair value gap in the picture below.

![Bullish fair value gap example — uptrend three-candle pattern with the gap between the high of the 1st candle and the low of the 3rd candle marked as a bullish FVG](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Bullish-fair-value-gap.png)

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: (II) Bearish Fair Value Gap
content:
#### (II) Bearish Fair Value Gap

A bearish fair value gap appears in a downtrend within a three-candle pattern.

It forms when the middle candle has a large body, creating a gap between the low of the first candle and the high of the third candle.

In a bearish trend, a fair value gap can act as good resistance, and mostly price tends to fill this gap before moving lower.

You can see the example of a bearish fair value gap in the picture below.

![Bearish fair value gap example — downtrend three-candle pattern with the gap between the low of the 1st candle and the high of the 3rd candle marked as a bearish FVG](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Bearish-Fair-Value-gap.png)

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: ICT FVG Trading Strategy
content:
#### ICT FVG Trading Strategy

To trade using an ICT fair value gap, follow the steps below.

**Step 1 — Determine Market Trend.** First, identify the market trend of any asset — bullish or bearish. You can use [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>) to anticipate the direction of the price move. In a bullish trend, price makes higher highs and higher lows; in a bearish trend, price makes lower lows and lower highs.

**Step 2 — Identify[Premium and Discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) Zone.** Look for the premium fair value gap in a bearish trend; in a bullish trend, look for the discount FVG.

**Step 3 — Identify the Large Candle.** Once the trend is determined, find a large candle with large body and small wicks. In a bullish trend look for a strong bullish candle with most body range; in a bearish trend look for a large bearish candle with most body range.

**Step 4 — Study Preceding and Proceeding Candles.** Now study the one candle before the large candle and the one candle after it. Both of these candles should have such a structure that their bodies do not overlap the body of the middle candle, confirming a fair value gap between the wicks of the 1st and 3rd candle.

**Step 5 — Mark the Fair Value Gap.** In a bullish trend, mark the gap between the high of the first candle and the low of the third candle. In a bearish trend, mark the gap between the low of the first candle and the high of the third candle.

**Step 6 — Execute the Trade.** If price is in a bullish trend, wait for price to retrace and test the discount fair value gap to balance the move. When price tests the discount fair value gap, execute a buy trade with other confirmations like rejection or a market structure shift on the lower timeframe.

In the picture given below, price is in a bullish trend making higher highs and higher lows. It retraces back to test the fair value gaps and rejects from them, eventually going higher.

![Bullish fair value gap trading example — price in a bullish trend retraces to multiple FVGs, rejects from each, and continues higher toward the next draw on liquidity](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/fair-value-gap-trading.png)

In a bearish trend, wait for price to retrace up and test the premium fair value gap to balance the bearish price delivery. When price visits this gap, it can offer sell opportunities — especially when combined with additional confirmations like rejection or a shift in market structure.

In the image below, the market is in a downtrend forming lower highs and lower lows. It repeatedly tests bearish fair value gaps and rejects from these levels, leading to further price declines.

![Bearish fair value gap trading example — price in a bearish trend retraces to bearish FVGs, rejects, and continues lower toward the next draw on liquidity](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy.png)

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: The FVG Family — Variants You Should Know
content:
#### The FVG Family — Variants You Should Know

The fair value gap has a family of related concepts on this site, each refining the basic FVG for a specific scenario.

**[First Presented FVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-1st-presented-fvg/>)** — the very first FVG of the trading day or session. Often the cleanest delivery FVG inside the daily Power-of-3 template.

**[Valid FVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/valid-ict-fair-value-gap/>)** — the FVG that survives the validity check (no overlapping wicks, sufficient displacement, bias-aligned).

**[Inversion FVG (iFVG)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>)** — an FVG broken in the opposite direction that flips polarity and now acts as the opposite-direction support or resistance.

**[Implied FVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-implied-fair-value-gap-ifvg/>)** — a structural FVG implied by the wicks of three candles even when the bodies overlap.

**[Balanced Price Range (BPR)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>)** — the overlap area of two opposite-direction FVGs in the same zone.

**[Breakaway Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breakaway-gap/>)** — an FVG that price never returns to, held by a breaker block, iFVG or BPR in front of it.

**[NWOG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-week-opening-gap-nwog/>)** — the weekend gap between Friday close and Monday open.

**[NDOG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-day-opening-gap-ndog/>)** — the daily gap between 5:00 PM close and 6:00 PM open New York time.

**[SIBI / BISI](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts/>)** — the directional naming convention for sell-side and buy-side FVGs.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: Step-by-Step FVG Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step FVG Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading off a fair value gap.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — bullish, bearish or neutral structure.
  2. **Identify premium / discount.** Bullish bias targets discount FVGs; bearish bias targets premium FVGs.
  3. **Mark the bias-aligned FVG.** Three-candle pattern with the gap between the 1st-candle and 3rd-candle wicks.
  4. **Wait for price to retrace to the FVG.** Bullish — price comes down to the discount FVG. Bearish — price rallies up to the premium FVG.
  5. **Drop to the lower timeframe (5-minute or 15-minute).** For the entry trigger.
  6. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS at the FVG.** A clean break of the most recent counter-trend swing point in the bias direction.
  7. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the consequent encroachment (50% of the FVG) or at the IOFED (the very edge of the FVG).
  8. **Set the stop.** Beyond the FVG far edge or beyond the MSS swing extreme, with a small buffer.
  9. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

content:
#### Best Timeframe for ICT FVG Identification

ICT FVG serves different purposes — it can be used on the 1-day chart to set the daily bias, on the 4-hour for the higher-timeframe PD array, and on the 15-minute or 5-minute for trade entries.

If you are using the fair value gap as a [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>) to find trade entries, look for an FVG on the 15-minute or lower timeframes.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: Common Mistakes Around the Fair Value Gap
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the Fair Value Gap

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the fair value gap concept.

  1. **Treating every imbalance as a tradeable FVG.** Not every fair value gap is tradeable — the FVG must be bias-aligned, in the premium / discount of the higher-timeframe range, and supported by a lower-timeframe MSS to qualify as a setup.
  2. **Marking FVGs in choppy ranges.** FVGs are most reliable inside a directional leg. In a range, every retracement creates noise FVGs that price ignores.
  3. **Entering at the FVG without confirmation.** The FVG is the zone — the entry trigger is the lower-timeframe MSS or order block formed at the zone, not the touch of the zone alone.
  4. **Confusing the regular FVG with the inversion FVG.** A regular FVG holds in the direction of the impulse leg. An inversion FVG flips polarity after being broken. Mixing them up flips the trade direction.
  5. **Stops parked at the FVG far edge.** Tight stops at the FVG boundary get hunted on the second test. The stop should sit beyond the FVG far edge with a buffer, or beyond the MSS swing extreme.
  6. **Trading FVGs against the higher-timeframe bias.** An FVG aligned with the higher-timeframe trend has a much higher hit rate than a counter-trend FVG.

title: fair-value-gap-trading-strategy
section: FAQs about ICT Fair Value Gap
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Fair Value Gap

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the fair value gap.

**What is an ICT Fair Value Gap?**

ICT FVG is a three-candle formation with an un-retraced area between the high and low of the 1st and 3rd candlesticks. It indicates an imbalance and acts as a support / resistance level that price often returns to before continuing in the original direction.

**How do I identify a fair value gap?**

Look for a large body candlestick. Mark the high of the candle before it and the low of the candle after it. The gap between those two levels is the fair value gap.

**What is the difference between a bullish and a bearish FVG?**

Bullish FVG forms in an uptrend — the gap is between the high of the 1st candle and the low of the 3rd candle, and acts as support. Bearish FVG forms in a downtrend — the gap is between the low of the 1st candle and the high of the 3rd candle, and acts as resistance.

**What is the consequent encroachment of an FVG?**

Consequent encroachment is the 50% midpoint of the FVG. It is often the most reactive level inside the gap and is used as a refined entry zone.

**What is the IOFED of an FVG?**

The IOFED (Institutional Order Flow Entry Drill) is the very edge of the FVG — the earliest possible entry. Bullish — just inside the low of the 3rd candle. Bearish — just inside the high of the 3rd candle. See my dedicated [IOFED guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-institutional-order-flow-entry-drill/>).

**Where do I place the stop loss on an FVG trade?**

Beyond the FVG far edge or beyond the lower-timeframe MSS swing extreme, with a small buffer. Not at the FVG boundary itself.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw on liquidity — old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What timeframe is best for FVG trading?**

Mark the higher-timeframe FVG on the daily or 4-hour for the bias. Use the 15-minute or 5-minute FVG for the entry trigger. The 1-minute can be used for very tight scalp entries.

**Does FVG work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook FVG entries, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases. ICT actually introduced FVG using NQ and ES.

**What is the difference between FVG and order block?**

The FVG is the IMBALANCE between three candles. The order block is the LAST opposing candle before the displacement that produced the FVG. Often you find both in the same setup — the FVG is the zone, the OB is the candle.

**Is every FVG tradeable?**

No — FVGs in choppy ranges, against the higher-timeframe bias, or without lower-timeframe MSS confirmation should be ignored. Only bias-aligned, displacement-confirmed FVGs are worth trading.

**What if price never returns to fill the FVG?**

That is a breakaway gap — an FVG held in place by a breaker block, inversion FVG or balanced price range in front of it. See my [Breakaway Gap guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breakaway-gap/>) for the full breakdown.

# What is Forex Trading? — Beginner’s Step-by-Step Guide to Currency Pairs & ICT

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/forex-trading/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/forex-trading/)

![What is Forex Trading — beginner-friendly step-by-step introduction to forex, currency pairs, the forex market, brokers, terminology and how money is made through currency exchange](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/What-is-Forex-Trading.png)

Forex trading is the world’s largest financial market and the entry point for almost every retail trader — yet for newcomers it can feel terrifying, especially without a finance background. The good news: the core concept is the same as exchanging physical currency at an airport, only done digitally for profit instead of for travel.

I have taught over 100,000+ users forex trading, and I have created this step-by-step guide on how to start forex trading for beginners without any technical knowledge. The process is easy to follow whether you are 20 years old or 60 years old — just follow the guide step by step.

In this guide I walk you through forex from the ground up — what forex is, what forex trading is, what the forex market is, what is traded, the market size, how much money you can make, the essential terminology, the next step into the ICT framework, common beginner mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: forex-trading
section: What is Forex?
content:
#### What is Forex?

The word forex is derived from two words — foreign and exchange. The word foreign here refers to **foreign currencies** , so it is basically the exchange of various currencies. You give one currency and take the other one.

In the old days, this exchange of currencies used to be for traveling to other countries or purchasing goods from abroad. All this exchange of currencies used to happen in physical locations like banks or money exchanges.

You must be wondering how you can make money from the exchange of these currencies. Take a deep breath — the world has evolved. Until now you have just understood what forex is. Your money will be generated in the next step of forex trading.

title: forex-trading
section: What is Forex Trading?
content:
#### What is Forex Trading?

Forex trading is the process of buying a currency with the intent of selling it when its price goes up. It is just like buying any physical asset in the market and then selling it once its price goes up. The hike in the price of any particular asset is dependent on demand and supply, along with other various economic factors.

The same is the case of currencies in forex trading. You buy any particular currency based on your analysis of various economic and technical factors, with the belief that price of this currency will go up in the near future. Once the price goes up, you make the profit.

But forex trading is not all about profits. You can have losses too if the price of your bought currency goes down.

This buying and selling of currencies happens in pairs. Understanding pairs now will get too complicated for you — but I have covered that in the next section on what is traded in forex.

For the purpose of buying and selling these currencies digitally from the comfort of your bed, different mobile and web apps provide services. These digital facilitators of your currency trades are called brokers in the world of forex trading. They receive your orders digitally and provide them to banks and other financial institutions.

More or less, forex trading happening nowadays is just like the exchange of physical currencies that happened in the old days, only at banks and money exchanges.

The only difference is that today exchange happens digitally via brokers, and the major purpose is to earn money on the exchange of currencies — unlike the old days where the purpose was to import goods from a certain country.

You have now understood why it is called **forex trading** — because here exchange of foreign currencies happens just for trading.

title: forex-trading
section: What is the Forex Market?
content:
#### What is the Forex Market?

The overall ecosystem of buying and selling currencies electronically is called the forex market. You will be surprised to know that this forex market has no physical location, no office, and no central international regulatory authority.

But this does not mean that online forex brokers are not regulated anywhere. Good brokers, which are trustable, are regulated by the relevant finance authorities of the country in which they are operating. To keep your money safe, you have to always go with regulated brokers.

Due to lack of regulations in some countries, some brokers have to go unregulated — but this does not mean that they are a scam.

title: forex-trading
section: What is Traded in Forex
content:
#### What is Traded in Forex

As explained in the definition of forex trading, different currency pairs are traded in forex. For example, one of the pairs is USD/JPY. When you buy this pair, you have actually bought USD against Japanese Yen.

You must be thinking about the role of the Japanese Yen here. In fact, in the background you bought JPY first, and then with that JPY you bought USD.

If the price of USD goes up and you close that trade, you can sell that USD back to the market and you will get more JPY than you initially invested.

Similarly, you can also sell USD/JPY. This sell actually means you have bought the Japanese Yen with the USD. Once the price of JPY goes up, you can close the trade and earn the profit this way too.

title: forex-trading
section: What is the Size of the Forex Market?
content:
#### What is the Size of the Forex Market?

Forex market is the largest market in the world, with daily trading volume of 6.6 trillion USD according to the Central Bank Survey of FX conducted in 2019. This 6.6 trillion means this amount of currency is bought and sold every day. The number has continued to grow since then.

title: forex-trading
section: How Much Money Can You Make from Forex Trading?
content:
#### How Much Money Can You Make from Forex Trading?

You have already got the numbers of daily trading volume, so the sky is the limit theoretically. But practically speaking, based on my experience, on average any good forex trader can earn 10% of their invested capital per month. This number can vary, but a professional forex trader earns approximately that much.

That will not be a constant journey. Some months you will be earning 20 to 50%, or even 100% of your invested capital — but for some months you will be losing too at the same pace. It is important to mention that controlling your greed in this market is a very important aspect of learning forex trading.

In sophisticated language: **risk management is the key to success.**

You have now got the broader picture of what forex trading is and how money can be made from forex trading. To practically master this art, you have to learn more. I am here to guide you step by step.

title: forex-trading
section: Forex Terminology
content:
#### Forex Terminology

Your next step in the journey of forex trading should be learning some basic terminology, which I have listed below with compact, easy-to-understand definitions.

**(01) Buy / Ask** — Buy and Ask are similar terms. Buy is the minimum price at which you will be able to purchase any currency pair in your broker account.

**(02) Sell / Bid** — Sell and Bid are similar terms. Sell is the maximum price at which you will be able to sell any currency pair in your broker account.

**(03) Lot** — Lot is the quantity of currency you will be purchasing or selling. It is just like a unit of quantity.

**(04) Leverage** — Leverage is the buying power provided to you by your broker so you can buy or sell more currency than the available amount in your account.

**(05) Pip** — Pip is the smallest change in value of any currency pair.

**(06) Take Profit Limit / TP** — A feature provided by your broker to set limits in your account to close any opened trade once it reaches a certain profit limit.

**(07) Stop Loss / SL** — A feature provided by your broker to limit your loss. Once you set a stop loss limit, your trades are closed automatically once they hit a certain loss limit.

**(08) Spread** — Technically its definition may vary, but simply it is the fee charged to you by the broker for opening your trades.

**(09) Fundamental Analysis** — Analysis and prediction of any currency pair price in the near future, based on the data of economic events worldwide.

**(10) Technical Analysis** — Analysis and prediction of any currency pair price in the near future, based on the historical data of forex charts.

title: forex-trading
section: The Next Step — Learning a Trading Framework
content:
#### The Next Step — Learning a Trading Framework

Once you have understood the basics and the terminology, the next step is choosing a trading framework — the rules you will use to decide when to buy or sell.

The framework I teach on this site is the [Inner Circle Trader (ICT) framework](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/most-important-ict-concepts-to-conquer-market-complete-list/>). It is built on three pillars — [liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>), [imbalance (fair value gap)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>), and [market structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/market-structure-in-trading/>). Master these three concepts and you have the foundation for every ICT setup.

For your very first deep-dive, I recommend reading these in order:

  1. [Market Structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/market-structure-in-trading/>) — read the chart correctly.
  2. [Support and Resistance](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/support-resistance-trading/>) — find where price reacts.
  3. [Break of Structure (BOS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>) — recognize trend continuation.
  4. [Change of Character (CHOCH)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>) — recognize trend reversal.
  5. [Fair Value Gap (FVG)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>) — institutional re-entry zone.

title: forex-trading
section: Common Beginner Mistakes in Forex
content:
#### Common Beginner Mistakes in Forex

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders are new to forex.

  1. **Trading without a stop loss.** The single fastest way to blow an account. Every trade must have a stop loss before it is opened.
  2. **Over-leveraging.** Leverage amplifies losses just as much as gains. Use the smallest leverage your broker allows for your size.
  3. **Skipping the demo phase.** Trade on a demo account for at least 1–3 months before risking real money.
  4. **Trading without a plan.** A trading plan with entry rules, stop rules, target rules and risk-per-trade rules is mandatory.
  5. **Revenge trading.** Doubling down after a loss to “make it back” is the second-fastest way to blow an account.
  6. **Risking more than 1–2% per trade.** Even good strategies have losing streaks. Risk small per trade so the inevitable streak does not wipe you out.

title: forex-trading
section: FAQs about Forex Trading
content:
#### FAQs about Forex Trading

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about forex trading.

**What is forex trading in simple terms?**

Forex trading is buying one currency and selling another in the hope that the price moves in your favor. It is the same idea as exchanging dollars for yen at the airport — but done digitally through a broker for profit.

**What is the forex market?**

The forex market is the worldwide electronic ecosystem of buying and selling currencies. It has no physical location and no central international regulator; brokers are regulated by the finance authority of each country they operate in.

**How big is the forex market?**

Daily trading volume was 6.6 trillion USD per day in the 2019 Central Bank Survey of FX, and has continued to grow. It is the largest financial market in the world.

**How much money can I make from forex trading?**

A professional forex trader averages around 10% of invested capital per month, but it is not consistent — some months 20–50% or more, other months losses at the same pace. Risk management is the key to long-term success.

**Do I need to know finance to start forex trading?**

No — the basics of forex can be learned without any finance background. The hard part is the discipline and risk management, not the technical knowledge.

**What are currency pairs?**

Currencies are traded in pairs — for example USD/JPY. Buying the pair means buying USD against JPY; selling the pair means buying JPY against USD. Every trade involves two currencies.

**What is a pip?**

A pip is the smallest change in the value of a currency pair. For most pairs, one pip is 0.0001 of the price. Profit and loss in forex are measured in pips.

**What is leverage?**

Leverage is the buying power your broker provides — letting you control a larger position than your account size. It amplifies both gains and losses, so use it carefully.

**What is the spread?**

The spread is the fee your broker charges to open a trade — the difference between the buy and sell prices. Smaller spreads are better for active trading.

**How do I start forex trading?**

(1) Open an account with a regulated broker. (2) Practice on a demo account for 1–3 months. (3) Learn a trading framework (I recommend ICT — start with market structure, support/resistance, BOS, CHOCH, FVG). (4) Use strict risk management — 1% to 2% per trade with a stop loss.

**Is forex trading legal?**

In most countries, yes — forex trading through regulated brokers is legal. Some countries impose restrictions or require specific licensing. Check your local regulations before opening an account.

**What is the difference between fundamental and technical analysis?**

Fundamental analysis predicts currency prices from economic data and global events (interest rates, GDP, employment). Technical analysis predicts prices from historical chart patterns and price action. Most professional traders use both.

**How long does it take to become profitable in forex?**

Realistically, 6 to 24 months of focused study and demo trading before consistent profitability. Anyone promising faster results is selling, not teaching.

**What is the best framework for beginners?**

The ICT (Inner Circle Trader) framework built on liquidity, imbalance, and market structure. Start with the [ICT concepts overview](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/most-important-ict-concepts-to-conquer-market-complete-list/>) for the full reading order.

# Gravestone Doji Candlestick — Bearish Reversal at Resistance with Long Upper Wick

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/gravestone-doji-candlestick/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/gravestone-doji-candlestick/)

![Gravestone Doji Candlestick — bearish reversal pattern with long upper wick and almost no real body, open low and close at the same price level](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Gravestone-Doji-Candlestick.png)

Gravestone Doji is the bearish mirror of the [Dragonfly Doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/dragonfly-doji-candlestick/>) — a single candle with a long upper wick and virtually no real body, signaling that buyers pushed price up but were forcefully overwhelmed by sellers who drove it back to the open. When it prints at a strong resistance area, it is one of the highest-conviction bearish reversal triggers in candlestick analysis.

In this guide I walk you through the Gravestone Doji — the definition, how to use it, stop and target rules, the limitations, comparisons with the shooting star and dragonfly doji, other bearish reversal candles, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: What is Gravestone Doji?
content:
#### What is Gravestone Doji?

A doji candlestick is one which has a small body range — almost 5% to 10% of its wick.

A Gravestone Doji candlestick has its open, low and close price at the same level, with a long wick at the top.

It signals potential reversal of price to the downside. As the candlestick opens, price initially goes up — but when sellers enter the market, they push price down, resulting in the close of the candlestick near its open price.

![Gravestone doji candlestick anatomy — open, low and close at the same level, with a long upper wick showing seller rejection of the highs](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/gravestone-doji.png)

It is named because its shape resembles a gravestone — having a long upper wick and a small body at the bottom.

Most traders wait for the follow-up candlestick to close below the low of the gravestone candlestick as a confirmation of the gravestone doji.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: How to Use Gravestone Doji
content:
#### How to Use Gravestone Doji

To trade using gravestone doji, look for a bullish market trend approaching a strong resistance area.

When price approaches the resistance zone, it gets strong rejection as sellers enter the market. Wait for the candlestick to close.

When you see a gravestone doji candlestick forming at the resistance zone, wait for the next candlestick to close below the low of the gravestone doji — it will confirm the reversal of price from the resistance zone.

After the confirmation of the gravestone doji, wait for price to retrace back and test the gravestone doji candlestick’s body or wick.

When price approaches the gravestone doji candlestick, you can execute a sell trade.

![Gravestone doji trade example — bullish trend tests resistance, gravestone doji forms with confirmation candle, then retraces back to the doji body for the sell entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/gravestone-trading.png)

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: Stop Loss and Take Profit
content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

When you sell at the resistance using a gravestone doji, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the high of the gravestone doji.

For profit target, set your take profit at the next support level — keeping in view your risk-reward ratio.

section: What Does Gravestone Doji Tell Us?
content:
#### What Does Gravestone Doji Tell Us?

Gravestone doji informs about the losing control of buyers and the entrance of sellers in the market — which indicates the potential reversal of price.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: Limitations of Gravestone Doji
content:
#### Limitations of Gravestone Doji

Gravestone doji sometimes may fail as an indicator of reversal — price may go up above the high of the gravestone doji.

Sometimes the follow-up candlestick may close much lower and price may not retrace back, so traders may not get into a sell position because of the larger stop loss disturbing the risk-reward ratio.

Gravestone doji candlestick does not define the profit target — so you have to use other strategies to find a safe exit.

section: Gravestone Doji vs Shooting Star Candlestick
content:
#### Gravestone Doji vs Shooting Star Candlestick

Both gravestone doji and shooting star are bearish reversal candlesticks formed at the end of an uptrend.

But gravestone doji has no real body — its open, low and close price are almost the same. The shooting star candlestick has a small real body, either bullish or bearish.

section: Can We Use Gravestone Doji for Scalping?
content:
#### Can We Use Gravestone Doji for Scalping?

Yes — gravestone doji can be used for scalping on lower timeframes like 15-minute or 5-minute.

But keep in mind that lower timeframes have less reliability as compared to higher timeframes, and they offer low risk-to-reward as well.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: Gravestone Doji vs Dragonfly Doji
content:
#### Gravestone Doji vs Dragonfly Doji

Both are doji candlesticks with almost no real bodies, and both candlesticks indicate reversal of price.

The main difference between gravestone doji and [dragonfly doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/dragonfly-doji-candlestick/>) is the direction of price.

Gravestone doji has a long UPPER wick — and its formation at a resistance level indicates lower prices in the future. Dragonfly doji has a long LOWER wick — and its formation at a support level indicates bullish reversal.

section: Gravestone Doji in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Gravestone Doji in the ICT Framework

In ICT terms, the gravestone doji is the single-candle signature of an [inducement sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) above resistance followed by a strong rejection.

The long upper wick is the sweep — buyers grab the liquidity above resistance. The close at the open is the candle-level [change in state of delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>) — buyers exhausted, sellers in control.

For the highest-conviction setup, look for gravestone doji at a higher-timeframe supply zone or bearish PD array, then drop to the 15-minute for the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation before entering.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: Step-by-Step Gravestone Doji Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Gravestone Doji Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for a gravestone doji trade.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Bullish — making higher highs and higher lows.
  2. **Mark the resistance zone.** Strong horizontal resistance, ideally aligned with a higher-timeframe PD array.
  3. **Wait for price to test resistance.** Patience is mandatory.
  4. **Watch for the gravestone doji to print.** Open, low and close at the same level with a long upper wick.
  5. **Wait for the candle to close.** Only the closed candle counts.
  6. **Wait for the confirmation candle.** Next candle must close below the gravestone’s low.
  7. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to test the gravestone’s body or wick.
  8. **Enter the sell.** On the retest, with bearish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.
  9. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips above the high of the gravestone doji.
  10. **Set the target.** Next support level, keeping the risk-reward ratio in view.

title: gravestone-doji-candlestick
section: Common Mistakes Around Gravestone Doji
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Gravestone Doji

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the gravestone doji.

  1. **Trading every gravestone doji.** Without a resistance level above the wick, the gravestone is just noise. The level is mandatory.
  2. **Skipping the confirmation candle.** The follow-up candle must close below the gravestone’s low. Without it, the doji may fail.
  3. **Trading gravestone doji on low timeframes.** 5-minute and 15-minute produce many fake gravestones. Higher timeframes (4-hour, daily) are far more reliable.
  4. **Stops too tight.** The 10–20 pip buffer above the high is mandatory — wicks often spike just past the doji high on the second test.
  5. **Confusing gravestone with shooting star.** Shooting star has a small real body; gravestone has no body. Treating them as identical is wrong — the no-body version is stronger.
  6. **Entering before retest.** The clean entry is on the retest of the doji body or wick, not on the confirmation candle close.

section: FAQs about Gravestone Doji Candlestick
content:
#### FAQs about Gravestone Doji Candlestick

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the gravestone doji.

**What is a gravestone doji?**

A single candlestick where open, low and close are at the same level, with a long upper wick. It signals strong bearish rejection from a high and potential reversal downward.

**What does gravestone doji tell us?**

It signals the losing control of buyers and the entrance of sellers, indicating potential reversal of price from an uptrend to a downtrend.

**Where does a gravestone doji form?**

Most reliably at strong horizontal resistance after a bullish trend. Gravestones in the middle of a range or against the trend have a much lower hit rate.

**How do I confirm a gravestone doji?**

Wait for the next candle to close below the low of the gravestone doji. That close confirms sellers have taken control.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After the confirmation candle, wait for price to retrace back to the gravestone’s body or wick. Enter on the retest with bearish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips above the high of the gravestone doji.

**Where do I take profit?**

Next support level, with risk-reward ratio kept in mind. For extended targets, use the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What is the difference between gravestone doji and shooting star?**

Both are bearish reversal candles with long upper wicks. Shooting star has a small real body; gravestone has virtually no real body (open and close at the same level). Gravestone is the stronger signal.

**What is the difference between gravestone doji and dragonfly doji?**

Gravestone doji has a long UPPER wick and signals bearish reversal at resistance. Dragonfly doji has a long LOWER wick and signals bullish reversal at support. They are direct opposites.

**Can I use gravestone doji for scalping?**

Yes — on 15-minute or 5-minute timeframes. But lower timeframes are less reliable and offer lower risk-to-reward ratios than 4-hour or daily gravestones.

**Can a gravestone doji fail?**

Yes — sometimes price continues higher above the gravestone high. That is why confirmation candle, resistance level alignment, and trend context are all required filters.

**How does gravestone doji fit in the ICT framework?**

It is a single-candle signature of an inducement sweep at a bearish PD array, with the close at the open functioning as a candle-level CISD. The strongest setup is gravestone doji at a higher-timeframe supply zone with lower-timeframe MSS confirmation.

**Does gravestone doji work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook gravestone dojis at higher-timeframe resistance and supply zones, especially during the New York AM session.

# Higher High and Higher Low — Identify Valid Bullish Market Structure with Inducement Sweep

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/higher-high-and-higher-low/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/higher-high-and-higher-low/)

![Higher High and Higher Low — identifying valid bullish market structure with inducement sweep and break of structure confirmation](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Identify-Higher-High-and-Higher-Low-in-Bullish-Market.png)

Higher High and Higher Low are the two building blocks of bullish market structure — but not every visible high or low qualifies as STRUCTURAL. The valid higher high requires an inducement sweep, and the valid higher low requires both an inducement sweep AND a follow-up break of structure to confirm.

In this guide I walk you through the identification of higher high and higher low — the inducement-sweep rule, the swing-formation sequence, the structural high and low after a bullish CHOCH, common mistakes and the FAQ. For the bearish mirror see my [Lower High and Lower Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/lower-high-and-lower-low/>) guide.

section: How to Identify Higher High in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Higher High in Bullish Market

In a bullish market, price makes higher highs — but every high is not a structural high.

To identify a valid higher high in a bullish market, you have to identify [Inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>) first.

After identifying the inducement, wait for price to make a [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>) and retrace down to sweep the inducement.

When price sweeps the inducement, the last swing high formed BEFORE sweeping the inducement is marked as the valid higher high.

![Higher high identification example — inducement marked, swing high forms, price sweeps the inducement, then the last swing high is confirmed as the valid higher high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Higher-High-market-structure.png)

When price breaks above the higher high, it is called a valid break of structure.

Every time price breaks the structure to the upside, you have to look for the inducement sweep to confirm the higher high.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: How to Identify Higher Low in Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Identify Higher Low in Bullish Market

In a bullish market, price makes higher lows — but every low is not a valid higher low.

To confirm a low as a valid higher low, follow the steps explained below.

When price sweeps the inducement and confirms the higher high, look for the formation of a [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>).

After the formation of the swing low, if price moves up and breaks the previous high, then the last swing low formed at the liquidity sweep is marked as the valid higher low.

![Higher low identification example — after inducement sweep and higher high confirmation, swing low forms, price breaks the previous high confirming the valid higher low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/higher-low-market-structure.png)

Every time after a break of structure to the upside, you have to look for a liquidity sweep and then the next break of structure to confirm a higher low.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: How to Identify Structural Low after Bullish CHOCH
content:
#### How to Identify Structural Low after Bullish CHOCH

To identify a structural low after a bullish CHOCH, mark the last lower low that was made before the CHOCH.

The last lower low of the bearish trend is marked as the structural low when the market changes its trend from bearish to bullish — because the bullish trend starts from that low.

![Structural low after bullish CHOCH — last lower low of the prior bearish trend marked as the structural anchor for the new bullish leg](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/structural-low.png)

Then after every break of structure, look for an inducement sweep and a break of structure to the upside to confirm the higher low.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: How to Identify Structural High after Bullish CHOCH
content:
#### How to Identify Structural High after Bullish CHOCH

[CHOCH](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>) means change of character — and when the market changes its trend from bearish to bullish, you have to mark a higher high.

To identify a structural high after a bullish CHOCH, identify the inducement and wait for the formation of a swing high.

After the formation of the swing high, when price sweeps the inducement, the last swing high is marked as the valid structural high.

![Structural high after bullish CHOCH — first valid higher high marked after the change of character with inducement sweep confirming the structural anchor](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/structural-high.png)

As the trend is bullish, price will expectedly rise and break the previous high making a new high. After every break of structure, look for the inducement sweep to confirm the higher high.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: Can We Mark a Higher High Without an Inducement Sweep?
content:
#### Can We Mark a Higher High Without an Inducement Sweep?

No — to confirm a higher high, the sweep of inducement is necessary.

If price breaks a high without sweeping the inducement, it is called a “Minor Break of Structure” — your high just shifts, but the overall market structure remains the same.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: Can We Mark a Higher Low Without an Inducement Sweep?
content:
#### Can We Mark a Higher Low Without an Inducement Sweep?

No — to confirm a higher low, both the inducement sweep AND a break of structure to the upside are crucial.

Without the inducement sweep and a break of structure to the upside, you cannot mark a higher low.

title: higher-high-and-higher-low
section: Step-by-Step Higher High / Higher Low Identification
content:
#### Step-by-Step Higher High / Higher Low Identification

This is the exact sequence I run to mark every valid higher high and higher low in a bullish leg.

  1. **Confirm the bullish trend.** Either a fresh bullish CHOCH or an existing bullish series of higher highs.
  2. **Mark the structural low.** Last lower low before the CHOCH (or the most recent confirmed higher low if mid-trend).
  3. **Wait for the first swing high.** The next visible high in the bullish leg.
  4. **Mark the inducement.** The first valid pullback inside the leg toward that swing high — the inducement low.
  5. **Wait for the inducement sweep.** Price retraces down and dips below the inducement low.
  6. **Confirm the higher high.** The last swing high formed BEFORE the inducement sweep is the valid higher high.
  7. **Wait for the BOS above that higher high.** A clean break above the higher high.
  8. **Confirm the higher low.** The last swing low formed at the inducement sweep is now the valid higher low.
  9. **Repeat for the next leg.** Each new bullish leg follows the same inducement-sweep-then-BOS sequence.
  10. **Watch for a bearish CHOCH.** The bullish series ends when price breaks the most recent higher low — that is the CHOCH that flips the bias.

section: Common Mistakes Around Higher High and Higher Low
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Higher High and Higher Low

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start working with higher highs and higher lows.

  1. **Marking every visible high as a higher high.** Only the swing high BEFORE an inducement sweep qualifies. Random highs are noise.
  2. **Marking a higher low before the BOS.** The higher low is only confirmed AFTER the next break of structure to the upside. Marking it earlier creates false structure.
  3. **Confusing minor BOS with valid BOS.** Breaking a high without an inducement sweep is a minor BOS — the high just shifts. It is NOT a valid higher high.
  4. **Skipping the structural low / high anchor.** After a CHOCH, the prior trend’s last extreme becomes the structural anchor. Without it, you have no reference for the new trend.
  5. **Trading higher highs on the wrong timeframe.** A higher high on the 5-minute against a bearish daily is unreliable. Use top-down alignment.
  6. **Ignoring the inducement after CHOCH.** The first valid higher high after a CHOCH still requires inducement sweep — do not skip it because it is the first leg.

section: FAQs about Higher High and Higher Low
content:
#### FAQs about Higher High and Higher Low

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about higher highs and higher lows.

**What is a higher high in trading?**

A higher high is the structural high of a bullish leg — the last swing high formed BEFORE price sweeps the inducement. Breaking above it is the valid bullish break of structure.

**What is a higher low in trading?**

A higher low is the structural low of a bullish leg — the last swing low formed at the inducement sweep, confirmed when price then breaks the previous higher high to the upside.

**How is a higher high different from a swing high?**

Every swing high is a visible local extreme. A higher high is the SPECIFIC swing high that exists before an inducement sweep — the only one that counts as structural.

**Can I mark a higher high without inducement?**

No — without the inducement sweep, breaking a high is just a minor BOS. The high shifts but the structure does not advance.

**Can I mark a higher low without a BOS?**

No — the higher low requires BOTH the inducement sweep AND a follow-up break of structure to the upside to confirm. Without the BOS, the swing low is not yet structural.

**What is the structural low after a bullish CHOCH?**

The last lower low of the prior bearish trend — that is where the new bullish trend starts. It anchors all the higher lows that follow.

**What is the structural high after a bullish CHOCH?**

The first valid higher high after the CHOCH — confirmed by the inducement sweep on the new bullish leg.

**Is market structure a reliable trading method?**

Yes — market structure is one of the most reliable trading methods. To achieve good results, learn it properly and mark the structure accurately.

**Can I trade using market structure alone?**

Yes — if you master market structure properly, you do not need anything else. You can trade using the market-structure method without any indicators.

**What ends the bullish series of higher highs and higher lows?**

A bearish CHOCH — when price breaks the most recent higher low. That is the structural signal the trend has flipped.

**What timeframe is best for marking higher highs and higher lows?**

Use top-down analysis. The 1-day and 4-hour for the macro structure, the 15-minute or 1-hour for the intraday structure, the 5-minute for execution.

**Does this work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook higher-high / higher-low sequences, especially in trending environments after a CHOCH.

# How to Trade an RSI Divergence — Bullish/Bearish Reversal Setup with Confirmation

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence/)

![RSI Divergence trading strategy — regular bullish and bearish divergence with price-RSI disconnect at support and resistance levels for trend reversal trades](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/RSI-divergence.png)

RSI Divergence is one of the most reliable momentum-based reversal signals in technical analysis — when price makes a new low but RSI makes a higher low (or price makes a new high but RSI makes a lower high), the momentum behind the trend is fading and a reversal is often near. Master the regular bullish and bearish divergence at strong support and resistance levels, and you have a high-conviction reversal filter.

section: What is an RSI Divergence?
content:
#### What is an RSI Divergence?

**The Relative Strength Index (RSI)** , created by J. Welles Wilder, serves as a momentum oscillator that gauges the velocity and direction of price changes.

RSI values fluctuate between zero and 100, tracking price movements and signaling instances of overbought and oversold conditions in the market.

But sometimes the price movement and the movement of RSI may diverge from each other — price moves in one direction while RSI moves in the other direction — and this is termed an **RSI divergence**.

RSI divergence is divided into two types:

**(I) Regular RSI Divergence**

**(II) Hidden RSI Divergence**

This guide primarily focuses on Regular RSI divergence — the type of divergence most commonly utilized in trading practices.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: Regular RSI Divergence
content:
#### Regular RSI Divergence

Regular RSI signals a trend reversal in the market. It has two types based on the trend of the market.

**(I) Bullish RSI Divergence** is mostly seen and reliable at the end of a bearish trend.

In a bearish trend, when price makes lower lows but the RSI diverges from price making higher lows, this indicates the losing momentum of sellers in the market and a possible change in the direction of market.

In the picture below you can see an example of bullish RSI divergence on a chart.

![Bullish RSI divergence example — price makes a new lower low while RSI prints a higher low, signaling weakening bearish momentum and potential reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Bullish-RSI-divergence-1.png)

**How to Trade Bullish RSI Divergence**

To trade using bullish RSI divergence, you have to identify the trend of the market — and it should be bearish.

Price should be seen making lower lows and is going to test a strong support area where you can expect a reversal of price or a deeper retracement.

When price tests the support area, you will be looking for a buy trade — and here the RSI divergence will act as confirmation of your buy trade.

At the support area, if you see RSI diverging from price, you can expect a price reversal.

But to execute a trade, the RSI divergence alone is not reliable — you have to look for other bullish evidences like a bullish candlestick pattern, [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>), or bullish chart pattern.

![Bullish RSI divergence trade example on XAU/USD 4H — 1932 support line tested with bullish RSI divergence, bullish engulfing candle confirmation and market structure shift](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/rsi-bullish-divergence.png)

As you can see in the picture above — XAU/USD 4-hourly chart where price was in a bearish trend and tested the 1932 support line.

When it tested the support line, RSI indicated a bullish divergence — and as a confirmation, the bullish engulfing candlestick pattern was also formed. Plus price shifted its structure too, so there were three confirmations of price reversal from here.

A buy trade is executed at support using RSI bullish divergence.

In this scenario, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the recent low or support zone, whichever is lower. For take profit, target the next resistance zone.

**(II) Bearish RSI Divergence** is typically observed and considered reliable towards the conclusion of a bullish trend.

During a bullish trend, when price makes higher highs but the RSI demonstrates lower highs — showing a divergence from price — it signifies diminishing momentum among buyers in the market, hinting at a potential reversal in market direction.

The provided image below illustrates an example of bearish RSI divergence on a chart.

![Bearish RSI divergence example — price makes a new higher high while RSI prints a lower high, signaling weakening bullish momentum and potential reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/RSI-bearish-divergence.png)

**How to Trade Bearish RSI Divergence**

To execute trades based on bearish RSI divergence, first identify a bullish trend in the market.

During this bullish trend, monitor the price action as it forms higher highs — indicating a potential test of a significant resistance level where a reversal or deeper retracement could occur.

As price approaches the resistance area, prepare to enter a sell trade. The bearish RSI divergence will serve as confirmation for your sell trade. Keep an eye on the RSI indicator as it diverges from price action at the resistance area.

This divergence suggests a weakening bullish momentum and hints at an impending price reversal. Therefore, when you observe the RSI diverging from price at the resistance level, anticipate a reversal — confirming your decision to enter a sell trade.

But to execute a trade, the RSI divergence alone is not reliable — you have to look for other bearish evidences like a bearish candlestick pattern, [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>), or bearish chart pattern.

![Bearish RSI divergence trade example on XAU/USD 4H — 2088 resistance area tested with bearish RSI divergence, evening star candle confirmation triggering the sell entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/rsi-bearish-divergence-trading.png)

In the picture above you can see the XAU/USD 4-hourly chart where price approaches the 2088 strong resistance area.

When it tests the resistance, you can see RSI indicating bearish divergence and a formation of the Evening Star candlestick pattern for confirmation.

A sell trade is executed on the test of the evening star pattern using RSI bearish divergence.

In this case, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the recent high or resistance level, whichever is higher. For take profit, target the next support area.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: RSI Divergence in the ICT Framework
content:
#### RSI Divergence in the ICT Framework

RSI divergence is a momentum filter that ICT traders can layer on top of the structural framework — not a replacement for it.

The cleanest setups occur when RSI divergence aligns with three structural conditions: (1) price at a higher-timeframe PD array, (2) an [inducement sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) at the level, and (3) a lower-timeframe MSS in the reversal direction.

Use RSI divergence to filter out structural reversal signals — if MSS prints but RSI agrees with the prior trend, the reversal is weaker. If MSS prints AND RSI diverges, the reversal is high-conviction.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: Step-by-Step RSI Divergence Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step RSI Divergence Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading an RSI divergence reversal.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Bearish for bullish divergence setup, bullish for bearish divergence setup.
  2. **Mark the key level.** Strong support (bullish setup) or strong resistance (bearish setup) — ideally aligned with a higher-timeframe PD array.
  3. **Wait for price to reach the level.** Patience — do not pre-position.
  4. **Check RSI for divergence.** Bullish — price makes a new low but RSI prints a higher low. Bearish — price makes a new high but RSI prints a lower high.
  5. **Wait for confirmation.** A bullish candlestick pattern (hammer, engulfing, morning star) at support — or bearish candle (evening star, shooting star, bearish engulfing) at resistance. Optional: lower-timeframe MSS in the reversal direction.
  6. **Enter on the confirmation candle close.**
  7. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips below the recent low / support (buy) or above the recent high / resistance (sell), whichever is the more extreme level.
  8. **Set the target.** Next opposite-direction level — next resistance for a buy, next support for a sell.
  9. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1 or at the first opposite-direction PD array, trail the runner.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: Best Pairs for RSI Divergence
content:
#### Best Pairs for RSI Divergence

RSI divergence works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, USD/JPY, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD, and indices like NQ and ES.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the RSI divergence framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for RSI divergence reversals.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: Common Mistakes Around RSI Divergence
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around RSI Divergence

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading RSI divergence.

  1. **Trading divergence in the middle of a range.** Divergence only matters at strong support / resistance. In a range, every minor reversal produces a divergence.
  2. **Entering on divergence alone.** RSI divergence is the FILTER — not the trigger. You need a candlestick pattern, MSS or structural confirmation to enter.
  3. **Confusing regular and hidden divergence.** Regular divergence signals reversal. Hidden divergence signals continuation. Mixing them flips the direction of the trade.
  4. **Tight stops at the recent extreme.** The 10–20 pip buffer below the support or above the resistance is mandatory — wicks hunt tight stops at the level.
  5. **Trading every divergence.** Some divergences fail. Stack the filters — divergence + level + candle pattern + MSS — for the highest hit rate.
  6. **Wrong RSI period.** Default RSI(14) works on every timeframe. Changing the period for “better signals” usually over-fits and produces fakes.

title: how-to-trade-an-rsi-divergence
section: FAQs about RSI Divergence
content:
#### FAQs about RSI Divergence

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about RSI divergence.

**What is an RSI divergence?**

When price and the RSI indicator move in opposite directions — for example, price makes a new high while RSI makes a lower high (bearish divergence), or price makes a new low while RSI makes a higher low (bullish divergence). It signals fading momentum behind the trend.

**What is regular RSI divergence?**

Regular RSI divergence signals trend reversal. Bullish regular divergence (in a downtrend) precedes a reversal up; bearish regular divergence (in an uptrend) precedes a reversal down.

**What is hidden RSI divergence?**

Hidden divergence signals trend continuation, not reversal. It is the opposite of regular divergence — bullish hidden divergence in an uptrend predicts continuation higher.

**How do I identify bullish RSI divergence?**

In a bearish trend, watch for price to make a new lower low while RSI prints a higher low. The disagreement signals fading sell-side momentum.

**How do I identify bearish RSI divergence?**

In a bullish trend, watch for price to make a new higher high while RSI prints a lower high. The disagreement signals fading buy-side momentum.

**Can I trade RSI divergence alone?**

No — RSI divergence alone is not reliable. Pair it with a strong support / resistance level, a candlestick pattern confirmation, and ideally a market structure shift.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After price reaches the support / resistance level, RSI diverges, and a confirmation candle prints (bullish at support, bearish at resistance). Enter on the candle close.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips below the recent low or support (buy trade), 10 to 20 pips above the recent high or resistance (sell trade) — whichever is the more extreme level.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next opposite-direction level — next resistance for a buy trade, next support for a sell trade.

**What RSI period works best?**

The default RSI(14) is the standard and works on every timeframe. Avoid changing the period — shorter periods produce too many false signals, longer periods miss the divergence entirely.

**What timeframe is best for RSI divergence?**

RSI divergence works on every timeframe but is most reliable on the 4-hour and daily. Lower timeframes (15-minute, 5-minute) produce more false divergences.

**Does RSI divergence work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook RSI divergence reversals at higher-timeframe key levels.

**How does RSI divergence fit in the ICT framework?**

Use it as a momentum filter on top of the structural framework — RSI divergence at a higher-timeframe PD array combined with an inducement sweep and a lower-timeframe MSS is the highest-conviction reversal setup.

title: ict-abbreviations
section: ICT Abbreviations List (A–Z)
content:
#### ICT Abbreviations List (A–Z)

**AMD** — Accumulation, Manipulation and Distribution. Also known as the [ICT Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>) daily template.

**BB** — [ICT Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>). The flipped order block that becomes opposite-direction support or resistance.

**BE** — Breakeven. Moving the stop loss to the entry price after a trade goes in your favor — if the stop is hit, no profit no loss.

**BISI** — Buy Side Imbalance Sell Side Inefficiency. The bullish [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>).

**BOS** — [Break of Structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>). Price breaks the previous swing high or low after taking inducement, confirming continuation.

**BPR** — [Balanced Price Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>). The overlap area between two opposite-direction fair value gaps in the same zone.

**BSL** — [Buy Side Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>). Buy stops at or above old highs, plus stop losses of sellers placed at or above the old highs.

**CBDR** — [Central Bank Dealers Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-central-bank-dealers-range/>). The 14:00–20:00 NY-time consolidation range used to project intraday targets.

**CE** — [Consequent Encroachment](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-consequent-encroachment/>). The 50% retracement level (midpoint) of an FVG, order block or any PD array.

**CHOCH** — [Change of Character](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>). The break of the most recent higher low (bullish trend) or lower high (bearish trend), confirming long-term trend reversal.

**CISD** — [Change in State of Delivery](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>). The candle-level confirmation that price delivery has shifted direction.

**CRT** — [Candle Range Theory](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/candle-range-theory-crt/>). The four-stage candle delivery model — open, sweep, reverse, close.

**D Bias / Daily Bias** — [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>). The anticipated direction of price for the day.

**ERL** — [External Range Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-internal-external-liquidity/>). Liquidity residing outside a price range — the swing highs and lows.

**FTR** — Failed To Return. A smart-money zone where price failed to return after a structural break.

**FVG** — [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>). A three-candle formation with a gap between the 1st and 3rd candlestick where price has not retraced previously.

**HRLR / LRLR** — [High-Resistance Liquidity Run / Low-Resistance Liquidity Run](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-hrlr-lrlr/>). The expected resistance level of a liquidity run before the algorithm reverses.

**HTF** — Higher Timeframe. 1-hour, 4-hour, 1-day, 1-week or 1-month.

**IDM** — [Inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>). The retail trap level smart money sweeps before delivering the real direction.

**iFVG** — [Inversion Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>). A regular FVG that has been broken in the opposite direction and now acts as opposite-direction support or resistance.

**Implied FVG** — [Implied Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-implied-fair-value-gap-ifvg/>). A structural FVG implied by the wicks of three candles even when bodies overlap.

**IOFED** — [Institutional Order Flow Entry Drill](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-institutional-order-flow-entry-drill/>). The very edge of an FVG used as the earliest possible entry.

**IPDA** — [Inter-bank Price Delivery Algorithm](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-ipda/>). The algorithm that delivers price online on the charts.

**IRL** — Internal Range Liquidity. Liquidity residing inside a dealing range — the FVGs and order blocks.

**ITH** — [Intermediate Term High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/>). A high in between two short-term highs.

**ITL** — [Intermediate Term Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/>). A low in between two short-term lows.

**LP** — [ICT Liquidity Pool](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-pool/>). A cluster of stop-loss and pending orders at a key level.

**LTF** — Lower Timeframe. 1-minute, 5-minute or 15-minute.

**LTH** — Long Term High. A high with lower intermediate-term highs on both sides.

**LTL** — Long Term Low. A low with higher intermediate-term lows on both sides.

**MB** — [ICT Mitigation Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-mitigation-block-explained/>). The unmitigated swing point that price returns to before continuing.

**MMBM** — [Market Maker Buy Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-buy-model/>). The institutional 4-phase bullish delivery template.

**MMSM** — [Market Maker Sell Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-sell-model/>). The institutional 4-phase bearish delivery template.

**MSS** — [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>). The break of a swing high or low signaling the initial change in delivery direction.

**MT** — Mean Threshold. The 50% retracement level of an [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>).

**NDOG** — [New Day Opening Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-day-opening-gap-ndog/>). The daily gap between 5:00 PM close and 6:00 PM open in New York time.

**NWOG** — [New Week Opening Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-week-opening-gap-nwog/>). The weekend gap between Friday close and Monday open.

**OB** — [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>). The last opposing candle before the displacement that produced a structural break.

**OTE** — [Optimal Trade Entry](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>). The 62%–79% Fibonacci retracement zone of the most recent impulsive leg.

**PD Array** — Premium / Discount Array. The collective name for FVG, order block, breaker, mitigation, OTE and any other PD-arrangement zones used as entries.

**PDH** — Previous Day High. The high (or wick) of yesterday’s daily candle.

**PDL** — Previous Day Low. The low (or wick) of yesterday’s daily candle.

**PO3** — [ICT Power of Three](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>). The Accumulation–Manipulation–Distribution daily template.

**QML** — [Quasimodo Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/qml-chart-pattern/>). A reversal chart pattern at higher-timeframe support or resistance.

**RB** — Rejection Block. See [ICT Rejection Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-rejection-block/>).

**RDRB / RRPR** — [Redelivered / Rebalanced Price Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-redelivered-rebalanced-price-range/>). The PD-array reset where price returns to a prior FVG and rebalances it before continuing.

**SCOB** — [Single Candle Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/single-candle-order-block-scob/>). The single-candle variant of the OB used for refined LTF entries.

**SIBI** — Sell Side Imbalance Buy Side Inefficiency. The bearish [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>).

**SMT** — [Smart Money Technique Divergence](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-smt-divergence-smart-money-technique/>). The disagreement between two correlated pairs at a key liquidity level.

**SSL** — Sell Side Liquidity. Sell stops at or below old lows, plus stop losses of buyers placed at or below old lows.

**STH** — [Short Term High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>). A swing high — local extreme between two lower highs on either side.

**STL** — [Short Term Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>). A swing low — local extreme between two higher lows on either side.

**TGIF** — [Thank God It Is Friday](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro/>). The Friday-only weekly-range retracement model.

If you are starting out, master these five abbreviations before any others — they appear in almost every ICT setup.

title: ict-abbreviations
section: FAQs about ICT Abbreviations
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Abbreviations

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about ICT abbreviations.

**What does ICT stand for in trading?**

ICT stands for Inner Circle Trader — the trading framework introduced by Michael J. Huddleston, built on the Interbank Price Delivery Algorithm and Smart Money Concepts.

**What is the difference between ICT and SMC?**

ICT and SMC overlap heavily — both are built on liquidity, imbalance and structure. SMC is essentially a derivative of ICT that some traders teach separately, but the mechanics are the same.

**What is the most important ICT abbreviation to learn first?**

FVG — the Fair Value Gap. Almost every ICT setup uses an FVG somewhere — as the entry, the target, or the bias confirmation.

**What does FVG stand for?**

FVG stands for Fair Value Gap — a three-candle formation with an unfilled gap between the 1st and 3rd candle wicks.

**What does BOS mean in trading?**

BOS stands for Break of Structure — price breaking the previous swing high or low after taking inducement, confirming the continuation of the trend.

**What does MSS stand for?**

MSS stands for Market Structure Shift — the break of a swing high or low signaling the initial change in price delivery direction.

**What does CHOCH mean?**

CHOCH stands for Change of Character — the break of the most recent structural higher low (bullish trend) or lower high (bearish trend), confirming long-term trend reversal.

**What does PO3 stand for?**

PO3 stands for Power of 3 — the daily Accumulation, Manipulation, Distribution template that describes how price is delivered each session.

**What does OTE stand for?**

OTE stands for Optimal Trade Entry — the 62%–79% Fibonacci retracement zone of the most recent impulsive leg, used as a refined entry zone.

**What does IPDA stand for?**

IPDA stands for Inter-bank Price Delivery Algorithm — the algorithm ICT teaches as the underlying engine that delivers price on the charts.

**What does IDM mean?**

IDM stands for Inducement — the retail-trap level smart money sweeps before delivering the real directional move.

**What does NWOG stand for?**

NWOG stands for New Week Opening Gap — the gap between Friday close and Monday open at the start of each week.

**What does NDOG stand for?**

NDOG stands for New Day Opening Gap — the daily gap between the 5:00 PM close and 6:00 PM open in New York time.

**What does CISD mean?**

CISD stands for Change in State of Delivery — the candle-level confirmation that price delivery has shifted direction.

**Where can I find the full tutorial for each abbreviation?**

Every abbreviation in the list above is linked to its dedicated tutorial. Click the abbreviation’s link for the deep-dive guide — definition, types, identification, trade flow, common mistakes and FAQ.
