# ICT Advance Market Structure – STH ITH & LTH

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/)

![ICT advanced market structure showing STH, ITH, and LTH hierarchy of highs on a price chart](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Advance-Market-Structure.png)

For years I marked every swing high on my chart and treated each one as resistance. Most of them broke a few candles later. The few that actually held the move — those were the LTHs. The hierarchy of highs — STH, ITH, LTH — is the difference between a high that matters to the trend and a wick that simply did not.

In ICT, **STH stands for Short Term High, ITH stands for Intermediate Term High, and LTH stands for Long Term High.** These three labels rank every swing high on your chart by structural importance. The highest rank — LTH — marks the levels that decide whether a market is still bullish or has lost its trend.

In this guide, I will show you exactly how each of these highs is identified, the hierarchy that connects them, the rule for reading bullish market structure, and how to use the three labels in actual trading.

If you also want the lows side of advanced market structure (STL, ITL, LTL), see our companion post on [ICT STL, ITL & LTL](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/> "ICT STL, ITL, LTL").

Do not worry — once you have seen the three-candle pattern a few times, identifying STHs, ITHs, and LTHs becomes mechanical.

Ready? Let us break it down.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: What Are STH, ITH, and LTH in ICT?
content:
## What Are STH, ITH, and LTH in ICT?

In ICT trading, every swing high on your chart belongs to one of three tiers:

  * **STH — Short Term High.** A basic three-candle swing high.
  * **ITH — Intermediate Term High.** An STH with a lower STH on each side.
  * **LTH — Long Term High.** An ITH with a lower ITH on each side, usually at a higher-timeframe PD Array.

Each tier is a stricter version of the one before it. An STH is just a local peak. An ITH is a meaningful high because the peaks around it were shallower. An LTH is a structural high because the meaningful highs around it were shallower still. The deeper you go in the hierarchy, the more weight that high carries for the larger trend.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: What is Market Structure?
content:
## What is Market Structure?

Market structure refers to the framework within which a market is trading at any given time. It provides insight into the market’s behaviour, condition, and current flow. Through swing highs and swing lows, market structure helps in understanding the overall dynamics of the market.

Market structure has three main types:

  * **Bullish Market Structure** — consistently rising prices of an asset, indicated by higher long-term highs and higher long-term lows on the price chart.
  * **Bearish Market Structure** — consistently falling prices of an asset, indicated by lower long-term lows and lower long-term highs on the price chart.
  * **Sideways Market Structure** — price is trading in a range and making equal highs and equal lows.

For a fuller walkthrough of market-structure types and how to spot transitions between them, see [Market Structure in Trading](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/market-structure-in-trading/> "Market Structure in Trading").

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: Why These Highs Matter (The Hierarchy of Market Structure)
content:
## Why These Highs Matter (The Hierarchy of Market Structure)

Every retail trader can mark a high. The hard part is knowing which high matters.

When price prints a fresh local peak, you do not yet know if it is a Short Term High that will be broken five candles later, an Intermediate Term High that defines the current pullback, or a Long Term High that holds the trend together. The hierarchy gives you a procedural answer: wait for the swing-high neighbours on each side, then label accordingly.

This matters in two practical situations:

  * **Identifying the trend.** A bullish market is one printing higher LTHs and higher LTLs. A bearish market is the inverse. Without LTH labelling, you are guessing whether a pullback is healthy or whether the trend has changed.
  * **Anticipating reversals.** LTHs that form after a reaction at a higher-timeframe PD Array are high-probability turning points. Knowing one has formed lets you watch for confirmation rather than guessing the top.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: (I) ICT Short Term High (STH)
content:
## (I) ICT Short Term High (STH)

ICT STH — Short Term High — is basically an [ICT Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/> "ICT Swing High") being a three-candle formation in such a way that the high (wick) of the 2nd (middle) candle is higher than the high of both candles — the 1st on the left and the 3rd on the right of it.

So the high of the 2nd (middle) candle is termed as the Short Term High (STH).

![ICT Short Term High \(STH\) example: a three-candle swing high with the middle candle wick higher than the left and right candles](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/short-term-high-STH.png)

Every peak on a chart that meets this three-candle test is an STH. They are common, they are everywhere, and they are the building block of the next two tiers.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: (II) ICT Intermediate Term High (ITH)
content:
## (II) ICT Intermediate Term High (ITH)

The word “intermediate” refers to something that is in the middle, or between two stages. So the Intermediate Term High (ITH) is basically a Short Term High — but with a **lower Short Term High on the left and right side of it**.

It is in the middle of two short term highs, and it is higher than both the left and right short term highs.

![ICT Intermediate Term High \(ITH\) example: a Short Term High flanked by two lower Short Term Highs on each side](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/intermediate-term-high.png)

ITHs are less common than STHs. Each ITH marks a higher peak that the surrounding STHs failed to match — a sign that the move into that high had real momentum.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: (III) ICT Long Term High (LTH)
content:
## (III) ICT Long Term High (LTH)

An ICT Long Term High (LTH) is also an Intermediate Term High by nature, but it is mostly formed at a higher-timeframe [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array") after a reaction of price.

A Long Term High (LTH) is indicated by an Intermediate High in the middle of two Intermediate Term Highs. It is the highest Intermediate Term High, having a lower Intermediate Term High on the left and right side of it.

![ICT Long Term High \(LTH\) example: an Intermediate Term High flanked by two lower Intermediate Term Highs, formed at a higher-timeframe PD Array](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/long-term-high.png)

LTHs are the most weighted highs on your chart. Each one is a structural anchor — until it is broken, the larger trend it belongs to remains intact.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: Reading Bullish Market Structure With LTHs and LTLs
content:
## Reading Bullish Market Structure With LTHs and LTLs

In bullish market structure, price will make higher Long Term Highs and higher long-term lows.

If price is supposed to go higher, then it should not violate the recent higher long-term low. But if it does so and breaks the long-term low, then it will no longer be bullish.

This is the rule that decides whether a bullish trend is still alive. As long as each new long-term high prints above the previous long-term high, and each new long-term low prints above the previous long-term low, the bullish structure is intact. The moment price closes below a recent long-term low, the structure has changed and the bias must be re-evaluated.

The same rule mirrors for bearish markets — lower LTHs and lower long-term lows, and the structure stays bearish as long as price does not violate the most recent long-term high.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: How to Use STH, ITH, and LTH in Your Trading
content:
## How to Use STH, ITH, and LTH in Your Trading

The hierarchy is a labelling system, not an entry signal on its own. Here is how it integrates into a trade:

  1. **Mark the LTHs first.** Identify the highest-tier highs on your bias timeframe. These define the trend.
  2. **Mark the ITHs.** These define the active swing structure inside the trend.
  3. **Mark the STHs.** These give you reaction levels for shorter-term entries.
  4. **Watch the most recent long-term low.** As long as it holds (in a bullish trend), you can keep buying pullbacks. If it breaks, the bias has shifted.
  5. **Use LTHs as targets.** A bearish trade looking for room runs to the next opposing level — often a recent LTL. Same logic mirrored for longs.
  6. **Use ITHs and STHs as entry zones.** When price retraces back into an ITH or STH during a continuation move, that is your refined entry area.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest LTH trades happen when the LTH forms inside a higher-timeframe PD Array — a [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap"), [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block"), or [breaker block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block"). The PD Array is the institutional level. The LTH is the structural confirmation. When both line up, the level holds with conviction.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: Bonus Tip: Pair STH, ITH, LTH With STL, ITL, LTL
content:
## Bonus Tip: Pair STH, ITH, LTH With STL, ITL, LTL

The highs side is only half of advanced market structure. The lows side — STL (Short Term Low), ITL (Intermediate Term Low), and LTL (Long Term Low) — uses the same three-candle hierarchy in reverse.

Read the highs for resistance structure, read the lows for support structure, and the chart tells you exactly where the trend is and what it has to break to change direction. For the full lows walkthrough, see [ICT STL, ITL & LTL — Short, Intermediate & Long Term Lows](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/> "ICT STL ITL LTL").

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does ITH mean in trading?

ITH stands for Intermediate Term High. It is an ICT market structure label for a Short Term High that has a lower Short Term High on each side of it — making it the highest STH in a sequence of three.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: What is the full form of STH, ITH, and LTH?
content:
### What is the full form of STH, ITH, and LTH?

STH is Short Term High, ITH is Intermediate Term High, and LTH is Long Term High. All three are ICT labels for swing highs ranked by structural importance.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: How is an LTH different from an ITH?
content:
### How is an LTH different from an ITH?

An LTH is an ITH with a lower ITH on each side of it — making it the highest ITH in a sequence of three. An LTH is also typically formed at a higher-timeframe PD Array. The hierarchy is STH → ITH → LTH, with each tier requiring two same-tier neighbours that are lower.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: How is an STH identified on a chart?
content:
### How is an STH identified on a chart?

An STH is a three-candle swing high. The high of the middle candle must be higher than the high of both the candle to its left and the candle to its right. The middle candle is then marked as the STH.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: What is the difference between an STH and a regular swing high?
content:
### What is the difference between an STH and a regular swing high?

In ICT, STH is the specific name for the standard three-candle swing high. A swing high and an STH are the same thing in ICT terminology — the abbreviation is just the labelling system used to rank highs by tier.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: How does a bullish market behave with these highs?
content:
### How does a bullish market behave with these highs?

In a bullish market, price will print higher LTHs and higher long-term lows. The trend is intact as long as the most recent long-term low is not violated. The moment price closes below that low, the bullish structure has shifted.

title: ict-advance-market-structure
section: Which timeframe should I use to mark STH, ITH, and LTH?
content:
### Which timeframe should I use to mark STH, ITH, and LTH?

Mark LTHs on your bias timeframe (Daily or 4-hour for swing trading; 1-hour for intraday). ITHs sit on the same timeframe but are less frequent. STHs can be marked on the bias timeframe or one timeframe lower for refined entries.

# ICT Asian Range Trading Strategy — Asian Session Liquidity Sweep + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-asian-range/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-asian-range/)

![ICT Asian Range Trading Strategy — Asian session liquidity sweep that traps retail traders before the New York directional move](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-Asian-Range-Trading-Strategy.png)

The ICT Asian range trading strategy is based on the liquidity sweep of the Asian range — the tight overnight consolidation that often traps retail traders before price reverses into the New York session.

The ICT Asian range lies between 07:00 PM and 12:00 AM New York local time. After the Asian range liquidity sweep, you can anticipate the next directional move of the day and align your trade with it.

This guide walks you through the Asian range — the session times, the bullish and bearish models, the entry options after the sweep, the stop and target placement, the common mistakes and the free PDF download.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the whole article for a complete view.

Table of Contents

title: ict-asian-range
section: What is the ICT Asian Range?
content:
#### What is the ICT Asian Range?

The ICT Asian range is the range of the Asian session, which starts at 07:00 PM and ends at midnight 12:00 AM (New York local time).

If you have a higher-timeframe directional bias you can use the ICT Asian range to anticipate the likely movement of price after the Asian session.

A tight consolidation within the Asian range often signals an impending shift to a trending algorithm, which means the market is likely to sweep liquidity either above or below the Asian range.

This liquidity sweep traps retail traders in the wrong direction and price reverses afterwards.

You can see an example of the ICT Asian range in the picture below.

![ICT Asian Range — overnight consolidation between 07:00 PM and 12:00 AM NY local time, with the high and low marked as future liquidity targets](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-Asian-Range.png)

title: ict-asian-range
section: ICT Asian Range Time (NY Local, EST & GMT)
content:
#### ICT Asian Range Time (NY Local, EST & GMT)

The Asian range is anchored to the New York local clock. Use the New York time as the base reference and let your charting platform translate to your local time zone.

  * **New York local time (EST):** 07:00 PM to 12:00 AM
  * **GMT:** approximately 12:00 AM to 05:00 AM (during EST; shifts by one hour during EDT)
  * **London time (BST):** approximately 12:00 AM to 05:00 AM

The most important reference is the New York midnight open price, which marks the close of the Asian range and the boundary that price often returns to during the New York session.

title: ict-asian-range
section: How to Trade the Asian Range
content:
#### How to Trade the Asian Range

To trade the ICT Asian range strategy you need to have a directional bias. You then mark the high and low of the Asian range and wait for a liquidity sweep above the high or below the low.

For better understanding I cover the bullish and bearish setups separately below.

title: ict-asian-range
section: ICT Asian Range in a Bullish Market
content:
#### ICT Asian Range in a Bullish Market

First of all you should have a correct bullish bias of the market.

Mark the high and low of the Asian range and extend both lines forward.

In a bullish market you look for price to drop below the low of the Asian range to sweep the liquidity and trap sellers.

Once the Asian-low has been taken, you may take any of the decisions below.

**(I)** You can take a buy trade below the New York midnight open price, but do not buy before the Asian range low has been taken.

**(II)** You may buy when price reverses and surpasses the high of the Asian range, as that confirms the bullish price direction.

**(III)** If you cannot buy below the midnight open or you have missed the opportunity, then wait for price to return to the Asian range high in the New York open time.

You may wait for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") for confirmation of the trade.

![ICT Asian Range bullish setup — sweep below the Asian low followed by an MSS to the upside and a long entry below the New York midnight open](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-asian-range-in-bullish-market.png)

In this scenario your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the low of the Market Structure Shift.

For profit you may target the next [low resistance liquidity run](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-hrlr-lrlr/>).

title: ict-asian-range
section: ICT Asian Range in a Bearish Market
content:
#### ICT Asian Range in a Bearish Market

First of all, you should have a correct bearish bias of the market.

Mark the high and low of the Asian range and extend both lines forward.

In a bearish market you look for price to rise above the high of the Asian range to sweep the liquidity and trap buyers.

Once the Asian high has been taken, you may make any of the following decisions.

**(I)** You can take a sell trade above the New York midnight open price, but do not sell before the Asian range high has been taken.

**(II)** You may sell when price reverses and falls below the low of the Asian range, confirming the bearish price direction.

**(III)** If you cannot sell above the midnight open or you have missed the opportunity, then wait for price to return to the Asian range low during the New York open time.

![ICT Asian Range bearish setup — sweep above the Asian high followed by an MSS to the downside and a short entry above the New York midnight open](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-asian-range-in-bearish-market.png)

In this scenario your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the high of the Market Structure Shift.

For profit you may target the next low resistance liquidity run.

title: ict-asian-range
section: Step-by-Step Asian Range Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Asian Range Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run before and during every Asian range trade.

  1. **Set the daily bias.** Read the higher-timeframe bias on the daily and H4 — bullish, bearish or neutral.
  2. **Mark the Asian range.** 07:00 PM to 12:00 AM NY local time. Highlight the high and low and extend both forward.
  3. **Mark the New York midnight open.** The opening price at 12:00 AM NY local time becomes the reference for entry placement.
  4. **Wait for the sweep.** Price must take out the Asian high (bearish setup) or the Asian low (bullish setup). The sweep almost always happens during the London open or the early NY-AM session.
  5. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry trigger.
  6. **Wait for an MSS.** A Market Structure Shift confirms intent.
  7. **Enter on the retracement.** Into the order block, fair value gap or mean threshold left behind by the displacement.
  8. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips beyond the MSS swing.
  9. **Take profit at LRLR.** The first low-resistance liquidity pool in the trend direction.

title: ict-asian-range
section: Best Pairs and Markets for the Asian Range Strategy
content:
#### Best Pairs and Markets for the Asian Range Strategy

The Asian range works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to, but the cleanest setups print on a specific subset.

  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — the Asian range is tight on these pairs and the London open routinely sweeps it before delivering the directional move.
  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — the overnight session forms a clean range that the New York open frequently sweeps.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — Asian range setups print especially well around the London-NY session overlap.
  * **USD/JPY** and **AUD/USD** — Asian-session-active pairs that often build the range itself rather than just being swept by it.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the Asian range setup is most natural on NQ and ES futures (CME Group). The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) often delivers the second leg of the move after the Asian range sweep, making the two strategies complementary on the same trading day.

title: ict-asian-range
section: What Confirmation to Look for After the Asian Liquidity Sweep?
content:
#### What Confirmation to Look for After the Asian Liquidity Sweep?

Once price has swept the liquidity of the Asian range you may look for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") for the confirmation of price reversal before executing your trade.

The MSS is the single most important filter for this strategy. A wick that takes out the Asian high or low without a clean MSS afterwards is not yet a tradeable reversal.

title: ict-asian-range
section: Does Price Sweep Asian Liquidity Every Day?
content:
#### Does Price Sweep Asian Liquidity Every Day?

No, it is not necessary.

As traders we anticipate prices rather than guarantee them. Therefore it is crucial to look for a liquidity sweep first — and only if it occurs do you plan the trade accordingly.

On a Sunday Asian session, on a holiday week, or when high-impact news lands inside the London open, the Asian range may either fail to form a tight range or be cleanly bypassed without the textbook sweep. On those days, sit out and wait for the next session.

title: ict-asian-range
section: Common Mistakes When Trading the Asian Range
content:
#### Common Mistakes When Trading the Asian Range

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the Asian range setup.

  1. **Pre-positioning before the sweep.** The sweep is the trigger. Entries placed before the Asian high or low is taken almost always end with a stopped trade.
  2. **No higher-timeframe bias.** The Asian range is a continuation pattern in the direction of the daily bias. Without a clear bias, every sweep looks like a setup, and most are not.
  3. **Skipping the MSS.** A wick alone is not the trade. A close-back-inside followed by a Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe is the trigger.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked exactly at the MSS swing get hunted on the second test. The 10 to 20 pip buffer is non-negotiable.
  5. **Trading every Asian range.** Not every Sunday-to-Friday session produces a tradeable Asian range. If the range is too wide or the daily bias is unclear, sit out.
  6. **Wrong pair for the wrong session.** Trying to trade the Asian range on US-only instruments during the actual Asian session itself usually produces no tradeable setup. Wait for the London or NY-AM open before acting on the sweep.

title: ict-asian-range
section: FAQs about the ICT Asian Range
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Asian Range

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the Asian range.

**What is the ICT Asian range?**

The ICT Asian range is the range of the Asian session — the high and low formed between 07:00 PM and 12:00 AM New York local time. The range is used as a future liquidity target during the London and New York sessions.

**What is the Asian range time?**

07:00 PM to 12:00 AM New York local time. The reference clock is New York; ICT recommends following the NY local time regardless of where you live.

**Why do retail traders get trapped in the Asian range?**

The Asian range is tight, so breakout traders take positions in the direction of the breakout. The institutional algorithm typically sweeps the breakout liquidity and then reverses, leaving the retail breakout entries trapped.

**How do I confirm an Asian range trade?**

Wait for an ICT Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe after the sweep. The MSS is the confirmation that price has rejected the swept level.

**Where is the stop loss on an Asian range trade?**

10 to 20 pips beyond the swing of the Market Structure Shift — below the MSS low for buy trades and above the MSS high for sell trades.

**Where is the take profit on an Asian range trade?**

The next low-resistance liquidity run (LRLR) in the direction of the trade — typically the prior session high/low or the next external pool.

**Does the Asian range work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD form clean overnight ranges that the New York session frequently sweeps, making this strategy effective across forex, indices and metals.

**What is the difference between the Asian range and the Asian session?**

The Asian session is the broader trading window of Tokyo plus Sydney. The Asian range is the specific 07:00 PM to 12:00 AM NY local time block ICT uses as a sweep reference.

**Does daylight saving change the Asian range time?**

The Asian range is anchored to New York local time, so the GMT and London-time references shift by an hour twice a year, but the NY local time stays constant.

**Can beginners trade the Asian range?**

Yes — the strategy is mechanical: mark the high and low, wait for the sweep, wait for the MSS, take the entry. The biggest hurdle for beginners is the daily bias, which improves with practice on a demo account.

![ICT Balanced Price Range BPR diagram showing the overlap zone between two opposite fair value gaps](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ict-Balanced-Price-Rnage-BPR.png)

The ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR) is the high-precision area where two opposite fair value gaps overlap on the price chart. It is one of the most reliable PD Arrays in the ICT toolkit because the overlap stacks two independent imbalance zones at the same price — and price reacts sharply when it returns to that combined level.

Used correctly, the BPR is a cleaner entry zone than a single fair value gap. The overlap of a bullish FVG and a bearish FVG produces a tighter, more reactive zone, and the trade win rate is meaningfully higher than entries based on a lone FVG.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT Balanced Price Range — what it is, how to identify it, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the difference between BPR and a regular FVG, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

section: What is the ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)?
content:
#### What is the ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)?

The ICT Balanced Price Range is built on top of the [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap"). To work with the BPR you should already understand the FVG — three-candle imbalance, gap between candle 1 high and candle 3 low (or inverse for bearish), unfilled price range that price tends to return to and rebalance.

The BPR is the area on the price chart where two opposite fair value gaps overlap. A bullish FVG (formed on a buy-side displacement leg) and a bearish FVG (formed on a sell-side displacement leg) intersect at a single price band. That intersection is the Balanced Price Range.

The overlap matters because it represents a level where both buyers and sellers have left unfilled imbalance. When price returns, both sides have unfinished business — and the reaction is sharper than at a level with only one imbalance.

title: ict-balanced-price-range-bpr
section: How to Identify the ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)
content:
#### How to Identify the ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)

To identify a BPR on any chart, follow this process:

  1. Mark a fair value gap on the sell side of price (a bearish FVG).
  2. Mark a fair value gap on the buy side of price (a bullish FVG).
  3. Confirm the two FVGs are horizontally opposite — meaning they cover overlapping price ranges from opposite directions.
  4. Mark the area where both fair value gaps intersect. That intersection is the BPR.

![ICT Balanced Price Range identification example — bullish FVG and bearish FVG intersecting, BPR shaded in the overlap zone](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ICT-BPR.png)

The shaded overlap area between the two opposite FVGs is the BPR. That is the entry zone.

title: ict-balanced-price-range-bpr
section: Why the Balanced Price Range Matters
content:
#### Why the Balanced Price Range Matters

The BPR matters because of its sensitivity to price. When price approaches the BPR it tends to deliver a quick, sharp reaction — a strong rejection or continuation move within minutes of the tap.

The reason: it is the combination of two fair value gaps. Each FVG individually is a point of interest for institutional traders looking to fill unfilled imbalance. When both FVGs sit at the same price level, the BPR doubles up the institutional attention on that zone. Smart money is positioning at the same level from both directions, and the trade reaction reflects that.

title: ict-balanced-price-range-bpr
section: Step-by-Step BPR Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step BPR Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every BPR setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Set the daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). BPR trades work cleanest in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe PD Array** on the daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour chart — the level where the institutional move is expected to begin.
  3. **Wait for price to approach** the higher-timeframe PD Array. Do not pre-position.
  4. **Drop to the 5-minute or 3-minute chart** at the moment of the tap.
  5. **Watch for a Market Structure Shift** on the lower timeframe in the direction of the daily bias.
  6. **Identify the displacement leg’s fair value gap** on the lower timeframe. This is your first FVG.
  7. **Look for the opposing FVG** — a fair value gap that printed earlier in the opposite direction at the same price band. The overlap of these two FVGs is the BPR.
  8. **Mark the BPR zone** precisely. The intersection — not either FVG individually — is the entry zone.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the retest of the BPR, with stop loss beyond the recent swing extreme that preceded the structural shift.
  10. **Take profit** at the next higher-timeframe draw on liquidity in the trade direction.

#### Is the ICT Balanced Price Range Reliable for Trading?

The BPR is one of the most reliable entry zones in the ICT method when used correctly. The win rate on a strict execution of the BPR setup sits in the 60–70% range with a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-to-reward target — better than entries on a lone FVG because the overlap stacks two imbalance zones at the same price.

The reliability is conditional on three filters: alignment with the daily bias, the BPR sitting in the right zone (discount for bullish trades, premium for bearish trades), and a confirming Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe. Outside those conditions, the BPR’s edge degrades sharply.

Yes — the BPR is timeframe-agnostic. It works for scalping, day trading, and swing trading. The only thing that changes is the timeframe on which you mark the FVGs.

For scalping, look for the BPR on the 1-minute, 3-minute, or 5-minute chart. For day trading, the 15-minute and 5-minute. For swing trading, the 4-hour and 1-hour. The mechanics are identical at every timeframe — just scaled.

section: ICT BPR vs ICT FVG — How They Differ
content:
#### ICT BPR vs ICT FVG — How They Differ

The ICT Fair Value Gap is a 3-candle formation with a gap between candle 1’s high and candle 3’s low (or inverse for bearish). The FVG itself is used as an entry zone — price returns to fill the gap, and the trade fires at the tap.

The Balanced Price Range is also built on fair value gaps, but it is specifically the overlap of two opposite FVGs at the same price band. The BPR is a stricter, narrower entry than a lone FVG because both buy-side and sell-side imbalance must intersect.

In practice: a lone FVG gives multiple entry levels through the day. The BPR gives fewer setups, but the win rate on each is meaningfully higher.

title: ict-balanced-price-range-bpr
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the BPR
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the BPR

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed BPR trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Marking BPRs that are not real overlaps.** The two FVGs must intersect at the same price band — not just be in the same general area. A “near miss” is not a BPR. Be strict on the overlap requirement.
  2. **Using FVGs that are not opposite.** The BPR requires one bullish FVG and one bearish FVG at the same price. Two same-direction FVGs stacked are not a BPR — they are just a more emphatic FVG.
  3. **Trading BPRs against the daily bias.** Counter-bias BPRs fail far more often than aligned BPRs. Filter every setup through the daily bias before acting.
  4. **Stop loss too tight on the BPR.** Place the stop beyond the recent swing extreme that preceded the structural shift, with a small buffer. Stops one pip past the BPR get tagged routinely on the typical re-test spike.
  5. **Forcing the BPR in trending markets without a PD Array tap.** The BPR works best at higher-timeframe PD Array taps where institutional flow is concentrating. In open trending price without a key level nearby, the BPR is just two random FVG shapes overlapping.

#### FAQs About the ICT Balanced Price Range

**What is the ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)?**

The ICT BPR is the area where two opposite fair value gaps — one bullish and one bearish — overlap on the price chart. The intersection is a high-precision entry zone that produces sharper price reactions than a lone FVG.

**How do I identify a BPR?**

Mark a fair value gap on the buy side and a fair value gap on the sell side, confirm they cover overlapping price ranges from opposite directions, then shade the intersection. That overlap is the BPR.

**What is a bullish BPR?**

A bullish BPR sits on the buy side of price and is used for long entries. It forms inside a discount zone where a bullish FVG (created during a recent up leg) overlaps with an older bearish FVG. The trade is buy on the retest of the overlap.

**What is a bearish BPR?**

A bearish BPR sits on the sell side of price and is used for short entries. It forms inside a premium zone where a bearish FVG (created during a recent down leg) overlaps with an older bullish FVG. The trade is sell on the retest of the overlap.

**Where do I place stop loss on a BPR trade?**

Beyond the recent swing extreme that preceded the structural shift — below the swing low for bullish BPRs, above the swing high for bearish BPRs — with a small buffer. Stops one pip past the BPR get tagged on the typical re-test spike.

**What is the difference between a BPR and an FVG?**

An FVG is a single 3-candle imbalance pattern. A BPR is the intersection of two opposite FVGs at the same price band. The BPR is narrower, fires less often, but produces sharper reactions because both buy-side and sell-side imbalance overlap.

**Can the BPR be used for scalping?**

Yes. The BPR works on every timeframe — 1-minute, 3-minute, and 5-minute for scalping; 15-minute and 5-minute for day trading; 4-hour and 1-hour for swing trading. The mechanics are identical at every scale.

**What is the win rate on the BPR?**

On a strict execution with daily-bias alignment, premium/discount filtering, and lower-timeframe MSS confirmation, the win rate sits in the 60–70% range at a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-to-reward target. Outside those conditions, the win rate drops sharply.

**What instruments work best for the BPR?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) produce the cleanest BPR setups. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect the same overlap mechanics.

section: What is an ICT Bearish Order Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Bearish Order Block?

The ICT bearish order block is the zone on a price chart where a large number of sell orders are placed by smart money, and the market shows a sudden, strong move from that area.

Retail traders follow smart-money footprints, so they wait for these order-block zones to sell in the market and profit alongside the big institutions like banks.

A bearish order block is a bullish candle followed by a strong bearish engulfing candle.

![ICT Bearish Order Block diagram — last bullish candle followed by a strong bearish engulfing candle that breaks below the bullish candle's low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Bearish-Order-Block.png)

title: ict-bearish-order-block
section: How to Identify a Bearish Order Block
content:
#### How to Identify a Bearish Order Block

A bearish order block is the last bullish candle before the bearish impulse move. It typically consists of two candles — the first candlestick is bullish and the second candlestick is bearish.

To identify a valid bearish order block you need to check the following four conditions.

**(I)** The second candle (bearish) grabs the high of the previous bullish candle. Price should go above the high of the previous bullish candle.

**(II)** The second candle (bearish) closes below the low of the previous bullish candle.

**(III)** Imbalance on the lower timeframe inside the order-block zone.

**(IV)** Structure shift on the lower timeframe.

To sum it up: the second candle should completely engulf the first candle — body-to-body and wick-to-wick.

title: ict-bearish-order-block
section: How to Trade a Bearish Order Block
content:
#### How to Trade a Bearish Order Block

To initiate a trade based on a bearish order block, it is essential to first identify the prevailing market order flow or trend.

Bearish order blocks typically hold greater reliability within a bearish trend. During a bullish trend they might offer only a brief retracement.

It is advisable to execute trades on bearish order blocks within a bearish market structure.

Once the market trend is determined, the next step is to identify a valid bearish order block as outlined previously.

Upon identifying a bearish order block, it is important to wait for price to retest it.

When price approaches the bearish order block, consider executing a sell trade at around the 50% retracement level of the bearish order block.

For additional confirmation, look for signals such as the [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift"), especially on lower timeframes like 15-minute or 5-minute.

![ICT Bearish Order Block trade example on EUR/USD daily — market structure shifts to the sell side, bearish OB forms at the top, price retests the OB and the short entry delivers 1:4 RR](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-order-block-trading.png)

In the picture above you can see the EUR/USD daily timeframe chart.

In this picture the market has shifted its structure to the sell side, indicating bearish momentum.

After the market structure shift and the formation of a bearish order block at the top, price came back to retest the bearish order block.

When price approached the bearish order block, a sell trade was executed after the confirmation on the lower timeframe.

You can see the result — it delivered a 1:4 risk-to-reward ratio.

title: ict-bearish-order-block
section: Step-by-Step Bearish Order Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Bearish Order Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a bearish order block.

  1. **Confirm bearish trend.** Lower highs and lower lows on the daily and H4. The bearish OB works best in a bearish higher-timeframe context.
  2. **Spot the candle pair.** A bullish candle followed by a strong bearish candle that fully engulfs it body-to-body and wick-to-wick.
  3. **Verify the four conditions.** The bearish candle must (a) grab the high of the bullish candle, (b) close below its low, (c) leave an imbalance on the LTF, and (d) print a structure shift on the LTF.
  4. **Mark the order block zone.** The body of the bullish candle defines the zone.
  5. **Mark the next draw on liquidity.** Old low or relative equal low below the OB — this is the profit target.
  6. **Wait for the retest.** Price must come back to the bearish order block.
  7. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 15-minute or 5-minute for the entry trigger.
  8. **Wait for the LTF MSS.** A clean Market Structure Shift to the downside confirms intent at the OB retest.
  9. **Enter at the 50% mark.** Take the sell at the 50% retracement of the bearish order block.
  10. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips above the high of the order block.
  11. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** The level identified in step 5.

content:
#### Stop Loss and Take Profit

When executing a trade based on a bearish order block, consider placing your stop loss approximately 10 to 20 pips above the high of the order block.

For setting a take profit, you can aim for the next significant liquidity draw — typically a relative equal low or the prior session low.

A typical 1:2 to 1:4 reward-to-risk ratio is achievable on most bearish OB setups when the higher-timeframe trend is aligned.

The next bearish candle fully engulfed the bullish candle and closed well below its low — leaving a lower-timeframe imbalance and breaking the prior swing low.

title: ict-bearish-order-block
section: Common Mistakes Trading the Bearish Order Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the Bearish Order Block

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading bearish OB setups.

  1. **Trading bearish OB in a bullish trend.** The bearish OB is a continuation pattern. Against the higher-timeframe bias, it usually fails to hold and price runs through to the next liquidity level.
  2. **Skipping the engulfing rule.** The bearish candle must engulf the bullish candle body-to-body AND wick-to-wick. Partial engulfing is not a valid OB.
  3. **No LTF MSS at the retest.** The retest alone is not the entry. The lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift is the trigger.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked at the body high of the OB get hunted on the wick. The 10 to 20 pip buffer above the OB high is non-negotiable.
  5. **Trading every two-candle engulfing.** A bullish candle followed by a bearish engulfing in the middle of a range is rarely a valid OB. The setup requires a strong impulse move away from the OB and a lower-timeframe imbalance left behind.
  6. **Mistaking continuation for reversal.** A bearish OB inside an ongoing uptrend is liquidity for the algorithm — not a reversal signal. Price often takes out the OB high to continue up.

section: FAQs about the ICT Bearish Order Block
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Bearish Order Block

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the bearish order block.

**What is a bearish order block?**

A bearish order block is the last bullish candle before a strong bearish impulse move. It marks the zone where institutional sell orders were filled and acts as a high-probability sell zone on the retest.

**How do I identify a bearish order block?**

Look for a bullish candle immediately followed by a bearish candle that (a) grabs the high of the bullish candle, (b) closes below its low, (c) leaves a lower-timeframe imbalance, and (d) prints a lower-timeframe structure shift. The bearish candle must engulf the bullish candle body-to-body and wick-to-wick.

**Where do I enter a bearish order block trade?**

At the 50% retracement of the bearish order block on the retest, ideally with confirmation from a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift on the 15-minute or 5-minute chart.

**Where is the stop loss on a bearish order block trade?**

10 to 20 pips above the high of the bearish order block.

**Where is the take profit on a bearish order block trade?**

The next draw-on-liquidity in the trend direction — typically a relative equal low or the prior session low.

**Is the bearish order block reliable?**

Yes — but mostly in a bearish trend. In a bullish trend, a bearish OB often acts as liquidity for the algorithm rather than as a reversal trigger.

**Can I trade a bearish order block alone without other confluences?**

Yes — provided the OB sits in the OTE zone (0.62 to 0.79 retracement of the prior swing) inside a bearish trend and is confirmed by a lower-timeframe MSS at the retest.

**What is the difference between a bearish order block and a bullish order block?**

A bearish OB is the last up-close candle before a strong down-move (used as a sell zone). A bullish OB is the last down-close candle before a strong up-move (used as a buy zone). The two are mirror opposites — see the [ICT Bullish Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bullish-order-block/>) guide for the bullish variant.

**What is a valid bearish order block?**

A bearish order block is valid only when the bearish candle fully engulfs the prior bullish candle (body-to-body and wick-to-wick), leaves a lower-timeframe imbalance, and prints a lower-timeframe structure shift. Without all four conditions, the pattern is unreliable.

**What timeframe is best for the bearish order block?**

The 4-hour and daily produce the highest-conviction OBs. The 15-minute and 5-minute are used for the entry trigger (the LTF MSS) at the retest.

**Does the bearish order block work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES, XAU/USD and XAG/USD all produce textbook bearish OB setups, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

ICT Bread and Butter Buy-Setup is an intraday trading model designed to capture at least 30 to 50 pips per session. Built on the two IPDA price engines — Offset-Accumulation and Re-Accumulation — it produces 2 to 3 buy setups per day across the London, New York, London Close and Asia sessions.

This guide focuses specifically on the BUY side of the ICT Bread and Butter model. For the sell-side variant see my [ICT Bread and Butter](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bread-and-butter/>) overview guide.

In this guide I walk you through the buy-setup — the two engines (offset-accumulation, re-accumulation), the four session entries (London, NY, London Close, Asia), the realistic objectives, the risk-reward profile, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

section: What is ICT Bread and Butter Buy-Setup?
content:
#### What is ICT Bread and Butter Buy-Setup?

ICT Bread and Butter Buy-Setup is an intraday model that focuses on bullish days.

When the market is poised to go higher based on higher-timeframe institutional order flow, we expect the opening at or near the low of the daily range.

There can be a small decline below the opening price.

London open posts the initial leg higher intraday, then waits for the New York open.

New York open sees a continuation of higher prices to 10:00 AM New York time.

Typically between 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM New York time, expect the high of the day to form — and then normally price will retrace lower.

In this buy program, [IPDA](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-ipda/>) will perform one of two price-engine models.

**(I) Offset-Accumulation:** IPDA will reprice the market below an old low to promote the sell stops residing there for current long holders — and this action engineers the sellers at a deep discount.

This happens frequently in a bullish market when the higher-timeframe institutional order flow suggests higher prices.

You can see the picture below showing the idea of offset-accumulation.

![ICT Bread and Butter offset-accumulation example — IPDA reprices the market below an old low to engineer sell stops, then reverses with a strong bullish move for long entries](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ICT-Bread-and-butter-Offsetaccumulation.png)

**(II) Re-Accumulation:** IPDA will reprice the market lower to a fair-value price array to provide smart money a discount price for long entries.

The retracement lower in price places pain on current long holders and tends to induce selling — thus providing the sell-side liquidity to pair the smart money long entries with.

You can see the picture below showing the idea of re-accumulation.

![ICT Bread and Butter re-accumulation example — IPDA reprices the market lower to a fair value PD array, inducing sells before reversing higher for the buy entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ICT-Bread-and-butter-Reaccumulation.png)

section: ICT Bread and Butter — London Open Setup
content:
#### ICT Bread and Butter — London Open Setup

When the higher-timeframe institutional order flow is bullish, anticipate the London session low of the day formation.

The open at 0 GMT or 12:00 AM New York time can see a protraction phase lower in price — this can be scalped from the open or just above it prior to 10:00 AM New York time.

The classic London [Judas Swing](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-judas-swing-complete-guide/>) lower can be scalped easier.

The market retraces 05:00 AM to 07:00 AM New York time, and this can provide a long scalp entry — once a discount [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>) is hit.

When London open confirms institutional sponsorship on the long side and posts the daily low, expect to see the New York open continue higher — unless a higher-timeframe premium array has been hit intraday.

Look for the intraday swings higher to determine the [discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) range to go long at, in the [NY open killzone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-kill-zones/>).

Use 08:20 AM New York time (CME Chicago Mercantile Exchange) to anticipate the New York Judas Swing to fade.

Target is the next higher-timeframe premium array found on the 1-hour, 4-hour or daily chart.

section: ICT Bread and Butter — London Close Setup
content:
#### ICT Bread and Butter — London Close Setup

When the New York and London sessions have moved in tandem and the higher-timeframe PD array has been reached — and it is at least 10:30 AM New York time — expect a retracement off the day’s high between 10:30 AM and 01:00 PM.

Look for the 5-minute chart failure swing at the high and a bearish order block to execute the trade.

Risk only 10 pips above the day’s high and target 20 to 30% of the total daily range on the retracement lower.

Keep in mind this trade can be very difficult to see often, and the daily range can exceed the higher-timeframe PD array.

Always aim for the 15 to 20 pips in this trade, as the range can be limited because it is the Asian range formation.

Below you can see the example of the ICT Bread and Butter — Asia Open setup.

title: ict-bread-and-butter-buy-setup
section: Step-by-Step Bread and Butter Buy Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Bread and Butter Buy Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for any Bread and Butter buy setup, regardless of which session.

  1. **Confirm higher-timeframe bullish institutional order flow.** 1-day and 4-hour structure plus the higher-timeframe PD array.
  2. **Set your chart to New York local time.** Every session window in the model uses NY time.
  3. **Identify the active session.** London (00:00 NY) / NY (07:00 NY) / London Close (10:30 NY) / Asia (19:00 NY).
  4. **Mark the discount PD array for that session.** Discount FVG, order block or breaker below the opening price.
  5. **Wait for the IPDA price engine.** Offset-accumulation (sweep below an old low) or re-accumulation (retrace to the PD array).
  6. **Drop to the 5-minute for the trigger.** Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS at the discount level.
  7. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the post-MSS PD array, in the bullish direction.
  8. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept discount extreme, with a small buffer.
  9. **Take 15 to 30 pips on the position.** Maximum 50 pips. Trail the runner only if the higher-timeframe premium array is still distant.
  10. **Risk 0.5% to 1% per trade.** Multiple setups per day require strict per-trade risk.

title: ict-bread-and-butter-buy-setup
section: Best Pairs for ICT Bread and Butter Buy
content:
#### Best Pairs for ICT Bread and Butter Buy

The model works on every major instrument that respects the four session windows — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, USD/JPY plus metals.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the Bread and Butter framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for the New York setup because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: ict-bread-and-butter-buy-setup
section: Common Mistakes Around the Bread and Butter Buy
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the Bread and Butter Buy

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the Bread and Butter buy.

  1. **Wrong timezone.** Every session window is defined in New York local time. Using your broker’s server time or local time produces the wrong windows.
  2. **Trading without confirmed bullish bias.** The buy-setup requires higher-timeframe bullish order flow. Without it, every discount looks like a setup.
  3. **Skipping the 5-minute MSS.** The discount PD array is the zone — the entry trigger is the 5-minute MSS. Touching the discount alone is not an entry.
  4. **Ignoring the session boundaries.** A ‘London’ trade taken at 06:00 AM NY is past the window. Stick to the session start times.
  5. **Greedy targets.** 15 to 30 pips is the model target. Holding for 100 pips converts the scalp into a swing and breaks the model.
  6. **Trading the London Close every day.** The London Close setup is the hardest — only take it when both London and NY have moved in tandem AND a higher-timeframe PD array has been reached.

An intraday bearish model that captures 30 to 50 pips per session, powered by two IPDA price engines — offset-distribution and re-distribution — across the London, NY, London Close and Asia sessions.

**What is offset-distribution?**

IPDA reprices the market above an old high to trigger buy stops from short holders, drawing in buyers at a premium before reversing lower.

**What is re-distribution?**

IPDA reprices the market higher to a fair-value premium PD array to provide smart money discount-of-shorts prices — inducing buying that pairs with the smart-money short entry.

**How many setups per day?**

2 to 3 setups typically — one per session across London, New York, London Close and Asia.

**What is the realistic pip target?**

15 to 30 pips per trade, with a maximum of 50 pips. Trade duration typically 1 to 2 hours.

**What is the risk-reward ratio?**

Typically 1:1 — but can be better. Risk 0.5% to 1% per trade.

**What chart interval do I use?**

5-minute for the execution. 1-hour or 4-hour for the higher-timeframe PD array.

**When does the London Open setup trigger?**

A market retracement between 5:00 AM and 7:00 AM NY time after the London Judas Swing — that retracement into a premium PD array is the short scalp entry.

**When does the New York Open setup trigger?**

08:20 AM New York time (CME open) — anticipate the New York Judas Swing to fade, then enter short at the intraday premium.

**When does the London Close setup trigger?**

Between 10:30 AM and 01:00 PM NY time — but only after London and NY have moved in tandem AND a higher-timeframe discount array has been reached. This trade is not always easy to spot.

**When does the Asia Open setup trigger?**

At or just above the 0 GMT open (07:00 PM NY time) — expect a 15 to 20 pip decline as the Asian range forms.

**What is the difference between the sell-setup and the buy-setup?**

The sell-setup focuses on bearish institutional order flow days. The buy-setup is the mirror image — see my [ICT Bread and Butter Buy-Setup](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bread-and-butter-buy-setup/>) guide.

**Does the Bread and Butter sell-setup work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook Bread and Butter sell setups, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

# ICT Breakaway Gap — Bullish/Bearish Identification, Three Holding Mechanisms & Trade Setup

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breakaway-gap/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breakaway-gap/)

![ICT Breakaway Gap — fair value gap that remains unmitigated after a strong displacement, with breaker block, inverse FVG and balanced price range holding price away from the gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/WhatsApp-Image-2024-09-05-at-07.03.32.jpeg)

ICT Breakaway Gap is a simple yet a complex ICT concept — at its core it is a fair value gap that price never returns to mitigate, and identifying one early is the difference between catching a clean directional move and getting stuck waiting for a retrace that never arrives.

To get the most out of this guide you should already have a basic understanding of the [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>), the [ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>), the [ICT Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) and the [ICT Balanced Price Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>).

In this guide I walk you through the breakaway gap concept — the meaning, the bullish and bearish variants, the three reasons it forms, the early-identification hints, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: What is ICT Breakaway Gap?
content:
#### What is ICT Breakaway Gap?

ICT Breakaway Gap is basically a fair value gap formed after a strong price move that price does not return to — it is left unmitigated.

It is named breakaway gap because, after breaking a swing high or swing low, price simply moves away and does not retrace to mitigate the fair value gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: How to Identify an ICT Breakaway Gap
content:
#### How to Identify an ICT Breakaway Gap

Anyone can identify an ICT breakaway gap after price has already moved away from it — but the test of your skill is identifying it before price moves further.

First we will look at the formation of a breakaway gap, then we will go through the hints that can tell you earlier.

ICT Breakaway Gap has two main types based on the direction of the price move.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: (I) Bullish Breakaway Gap
content:
#### (I) Bullish Breakaway Gap

Bullish Breakaway Gap is basically a [BISI](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts/>) formed near a swing high after price broke that swing high with a strong upside move.

![Bullish ICT breakaway gap example — BISI formed near a swing high after upside displacement, with price moving away without rebalancing the BISI](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/bullish-ICT-Breakaway-gap.png)

Mostly we look for price to balance the BISI, but here we anticipate that price will not retrace to the BISI and will move away from it — that is what makes it the breakaway gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: Reasons of a Bullish Breakaway Gap
content:
#### Reasons of a Bullish Breakaway Gap

These are the reasons that indicate price will not be able to retrace down to the BISI.

**(I)[Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>):** the very first and most powerful reason for a breakaway gap.

A breaker block forms when price breaks a swing high moving to the upside, and when it retraces back the first hurdle it faces is the breaker block, which may refrain price from moving further down. When price does not retrace further down, the BISI remains unmitigated — a breakaway gap.

**(II)[Inverse Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>):** the second most powerful reason for a breakaway gap.

When price moves up breaking above a bearish fair value gap, that bearish FVG becomes a bullish inverse fair value gap. When price retraces back, the inversion fair value gap has the ability to hold price and not let it move further down, which makes the BISI unmitigated and creates the breakaway gap.

**(III)[Balanced Price Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>):** the third most powerful tool to indicate a breakaway gap.

When price moves up breaking a bearish fair value gap and also making a bullish fair value gap, the overlapping area between these two FVGs is the balanced price range. The BPR has the ability to hold price and not let it move further down, making the BISI a breakaway gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: (II) Bearish Breakaway Gap
content:
#### (II) Bearish Breakaway Gap

Bearish Breakaway Gap is basically a [SIBI](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts/>) formed near a swing low after price broke that swing low with a displacement to the downside.

![Bearish ICT breakaway gap example — SIBI formed near a swing low after downside displacement, with price moving away without rebalancing the SIBI](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/ICT-breakaway-gap.png)

Mostly we look for price to balance the SIBI, but here we anticipate that price will not retrace to the SIBI and will move away from it — that is what makes it the breakaway gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: Reasons of a Bearish Breakaway Gap
content:
#### Reasons of a Bearish Breakaway Gap

These are the reasons that indicate price will not be able to retrace up to the SIBI.

**(I)[Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>):** the very first and most powerful reason for a bearish breakaway gap.

A bearish breaker block forms when price breaks a swing low moving to the downside, and when it retraces back the first hurdle it faces is the breaker block, which may refrain price from moving further up. When price does not retrace further up, the SIBI remains unmitigated — a breakaway gap.

**(II)[Inverse Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>):** the second most powerful reason for a bearish breakaway gap.

When price moves down breaking below a bullish fair value gap, that bullish FVG becomes a bearish inverse fair value gap. When price retraces back, the inversion fair value gap has the ability to hold price and not let it move further up, which makes the SIBI unmitigated and creates the breakaway gap.

**(III)[Balanced Price Range](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>):** the third most powerful tool to indicate a bearish breakaway gap.

When price moves down breaking a bullish fair value gap and also making a bearish fair value gap, the overlapping area between these two FVGs is the balanced price range. The BPR has the ability to hold price and not let it move further up, making the SIBI a breakaway gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: What does a Breakaway Gap Tell?
content:
#### What does a Breakaway Gap Tell?

A breakaway gap confirms the price direction and the strength of the move — and it gives you confidence in your trade setup.

It tells you that the algorithmic delivery is committed to the new direction. The original FVG inside the leg is intentionally left unmitigated as evidence of momentum, and price is heading toward the next draw on liquidity rather than balancing back into the gap.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: Step-by-Step Trade Flow Around a Breakaway Gap
content:
#### Step-by-Step Trade Flow Around a Breakaway Gap

This is the exact sequence I run when I want to trade in the direction of a breakaway gap rather than fade into the unmitigated FVG.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — bullish, bearish or neutral structure.
  2. **Identify the displacement and the FVG it left behind.** Bullish — strong upside break of a swing high with a BISI inside the leg. Bearish — strong downside break of a swing low with a SIBI inside the leg.
  3. **Look for one of the three holding mechanisms.** Breaker block, inverse FVG, or balanced price range — between the FVG and the current price. If at least one is present, the FVG is a candidate breakaway gap.
  4. **Wait for price to test the holding mechanism (not the FVG).** Price retraces to the breaker / iFVG / BPR — not all the way back to the original FVG.
  5. **Wait for confirmation at the holding mechanism.** Lower-timeframe MSS, fair value gap or order block formed at the breaker, iFVG or BPR.
  6. **Enter on the retest in the direction of the original displacement.** Bullish — buy at the holding mechanism. Bearish — sell at the holding mechanism.
  7. **Set the stop.** Beyond the holding mechanism extreme, with a small buffer.
  8. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: Best Pairs for Breakaway Gap Trading
content:
#### Best Pairs for Breakaway Gap Trading

Breakaway gaps form on almost every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD. They are most reliable on instruments that produce clean displacement legs.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the breakaway gap framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for breakaway gaps because the displacement legs there are most concentrated.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: Common Mistakes Around the Breakaway Gap
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the Breakaway Gap

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using the breakaway gap concept.

  1. **Calling every unmitigated FVG a breakaway gap.** A breakaway gap requires displacement that broke a swing high or swing low PLUS a holding mechanism between the FVG and current price. Without both, the FVG may still be filled.
  2. **Waiting for the FVG to be mitigated when it has already broken away.** If a breaker block, inverse FVG or BPR is holding price, the FVG will not be filled. Trade the holding mechanism instead.
  3. **Confusing the breakaway gap with a regular FVG entry.** A regular FVG is the entry zone. A breakaway gap is the FVG you do NOT enter — you trade the holding mechanism in front of it.
  4. **No higher-timeframe directional context.** Breakaway gaps in a choppy higher timeframe are unreliable. The higher-timeframe bias has to support the displacement direction.
  5. **Tight stops at the holding mechanism boundary.** The stop must sit beyond the breaker / iFVG / BPR extreme, with a buffer — not at the boundary itself.
  6. **Trading every breaker as a breakaway gap setup.** Only the breaker that sits between the FVG and the current price counts. Random breakers elsewhere on the chart do not protect the FVG.

title: ict-breakaway-gap
section: FAQs about ICT Breakaway Gap
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Breakaway Gap

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the ICT Breakaway Gap.

**What is an ICT Breakaway Gap?**

An ICT Breakaway Gap is a fair value gap formed after a strong displacement that breaks a swing high or swing low, where price moves away without retracing to mitigate the gap. It is left unmitigated because a holding mechanism (breaker, inverse FVG, or BPR) prevents price from returning.

**What are the reasons a breakaway gap forms?**

The three main reasons are: (1) a Breaker Block holding price after the structural break, (2) an Inverse Fair Value Gap created by the displacement breaking through an opposite-direction FVG, and (3) a Balanced Price Range formed by overlapping bullish and bearish FVGs.

**What is the difference between a breakaway gap and a regular FVG?**

A regular FVG is a re-entry zone — price typically retraces to mitigate it. A breakaway gap is a special FVG that price does NOT mitigate because a holding mechanism in front of it prevents the retrace. The breakaway gap signals strong directional commitment.

**How do I identify a breakaway gap before price moves further?**

Look for the displacement leg that broke a swing high or swing low, then check whether a breaker block, inverse FVG, or balanced price range exists between the new FVG and the current price. If at least one is present, the FVG is a candidate breakaway gap.

**Where do I enter on a breakaway gap setup?**

You do not enter at the breakaway gap itself. Enter at the holding mechanism — the breaker block, inverse FVG, or BPR — when price retraces to it. Wait for lower-timeframe MSS or order block confirmation before entering.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the holding mechanism extreme — below the bullish breaker / iFVG / BPR low or above the bearish equivalent high, with a small buffer.

**What does a breakaway gap tell me about the trade?**

It confirms the direction and strength of the move. The unmitigated FVG is evidence that the algorithmic delivery is committed to the new direction and is targeting the next draw on liquidity rather than rebalancing the gap.

**Does the breakaway gap concept work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook breakaway gaps, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What timeframe is best for spotting breakaway gaps?**

15-minute and 1-hour for marking and execution. 1-day and 4-hour for the higher-timeframe directional context.

**Is a breakaway gap the same as a NWOG or NDOG?**

No. A [NWOG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-week-opening-gap-nwog/>) is the specific Sunday-open weekly gap and a [NDOG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-day-opening-gap-ndog/>) is the daily open gap. A breakaway gap is any FVG inside a leg that remains unmitigated due to a holding mechanism. Different concepts.

# ICT Breaker Block Trading — Failed Order Block Strategy (Free PDF)

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/)

![ICT Breaker Block diagram showing a failed order block flipping into support or resistance after liquidity sweep](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Supply-and-Demand-trading-strategy-1.png)

An ICT Breaker Block is a failed order block — an order block that price has broken through, which then flips and acts as support or resistance from the opposite side. It is one of three “block trio” PD Arrays in the ICT toolkit, alongside the Rejection Block and the Mitigation Block, and it serves a distinct role: it is the trigger for trend-reversal trades after a liquidity sweep.

The Breaker is what I look for when an old order block has been swept and price has shifted structure in the opposite direction. The broken OB becomes the new entry zone — same level, opposite side.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT Breaker Block — how to identify it, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the difference from a regular order block, the common mistakes, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

Table of Contents
