title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: What is the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy?
content:
#### What is the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy?

The ICT consolidation strategy helps you trade range-bound markets and maximise your gains.

It enables you to think ahead of retail traders — to anticipate what the retail traders are thinking and where their stop orders are resting.

Most retail traders wait for price breakouts from consolidation, or stick to the basics — selling near resistance and buying near support.

But smart money buys the retail trader’s sell-stops and sells the retail trader’s buy-stops.

You can see the example of a consolidated price range in the picture below.

![ICT consolidated price range example — horizontal range bounded by support and resistance with retail stop-loss clusters above and below](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Consolidated-price-range.png)

In ICT terminology this is the “Original Consolidation” — the range from which the next directional leg expands. It pairs naturally with the [ICT Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>) framework, where consolidation is the accumulation phase before the manipulation sweep and the distribution leg.

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: How to Trade the Sideways Market
content:
#### How to Trade the Sideways Market

To trade the sideways market you should have a potential bias for the day using the daily or 4-hour chart.

After confirming a directional bias for the day and identifying sideways market conditions, you wait for the [liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) in the opposite direction of the daily bias.

A liquidity sweep can be in the form of a false breakout or just a price wick outside of the consolidation targeting the stop orders of retail traders.

On the basis of your daily bias, the sideways market can be traded in two different ways.

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy in a Bullish Market
content:
#### ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy in a Bullish Market

If your daily and 4-hour timeframe bias is bullish and the market is sideways on a lower timeframe, look for the following.

A liquidity sweep below the support of the consolidation area, because the stop losses of retail traders who bought at support are resting below that level.

The liquidity sweep can be in the form of just a wick or a false breakout.

Retail traders will mark the price expansion to the downside as a breakout of the support level and start selling.

Smart money will fade this expansion by buying against the retail traders.

After the liquidity sweep, you can buy immediately below the support level — or look for a price reversal like an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on a lower timeframe like 5-minute or 1-minute.

Below you can see the example of the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy in a bullish market.

![ICT consolidation bullish setup — sweep below support, MSS on the lower timeframe and long entry from the consolidation low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ICT-consolidation-trading-startegy.png)

**But sometimes price may not sweep below the support of consolidation — instead it may directly shoot to the upside.**

In this scenario you have to mark the [consequent encroachment](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-consequent-encroachment/>) level of the consolidation and look for the relative equal lows below the CE level.

Wait for price to sweep these equal lows below the consequent encroachment level.

After the liquidity sweep of the relative equal lows, monitor price for the break of the resistance of consolidation.

When price closes above the resistance of consolidation, you can buy immediately or wait for price to test the consequent encroachment level again and initiate a buy position at the CE.

Below is the example explaining the ICT consolidation trading strategy in this alternative bullish scenario.

![ICT consolidation bullish alternative — sweep of relative equal lows below the CE level, breakout above resistance and long entry on the CE retest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/ICT-consolidation-trading.png)

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy in a Bearish Market
content:
#### ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy in a Bearish Market

When the daily and 4-hour timeframes indicate a bearish bias but the market moves sideways on a lower timeframe, watch for the following.

A liquidity sweep above the resistance zone of the consolidation, targeting stop-loss orders from retail traders who went short at the resistance.

This liquidity grab could appear as a sharp wick or a false breakout above the resistance level.

Retail traders might misinterpret this as a bullish breakout and start buying.

Meanwhile, smart money steps in, fading the upward move by selling.

After the liquidity sweep, you can either sell right above the resistance or wait for a lower-timeframe reversal signal — such as an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on the 5-minute or 1-minute chart.

See the illustration below for how the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy applies in a bearish scenario.

![ICT consolidation bearish setup — sweep above resistance, MSS on the lower timeframe and short entry from the consolidation high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/consolidation-trading-startegy.png)

**However, price might sometimes skip the liquidity sweep and drop directly from the consolidation.**

In this situation, identify the [consequent encroachment](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-consequent-encroachment/>) within the consolidation range and locate any relative equal highs near the CE level.

Wait for price to sweep these equal highs.

Once the liquidity sweep occurs, observe whether price breaks below the consolidation support.

You can either sell immediately after the support break or wait for a retest of the CE level to confirm your position.

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: Step-by-Step ICT Consolidation Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT Consolidation Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading sideways markets with the ICT framework.

  1. **Set the higher-timeframe bias.** Daily and H4 — bullish or bearish. Neutral days should be skipped.
  2. **Identify the consolidation.** A clear horizontal range on the lower timeframe with defined support and resistance.
  3. **Mark the support, resistance and CE.** The high, the low, and the 50% midpoint (consequent encroachment) of the range.
  4. **Locate retail liquidity.** Stops above resistance (buy stops to fade) for bearish bias; stops below support (sell stops to fade) for bullish bias.
  5. **Wait for the sweep in the opposite direction of bias.** Bullish bias — sweep below support. Bearish bias — sweep above resistance.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry trigger.
  7. **Wait for the MSS.** A clean Market Structure Shift in the bias direction confirms the reversal at the swept level.
  8. **Enter the trade.** Buy on the bullish-bias setup; sell on the bearish-bias setup.
  9. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept extreme (with a small buffer).
  10. **Take profit at the opposite side of the range.** First target — then extend to the next external liquidity pool if the breakout follows through.
  11. **Alternate path: no sweep.** If price skips the sweep and breaks the range in the bias direction, mark the CE and wait for the retest. Enter at the CE retest after the breakout closes.

section: Best Markets for the ICT Consolidation Strategy
content:
#### Best Markets for the ICT Consolidation Strategy

The consolidation strategy works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to.

  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — clean lower-timeframe consolidations form daily during the New York lunch hour and the early NY-AM session.
  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — pre-London Asian-range consolidations are textbook setups for the bullish or bearish bias-aligned sweep.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — consolidations around US economic news (NFP, CPI, FOMC) deliver the largest sweep-and-reverse moves.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the ICT consolidation strategy fits naturally into NQ and ES intraday trading. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) often delivers the consolidation sweep on a lower timeframe — making this strategy especially time-efficient for US-based readers during the morning session.

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: Common Mistakes Around the ICT Consolidation Strategy
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the ICT Consolidation Strategy

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading consolidation setups.

  1. **Trading consolidation without a daily bias.** The strategy requires the daily and 4-hour bias to filter the trade direction. Without bias, both sweeps look like setups and most fail.
  2. **Following retail behaviour.** The strategy is designed to fade retail stops, not to join retail breakouts. Buying breakouts above resistance or selling breakouts below support is the wrong side of the trade.
  3. **No MSS confirmation.** The sweep alone is not the entry. The lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift is the trigger that filters out failed sweeps.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked exactly at the swept extreme often get hunted on the second test. Leave a small buffer beyond the wick.
  5. **Skipping the alternate (CE) path.** When price skips the sweep and breaks the range directly, the CE retest is the correct entry. Many traders abandon the strategy at this point and miss the move.
  6. **Trading every range.** Not every flat period is a tradeable consolidation. Only ranges with clear support, clear resistance and a definable CE are worth trading.

title: ict-consolidation-trading
section: FAQs about the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Consolidation Trading Strategy

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the consolidation strategy.

**What is ICT consolidation?**

ICT consolidation is the sideways or range-bound phase of price where the market compresses between a defined support and resistance. In ICT terminology it corresponds to the “Original Consolidation” that precedes the manipulation sweep and the directional expansion.

**How do I trade ICT consolidation?**

Set a daily and H4 directional bias. Mark the support, resistance and consequent encroachment of the range. Wait for a liquidity sweep in the opposite direction of the bias, confirm with a lower-timeframe MSS, then enter in the bias direction targeting the opposite side of the range.

**What is the consolidation expansion retracement reversal sequence?**

This is a 4-stage description of the ICT range-to-trend cycle. Consolidation is the range. Expansion is the directional move out of the range after the sweep. Retracement is the pull-back into the range or the consequent encroachment. Reversal is the return to the higher-timeframe bias direction after the retracement.

**What is the difference between consolidation and accumulation?**

In ICT terminology the two are closely related. Consolidation is the broad sideways pattern; accumulation is the specific Power-of-3 phase inside the consolidation where smart money builds the position before the sweep. Most consolidations contain an accumulation phase.

**Where do I enter a consolidation trade?**

After the liquidity sweep in the opposite direction of bias, drop to the 5-minute or 1-minute chart and enter on the MSS confirmation. Alternatively, on the no-sweep direct-breakout path, enter on the retest of the consequent encroachment after the range break.

**Where is the stop loss?**

Beyond the swept extreme with a small buffer (a few pips on forex, a few ticks on indices). On the CE-retest path, the stop sits beyond the broken range edge.

**Where is the take profit?**

The opposite side of the consolidation as the first target. Extended targets are the next external liquidity pool, the prior session high/low or the next higher-timeframe FVG.

**Does the consolidation strategy work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce clean consolidation-and-sweep patterns daily, especially around the lunch-hour compression and the morning pre-news consolidation.

**What happens if there is no liquidity sweep?**

Mark the consequent encroachment of the range and wait for relative equal levels above (or below) it to be swept. After the sweep, price often breaks the range directly. Enter on the CE retest after the breakout closes.

**Can I trade consolidation against the daily bias?**

Counter-trend consolidation trades have a much lower hit rate. The bias-aligned sweep-and-reverse setup is the standard high-probability application of the strategy.

**How do I identify the right timeframe for consolidation?**

Use the daily and H4 for the bias and to identify whether the broader market is trending or compressed. Use the 15-minute and 5-minute to find the actual consolidation range. Use the 1-minute to time the MSS entry trigger.

![ICT Daily Bias diagram showing bullish and bearish order flow patterns on the daily timeframe](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-daily-bias.png)

ICT daily bias is the assumed direction of the trading day — bullish or bearish — that anchors every intraday entry I take. Without a correct daily bias, the rest of the ICT method does not work. The daily bias is the input to every PD Array tap, every kill-zone setup, every Market Structure Shift trigger.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT daily bias — what it is, the three signals I use to identify it, how to read daily timeframe order flow, the bullish and bearish variants with chart examples, the step-by-step bias workflow I run before every session, the common mistakes that produce wrong bias calls, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: What is ICT Daily Bias?
content:
#### What is ICT Daily Bias?

ICT daily bias is the anticipated direction of price movement for a given trading day. To trade the ICT method consistently, I need to call this bias correctly — the rest of the model is built on top of it.

A bullish daily bias means I expect the day to deliver upside, so I look for buy entries at higher-timeframe PD Arrays. A bearish daily bias means I expect the day to deliver downside, so I look for sell entries. A neutral or unclear bias means I stay on the sidelines until the higher timeframe gives me a clean read.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: How to Identify ICT Daily Bias
content:
#### How to Identify ICT Daily Bias

To call the correct daily bias, I check three elements before the session opens.

**(I) Daily timeframe order flow.** This is the most important input. According to Michael Huddleston, banks and institutional traders use the daily chart to position their orders. The structure of the daily chart — higher highs and higher lows for bullish, lower highs and lower lows for bearish — gives the dominant directional read.

**(II) Any imbalance to rebalance.** Price moves for two reasons, and the first is to rebalance an imbalance. I scan the higher timeframes for unfilled fair value gaps, premium-discount imbalances, and weekly opening gaps. Price tends to revisit and rebalance these zones, which gives a directional signal.

**(III) Draw on liquidity.** The second reason price moves is to take liquidity. I identify the next significant draw on liquidity — old highs, old lows, equal-highs/equal-lows, session extremes — because price gravitates toward those pools. The direction of the next major draw on liquidity is often the direction of the day.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: How to Identify Daily Timeframe Order Flow
content:
#### How to Identify Daily Timeframe Order Flow

Order flow is the current structure of price movement on the daily chart.

**Bullish order flow** means price is expected to move higher. The structure prints higher highs and higher lows. Price moves up to take liquidity above old highs or to rebalance an imbalance. In a bullish market, I look for buy entries and my daily bias points higher.

![Bullish daily order flow example — daily chart printing higher highs and higher lows with bullish bias](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BULLISH-ORDERFLOW.png)

**Bearish order flow** means price is expected to move lower. The structure prints lower lows and lower highs. Price moves down to take liquidity below old lows or to rebalance an imbalance. In a bearish market, I look for sell entries and my daily bias points lower.

![Bearish daily order flow example — daily chart printing lower lows and lower highs with bearish bias](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BEARISH-ORDER-FLOW.png)

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: Step-by-Step Daily Bias Workflow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Daily Bias Workflow

This is the exact sequence I run before every trading session to set the bias. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Open the daily chart** at least 30 minutes before the London or New York session.
  2. **Read the daily order flow** — is the chart printing higher highs and higher lows (bullish), or lower lows and lower highs (bearish)?
  3. **Identify any unfilled imbalance** on the daily — fair value gaps or weekly opening gaps that price has not yet rebalanced.
  4. **Mark the next significant draw on liquidity** — the closest old high or old low above and below current price.
  5. **Check the previous day close** — close above midpoint of prior day’s range suggests bullish carry; close below suggests bearish carry.
  6. **Confirm with the 4-hour structure** — the 4-hour should not be in obvious conflict with the daily read.
  7. **Set the bias** as bullish or bearish based on the alignment of the three primary signals (order flow, imbalance, draw on liquidity).
  8. **Skip the day** if the three signals point in three different directions. Unclear bias means no trade.

section: What is Bullish Bias in Forex?
content:
#### What is Bullish Bias in Forex?

Bullish bias in forex is the trader’s expectation that the next major move on a given currency pair, index, or instrument will be to the upside. The term is interchangeable with “bullish daily bias” when applied at the daily timeframe. A bullish bias is set by reading higher-timeframe order flow (higher highs and higher lows on the daily chart), spotting an unfilled imbalance above current price, or identifying the next major draw on liquidity sitting above. Bullish bias does not mean every candle moves up — it means the dominant move of the session is expected to be up.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: What is Bearish Bias in Forex?
content:
#### What is Bearish Bias in Forex?

Bearish bias in forex is the trader’s expectation that the next major move on a given instrument will be to the downside. Like its bullish counterpart, the term mirrors “bearish daily bias” when applied at the daily timeframe. A bearish bias is set by reading lower lows and lower highs on the daily chart, spotting an unfilled imbalance below current price, or identifying the next major draw on liquidity sitting below. Bearish bias does not predict every minute of the session — it sets the directional anchor for where the dominant institutional flow expects to deliver price.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: Bias vs Trend — What is the Difference?
content:
#### Bias vs Trend — What is the Difference?

Bias and trend are related but distinct. Trend is what price has already done — visible higher highs and higher lows for an uptrend, lower lows and lower highs for a downtrend. Bias is what price is expected to do next, given the trend, the imbalances, and the next draw on liquidity. A market can be in a clear uptrend with a temporary bearish bias for a single session if the next draw on liquidity sits below current price. The bias is the directional read for the immediate session; the trend is the structural read across many sessions. Both feed each other, but they are not the same thing.

title: ict-daily-bias-explained
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on Daily Bias
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on Daily Bias

Five mistakes account for the majority of wrong-direction trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the bias call gets dramatically more reliable.

  1. **Reading bias from a lower timeframe.** The daily bias must come from the daily chart. Reading bias off the 1-hour or 15-minute is the most common error and produces conflicting signals every time intraday volatility kicks in.
  2. **Ignoring the next draw on liquidity.** Order flow alone is not enough. Price often sweeps the closer liquidity pool first, then reverses to the dominant direction. The draw on liquidity tells you which side is the magnet.
  3. **Forcing a bias when the daily is unclear.** If the daily prints inside-bar consolidation or a balanced range, there is no clean bias. Sit out. There is no rule that says I must trade every session.
  4. **Switching bias mid-session.** Once the bias is set, it stays set for the day. Switching after the manipulation phase looks rational but is almost always the wrong call. Trust the morning read.
  5. **Confusing bias with direction of the current move.** Bias is the predicted direction for the day, not where price is right now. If price is moving up against a bearish bias, that is the manipulation phase — wait for the reversal.

content:
#### FAQs About ICT Daily Bias

**What is ICT daily bias?**

ICT daily bias is the anticipated direction of price for a given trading day — bullish or bearish — anchored on the daily timeframe. It is the input to every ICT entry trigger, kill-zone setup, and PD Array tap.

**How do I identify the correct daily bias?**

Cross-reference three signals on the daily chart: order flow direction, any unfilled imbalance to rebalance, and the next significant draw on liquidity. When all three align, the bias is reliable.

**What is bullish order flow?**

Bullish order flow is when the daily chart prints higher highs and higher lows. It signals the institutional direction is up, and I look for buy entries at higher-timeframe PD Arrays.

**What is bearish order flow?**

Bearish order flow is when the daily chart prints lower lows and lower highs. It signals the institutional direction is down, and I look for sell entries at higher-timeframe PD Arrays.

**What is a draw on liquidity?**

A draw on liquidity is the next significant pool of stop-loss orders sitting above or below current price — typically at old highs, old lows, equal highs, or equal lows. Price tends to gravitate toward these pools.

**Can the daily bias change during the session?**

Once set in the morning, the bias should remain fixed for the session. Switching mid-session usually means reacting to the manipulation phase, which is the opposite of the real move. Trust the morning read.

**What timeframe should I use to set daily bias?**

The daily chart, validated against the 4-hour. Bias read from lower timeframes is unreliable because intraday noise drowns out the institutional structure.

**What if the daily bias is unclear?**

Sit out. If the three primary signals point in three different directions, or the daily prints inside-bar consolidation, there is no clean bias. Skip the session and wait for clarity.

content:
#### Step-by-Step Daily Bias Trick Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when applying the daily bias trick.

  1. **Open the 1-day chart.** Only the daily timeframe is needed for the bias read.
  2. **Identify the most recent daily MSS.** Bullish — price broke above a recent swing high. Bearish — price broke below a recent swing low.
  3. **Lock the bias direction.** Bullish MSS = bullish bias. Bearish MSS = bearish bias.
  4. **Mark the bias-aligned PD array.** Discount zone (bullish) or premium zone (bearish), using FVG, order block or OTE sweet spot.
  5. **Wait for price to retrace into the PD array.** While retracing, the daily structure must NOT flip to the opposite direction.
  6. **Drop to the confirmation timeframe.** 15-minute or 1-hour — not lower than 15 minutes.
  7. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS.** In the bias direction at the PD array.
  8. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the post-MSS PD array.
  9. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept PD-array extreme, with a small buffer.
  10. **Target the low-resistance liquidity run.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe FVG.
  11. **Continue trading the same bias until the daily structure flips.** One bias-aligned trade per day; new bias only after a fresh daily MSS in the opposite direction.

content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the Daily Bias Trick

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using the daily bias trick.

  1. **Flipping the bias on every intraday wick.** The bias is set by the DAILY MSS — not by the 15-minute. Intraday counter-moves do not invalidate the daily bias.
  2. **Using lower-than-15-minute confirmation.** The trick caps the confirmation timeframe at 15-minute. Lower than that produces too much noise.
  3. **Entering at the PD array without confirmation.** The PD array is the zone — the entry trigger is the lower-timeframe MSS. Touching the discount or premium alone is not a trigger.
  4. **Trading after a counter-direction daily MSS.** If the daily structure has flipped, the previous bias is invalid. Wait for the new MSS to confirm.
  5. **Skipping the structural protection rule.** While price retraces into the PD array, the daily structure must NOT flip. If it does, abandon the setup.
  6. **Trying to trade both directions on the same day.** The trick is a one-bias-per-day model. Once the daily MSS sets the bias, that is the only direction you trade.

title: ict-daily-bias-trick
section: FAQs about the ICT Daily Bias Trick
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Daily Bias Trick

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the daily bias trick.

**What is the ICT daily bias trick?**

A simplified single-timeframe method for determining the daily bias — read the most recent daily MSS, and that direction is your bias for the trading session.

**What timeframe do I use for the trick?**

Only the 1-day chart for the bias. 15-minute or 1-hour for the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation — never lower than 15-minute.

**How do I find the bullish daily bias?**

If price has shifted its structure to the buy-side on the daily chart (most recent MSS up), the bias is bullish. Then find the discount zone or OTE and wait for a 15-minute MSS to the up-side as the entry trigger.

**How do I find the bearish daily bias?**

If price has shifted its structure to the sell-side on the daily chart (most recent MSS down), the bias is bearish. Find the premium zone or OTE and wait for a 15-minute MSS to the down-side as the entry trigger.

**What is the OTE sweet spot?**

Optimal Trade Entry — the 62%–79% Fibonacci retracement zone of the most recent impulsive leg. It is one of the most refined entry zones inside the discount (bullish) or premium (bearish) area.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the swept PD-array extreme — below the discount low for buy trades, above the premium high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The low-resistance liquidity run — old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**How long does the bias stay valid?**

Until the daily structure flips. Continue trading the same bias-aligned direction until a fresh daily MSS prints in the opposite direction.

**What if the daily structure flips while I am in a trade?**

That is a strong signal to take partial profits or move the stop to breakeven. The bias has changed, and the next setup should align with the new direction.

**How is the trick different from the full daily bias framework?**

The trick uses only the daily MSS. The full framework adds the higher-timeframe PD array, the weekly profile, the IPDA range and the daily Power-of-3 template. The full framework has a higher win rate; the trick is faster.

**Does the daily bias trick work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook daily bias prints, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**Can I trade multiple times per day using the trick?**

Yes — but all trades on the same day must align with the daily bias. The trick does not flip direction intraday; it locks the bias from the daily MSS for the entire session.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: What is the ICT Displacement Move?
content:
## What is the ICT Displacement Move?

The word “displacement” means changing position from one place to another. ICT displacement means an energetic and quick price movement having strong momentum, which can be bullish or bearish.

The idea behind the displacement move is that whenever price moves quickly with strong momentum, it indicates the participation of Smart Money with large orders involved in that move. So the ICT displacement move helps you identify the direction of Smart Money.

Three structural traits separate a real displacement from random noise:

  * At least three consecutive same-direction candles with large bodies.
  * Small wicks or no wicks at all — the move is one-sided.
  * A fair value gap somewhere between those candles, confirming an unfilled imbalance.

If any one of those three is missing, you do not have a displacement — you have a fast move with no institutional commitment.

title: ict-displacement-move

content:
## Bullish ICT Displacement Move

A bullish ICT displacement move means a strong buy-side price movement which indicates bullish momentum.

To identify a bullish displacement move, look for at least 3 consecutive bullish candlesticks having large bodies and small wicks (or no wicks at all). It should be a clear price movement — there should not be much retracement in price between the candles. And a fair value gap between the candlesticks is the key for the confirmation of displacement.

![Bullish ICT Displacement Move example: three consecutive bullish candles with large bodies, minimal wicks, and a fair value gap inside](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bullish-ICT-displacement.png)

To trade a bullish displacement move:

  1. **First, look for a bullish market structure.**
  2. **If the market structure is bullish and price displaced from a higher-timeframe[PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array")**, identify the relevant [Premium Zone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/> "ICT Premium Zone") formed by the displacement leg.
  3. **When price retraces back and tests the premium zone** , look for bullish trade confirmations like an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift").
  4. **After confirmation** , execute a buy trade targeting the next draw on liquidity levels.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: Bearish ICT Displacement Move
content:
## Bearish ICT Displacement Move

A bearish ICT displacement move signifies a strong downward price movement, characterised by significant selling pressure.

To recognise a bearish ICT displacement move, observe at least three consecutive bearish candlesticks with substantial bodies and minimal or absent wicks. Additionally, the movement should exhibit clear directional momentum with limited price retracement. Confirmation of displacement is supported by a noticeable fair value gap between candlesticks.

![Bearish ICT Displacement Move example: three consecutive bearish candles with large bodies, minimal wicks, and a fair value gap inside](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-ICT-displacement.png)

To trade a bearish displacement move:

  1. **First, look for a bearish market structure.**
  2. **If the market structure is bearish and price displaced from a higher-timeframe PD Array** , identify the relevant [Discount Zone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/> "ICT Discount Zone") formed by the displacement leg.
  3. **When price retraces back and tests the discount zone** , look for bearish trade confirmations like an ICT Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe.
  4. **After confirmation** , execute a sell trade targeting the next draw on liquidity levels.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest displacement entries print when the displacement leg leaves a clean fair value gap inside a higher-timeframe PD Array. Price returning to that FVG offers a tight, well-defined entry — the FVG is the level, the displacement is the proof Smart Money has moved that direction. Skip displacements that close far from any PD Array — without a confluence level to defend the move, you have momentum but no edge.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does displacement in price indicate?

A displacement in price indicates the entry of a big player with large orders in the market. People also call them Smart Money, because they have enough capital to move the markets.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: Does ICT displacement occur on every timeframe?
content:
### Does ICT displacement occur on every timeframe?

Yes. ICT displacement can be seen on any timeframe ranging from minutes to weeks. But every timeframe has its own pace — shorter timeframes may deliver a small move of 20 to 30 pips while bigger timeframes can deliver a move of 50 to 100 pips.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: Does price continue its move in the direction of displacement after retracement?
content:
### Does price continue its move in the direction of displacement after retracement?

No. It is not necessary. The direction of price movement after a displacement depends on the overall market structure. If the displacement move is just a retracement of a larger trend, then price may not continue in the direction of the displacement — it can break the high or low of the displacement instead.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: What is the difference between a displacement and a regular price move?
content:
### What is the difference between a displacement and a regular price move?

A regular price move can be made up of any candles in any sequence. A displacement requires three structural traits at once: at least three consecutive same-direction large-body candles, minimal wicks, and a fair value gap between the candles. Without all three, it is a regular move and not a displacement.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: How is the fair value gap inside a displacement used?
content:
### How is the fair value gap inside a displacement used?

The fair value gap inside the displacement is the institutional level. After the displacement leg ends, price often retraces back to fill that FVG before continuing in the displacement direction. Traders use the FVG as the entry point with a stop loss beyond the far side of the gap.

title: ict-displacement-move
section: Can I trade displacement on its own without other ICT confirmations?
content:
### Can I trade displacement on its own without other ICT confirmations?

No. Displacement signals direction and Smart Money participation, but you still need a Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe and a price retest of the displacement-leg PD Array (Premium or Discount Zone) before entering. Displacement on its own is signal, not setup.

# ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap Projection and Protraction

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-enigma-fair-value-gap/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-enigma-fair-value-gap/)

![ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap diagram showing the origin candle, the volume imbalance, and the projected reaction zones drawn ahead of price](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ict-enigma.png)

The ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap Projection model is one of the most advanced concepts introduced by Inner Circle Trader. Unlike the traditional [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>) strategy, where you wait for an imbalance to form before trading it, the Enigma model tries to project the future institutional reaction zones before price ever gets there.

That is the whole appeal. Instead of reacting after the move has already happened, you anticipate where smart money is likely to become active and have your levels drawn in advance.

There is one honest caveat worth stating up front. ICT explained the ideas of Projection and Protraction publicly, but he never released a complete mechanical model with exact entry, stop loss and take profit rules. So this guide combines his public teaching with proven ICT execution concepts to turn it into a practical, repeatable framework you can actually trade.

Table of Contents

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: What is the ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap?
content:
#### What is the ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap?

A traditional Fair Value Gap is an imbalance created when a strong displacement candle leaves an inefficient area between three consecutive candles. The Enigma Fair Value Gap takes that idea one step further. Instead of waiting for the gap to form and then trading its retracement, the Enigma model projects where future institutional delivery is expected to occur.

The key difference is what it measures. Rather than the wick to wick gap, the Enigma model focuses on the volume imbalance between the first candle and the displacement candle. Specifically, the imbalance between:

  * The **close of candle 1**
  * The **open of candle 2**

That area is the true institutional inefficiency created when aggressive buying or selling entered the market. Because the imbalance originates from candle 2, ICT calls candle 2 the origin candle of the Enigma model. An example is shown below:

![ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap example marking the volume imbalance between the close of candle 1 and the open of candle 2, the origin candle](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ICT-Enigma-FVG.png)

**Why candle 2 is so important**

Candle 2 serves three purposes:

  * It identifies the beginning of institutional [displacement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/>)
  * It defines the volume imbalance used in the Enigma calculation
  * It becomes the anchor point for the Projection and the Protraction

Without a valid displacement candle, there is no Enigma setup.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Bullish Enigma Fair Value Gap
content:
#### Bullish Enigma Fair Value Gap

A bullish Enigma FVG should have the following characteristics:

  * A strong bullish displacement candle (candle 2)
  * A visible volume imbalance between the close of candle 1 and the open of candle 2
  * A traditional bullish Fair Value Gap formed by the three candle sequence
  * A clear [break in market structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) or strong directional expansion

The volume imbalance inside candle 2 becomes the measurement used to project future institutional buying zones. An example is shown below:

![Bullish ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap example, a strong bullish displacement candle with a volume imbalance and a bullish FVG](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/BULLISH-ENIGMA-FVG.png)

content:
#### Bearish Enigma Fair Value Gap

A bearish Enigma FVG follows the opposite logic. It should include:

  * A strong bearish displacement candle (candle 2)
  * A volume imbalance between the close of candle 1 and the open of candle 2
  * A bearish Fair Value Gap created by the three candle sequence
  * Strong bearish displacement showing institutional selling

The volume imbalance created by candle 2 becomes the origin for projecting future bearish reaction zones. An example is shown below:

![Bearish ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap example, a strong bearish displacement candle with a volume imbalance and a bearish FVG](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/BEARISH-ENIGMA-FVG.png)

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: ICT Enigma Projection
content:
#### ICT Enigma Projection

Projection measures the entire displacement leg that begins with the displacement candle (candle 2). The purpose is to estimate how far institutional price delivery may extend from the origin of the displacement.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: How to Draw the Bullish Projection
content:
#### How to Draw the Bullish Projection

**Step 1: Identify the displacement candle**

Locate a strong bullish displacement candle (candle 2). A valid displacement candle should:

  * Have a large bullish body
  * Create a Fair Value Gap
  * Create a volume imbalance
  * Show aggressive institutional buying

This candle becomes the origin of the projection.

**Step 2: Select the Fibonacci retracement tool**

Set up the Fibonacci retracement tool with the coordinates 0.00, 1.00 and 1.25. The Enigma model uses the Fibonacci differently from a traditional retracement. Instead of measuring an entire market swing, it measures the displacement leg that starts from candle 2.

**Step 3: Draw the projection**

For a bullish Enigma projection, draw the Fibonacci from the open of candle 2 to the low of candle 3, which is the point where the initial displacement leg completes. This measures the full displacement generated by the origin candle. The projected Fibonacci levels then extend beyond the displacement and estimate the future institutional reaction zones.

**Step 4: Read the projection levels**

The most important projected level is the 1.25 Fibonacci level. ICT refers to this area as the Low Hanging Fruit, representing the first anticipated institutional reaction. Higher projected levels create the Extreme Projection, defining the outer boundary of the expected reaction zone. Do not treat these levels as exact reversal prices. Read them as high probability points of interest where you begin looking for confirmation. A bullish Enigma projection example is shown below:

![Bullish ICT Enigma projection example, Fibonacci drawn from the open of candle 2 to the low of candle 3 with the 1.25 Low Hanging Fruit level projected ahead](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/bullish-enigma-projection.png)

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Bearish Enigma Projection
content:
#### Bearish Enigma Projection

The bearish model follows the exact opposite procedure. Draw the Fibonacci from the open of candle 2 to the high of candle 3, using the same 0.00, 1.00 and 1.25 coordinates. This measures the bearish displacement leg, and the 1.25 Fibonacci level represents the projected reaction price. A bearish Enigma projection example is shown below:

![Bearish ICT Enigma projection example, Fibonacci drawn from the open of candle 2 to the high of candle 3 with the 1.25 level projected below price](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/bearish-enigma-projection.png)

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: ICT Enigma Protraction
content:
#### ICT Enigma Protraction

While Projection measures the displacement, Protraction measures the complete institutional imbalance. Instead of beginning at the open of candle 2, Protraction begins at the close of candle 1, which is the start of the volume imbalance. This creates a wider institutional measurement by combining both the volume imbalance and the displacement.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: How to Draw the Bullish Protraction
content:
#### How to Draw the Bullish Protraction

Draw the Fibonacci retracement tool from the close of candle 1 to the low of candle 3 of the Fair Value Gap, using the coordinates 0.00, 1.00 and 1.25. This measurement includes:

  * The volume imbalance
  * The complete displacement leg

After drawing the measurement, extend the Fibonacci levels into future price action. These protracted levels stay on the chart until price eventually revisits them. A bullish Enigma protraction example is shown below:

![Bullish ICT Enigma protraction example, Fibonacci drawn from the close of candle 1 to the low of candle 3 combining the volume imbalance and the displacement](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Bullish-enigma-protraction.png)

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Bearish Enigma Protraction
content:
#### Bearish Enigma Protraction

For the bearish version, draw the Fibonacci from the close of candle 1 to the high of candle 3. This measures the complete bearish volume imbalance together with the displacement. The 1.25 Fibonacci level is then extended into future candles until price revisits the reaction zone. A bearish Enigma protraction example is shown below:

![Bearish ICT Enigma protraction example, Fibonacci drawn from the close of candle 1 to the high of candle 3 with the 1.25 level projected into future candles](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/bearish-enigma-protraction.png)

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: How to Trade the Enigma Projection
content:
#### How to Trade the Enigma Projection

The Projection and Protraction levels are not immediate entry signals. They identify the areas where institutional activity is likely to occur. When price revisits a projected reaction zone, you wait for confirmation before entering. Never enter on the level alone.

**Bullish confirmation**

At a bullish reaction zone, look for:

  * A sell side [liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>) sweep
  * A bullish [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>)
  * Strong bullish displacement
  * A newly formed bullish Fair Value Gap
  * Extra confluence such as an [IFVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>), [SMT divergence](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-smt-divergence-smart-money-technique/>), or a BPR

Enter on the first retracement into the newly formed bullish Fair Value Gap after confirmation. Place the stop loss below the liquidity sweep or the projected reaction zone. Target internal liquidity first, then external buy side liquidity.

**Bearish confirmation**

At a bearish reaction zone, look for:

  * A buy side liquidity sweep
  * A bearish Market Structure Shift (MSS)
  * Strong bearish displacement
  * A newly formed bearish Fair Value Gap
  * Extra confluence such as an IFVG, SMT divergence, or a BPR

Enter on the first retracement into the newly formed bearish Fair Value Gap after confirmation. Place the stop loss above the liquidity sweep or the projected reaction zone. Target internal liquidity first, then external sell side liquidity.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make with the Enigma Model
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make with the Enigma Model

The Enigma model is powerful but easy to misuse. These are the errors that ruin it most often.

  1. **Anchoring from the wrong candle.** Projection starts from the open of candle 2, and Protraction starts from the close of candle 1. Mixing the two anchors gives you the wrong levels every time. Know which one you are drawing before you start.
  2. **Trading the 1.25 level as an exact reversal.** The projected levels are points of interest, not automatic entries. Price can push past the Low Hanging Fruit into the Extreme Projection. Always wait for confirmation at the zone.
  3. **Skipping the displacement requirement.** No strong displacement candle means no valid origin candle, which means no Enigma setup. A weak, overlapping candle does not qualify no matter how clean the Fibonacci looks.
  4. **Entering without a lower timeframe confirmation.** The reaction zone only tells you where to look. The trade is triggered by a liquidity sweep, an MSS, and a fresh Fair Value Gap, not by price simply tagging the level.
  5. **Forcing the model on a quiet market.** The Enigma projection works best after genuine institutional displacement. In slow, ranging conditions the projected levels rarely deliver, so stand aside until real displacement appears.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Final Thoughts
content:
#### Final Thoughts

The Enigma Fair Value Gap is an anticipation tool. Where most traders react to an imbalance after it forms, the Projection and Protraction let you map the likely institutional reaction zones in advance and then wait patiently for price to come to you. Keep the honest caveat in mind. This is a framework built on top of ICT’s public teaching, not a fixed mechanical system he published, so treat the projected levels as points of interest and let confirmation do the final work. For the building blocks, revisit the [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>), [displacement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/>), and [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) guides.

title: ict-enigma-fair-value-gap
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
#### Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the ICT Enigma Fair Value Gap?**

It is an advanced ICT concept that projects future institutional reaction zones ahead of price. Instead of trading a Fair Value Gap after it forms, the Enigma model measures the volume imbalance around the displacement candle and projects where smart money is likely to become active next.

**What is the difference between Projection and Protraction?**

Projection measures only the displacement leg and starts from the open of candle 2. Protraction measures the complete institutional imbalance and starts from the close of candle 1, so it includes both the volume imbalance and the displacement. Protraction produces the wider measurement.

**What Fibonacci settings does the Enigma model use?**

Use the retracement tool with the coordinates 0.00, 1.00 and 1.25. The 1.25 level is the key projected reaction area, which ICT calls the Low Hanging Fruit. Levels beyond it form the Extreme Projection.

**What is the Low Hanging Fruit level?**

The 1.25 Fibonacci projection is the Low Hanging Fruit, the first anticipated institutional reaction zone. It is a high probability point of interest, not a guaranteed reversal, so you still wait for confirmation before entering.

**How do I enter a trade using the Enigma projection?**

Wait for price to revisit the projected zone, then look for a liquidity sweep, a Market Structure Shift, strong displacement, and a newly formed Fair Value Gap. Enter on the first retracement into that fresh FVG, with the stop beyond the sweep and targets at internal then external liquidity.

**Is the Enigma model an official ICT strategy?**

The Projection and Protraction concepts come from ICT’s public teaching, but he never released a complete mechanical model with fixed entry, stop and target rules. The execution framework in this guide combines those concepts with broader ICT principles to make the idea tradable.

In this guide I will walk you through the exact ICT Fibonacci settings I use on TradingView — the retracement levels, the OTE entry zone, the standard-deviation profit projections and how to apply the tool in both bullish and bearish setups.

Fibonacci is a tool used to measure retracements in price. It helps traders trade the continuation of a trend after a retracement and it sits at the heart of the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) pattern.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: What are ICT Fibonacci Levels?
content:
#### What are ICT Fibonacci Levels?

ICT Fib Levels are the customised Fibonacci retracement and extension settings used personally by [Michael Huddleston](<https://innercircletrader.net/opinion/who-is-inner-circle-trader-ict/> "Michael Huddleston") AKA [Inner Circle Trader (ICT)](<https://innercircletrader.net/opinion/who-is-inner-circle-trader-ict/> "Inner Circle Trader \(ICT\)").

Fibonacci levels are a crucial part of the [ICT Trading Strategy](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022/> "ICT Trading Strategy") including the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/> "ICT Optimal Trade Entry – OTE Pattern") and they pair directly with the [ICT Premium & Discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) framework.

So you need to set up your Fibonacci tool according to the ICT specification before you can trade his strategy.

The standard ICT Fibonacci retracement set replaces the default tool levels with the values below.

1| Start  
---|---  
0.5| Equillibrium  
0.62| 62% Retracement  
0.705| OTE 70.5  
0.79| 79% Retracement  
0| Profit Scale

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: ICT Fib Settings on TradingView (Step-by-Step)
content:
#### ICT Fib Settings on TradingView (Step-by-Step)

This is exactly how I configure the Fibonacci retracement tool on TradingView so the OTE zone, equilibrium and the standard-deviation extensions render correctly.

  1. Open the Fibonacci retracement tool on the left toolbar (or press **Alt+F**).
  2. Right-click the tool and choose **Settings**.
  3. Under the **Coefficients** tab, remove every default level except **0** and **1**.
  4. Add the ICT retracement levels: **0.5** , **0.62** , **0.705** and **0.79**. The 0.705 level is the centre of the OTE zone.
  5. Add the ICT standard-deviation extensions for profit targets: **-0.27** , **-0.62** , **-1.0** , **-2.0** , **-2.5** and **-4.0**.
  6. Tick **Show prices** and **Levels line** so the price labels print on every level.
  7. Save the configuration as a template named _“ICT Fib”_ so you can reapply it on every chart.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: How to Use ICT Fibonacci Levels in a Bullish Market
content:
#### How to Use ICT Fibonacci Levels in a Bullish Market

In a bullish market price makes higher highs and higher lows. Before making a new high price retraces down and then continues its bullish trend.

When price retraces back you use the ICT fib levels to identify Premium and Discount, and the entry comes from the discount area using the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/> "ICT Optimal Trade Entry – OTE Pattern").

**(I)** Identify a [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/uncategorized/ict-swing-high-explained/> "Swing High") and the most recent [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "Swing Low").

**(II)** Draw the Fibonacci tool from swing low to swing high as shown in the picture below.

**(III)** Wait for price to retrace back to the 70.5% OTE level.

![ICT Fibonacci settings on TradingView showing 0.5, 0.62, 0.705 \(OTE\) and 0.79 retracement levels in a bullish setup](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-fib-settings.png)

**(IV)** Look for bullish evidence such as an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") on lower timeframes at the OTE level.

**(V)** After confirmation you can execute a buy trade at the OTE level with stop loss below the swing low. For profit targets you use the ICT fib extensions on the negative side of the tool (standard deviation projections).

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: How to Use ICT Fibonacci Levels in a Bearish Market
content:
#### How to Use ICT Fibonacci Levels in a Bearish Market

In a bearish market price makes lower highs and lower lows. Before making a new low price retraces up and then continues its bearish trend.

When price retraces back you use the ICT fib levels to identify the Premium zone and you enter from the premium using the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) Pattern](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/> "ICT Optimal Trade Entry – OTE Pattern").

**(I)** Identify a [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/uncategorized/ict-swing-high-explained/> "Swing High") and the most recent [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "Swing Low").

**(II)** Draw the Fibonacci tool from swing high to swing low as shown in the picture below.

**(III)** Wait for price to retrace back to the 70.5% OTE level.

![ICT Fibonacci settings on TradingView showing the 0.705 OTE level on a bearish retracement back into the premium zone](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-fib-levels.png)

**(IV)** Look for bearish evidence such as an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") on lower timeframes at the OTE level.

**(V)** After confirmation you can execute a sell trade at the OTE level with stop loss above the swing high. For profit targets you use the ICT fib extensions on the negative side of the tool.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: Ideal Fibonacci Retracement Levels for Trade Entry
content:
#### Ideal Fibonacci Retracement Levels for Trade Entry

According to Michael Huddleston the ideal fibonacci entry zone in a bullish trend sits below the 50% retracement — specifically at the 62%, 70.5% and 79% levels.

In a bearish trend the ideal fibonacci entry levels sit above the 50% line, which is called the [ICT Premium Zone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/> "ICT Premium Zone").

So price is expected to bounce back from these fib levels and traders anticipate the entry here with confluence from a fair value gap, an order block or a liquidity sweep.

The 70.5% level is the central OTE level and is the most commonly cited entry on the ICT model.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: ICT Standard Deviation Fib Settings (Profit Targets)
content:
#### ICT Standard Deviation Fib Settings (Profit Targets)

The negative side of the Fibonacci tool — the **standard deviation** projection — is how I set my profit targets. ICT teaches a specific extension set that aligns with how the algorithm delivers price after a clean displacement.

The canonical ICT standard-deviation projections are:

  * **-0.27** — short-term internal target, often the first liquidity pool above/below the swing.
  * **-0.62** — measured-move continuation; useful trail point.
  * **-1.0** — symmetrical projection, typical “1× the leg” target.
  * **-2.0** — full standard deviation expansion; often coincides with prior session highs/lows.
  * **-2.5** — extended target on strong trend days.
  * **-4.0** — maximum projection used in weekly bias trades and during high-impact news drives.

These are the targets I work down through, taking partials at -1.0 and trailing the rest toward -2.0 and beyond when the higher-timeframe draw on liquidity supports it.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: Where to Set Stop Loss while Using ICT Fib Levels for Trade Entry
content:
#### Where to Set Stop Loss while Using ICT Fib Levels for Trade Entry

While using ICT fib levels to execute a trade, your stop loss should sit 10 to 20 pips below the 1.0 (100%) fibonacci level for a buy trade.

For a sell trade your stop loss should sit 10 to 20 pips above the 1.0 (100%) level of fibonacci.

On indices like NQ and ES the equivalent buffer is roughly 5 to 10 ticks beyond the 1.0 level. On gold (XAU/USD) I leave 50 to 100 cents of buffer beyond the 1.0 level.

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: Best Pairs for ICT Fibonacci Levels
content:
#### Best Pairs for ICT Fibonacci Levels

The ICT fib settings work on every instrument that the ICT methodology is applied to — major forex pairs, indices and metals.

I personally use them most on GBP/USD, EUR/USD, NQ (NASDAQ futures), ES (S&P 500 futures) and XAU/USD because these instruments deliver clean impulse legs that retrace cleanly into the OTE zone.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the ICT fib settings are particularly useful on NQ and ES futures (CME Group). The standard-deviation projections (-1.0 to -4.0) align well with the algorithmic delivery seen during the 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>).

title: ict-fibonacci-levels
section: Common Mistakes When Using ICT Fibonacci Levels
content:
#### Common Mistakes When Using ICT Fibonacci Levels

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first adopt the ICT fib settings.

  1. **Drawing from the wrong swing.** The Fibonacci must be drawn on the most recent valid impulse leg — not from a random high to a random low. The leg has to start with a clear sweep of liquidity or an MSS.
  2. **Entering at every retracement.** Not every retracement reaches the OTE zone. If price stalls before 62%, the move is weak and the setup is invalid — wait for the next leg.
  3. **Ignoring confluence.** The 70.5% level is meaningful only when paired with a fair value gap, an order block or relative equal liquidity inside the OTE zone. The level alone is not the trade.
  4. **Stop loss too tight.** Stops parked exactly at the 1.0 level get hunted on the wick. The 10 to 20 pip buffer below/above the 1.0 line is non-negotiable.
  5. **Confusing retracement direction.** In a bullish setup you draw from swing low to swing high. In a bearish setup you draw from swing high to swing low. Reversing the direction inverts the entire OTE zone.
  6. **No extension targets.** Many traders set up the retracement levels but skip the standard-deviation extensions. Without -1.0, -2.0 and -2.5 mapped, partials and trailing become guesswork.

section: FAQs about ICT Fibonacci Settings
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Fibonacci Settings

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the ICT fib settings.

**What are the exact ICT Fibonacci settings?**

The retracement levels are 0, 0.5, 0.62, 0.705, 0.79 and 1.0. The standard-deviation extensions are -0.27, -0.62, -1.0, -2.0, -2.5 and -4.0.

**What is the OTE level on the ICT fib?**

The OTE (Optimal Trade Entry) level is 0.705, which is the central level of the ICT fib retracement set. The 62% and 79% levels bracket the OTE zone.

**How do I apply the ICT fib settings on TradingView?**

Open the Fibonacci retracement tool, go to its Settings, replace the default levels with the ICT retracement and extension values listed above, and save the configuration as a template.

**Can I use the ICT fib settings on stocks and indices?**

Yes — the settings are agnostic to the instrument. They apply equally to NQ, ES, forex majors and XAU/USD.

**What is the standard deviation in the ICT fib?**

The negative side of the fib tool is treated as standard-deviation projection. ICT uses -1.0, -2.0, -2.5 and -4.0 as the principal profit target levels.

**Why does ICT use 70.5% instead of the classic 78.6%?**

The 70.5% level is the centre of the OTE zone in ICT methodology. It typically sits inside a fair value gap or an order block on a clean retracement, which is why it is used as the primary entry trigger.

**Where should the stop loss go?**

Place the stop 10 to 20 pips beyond the 1.0 level — below it for a buy trade, above it for a sell trade.

**Can I trade only with ICT fib levels?**

The fib levels work best with confluence — a fair value gap, an order block or liquidity inside the OTE zone. The 70.5% level on its own is not a complete setup.

**How do I read the negative levels?**

The negative levels are profit projections. -1.0 equals one full standard deviation beyond the swing. -2.0 is two standard deviations, and so on.

**Which timeframe is best for ICT fib levels?**

The 15-minute timeframe is ideal for drawing the impulse leg and the 5-minute, 3-minute or 1-minute timeframe is used to time the entry inside the OTE zone.

# ICT HRLR & LRLR — High vs Low Resistance Liquidity Run Explained + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-hrlr-lrlr/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-hrlr-lrlr/)

![ICT HRLR vs LRLR — high resistance vs low resistance liquidity runs illustrated on bullish and bearish trends](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-HRLR-LRLR.png)

LRLR (Low Resistance Liquidity Run) and HRLR (High Resistance Liquidity Run) are two ICT classifications of how easily price can reach a pool of liquidity. LRLR liquidity runs through quickly with little resistance — HRLR liquidity has multiple short-term swings defending it and takes effort to reach.

This guide walks you through both — the meaning, the chart structure that creates each one, how to use them as profit targets, the link to fair value gaps and the bullish/bearish examples.

Before moving forward you should understand the meaning of liquidity itself.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: What is Liquidity in Trading?
content:
#### What is Liquidity in Trading?

The word [liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/> "Liquidity") means willing sellers and buyers of an asset at the current market price.

It is the degree to which an asset can easily be bought and sold in the market without affecting its price.

According to Michael Huddleston (ICT), liquidity in trading refers to the buy and sell orders in the market.

As a trader you should know where the high probability of liquidity is resting because price seeks liquidity. Old highs have buy stops resting above them, and old lows have sell stops resting below them.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: (I) What is High Resistance Liquidity Run (HRLR)?
content:
#### (I) What is High Resistance Liquidity Run (HRLR)?

An old high having so many swing highs defending it — and the old low having so many swing lows defending it — is termed as high resistance liquidity.

A high resistance liquidity run (HRLR) occurs when price struggles to sweep out liquidity and takes a long time to reach an old swing high or swing low.

This situation arises when a liquidity level is defended by multiple resistance levels like short-term highs and lows in the way.

![ICT HRLR — old high defended by multiple short-term swing highs creating high resistance liquidity that price struggles to reach](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-HRLR.png)

For example, if price is making higher highs and higher lows with a clear and strong uptrend after taking out sell-side liquidity, it would face difficulty dropping all the way down below the long-term low (or the long-term high in a bearish scenario) due to multiple resistance levels.

This resistance can often prevent price from reaching those stops. Significant news days such as NFP, FOMC or CPI releases can drive price through these high resistance liquidity pools.

High Resistance Liquidity Runs are generally considered less favourable for trading because it becomes challenging for traders to reach their targeted liquidity levels.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: (II) What is Low Resistance Liquidity Run (LRLR)?
content:
#### (II) What is Low Resistance Liquidity Run (LRLR)?

The short-term swing highs and lows forming between an old high and an old low are termed as low resistance liquidity because these highs and lows are easy to sweep.

In contrast to a High Resistance Liquidity Run, a Low Resistance Liquidity Run occurs when there is aggressive acceleration in price movement, leaving behind liquidity voids or [fair value gaps (FVG)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>).

In this scenario, price moves quickly and easily through areas of liquidity due to the presence of fewer resistance points.

![ICT LRLR — short-term swing highs/lows form low resistance liquidity that price runs through quickly leaving fair value gaps behind](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-LRLR.png)

In a bearish trend price makes lower short-term lows, so it is easy for price to run below a recent short-term low to sweep out sell stops because it faces low resistance.

In a bullish trend price makes higher short-term highs, making it easier for price to run above a recent short-term high to sweep out buy stops due to the low resistance it encounters.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: HRLR vs LRLR — Side-by-Side Comparison
content:
#### HRLR vs LRLR — Side-by-Side Comparison

The two classifications are mirror opposites of each other. Use this side-by-side as a quick reference.

  * **LRLR** — short-term liquidity, few defenders, fast delivery, leaves FVGs behind, ideal profit-target zone for the next leg.
  * **HRLR** — long-term liquidity, multiple defenders, slow delivery, requires displacement from a high-impact news catalyst (NFP, FOMC, CPI), ambitious profit-target zone reserved for higher-conviction setups.

A practical rule I use: target LRLR for daily and intraday profit-taking; reserve HRLR as a stretch target only on news days or on multi-day swing trades.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: How to Utilise ICT HRLR and LRLR
content:
#### How to Utilise ICT HRLR and LRLR

HRLR and LRLR are utilised to set profit targets. As a trader I prefer simple, quick and effortless trade setups.

So Low Resistance Liquidity Runs (LRLR) are the most ideal, easiest conditions to trade — targeting low-resistance liquidity has a higher probability of success.

It is the easiest area to trade in price action. These trades feel simple, quick and effortless because it takes minimal effort for price to sweep those areas of liquidity.

If you want to target a high-resistance liquidity area like an old low or old high, then you should know it may take time and you may need a fundamental event like NFP or FOMC to align with your bias before the target can be achieved.

Also note that **institutional order flow** is important. If institutional order flow is bullish and price has created a long-term low, every swing high should be seen as a low-resistance liquidity run, while the long-term low is considered a high-resistance liquidity run.

In contrast, if institutional order flow is bearish and price has created a long-term high, every swing low should be viewed as a low-resistance liquidity run, and the long-term high as a high-resistance liquidity run.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: Step-by-Step Trade Flow Using HRLR and LRLR as Targets
content:
#### Step-by-Step Trade Flow Using HRLR and LRLR as Targets

This is the exact sequence I run when I am setting up a trade and using HRLR and LRLR as my profit targets.

  1. **Read the institutional order flow.** Daily and H4 — bullish, bearish or neutral.
  2. **Identify the long-term high and low.** The structural extremes that define the larger range — these become your HRLR.
  3. **Map the short-term swings.** Every short-term swing high (in a bullish IOF) and every short-term swing low (in a bearish IOF) becomes your LRLR.
  4. **Set the entry.** Use a standard ICT entry — order block, fair value gap or breaker block on a lower-timeframe MSS.
  5. **Set the first target as LRLR.** The closest unswept short-term swing — this is the high-probability take-profit.
  6. **Set the second target as HRLR (optional).** The long-term high or low — only used as a stretch target on news days or higher-conviction days.
  7. **Manage at first LRLR.** Move stop to break-even and trail the rest if you are still working a stretch HRLR target.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: Best Markets for HRLR / LRLR Targeting
content:
#### Best Markets for HRLR / LRLR Targeting

The HRLR/LRLR framework works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to.

  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — short-term LRLR pools form constantly during the New York AM session, making the framework very repeatable on indices.
  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — Asian range high/low typically becomes the first LRLR target during the London open.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — HRLR runs are most common around 08:30 AM ET news releases, when an NFP or CPI can drive price through long-term liquidity.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the LRLR concept maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group). Most NY-AM index setups deliver to LRLR targets without ever needing the news-day push that HRLR usually requires.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: Common Mistakes Around HRLR and LRLR
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around HRLR and LRLR

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using these concepts.

  1. **Targeting HRLR on a clean intraday setup.** A 5-minute trade rarely has the runway to reach a long-term high or low. Set the LRLR as the first target and let the trade prove itself before considering HRLR.
  2. **Treating every swing as LRLR.** Only swings in the direction of the institutional order flow qualify as LRLR. Counter-trend swings are HRLR.
  3. **Ignoring the FVG signature.** An LRLR run almost always leaves a fair value gap behind. If there is no FVG and no displacement, the move was probably already a sweep — not a run.
  4. **Forcing HRLR without a catalyst.** Targeting HRLR on a Tuesday with no scheduled news rarely fills. The framework explicitly calls out NFP, FOMC and CPI as the catalysts that drive HRLR delivery.
  5. **No stop management at LRLR.** The first LRLR target is where you move to break-even. Letting a winner reverse to a loss after reaching LRLR is a position-sizing mistake.
  6. **Confusing LRLR with a regular liquidity sweep.** A [liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) reverses after taking liquidity. An LRLR runs through and continues. The structure that follows is what tells the two apart.

title: ict-hrlr-lrlr
section: FAQs about ICT HRLR and LRLR
content:
#### FAQs about ICT HRLR and LRLR

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about HRLR and LRLR.

**What does LRLR mean in trading?**

LRLR stands for Low Resistance Liquidity Run. It is short-term liquidity (a swing high or swing low between an old high and an old low) that price can sweep through with very little resistance.

**What is the full form of LRL or LRLR?**

The full form of LRLR is Low Resistance Liquidity Run. Sometimes the term is shortened to LRL by readers, but the original ICT term uses the double-R for “Liquidity Run”.

**What does HRLR mean in trading?**

HRLR stands for High Resistance Liquidity Run. It is long-term liquidity (an old high or old low) that is defended by multiple short-term swings, making it slow and difficult for price to reach.

**What is the difference between HRLR and LRLR?**

LRLR is short-term, low-defence liquidity that price runs through quickly. HRLR is long-term, high-defence liquidity that takes time and usually a news catalyst (NFP, FOMC, CPI) to reach.

**How do I use HRLR and LRLR in trading?**

Use them as profit targets. LRLR is the first, high-probability target. HRLR is a stretch target reserved for higher-conviction days or news catalysts.

**Does LRLR leave a fair value gap?**

Yes — an LRLR run almost always leaves a fair value gap (FVG) behind because of the displacement. The presence of an FVG is a strong signature that the move was an LRLR rather than a stalled sweep.

**How does institutional order flow affect HRLR/LRLR?**

If institutional order flow is bullish, every swing high in the trend is an LRLR and the long-term low is an HRLR. If institutional order flow is bearish, every swing low is an LRLR and the long-term high is an HRLR.

**What news drives HRLR delivery?**

High-impact news such as NFP, FOMC and CPI typically provides the displacement needed to drive price through high-resistance liquidity pools.

**Is LRLR the same as a liquidity sweep?**

No. A [liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) takes liquidity and reverses. An LRLR takes liquidity and continues. Both can target the same level — the structure that follows determines the classification.

**Which timeframe should I use to identify HRLR and LRLR?**

Use the daily and H4 to identify the long-term high and low (HRLR). Use the 15-minute and 5-minute to identify short-term swings (LRLR). Always reference the higher-timeframe institutional order flow before classifying any level.
