The model works best on instruments that respond to high-impact economic events — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, USD/JPY plus the major US indices.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the One Shot One Kill framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. FOMC, NFP and CPI release windows are the highest-conviction volatility injections for this model.

title: ict-one-shot-one-kill
section: Common Mistakes Around One Shot One Kill
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around One Shot One Kill

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading One Shot One Kill.

  1. **Skipping the 20-week IPDA range.** The 20-week range is the dealing-range filter. Without it, every weekly setup looks the same.
  2. **Trading without a calendar event.** The volatility injection is the trigger. Setups without a high-impact event have a much lower hit rate.
  3. **Trading anchor points later in the week.** The anchor must form Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. Thursday and Friday anchors usually do not deliver the full 50–75 pips.
  4. **Skipping the 15-minute OTE.** The OTE is the entry refinement — entering on the touch of the PD array without OTE confirmation produces unnecessary stop-outs.
  5. **Not closing 80% at 50 pips.** The model is a fixed-target plan. Holding for 200 pips converts it into something else.
  6. **Trading outside the killzones.** The execution window is London open or New York open. Setups outside those windows lose the institutional volume.

title: ict-one-shot-one-kill
section: FAQs about ICT One Shot One Kill
content:
#### FAQs about ICT One Shot One Kill

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the One Shot One Kill model.

**Which day to expect for the trade setup formation?**

Expect an anchor point to form on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday in order to frame a trade setup.

**Is ICT One Shot One Kill a reliable trading model?**

Yes — it is one of the most reliable ICT models, especially suited for traders who cannot sit and watch the market daily. You mark the 20-week range and look for the setup in the first 3 days of the week.

**Can the profit target go beyond 75 pips?**

75 pips is just the recommended easily-achievable target. You can trail your trade up to 100 pips and beyond, or use [ICT Fibonacci Levels](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-fibonacci-levels/>) to set the profit target.

**What is the dealing range?**

The dealing range is the highest high and lowest low of the past 20 weeks on the weekly chart. It is the IPDA reference range that defines the institutional draw on liquidity.

**Which economic events count?**

FOMC, NFP, CPI, central bank rate decisions, and any tier-1 release that produces volatility injection. The model is built around these events as the catalyst.

**What is the weekly bias?**

The directional read of the weekly chart inside the 20-week dealing range — bullish if price is targeting the dealing-range high, bearish if it is targeting the low.

**How is One Shot One Kill different from the One Trade Setup for Life?**

The One Trade Setup is a daily intraday model based on five session ranges. One Shot One Kill is a weekly model based on the 20-week IPDA range and a single high-impact event-driven trade per week.

**What timeframes do I use?**

Weekly for the dealing range and bias. 4-hour for the PD array. 15-minute for the OTE and entry trigger.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the 15-minute OTE swing extreme, with a small buffer.

**What killzones do I trade?**

London open and New York open. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong execution slot.

**How do I manage the trade once entered?**

Place a limit order at 50 pips as the primary target. If the limit fills, close 80% of the position and trail the remaining 20% to 75+ pips.

**Does this model work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook One Shot One Kill setups, especially around FOMC and NFP windows.

section: What is Draw on Liquidity?
content:
#### What is Draw on Liquidity?

[Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>) means willing buyers and sellers at the current market price.

In trading terms, liquidity means the liquidation price of active traders — either sellers or buyers.

Draw on liquidity means hunting the liquidity of active traders — hitting their stop losses or activating their pending orders such as sell stops or buy stops.

Draw on liquidity is the sole purpose of price delivery.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: How to Trade Using ICT One Trade Setup for Life
content:
#### How to Trade Using ICT One Trade Setup for Life

To trade using the ICT One Trade Setup for Life, follow the steps below as told by ICT himself, and set your TradingView time window to New York local time.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: (I) PM Session Range
content:
#### (I) PM Session Range

PM session range is the previous day’s price delivery. For the PM session range, look at the 01:30 PM to 04:00 PM (New York local time) range.

Mark the highest high and lowest low of the PM session range. Above the highest high rests the buy-side liquidity; below the lowest low rests the sell-side liquidity.

If your [Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>) is bullish, anticipate price to run below the PM session range low to raid the sell-side liquidity and create an [ICT Judas Swing](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-judas-swing-complete-guide/>).

If you are bearish, look for price to run above the PM session high for the liquidity raid and the [ICT Judas Swing](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-judas-swing-complete-guide/>).

![PM session range example for ICT One Trade Setup — 1:30 PM to 4:00 PM NY range marked, with sell-side liquidity below the low and buy-side liquidity above the high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/PM-session-ranges.png)

After the liquidity raid, wait for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) in the direction of your daily bias. Then execute a trade at the retest in the direction of your daily bias.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: (II) London Session Raid
content:
#### (II) London Session Raid

If the PM session is not a factor or price is far away from the PM session range, look for the London session liquidity raid for trade execution.

Mark the London session range 02:00 AM to 05:00 AM — highest high and lowest low.

On the New York opening, if you are bullish, anticipate a run below the low of the London session range for the sell-side liquidity raid.

If your daily bias is bearish, anticipate a run above the high of the London session range for the buy-side liquidity hunt.

![London session range example — 2:00 AM to 5:00 AM NY range marked, with buy-side liquidity above the London high targeted by a bearish bias](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/london-session-raid.png)

The process after the liquidity hunt is the same for every session — look for a market structure shift in the direction of your daily bias and then execute a trade on the retracement.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: (III) Opening Range Gaps
content:
#### (III) Opening Range Gaps

The opening gap is the event that takes place when trading stops and the market reopens at 08:30 AM for forex and 09:30 AM (New York local time) for indices like Nasdaq and S&P500.

If your daily bias is bearish and price opens with a gap, wait until New York lunch hour — the algorithm engineers liquidity in the morning and during lunch hour at 01:30 PM NY local time.

After lunch hour, anticipate price to approach the opening gap and then sell off to take the liquidity engineered during the AM session and lunch hour.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: (IV) New York Lunch Raid
content:
#### (IV) New York Lunch Raid

If price has not done anything yet — no PM session raid, no London session raid, no opening gap range — look for the New York lunch raid.

Mark the New York lunch range (highest high and lowest low) from 12:00 PM to 01:30 PM (New York local time).

If you are bearish, look for the New York lunch range high to be raided for buy-side liquidity, and then a market structure shift to the downside to execute a sell trade.

![New York lunch raid example — 12:00 PM to 1:30 PM NY range marked, with the high being raided for buy-side liquidity before a bearish MSS confirms the sell entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/NY-Lunch-Riad.png)

If your daily bias is bullish, look for the New York lunch range low to be raided for sell-side liquidity, and then a market structure shift to the upside to execute a buy trade.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: (V) AM Session Liquidity Raid (Target)
content:
#### (V) AM Session Liquidity Raid (Target)

The previous day’s AM session (09:30 AM to Noon) liquidity is the target.

If you are bullish and have the trade setup, your final target is the previous day’s AM session high.

If you are bearish and have the trade opportunity, your final profit target is the previous day’s AM session low.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: Step-by-Step One Trade Setup Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step One Trade Setup Flow

This is the exact sequence I run every morning to find the One Trade Setup.

  1. **Set your chart to New York local time.** Every session range in the model is defined in NY time.
  2. **Set the daily bias.** 1-day and 4-hour structure plus the higher-timeframe PD array — bullish, bearish or neutral.
  3. **Mark the previous day’s AM session high and low.** 09:30 AM to Noon — this is the final target zone.
  4. **Mark the PM session range.** 01:30 PM to 04:00 PM of the previous day.
  5. **Mark the London session range.** 02:00 AM to 05:00 AM NY time of the current day.
  6. **Mark the NY lunch range.** 12:00 PM to 01:30 PM NY time once the period closes.
  7. **Identify the opening range gap.** Forex 08:30 AM, indices 09:30 AM — note the gap if present.
  8. **Wait for the first session raid against your bias.** Bullish bias — wait for a sell-side raid below one of the session lows. Bearish bias — wait for a buy-side raid above one of the session highs.
  9. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS.** 5-minute or 1-minute MSS in the direction of your daily bias after the liquidity raid.
  10. **Enter on the retest.** Take the trade in the bias direction at the post-MSS PD array.
  11. **Set the stop.** Beyond the swept session extreme, with a small buffer.
  12. **Take profit at the AM session target.** Bullish — previous AM session high. Bearish — previous AM session low. Use partial profits at the relative equal level along the way.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: Best Pairs for ICT One Trade Setup
content:
#### Best Pairs for ICT One Trade Setup

The One Trade Setup works on every major instrument that respects the New York session — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus indices and metals.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the One Trade Setup maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is the highest-conviction window for the entry trigger because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: ict-one-trade-setup-for-life
section: Common Mistakes Around the One Trade Setup
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the One Trade Setup

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the One Trade Setup.

  1. **Wrong timezone.** Every range is defined in New York local time. Using broker-server time or local time produces the wrong session ranges.
  2. **Trading the first raid that prints, regardless of bias.** The raid must align with your daily bias. A buy-side raid against a bullish bias is a stop hunt, not the setup trigger.
  3. **Skipping the MSS confirmation.** The session raid is the trigger zone — the entry is the post-raid lower-timeframe MSS. Do not enter on the touch of the session level alone.
  4. **Marking the lunch range too early.** The 12:00 PM to 01:30 PM range is only valid AFTER 01:30 PM. Marking it at 12:30 PM produces a half-formed range.
  5. **Targeting the same-day AM session.** The AM session target is the PREVIOUS day’s AM range, not today’s.
  6. **Trading every session raid every day.** The model is a “first opportunity wins” framework. Once one session triggers a clean trade, the rest of the day is monitoring — not new entries.

content:
#### FAQs about ICT One Trade Setup for Life

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the One Trade Setup.

**What is the ICT One Trade Setup for Life?**

A complete daily trading model based on five session-based liquidity raids — PM session, London session, opening range gap, NY lunch raid and the previous AM session as the target — anchored to the daily bias.

**What time zone do I use?**

New York local time. Every range in the model is defined in NY time.

**What is the PM session range?**

01:30 PM to 04:00 PM NY time of the previous day. Mark the highest high and lowest low — buy-side liquidity sits above the high, sell-side liquidity sits below the low.

**What is the London session range?**

02:00 AM to 05:00 AM NY time. Mark the highest high and lowest low for the New York open liquidity raid.

**What is the NY lunch range?**

12:00 PM to 01:30 PM NY time. Mark the highest high and lowest low. Used as the trigger range when no earlier session has produced a setup.

**What is the AM session target?**

The previous day’s 09:30 AM to Noon session high (bullish target) or low (bearish target). This is the final profit target of the model.

**How does the daily bias fit in?**

The daily bias decides which side of every session range you target. Bullish bias — sell-side raids below session lows. Bearish bias — buy-side raids above session highs.

**Where do I enter?**

After the session raid in the direction of your bias, wait for the lower-timeframe MSS, then enter on the retest of the post-MSS PD array. Not on the touch of the session level alone.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the swept session extreme, with a small buffer.

**What timeframe is best for the entry trigger?**

5-minute or 1-minute for the MSS. 15-minute for the post-MSS PD array.

**Does this setup work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all respect the same session ranges, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**Why is it called One Trade Setup for Life?**

Because the model repeats every day and covers every session — if you master it, you do not need a second strategy. It scales from scalping to day trading without changing the framework.

# Master ICT Optimal Trade Entry (OTE) — Fibonacci Setup with Examples + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/)

![ICT Optimal Trade Entry \(OTE\) diagram showing fibonacci retracement zone between high and low of dealing range](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-optimal-trade-entry-OTE.png)

ICT OTE — Optimal Trade Entry — is the fibonacci retracement zone between an established high and low from which I expect price to reverse. It is one of the cleanest entry tools in the ICT method because the risk at the OTE level is neither too small nor too large, and the risk-to-reward potential is consistently strong.

I use OTE for scalping, intraday trading, and swing trading alike. The same fibonacci levels work across timeframes — what changes is the size of the dealing range and the size of the move that follows.

This guide is the full breakdown of ICT OTE — what it is, the exact fibonacci levels Huddleston uses, how to identify the dealing range, how to trade it in bullish and bearish markets, the common mistakes I see, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern
section: What is ICT OTE?
content:
#### What is ICT OTE?

ICT OTE is a trading model built on the retracement of price inside a trending market. The fibonacci retracement levels defined by the Inner Circle Trader are the key to identifying the OTE zone — they are explained below.

When price moves in a trend — bullish or bearish — it does not travel in a straight line. It retraces, gathers liquidity, and continues. OTE is the framework I use to enter on those retracements with controlled risk.

OTE has two clean uses: **joining a continuation** at the retracement of an established trend, and **fading a reversal** at the tap of a higher-timeframe PD Array.

**ICT Fibonacci Levels for the OTE Setup**

To use the ICT optimal trade entry pattern, set your fibonacci retracement levels to the values Huddleston specifies, listed in the table below.

0| First Profit Scale  
---|---  
0.5| Equilibrium  
0.62| OTE level 1  
0.705| 0TE level 2  
0.79| Optimal Trade Entry  
1| 100% retracement level (Starting Position)  
-0.5| Target 1  
-1| Target 2  
-2| Symmetrical Price  
  
**How to Identify the OTE Zone**

To identify an OTE pattern, set the fibonacci retracement levels first.

If you are using TradingView, the levels look like this on the chart.

![TradingView fibonacci retracement settings for ICT OTE — 0.62, 0.705, and 0.79 levels marked as Optimal Trade Entry zone](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-OTE-Fib-levels.png)

Next, identify the established high and low to mark the **ICT Dealing Range** , as shown in the picture below.

![ICT dealing range illustration — high and low marked between fibonacci retracement zone for OTE setup](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-OTE-illustration.png)

Then apply the fibonacci retracement tool from the high to the low of the ICT dealing range.

The precise OTE level is **0.705**. Any value between **0.62 and 0.79** still sits inside the OTE range and is tradable.

title: ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern
section: Step-by-Step OTE Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step OTE Trade Flow

This is the ten-step checklist I run before every OTE trade. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Establish the daily bias** on the daily and 4-hour charts before the session opens.
  2. **Identify the dealing range** — the most recent established high and low on your trade timeframe.
  3. **Confirm the trend direction** matches the daily bias. Do not take counter-trend OTE without a higher-timeframe PD Array reason.
  4. **Apply the fibonacci retracement** from low to high (bullish) or high to low (bearish) of the dealing range.
  5. **Mark the OTE zone** — the area between 0.62 and 0.79, with 0.705 as the precise level.
  6. **Wait for price to retrace** into the OTE zone. Do not chase.
  7. **Watch for confirmation** at the OTE tap — price rejection, an ICT Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe, or a clean candle pin.
  8. **Execute the trade** at the OTE level after confirmation, with stop loss beyond the swept extreme of the dealing range.
  9. **Set the take profit** at the opposing extreme of the dealing range or the next significant liquidity pool.
  10. **Manage the trade** — trail the stop to break-even after the first 1:1 of risk-to-reward is captured.

content:
#### (II) ICT OTE in a Bearish Market

In a bearish market, price moves to the downside in a zigzag — declining, rallying briefly, and declining again.

After the OTE level is marked, wait for price to rally back and tap the OTE area.

When price approaches the OTE level, I either enter the sell trade immediately or wait for additional confirmation — a price rejection candle or an ICT Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe.

title: ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on OTE
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on OTE

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed OTE trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading OTE against the daily bias.** OTE is a continuation tool first. Counter-trend OTE without a higher-timeframe PD Array reason fails far more often than aligned OTE. Filter every setup through the daily bias.
  2. **Using the wrong dealing range.** The dealing range must use the most recent established high and low — not arbitrary swing points. A bad range produces OTE levels that price ignores.
  3. **Entering at 0.705 without confirmation.** The 0.705 level is the precise OTE, but price often wicks past it before reversing. Wait for a rejection candle or a lower-timeframe MSS at the OTE before pulling the trigger.
  4. **Stop loss inside the dealing range.** Place the stop beyond the extreme of the dealing range that the OTE is retracing from, with a small buffer. Stops inside the range get tagged routinely.
  5. **Ignoring the time of day.** OTE setups taken during low-volatility windows (Asia lunch, NY lunch) deliver weaker results. Pair OTE with kill-zone times for the cleanest entries.

title: ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern
section: Final Thoughts
content:
#### Final Thoughts

No strategy is foolproof, OTE included. Do not risk all your capital on a single setup, and always trade with a stop loss in place to keep your equity safe. The 0.705 level is the precise reference, but the real edge in OTE comes from combining it with the daily bias, a higher-timeframe PD Array, and confirmation on the lower timeframe.

section: FAQs About ICT OTE / Optimal Trade Entry
content:
#### FAQs About ICT OTE / Optimal Trade Entry

**What is OTE / Optimal Trade Entry in trading?**

ICT OTE stands for Optimal Trade Entry. It is the fibonacci retracement zone between an established high and low from which price is expected to reverse. The precise OTE level is 0.705, with the broader zone running from 0.62 to 0.79.

**Is ICT Optimal Trade Entry a reliable model?**

Yes. OTE is one of the most reliable models in the ICT toolkit because it is a trend-continuation method. As long as the trend is intact, OTE produces clean entries. The model loses reliability when traded against the higher-timeframe bias.

**Is ICT OTE a day-trading strategy?**

OTE is a flexible model. It works for day trading, swing trading, and scalping because the same fibonacci levels apply across timeframes. For swing setups, use the daily timeframe trend and OTE levels for entry. For intraday, use a 1-hour or 15-minute trend and OTE on the lower timeframe.

**Is there a specific time for the ICT OTE setup?**

There is no specific time of day for OTE itself. That said, kill-zone times deliver the cleanest setups because volatility is concentrated there. Look for OTE during the [ICT Kill Zone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-kill-zones/> "ICT Kill Zones") windows for the highest-probability entries.

**What is the precise OTE level?**

The precise ICT OTE level is 0.705 on the fibonacci retracement. Any value between 0.62 and 0.79 sits inside the broader OTE range and is tradable when paired with confirmation.

**Can OTE be used with other ICT concepts?**

Yes — OTE is at its strongest when combined with a higher-timeframe PD Array, the daily bias, and a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift or CISD as the entry trigger. The fibonacci zone identifies the price; the other tools confirm the timing.

# ICT Order Block Explained — Bullish & Bearish OB Setup with Examples + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/)

![ICT Order Block diagram showing the institutional order zone where a strong bullish or bearish move originates](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/order-block-trading-strategy.png)

The ICT Order Block is one of the most important PD Arrays in the entire ICT method. It is the area on the price chart where institutions executed a large block of orders before a strong impulse move — and that area becomes a magnet for price every time it returns. The Order Block is the foundation of dozens of other ICT setups, including the Breaker Block, the Mitigation Block, the Unicorn Model, and the entry leg of the Silver Bullet.

Used correctly, the Order Block tells me where institutional buyers or sellers are positioned. Retail traders follow the institutional footprint by waiting for price to retest these zones, then entering alongside the institutions instead of fighting them.

This guide is the foundational explainer for the ICT Order Block — what it is, how to identify it on any chart, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often. If you are new to Order Blocks, start here. For deeper coverage of either variant, see the dedicated [Bullish Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bullish-order-block/>) and [Bearish Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bearish-order-block/>) guides.

title: ict-order-block
section: What is an ICT Order Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Order Block?

An ICT Order Block is the price area where a large number of orders were executed by institutional traders before the market made a sudden, strong move away from that level. It is the visible footprint of institutional positioning on the chart.

The mechanic is simple: institutions cannot fill all of their large orders at one price — that would move the market against them. Instead, they accumulate gradually over a small price range. When their position is fully built, they push price out of that range with force, leaving a clear order block behind.

Retail traders watch for these zones because price tends to return to them. When price comes back to test an Order Block, the unfilled portion of the institutional order gets mitigated, and price reacts sharply — usually continuing in the original direction of the impulse move.

![ICT Order Block example chart showing a bullish OB at the bottom of an impulse move and a bearish OB at the top](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/ICT-Order-Block-1.png)

title: ict-order-block
section: Types of ICT Order Block
content:
#### Types of ICT Order Block

By market direction, the Order Block splits into two clean types — bullish and bearish — each with its own validation criteria and trading mechanics.

**(I) Bullish Order Block** — the last bearish candle before a strong bullish impulse move.

**(II) Bearish Order Block** — the last bullish candle before a strong bearish impulse move.

Both variants are 2-candle formations at minimum, with the first candle in the opposite direction of the move that follows.

title: ict-order-block
section: Bullish Order Block
content:
#### Bullish Order Block

A bullish Order Block is the last bearish candle before a bullish impulse move. It typically consists of two candles — the first being bearish (the OB itself) and the second being bullish (the impulse candle that engulfs the OB).

**How to Identify a Bullish Order Block**

To validate a bullish Order Block, four conditions must be true:

  1. The second candle (bullish) must grab the low of the previous bearish candle — price goes below the low of the bearish OB before reversing.
  2. The second candle must close above the high of the previous bearish candle — a clean engulf.
  3. An imbalance (fair value gap) prints on the lower timeframe inside or just above the Order Block zone.
  4. A market structure shift to the upside on the lower timeframe confirms the bullish intent.

In short: the second candle should completely engulf the first — body to body and wick to wick — and that engulf should occur at a place where the lower timeframe shows imbalance and structural shift.

![Bullish ICT Order Block example — last bearish candle before bullish impulse, with bullish engulfing candle taking out the OB low and closing above its high](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/bullish-order-block.png)

title: ict-order-block
section: Bearish Order Block
content:
#### Bearish Order Block

A bearish Order Block is the last bullish candle before a bearish impulse move. It typically consists of two candles — the first being bullish (the OB itself) and the second being bearish (the impulse candle that engulfs the OB).

**How to Identify a Bearish Order Block**

To validate a bearish Order Block, four conditions must be true:

  1. The second candle (bearish) must grab the high of the previous bullish candle — price goes above the high of the bullish OB before reversing.
  2. The second candle must close below the low of the previous bullish candle — a clean engulf to the downside.
  3. An imbalance (fair value gap) prints on the lower timeframe inside or just below the Order Block zone.
  4. An [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) to the downside on the lower timeframe confirms the bearish intent.

Same rule: the second candle completely engulfs the first — body to body and wick to wick — at a level showing lower-timeframe imbalance and structural shift.

![Bearish ICT Order Block example — last bullish candle before bearish impulse, with bearish engulfing candle taking out the OB high and closing below its low](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Bearish-Order-Block.png)

title: ict-order-block
section: Step-by-Step Order Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Order Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every Order Block setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Set the daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). Order Block trades work cleanest in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe[PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>)** on the daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour chart — the level where institutional positioning is expected.
  3. **Wait for price to approach** the higher-timeframe PD Array. Do not pre-position.
  4. **Drop to the 5-minute or 3-minute chart** at the moment of the tap.
  5. **Watch for the impulse move** in the direction of your bias — large bodies, short wicks, ideally a fair value gap left behind.
  6. **Identify the last opposing candle before the impulse** — the bearish candle before a bullish impulse, or the bullish candle before a bearish impulse. That candle is the Order Block.
  7. **Validate the four conditions** — engulf body and wick, lower-timeframe imbalance, market structure shift in the direction of the impulse.
  8. **Wait for the retest** back to the Order Block zone. Do not chase the impulse.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the OB tap, with stop loss 10–20 pips beyond the OB extreme — below the OB low for bullish, above the OB high for bearish.
  10. **Take profit** at the next significant draw on liquidity in the trade direction.

title: ict-order-block
section: Bullish Order Block Trading Strategy
content:
#### Bullish Order Block Trading Strategy

For a bullish Order Block trade, I look for the shift of price delivery from bearish to bullish. When the prevailing trend is bearish and price approaches a higher-timeframe demand zone (a discount PD Array), I drop to the lower timeframe and watch for the structure to shift to the upside.

The shift creates the impulse move. The last bearish candle before that impulse — the one that just got engulfed by the bullish push — is the bullish Order Block.

I wait for price to retrace back and tap the OB zone. The retest is the buy entry.

![Bullish Order Block trade strategy chart — discount PD Array tap, MSS to upside, bullish OB identified at start of impulse leg, retest as buy entry](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/bullish-order-block-trading-strategy.png)

Stop loss on a bullish Order Block trade sits 10–20 pips below the low of the Order Block zone. Take profit targets the next buy-side liquidity above — equal highs, the previous swing high, or the higher-timeframe premium PD Array.

The shift creates the impulse move. The last bullish candle before that impulse — the one that just got engulfed by the bearish push — is the bearish Order Block.

title: ict-order-block
section: Order Blocks in Trends — Continuation Setups
content:
#### Order Blocks in Trends — Continuation Setups

Order Blocks are not only reversal tools. They also form during trend continuation, and these continuation Order Blocks are some of the highest-probability entries in the ICT method.

In a bearish trend, after a bullish pullback, a bearish Order Block may print to confirm the strength of the dominant downtrend. I can use that OB to add a new sell order alongside the existing trend.

Likewise, in a bullish trend, after a bearish pullback, a bullish Order Block may print to confirm the strength of the dominant uptrend. That OB is a clean entry to add a new buy order in the trend’s direction.

The validation rules are identical to a reversal Order Block — engulf body and wick, lower-timeframe imbalance, MSS in the trend direction. What differs is the context: continuation OBs sit in the middle of an existing move, not at the higher-timeframe PD Array reversal point.

title: ict-order-block
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on Order Blocks
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on Order Blocks

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed Order Block trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Treating any opposing candle as an Order Block.** Not every bearish candle before a bullish move is a valid OB. The four conditions must be true — engulf body and wick, lower-timeframe imbalance, market structure shift, and clean impulse move. Without all four, it is just a candle.
  2. **Trading Order Blocks against the daily bias.** Counter-bias OBs fail far more often than aligned OBs. Filter every setup through the daily bias before acting.
  3. **Stop loss too tight on the OB extreme.** Place the stop 10–20 pips beyond the OB low (bullish) or OB high (bearish), with a small buffer. Stops one pip past the OB get tagged routinely on the typical re-test spike.
  4. **Missing the imbalance / FVG requirement.** An Order Block without an associated fair value gap on the lower timeframe is much weaker. The FVG confirms the impulse was strong enough to qualify the candle as a real OB.
  5. **Confusing an Order Block with a Breaker Block.** An OB is a fresh institutional level — price retraces and continues in the OB direction. A Breaker Block is a failed OB — price closed past it, swept liquidity, and now trades the opposite direction. Same level on the chart, opposite trade idea. See the [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) guide for the full distinction.

title: ict-order-block
section: FAQs About the ICT Order Block
content:
#### FAQs About the ICT Order Block

**What is an ICT Order Block?**

An ICT Order Block is the price area where institutional traders executed a large block of orders before a strong impulse move. The OB is the visible footprint of institutional positioning, and price tends to return to retest the level where unfilled orders mitigate.

**What is a bullish Order Block?**

A bullish Order Block is the last bearish candle before a bullish impulse move. It is validated when the next bullish candle takes out the OB low and closes above the OB high, with imbalance and structural shift on the lower timeframe.

**What is a bearish Order Block?**

A bearish Order Block is the last bullish candle before a bearish impulse move. It is validated when the next bearish candle takes out the OB high and closes below the OB low, with imbalance and structural shift on the lower timeframe.

**How do I identify a valid Order Block?**

Four conditions: the impulse candle engulfs the OB body and wick, the lower timeframe shows a fair value gap inside or adjacent to the OB zone, a Market Structure Shift confirms the impulse direction, and the move follows from a higher-timeframe PD Array tap.

**Where do I place stop loss on an Order Block trade?**

10–20 pips beyond the OB extreme — below the OB low for bullish trades, above the OB high for bearish trades. The buffer absorbs the typical re-test spike before the move resolves.

**What is the difference between an Order Block and a Breaker Block?**

An Order Block is a fresh institutional zone — price retraces to it and continues in the OB direction. A Breaker Block is a failed Order Block — price closed past the OB extreme, swept liquidity, and now trades in the opposite direction. Same level on the chart, opposite trade.

**Can Order Blocks be used in trending markets?**

Yes. Continuation Order Blocks form during trends — after a pullback, the OB at the start of the next leg confirms trend strength and gives a clean entry to add to the existing trend.

**What is the best timeframe for Order Blocks?**

Daily and 4-hour for the higher-timeframe Order Blocks that produce the biggest moves. 15-minute and 5-minute for entry-level Order Blocks inside a higher-timeframe PD Array tap. Use both — the higher TF for context, the lower TF for execution.

**What instruments work best for Order Blocks?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) produce the cleanest Order Blocks because the CME session structure delivers tight impulse moves. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect OB mechanics.

# ICT PD Array Matrix — Premium & Discount Trade Execution Framework + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/)

![ICT PD Array Matrix diagram showing premium and discount zones with the eight institutional trigger tools](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-PD-array-1.png)

The ICT PD Array stands for “Premium and Discount Arrangement” — the canonical framework Michael Huddleston taught for choosing where to enter a trade. The PD Array is not a single tool. It is a checklist of eight institutional trigger tools, each placed in either the premium zone (top half of a dealing range) or the discount zone (bottom half), used to identify the optimal price for buying and selling.

I use the PD Array on every trade I take. It is the input to the daily bias call, the input to every kill-zone setup, and the framework I use to decide whether a particular fair value gap, order block, or breaker is worth trading in the current context. Without the PD Array, every other ICT setup is just a chart pattern in isolation.

To find the PD Arrays on any chart, draw a fibonacci retracement from an established old high to an established old low — using the dealing range as the anchor. The 50% line splits the range into premium (top half) and discount (bottom half). The eight ICT trigger tools then arrange themselves in either zone based on direction, and the right tool in the right zone is the entry.

This guide is the canonical breakdown of the ICT PD Array Matrix — what it is, how to identify the premium and discount zones, the eight tools in each direction, the step-by-step trade flow, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: What is the ICT PD Array Matrix?
content:
#### What is the ICT PD Array Matrix?

The ICT PD Array Matrix is the arrangement of eight ICT trade-entry tools across the premium and discount zones of a dealing range. The matrix is a checklist — when price reaches a level inside the right zone where one of the eight tools fires, that confluence is the trade.

The logic is simple. As a seller, I always want to sell at a premium price. As a buyer, I always want to buy at a discounted price. The PD Array Matrix shows me where premium and discount sit on the chart, and which tool to use in each zone to time the entry precisely.

![ICT PD Arrays diagram showing the premium zone above 50% and the discount zone below 50% with the institutional tools arranged in each](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-PD-arrays.png)

**Elements of ICT PD Arrays**

The PD Array contains the following eight ICT trigger tools — each one a complete model in its own right:

  1. [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>) (FVG)
  2. [ICT Inverse Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>) (IFVG)
  3. [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>)
  4. [ICT Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>)
  5. [ICT Mitigation Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-mitigation-block-explained/>)
  6. [ICT Unicorn Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-unicorn-model/>)
  7. ICT NWOG (New Week Opening Gap)
  8. ICT NDOG (New Day Opening Gap)

When more than one of these tools sits at the same price level in the correct zone, the confluence is meaningfully stronger than any single tool alone.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: How to Identify the ICT PD Arrays
content:
#### How to Identify the ICT PD Arrays

To identify the premium and discount zones on any chart, plot the fibonacci retracement tool with these three levels:

  * **1.0** — Start (the upper end of the dealing range)
  * **0.5** — Equilibrium (the midpoint, where premium and discount split)
  * **0.0** — End (the lower end of the dealing range)

Plot the fibonacci from an established old high to an established old low. The 50% level is the midpoint. The area above the 50% line on the chart is the **premium zone**. The area below the 50% line is the **discount zone**.

![ICT PD Array fibonacci setup chart showing premium zone above 50% and discount zone below 50% on the dealing range](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-PD-array.png)

For more on the dealing range itself and the related concept of [Internal and External Range Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-internal-external-liquidity/>), see the dedicated guide.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: Step-by-Step PD Array Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step PD Array Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading inside the PD Array framework. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Identify the dealing range** on the higher timeframe (daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour). Mark the established swing high and swing low that have already swept liquidity.
  2. **Plot the fibonacci** from the swing high to the swing low, with levels at 1.0, 0.5, and 0.0.
  3. **Mark premium and discount zones** on the chart — above 50% is premium, below 50% is discount.
  4. **Set the daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). If bullish, hunt for buy setups in the discount zone. If bearish, hunt for sell setups in the premium zone.
  5. **Wait for price to enter the correct zone** for your bias direction.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe** (15-minute, 5-minute, or 3-minute) and watch for one or more PD Array trigger tools to print.
  7. **Confirm with a Market Structure Shift** on the lower timeframe in the direction of your bias.
  8. **Identify the strongest PD Array** at the level — when multiple tools stack (FVG + OB, OB + Breaker, etc.), confluence makes the entry stronger.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the retest of the PD Array, with stop loss beyond the structural extreme that preceded the MSS.
  10. **Take profit** at the opposite end of the dealing range (the 1.0 level for buys, the 0.0 level for sells), or at the next significant draw on liquidity.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: How to Use ICT PD Arrays
content:
#### How to Use ICT PD Arrays

PD Arrays serve two major purposes for ICT traders.

**(I) Daily bias identification.** If price has already shifted structure to the downside and is now in the premium zone, the bias is bearish — hunt for sell setups. If price has already shifted to the upside and is now in the discount zone, the bias is bullish — hunt for buy setups. The combination of structural direction and current zone tells me which side of the market to trade.

**(II) Trade execution.** When the daily bias is bearish and price is in the premium zone, I drop to the lower timeframe, wait for a Market Structure Shift, and find a bearish PD Array at the level to execute the sell. When the bias is bullish and price is in the discount zone, the same workflow applies in the opposite direction — wait for the MSS, find a bullish PD Array, and execute the buy.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: Best Time Frame for ICT PD Arrays
content:
#### Best Time Frame for ICT PD Arrays

The right timeframe depends on the use case.

For **daily bias identification** , the 1-day timeframe is the canonical reference. Daily PD Arrays produce the most reliable bias reads because they reflect the institutional positioning over many sessions.

For **trade entry execution** , drop to the lower timeframes — 15-minute and 5-minute. Lower-timeframe PD Arrays inside a higher-timeframe zone give the precise entry timing.

The two timeframes work together. Higher-timeframe PD Array sets the directional context; lower-timeframe PD Array fires the entry.

content:
#### Best Trading Pair for ICT PD Arrays

ICT PD Arrays were originally developed and tested on US index futures — **NASDAQ 100 (NQ Futures)** and the **E-mini S &P 500 (ES Futures)**. These remain the cleanest instruments for the framework because the time-of-day delivery on US index futures is the most predictable.

The PD Array framework also works very well on the major forex pairs and metals: **GBP/USD** , **EUR/USD** , and **XAU/USD** (Gold). Same fibonacci-based zones, same eight trigger tools — just different volatility profiles.

For US-based futures traders, ES and NQ are CFTC-regulated futures and execute through a US futures broker (NinjaTrader, AMP, Tradovate, or a prop firm such as Topstep). TradingView is for chart analysis only.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on PD Arrays
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on PD Arrays

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed PD Array trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the framework converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading the wrong PD Array in the wrong zone.** Bullish PD Arrays only work in the discount zone. Bearish PD Arrays only work in the premium zone. A bullish FVG in the premium zone is not a buy entry — it is just a fair value gap waiting to fail.
  2. **Skipping the dealing range marking.** Without an established swing high and swing low (each having swept liquidity), the dealing range is not valid. Without the dealing range, the fibonacci has no anchor and the premium / discount zones are guesses.
  3. **Trading PD Arrays against the daily bias.** The PD Array framework requires bias alignment. A discount-zone bullish setup against a bearish daily bias is a coin flip at best.
  4. **Treating any FVG, OB, or Breaker as a PD Array.** The matrix has eight specific tools, and each must be validated against its own rules (Order Block engulf, Breaker liquidity sweep, Mitigation OB hold, etc.). Loose pattern recognition is the fastest way to misread the matrix.
  5. **Forcing a single tool when no confluence exists.** The strongest PD Array setups stack two or more tools at the same level. A lone FVG in the discount zone is tradable, but a lone FVG plus a bullish Order Block plus a Breaker stacked at the same level is dramatically higher probability.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: Final Thoughts
content:
#### Final Thoughts

The PD Array Matrix is the master framework of the ICT method. Use it in conjunction with the higher-timeframe directional models — [ICT 2022 Trading Strategy](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022/>), [Silver Bullet](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-silver-bullet-strategy/>), [Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>), and the [Weekly Profiles](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-profiles/>). Together, the higher-timeframe model gives the directional anchor and the PD Array gives the execution.

No strategy is foolproof. Do not risk all your capital on a single PD Array setup, and always trade with a stop loss in place. The PD Array maximises the win rate; risk management protects the capital that compounds over time.

title: ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution
section: FAQs About the ICT PD Array
content:
#### FAQs About the ICT PD Array

**What is the ICT PD Array?**

ICT PD Array stands for “Premium and Discount Arrangement” — the canonical framework for choosing trade entry points in the ICT method. It is a matrix of eight institutional trigger tools (FVG, IFVG, Order Block, Breaker, Mitigation, Unicorn, NDOG, NWOG) arranged across the premium and discount zones of a dealing range.

**How do I identify premium and discount zones?**

Plot the fibonacci retracement tool from an established old high to an established old low, with levels at 1.0, 0.5, and 0.0. Above the 50% line is the premium zone. Below the 50% line is the discount zone.

**What are the eight ICT PD Array trigger tools?**

Fair Value Gap, Inverse Fair Value Gap, Order Block, Breaker Block, Mitigation Block, Unicorn Model, NDOG (New Day Opening Gap), and NWOG (New Week Opening Gap). Each one fires entries when price taps it inside the correct zone.

**What is a bullish PD Array?**

A bullish PD Array is any of the eight trigger tools positioned in the discount zone (below the 50% fibonacci line). It is used to identify buy entries when the daily bias is bullish.

**What is a bearish PD Array?**

A bearish PD Array is any of the eight trigger tools positioned in the premium zone (above the 50% fibonacci line). It is used to identify sell entries when the daily bias is bearish.

**How do I use PD Arrays for daily bias?**

Read the structural direction and the current zone together. Structure shift to the upside plus price in the discount zone equals bullish bias. Structure shift to the downside plus price in the premium zone equals bearish bias.

**What is the best timeframe for PD Arrays?**

1-day for daily bias identification. 15-minute or 5-minute for trade execution inside a higher-timeframe zone. The higher TF gives context; the lower TF fires the entry.

**What instruments work best with PD Arrays?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) produce the cleanest PD Arrays. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect the same fibonacci zones and trigger tools.

**Should I use one PD Array tool or stack multiple?**

Stack when possible. A lone FVG or OB inside the right zone is tradable, but the strongest setups have two or more PD Array tools at the same level — the confluence dramatically improves the win rate.

# ICT PD Array Matrix Revealed — 20-Day IPDA Data Range & Quadrant Grading

**Source:** ICT PD Array Matrix Revealed — October 18, 2025 (The Inner Circle Trader channel). Compiled instructional report synthesizing the live teaching by Michael J. Huddleston.

This report covers: the 20-day look-back as the primary framing tool, quadrant grading of ranges AND individual PD arrays (wicks, FVGs, order blocks), the middle focus zone, liquidity draws, market structure shifts, intermarket risk-on/off analysis via the Dollar Index, and practical intraday application.

ICT PD Array Matrix Revealed
Detailed Instructional Report & Insights
Based on the Live Teaching Session by Michael J. Huddleston (The Inner Circle Trader)
October 18, 2025 | YouTube Live Stream
Source:
 ICT PD Array Matrix Revealed \227 October 18, 2025 (The Inner Circle Trader channel). This report
synthesizes the core methodology, practical instructions, intermarket analysis, and all major insights shared
during the session for structured study and application.
Disclaimer: Hypothetical/simulated performance results have inherent limitations. This material is
for educational purposes only and does not constitute trading advice. Trading involves substantial
risk of loss. Past performance is not indicative of future results. Always trade at your own risk and
seek licensed advice if needed.
1. Session Overview & Core Thesis
This live session is a relaxed but highly instructional deep-dive into ICT\222s proprietary 
PD Array Matrix
(Premium & Discount Array Matrix). The focus is on algorithmic price action using only time-based candlesticks
(Open, High, Low, Close). ICT emphasizes that the market is driven by an algorithm that references specific
data arrays derived from fixed look-back periods. The primary tool for framing current relevant price levels is a
20-day look-back range
 graded into quadrants.
Key themes covered: time-based price delivery, 20-day IPDA (Interbank Price Delivery Algorithm) data ranges,
quadrant grading of ranges and individual PD arrays (wicks, FVGs, Order Blocks), liquidity draws, market
structure shifts, intermarket risk-on/risk-off analysis via the Dollar Index, and practical intraday application
across indices, forex, commodities, and bonds. Crypto is explicitly excluded as ICT has no expertise or
conviction in it.
2. Foundational Principle: Time-Based Candlesticks Only
ICT strongly criticizes non-time-based bars (range bars, volume bars, tick charts, etc.) because they distort the
natural order of price delivery and reduce predictive power. The algorithm operates on fixed daily ranges and
the OHLC data of each individual candlestick. Every single daily candle is a specific data array that the
algorithm can reference when deciding where to deliver price next.
When analyzing any market, the first action is always to establish the relevant look-back range on the daily
chart using pure time-based candles. Lower timeframes (5-minute, 15-minute, etc.) are then used for precise
entry timing once the higher-timeframe PD arrays and bias are identified.
3. The 20-Day Look-Back Range \227 The Core Framing Tool
For day trading and short-term trading, the 
20-day look-back
 is the primary (and often only necessary) data
range ICT uses. Longer look-backs (40-day or 60-day) exist in the broader IPDA framework but are secondary
for most active trading. The process is:
Step-by-Step Construction
1.
 On the daily chart, count back exactly 20 trading days from the current (or most recent completed) day.
2.
 Identify the absolute highest high and lowest low within those 20 days. This forms the dealing range / data
range.
3.
 Draw a box or use horizontal lines from the high to the low of that range for visual reference (optional but
helpful while learning).
4.
 Grade the entire range into equal quadrants using Fibonacci or simple percentage levels: 0% (low), 25%,
50% (equilibrium / midpoint), 75%, and 100% (high).
5.
 The upper quadrant (75\226100%), equilibrium (around 50%), and lower quadrant (0\22625%) become the
primary focus zones. The \223heart\224 of most actionable price delivery usually resides between the 25% and 75%
levels.
ICT states that this 20-day graded range is the algorithm\222s current reference frame. You do not need to concern
yourself with PD arrays outside this active range until price closes beyond the extremes on a closing basis. This
dramatically reduces noise and focuses attention on the highest-probability levels.
Important Insight: When the market has been trending higher within the 20-day range, focus
primarily on PD arrays in the upper half / premium side for potential shorts or on lower-quadrant
arrays for continuation longs after retracements. The reverse applies in downtrends. Extremes (very
top or bottom quadrants) are only prioritized when a full reversal or major liquidity run is expected.
4. Quadrant Grading of Ranges and Individual Arrays
Every significant range and every individual PD array (especially wicks) can itself be graded into quadrants.
This provides multi-layered precision:
\177 
Range Quadrants
 (from the 20-day high\226low): Lower quadrant, Equilibrium, Upper quadrant.
\177 
Wick / Array Quadrants
: For any candle wick or inefficiency, project its own 0/25/50/75/100% levels forward
in time. Price frequently reacts precisely at these projected quadrant levels of prior premium or discount wicks.
Example from the session (Dollar Index): A premium wick on a prior daily candle is graded; its upper quadrant,
equilibrium, and lower quadrant levels later act as precise reaction points on the 5-minute chart (e.g., price
stopping at 98.499, then 98.402 which was the upper quadrant of that wick, then equilibrium at 98.306).
This nested grading is how the algorithm \223knows\224 where to stop or reverse on a dime. ICT demonstrates
repeated precise reactions at these levels across timeframes as evidence of algorithmic delivery rather than
random price action.
5. PD Arrays (Premium & Discount Arrays) \227 The Matrix Elements
PD Array stands for 
Premium and Discount Arrangement
 (or Array). It is the hierarchical collection of
institutional price-delivery tools that the algorithm uses to deliver price into premium (above equilibrium) or
discount (below equilibrium) zones of a dealing range.
Within the graded 20-day range, identify and rank all relevant PD arrays that sit inside the active quadrants. The
classic ICT PD Array Matrix typically includes (in rough hierarchical order of strength when aligned with bias
and zone):
PD Array Tool
Typical Use in Premium Zone (Bearish
Bias)
Typical Use in Discount Zone (Bullish
Bias)
Fair Value Gap (FVG / SIBI or BISI)
Sell-side Imbalance (bearish FVG) for
shorts
Buy-side Imbalance (bullish FVG) for longs
Order Block (OB)
Bearish Order Block (last up-close before
down move)
Bullish Order Block (last down-close before
up move)
Breaker Block
Bearish Breaker after failed bullish
structure
Bullish Breaker after failed bearish
structure
Mitigation Block
Bearish Mitigation
Bullish Mitigation
Inverse Fair Value Gap (IFVG)
Bearish IFVG after inversion
Bullish IFVG after inversion
Rejection Block
Bearish Rejection
Bullish Rejection
NWOG / NDOG (New Week/Day
Opening Gap)
In premium for shorts
In discount for longs
Unicorn Model / OTE confluence
When stacked with other arrays
When stacked with other arrays
Confluence of two or more PD arrays at the same level inside the correct zone (premium for shorts, discount for
longs) dramatically increases probability. A lone FVG is tradable; an FVG + Order Block + Breaker stack is far
higher probability.
6. Practical Instructions: How to Apply the PD Array Matrix
Daily Workflow (Recommended Sequence)
1. Establish Daily Bias & Risk Context
 \227 Check the Dollar Index (DXY). Dollar rallying = Risk-Off (favor
shorts in indices/commodities if technicals align). Dollar declining = Risk-On (favor longs). This is a
barometer, not a guarantee.
2. Frame the 20-Day Look-Back
 \227 Mark the high and low of the last 20 trading days on the daily chart of
your instrument (NQ, ES, EURUSD, GBPUSD, Gold, etc.). Grade into 0/25/50/75/100%.
3. Identify Active Quadrants
 \227 Determine where current price sits relative to equilibrium. Focus attention
on PD arrays inside the upper or lower quadrants that are relevant to the expected direction.
4. Catalogue PD Arrays
 \227 List every relevant FVG, Order Block, Breaker, Mitigation Block, wick (with its
own quadrant grades), NWOG/NDOG, etc., that sit inside the active 20-day range. Rank them by location
(premium vs discount) and confluence.
5. Wait for Price to Enter the Correct Zone
 \227 For a bullish bias, wait for price to trade into discount. For
bearish bias, wait for premium.
6. Drop to Lower Timeframe for Entry
 \227 On 15-min, 5-min, or even lower, look for a Market Structure Shift
(MSS / break of a swing high or low) in the direction of bias, then enter on the retest of the strongest PD
array at that level.
7. Risk Management
 \227 Place stop beyond the structural extreme that preceded the MSS. Target the
opposite side of the dealing range, the next significant liquidity pool (equal highs/lows), or a higher-timeframe
PD array. Scale out partially.
8. Time of Day Awareness
 \227 Certain windows (e.g., late New York session macros around 2:50\2263:10 PM
ICT stresses: do not chase perfect highs or lows. Trade the high-probability arrays that appear inside the
graded range. Build confidence gradually through back-testing and forward observation.
7. Intermarket Analysis & Dollar Index Context
The Dollar Index is used purely as a risk-on / risk-off barometer \227 ICT does not trade the DXY itself. Key rules
shared:
\177 When DXY is rallying (especially after rejecting a buy-side imbalance / fair value gap or breaking below
consequent encroachment of a prior structure), it creates a risk-off environment that supports high-probability
shorts in equity indices if technicals confirm.
\177 When DXY drops and digs below key lows or consequent encroachment, it supports risk-on conditions
favorable for longs in NASDAQ, S
&P;
, etc., or dollar-based forex pairs.
\177 This is contextual confirmation only. Strong technical PD-array setups on the instrument itself are still
required.
In the session, ICT revisited a prior DXY analysis: price entered an old buy-side imbalance, pierced the upper
end, spent time inside, then failed and moved lower. He had previously stated that a move below consequent
encroachment of a key low would open the door for another challenge of NASDAQ all-time highs (via risk-on).
The 20-day graded range on DXY itself was used to identify the relevant PD arrays driving the move.
8. Market Structure Shifts & Liquidity Draws
Within the graded 20-day range, shifts in market structure are confirmed by price closing above or below key
swing highs/lows and interacting with quadrant levels. Liquidity draws frequently occur at:
\177 Relative equal highs or equal lows (classic buy-side or sell-side liquidity pools).
\177 The extremes of the 20-day range (or its quadrant boundaries).
\177 Unfilled fair value gaps or order blocks that sit at those levels.
The algorithm systematically \223orders\224 price to these levels. By knowing the active 20-day range and its graded
PD arrays, the trader can anticipate the most likely next draw on liquidity rather than reacting after the fact.
9. Key Examples Covered in the Session
Dollar Index (Daily + 5-min)
: Full demonstration of 20-day look-back grading, identification of premium wicks,
projection of their quadrants onto the lower timeframe, and precise reactions at those levels (stops on a dime at
specific quadrant prices). Showed how price respected graded inefficiencies and order flow.
NASDAQ
: Linked to DXY risk-on/off. Discussed a major gap from two Fridays prior and how price respects the
graded ranges around it. Emphasis on waiting for the correct side of the 20-day structure before looking for
longs toward prior highs.
Gold (December contract)
: Examined a parabolic run. Used quadrant grading of the recent range to identify
logical profit-taking zones and where institutional players would likely begin to distribute after volatility
expansion.
Practice Markets Suggested
: EUR/USD and GBP/USD are recommended for students to practice applying
the exact same 20-day quadrant + PD Array process. The methodology is universal across forex, indices,
commodities, and bonds.
10. Additional Insights & Teaching Points from the Session
\177 ICT deliberately keeps the presentation casual and energy-efficient (\223not a shotgun Saturday\224). He still
covers the complete core process.
\177 He writes key levels and PD arrays in a personal notepad (highest to lowest) rather than cluttering the live
chart while trading. Charts are annotated heavily only when teaching.
\177 Back-testing method recommended: pick any random historical day, treat it as \223today,\224 count back 20 days,
grade the range, identify PD arrays, and observe how price subsequently respected those levels. Repeat
across many samples.
\177 Avoid reliance on Level 2 data, volume profile, footprint charts, or other \223gimmicks.\224 Time and price alone,
properly framed, are sufficient.
\177 Big institutional players often wait for price to break out of major volatility bands before committing
significant capital. Graded ranges help identify when that condition is present.
\177 Partial profit-taking and strict risk management are essential, especially in volatile or uncertain conditions.
\177 Do not publicly share personal trade results obsessively; it creates distraction and unnecessary pressure.
Focus on the process.
\177 The system is proprietary in its specific combination and emphasis on the 20-day matrix, yet the individual
tools (FVG, OB, etc.) are taught freely. Mastery comes from consistent application and verification.
\177 When a 20-day range is strongly directional (e.g., higher highs), the trader can ignore the extreme opposite
quadrant until a closing breach occurs. This keeps focus on the high-probability \223heart\224 of the range.
11. Common Pitfalls to Avoid (Synthesized from Session Logic)
\177 Trading PD arrays in the wrong zone relative to bias (e.g., buying a bullish FVG that sits in premium while
bias is bearish).
\177 Ignoring the 20-day look-back and marking random historical arrays that are no longer relevant to the
algorithm\222s current data set.
\177 Failing to grade the range or the individual arrays, thereby missing the precise reaction levels.
\177 Using non-time-based charts that destroy the algorithmic reference points.
\177 Over-complicating with external indicators instead of mastering pure price and time delivery.
\177 Chasing extremes instead of trading the high-probability arrays inside the active quadrants.
\177 Skipping intermarket context (DXY risk-on/off) when trading correlated markets.
12. Quick-Reference Checklist for Daily Use
n
 Dollar Index direction and key structure checked (risk-on or risk-off context).
n
 20-day high and low identified on daily chart of the instrument.
n
 Range graded: 0% / 25% / 50% (EQ) / 75% / 100%.
n
 Current price location relative to equilibrium noted (premium or discount).
n
 Relevant PD arrays (FVGs, OBs, Breakers, wicks with their own quadrants, gaps) listed inside active
zones.
n
 Highest-confluence arrays prioritized.
n
 Bias confirmed (bullish 
\256
 hunt discount arrays; bearish 
\256
 hunt premium arrays).
n
 Lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift awaited in direction of bias.
n
 Entry on retest of the strongest aligned PD array; stop beyond structural extreme.
n
 Targets set at opposing liquidity or opposite side of the graded range; partials taken.
n
 Time-of-day macro windows considered for scalping precision.
Closing Notes
The October 18, 2025 session reveals the PD Array Matrix as a focused, algorithmic framework built on a
simple but powerful foundation: the 20-day look-back range graded into quadrants, populated with precisely
defined institutional arrays (FVGs, Order Blocks, etc.), and filtered by intermarket risk context and time-based
delivery. By systematically applying the steps above, a trader can dramatically reduce noise, identify the levels
the algorithm is most likely to reference next, and execute with defined risk and logical targets.
ICT repeatedly invites students to verify everything independently through back-testing and live observation.
The tools are free; the edge comes from disciplined, repeated application of the matrix logic rather than from
any single indicator or secret.
Study the original recording for the live chart walkthroughs and the exact price levels demonstrated. This report
is intended as a structured companion that captures the instructions and insights without omitting the critical
operational details shared in the session.

# ICT Power of 3 — Accumulation, Manipulation, Distribution Explained (Free PDF)

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/)

![ICT Power of 3 diagram showing the three phases of price delivery — Accumulation, Manipulation, and Distribution](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ICT-power-of-3.png)

The ICT Power of 3 — also called the Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) model — is a trading framework introduced by Michael Huddleston that helps retail traders follow the moves of smart money rather than fall into their traps.

The model breaks every trading day into three phases: Accumulation, where smart money builds positions inside a tight range; Manipulation, where price runs the opposite way to trigger retail stops; and Distribution, where the real move of the day delivers in the institutional direction.

Once you understand these three phases, you can time your entries with the institutions, avoid the manipulation traps, and trade the only phase that actually pays — the distribution. This guide walks through the model, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the common mistakes traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: What is the ICT Power of 3?
content:
#### What is the ICT Power of 3?

The ICT Power of 3 is the trading model Michael Huddleston designed to expose smart-money manipulation in intraday markets. It is built on three sequential phases of price delivery: Accumulation, Manipulation, and Distribution.

Accumulation is where institutions quietly build their positions inside a horizontal range. Manipulation is the engineered move that runs the opposite side of the range to trigger retail stops and sweep liquidity. Distribution is the real, sustained move of the day in the institutional direction.

Master the three phases and you stop trading against the algorithm. You start trading with it.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: What is Accumulation Manipulation Distribution?
content:
#### What is Accumulation Manipulation Distribution?

Accumulation Manipulation Distribution — known as AMD — describes the three phases of a complete intraday price move. Each phase has a precise definition and a precise role in the daily delivery.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Accumulation Phase
content:
#### Accumulation Phase

The Accumulation phase begins at the daily open. Price ranges in a tight horizontal zone near the opening price while smart money quietly builds its position at favourable levels.

This phase is recognised by the chart pattern: price appears trapped inside a horizontal band, drifting between a clear support and resistance with little net movement.

During Accumulation, retail traders place buy orders at the horizontal support and sell orders at the horizontal resistance. Their stop losses sit just above the range high and just below the range low — exactly where the next phase will hunt.

![ICT Accumulation phase example — horizontal price range at daily open with retail stops above and below](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Accumulation-Phase.png)

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Manipulation Phase
content:
#### Manipulation Phase

The Manipulation phase does exactly what the name suggests — it manipulates retail traders. After accumulation completes, smart money pushes price in the opposite direction of the day’s true bias.

On a bearish day, the manipulation runs to the upside, dragging in retail buyers and stopping out the early sellers. On a bullish day, the manipulation runs to the downside, dragging in retail sellers and stopping out the early buyers.

The mechanism is mechanical: when price breaks above the accumulation range, short-seller stops are triggered and breakout buyers enter long. When price breaks below the accumulation range, long-trader stops are triggered and breakout sellers enter short. Either way, retail loses money and feeds liquidity to the institutions.

The manipulation phase is also called the false breakout of the accumulation range.

![ICT Manipulation phase example — false breakout sweeps retail stops outside the accumulation range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Manipulation-Phase.png)

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Distribution Phase
content:
#### Distribution Phase

The Distribution phase is the final stage of AMD and the only phase that pays. After harvesting all the liquidity created by retail traders during manipulation, smart money adds to its position and drives the market in the original institutional direction.

This is the real move of the day. Distribution is where I take the trade.

![ICT Distribution phase example — institutional direction takes hold, real move of the day delivers](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Distribution-Phase.png)
