title: ict-power-of-3
section: The Concept Behind the AMD Setup
content:
#### The Concept Behind the AMD Setup

The Power of 3 is rooted in market psychology. The Accumulation phase tests trader patience. The Manipulation phase triggers emotional, impulsive decisions. The Distribution phase rewards only those who understand the cycle.

This loop reflects the predictable behaviour of retail participants — buying breakouts, panicking on pullbacks, chasing strength — and gives the patient trader a structural advantage. Recognise the cycle, and you stop reacting emotionally with the crowd.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Step-by-Step Power of 3 Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Power of 3 Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every Power of 3 setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Establish daily bias** on the daily and 4-hour charts before the session opens. Bullish or bearish — the AMD model only works with a clear bias.
  2. **Mark the daily opening price** at midnight New York time. The accumulation forms around this level.
  3. **Wait for accumulation** — a tight horizontal range to form near the opening price. Do not pre-position.
  4. **Mark the accumulation range high and low**. These are the levels manipulation will target.
  5. **Wait for the manipulation move** — price runs in the opposite direction of your bias, sweeping the stops on that side of the range.
  6. **Confirm the sweep** by watching for price to fail at the swept extreme and reverse.
  7. **Drop to the lower timeframe** (5-minute or 3-minute) for entry confirmation — Market Structure Shift or CISD in the direction of your bias.
  8. **Mark the PD Array** created during the displacement leg of the distribution — fair value gap, order block, or breaker block.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the PD Array tap, with stop loss beyond the swept extreme of the manipulation phase.
  10. **Set take profit** at the opposite end of the daily range or the next significant liquidity pool.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: How to Trade the ICT Power of 3
content:
#### How to Trade the ICT Power of 3

To trade the Power of 3, I need a correct [Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>) for the session. Daily bias is the predicted direction of the day’s candle and the dominant intraday move.

With the bias set, I drop to a lower timeframe (15-minute, 5-minute, or 3-minute) and wait for the distribution phase, because that is where the real move of the day delivers.

The model splits cleanly into two variants based on the daily bias.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: ICT Power of 3 in a Bullish Market
content:
#### ICT Power of 3 in a Bullish Market

On a bullish day, price accumulates near the opening price. Smart money quietly builds long positions inside this range.

After accumulation, smart money runs the manipulation move to the downside — a sharp sell that engineers liquidity below the open and targets any nearby old lows. Retail traders read this move as a bearish breakout and start selling. Meanwhile, the early buyers who positioned during accumulation get their stops triggered below the old lows, neutralising the long side.

Now the institutions buy aggressively in the discount zone below the opening price. Price reverses and drives upside in the distribution leg, targeting old highs as liquidity. The bullish day prints a wick below the open (the manipulation low), runs to the high of the day to clear external liquidity, and closes near the high of the daily range.

![ICT Power of 3 in a bullish market — accumulation, sell manipulation below open, bullish distribution to old highs](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ICT-power-of-3-in-bullish-market.png)

title: ict-power-of-3
section: ICT Power of 3 in a Bearish Market
content:
#### ICT Power of 3 in a Bearish Market

On a bearish day, price accumulates near the opening price. Smart money builds short positions inside the range.

After accumulation, smart money runs the manipulation move to the upside — a sharp buy that engineers liquidity above the open and targets any nearby old highs. Retail traders read this as a bullish breakout and start buying. The early sellers who positioned during accumulation get their stops triggered above the old highs, neutralising the short side.

Now the institutions sell aggressively in the premium zone above the opening price. Price reverses and drives downside in the distribution leg, targeting old lows as liquidity. The bearish day prints a wick above the open (the manipulation high), runs to the low of the day to clear external liquidity, and closes near the low of the daily range.

![ICT Power of 3 in a bearish market — accumulation, buy manipulation above open, bearish distribution to old lows](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ICT-power-of-3-in-bearish-Market.png)

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Best Pair for Accumulation Manipulation Distribution
content:
#### Best Pair for Accumulation Manipulation Distribution

The Power of 3 was originally developed and tested on US index futures — **NASDAQ 100 (NQ Futures)** and the **E-mini S &P 500 (ES Futures)**. These remain the cleanest instruments for the model because the time-of-day delivery on US index futures is the most predictable.

It also works very well on forex majors and metals: **GBP/USD** , **EUR/USD** , and **XAU/USD** (Gold) all respect the same AMD logic.

For US-based futures traders, ES and NQ are CFTC-regulated futures and execute through a US futures broker (NinjaTrader, AMP, Tradovate, or a prop firm such as Topstep). TradingView is for chart analysis only.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Best Timeframe to Spot Accumulation Manipulation Distribution
content:
#### Best Timeframe to Spot Accumulation Manipulation Distribution

The Power of 3 is an intraday model, so I always use a higher-timeframe bias as the anchor. For spotting the three phases on the chart I drop to the 15-minute or 5-minute timeframes.

The 15-minute is where I read the accumulation and manipulation cleanly. The 5-minute and 3-minute are where I refine the entry inside the distribution leg.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Best AMD Phase to Trade
content:
#### Best AMD Phase to Trade

Only one of the three phases is tradable: Distribution.

Accumulation is preparation — institutions are still building positions; the move has not started. Manipulation is a trap — it runs the opposite direction of the real move and stops out anyone who took the bait. Distribution is the real, sustained move of the day, and it is the only phase where the risk-to-reward profile makes sense.

title: ict-power-of-3
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Power of 3
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Power of 3

Five mistakes show up in nearly every Power of 3 comment thread. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading the manipulation phase as a breakout.** The manipulation looks identical to a breakout — that is the whole point. Filter every breakout against the daily bias before acting. If the breakout direction is opposite to your bias, it is the manipulation, not the move.
  2. **Entering before the distribution leg confirms.** A liquidity sweep on its own is not a signal. Wait for a Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe in the direction of your bias before pulling the trigger.
  3. **Trading without a daily bias.** The Power of 3 is a directional model. Without a higher-timeframe bias, the manipulation and distribution phases cannot be distinguished from each other.
  4. **Stop loss inside the manipulation range.** The sweep candle often runs a few pips beyond the prior extreme before reversing. Place the stop beyond the wick of the sweep candle, with a small buffer.
  5. **Forcing the model in low-volatility windows.** AMD setups taken during Asia lunch or NY lunch are weaker. The model performs best during London open and New York AM, when the institutional flow is concentrated.

section: FAQs About the ICT Power of 3
content:
#### FAQs About the ICT Power of 3

**What is the ICT Power of 3?**

The ICT Power of 3 is the trading model Michael Huddleston designed to expose smart-money manipulation in intraday markets. It is built on three sequential phases — Accumulation, Manipulation, and Distribution — that describe how price is delivered through every trading session.

**What does AMD stand for in trading?**

AMD stands for Accumulation Manipulation Distribution — the three phases of the ICT Power of 3 model.

**Which phase of the Power of 3 do I trade?**

Only the Distribution phase. Accumulation is preparation, Manipulation is a trap, and Distribution is the real, sustained move of the day. Take entries during distribution only.

**What is the best timeframe for the Power of 3?**

Daily for bias, then 15-minute or 5-minute for spotting the three phases. The 5-minute and 3-minute are useful for refining the entry inside the distribution leg.

**What are the best instruments to trade the Power of 3?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) work cleanest. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect the AMD logic.

**What is the difference between manipulation and distribution?**

Manipulation runs the opposite direction of the daily bias to sweep retail stops and engineer liquidity. Distribution runs in the direction of the daily bias and delivers the real move. They are mirror images of each other in price action but opposite in intent.

**Can I trade the Power of 3 on forex?**

Yes. The model was originally developed on US index futures but has proven effective on the major forex pairs and on Gold. Use the same daily-bias-first approach.

**Is the Power of 3 the same as the Market Maker Buy/Sell Model?**

The Power of 3 is the daily-cycle expression of the same logic that drives the Market Maker Buy/Sell Models. AMD describes the daily phases in three steps; the MMBM and MMSM describe the longer multi-day delivery sequence in five.

# ICT Premium and Discount Zone Identification

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/)

![ICT Premium and Discount Zone identification using Fibonacci retracement on a price chart with the 50% midline marked](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-premium-and-discount.png)

For my first two years of trading, I sold tops and bought bottoms by feel. I lost more often than I won. The day I learned to draw a Fibonacci between my swing high and swing low and force myself to sell only above the 50% line and buy only below it, my win rate jumped without changing anything else about my analysis. That single rule is what ICT calls Premium and Discount.

The **ICT Premium and Discount Zone** is a part of the broader [ICT Trading Strategy](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/complete-ict-trading-strategy-2022/> "ICT Trading Strategy"). It helps you decide where in a range a trade entry actually belongs — selling only when price is in premium territory, buying only when price is in discount territory.

In this guide, I will show you what premium and discount mean using a simple real-world example, the exact Fibonacci settings used to identify the zones, how to mark a Premium Zone in a bearish trend, how to mark a Discount Zone in a bullish trend, and how to trade them with proper confirmation.

Do not worry — once you know which side of 50% to trade from, this becomes a one-line discipline rule.

Ready? Let us break it down.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: The Meaning of Premium and Discount
content:
## The Meaning of Premium and Discount

Let us understand it with an example.

Suppose you want to buy a car with a market value of $120,000. The basic or fair value of the car is $120,000. **Premium** is the amount paid above the basic or fair value, so anything above $120k is a premium price. **Discount** is the price less than the fair or basic value, so the price of the car below $120k is a discounted price.

Now ask yourself: would you buy the car at premium or at discount? Of course at discount.

The same logic applies to trading. To buy anything, you want to buy it at discount. To sell anything, you want to sell it at premium.

Premium and Discount zones simply project that intuition onto a price chart using Fibonacci.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Fibonacci Settings for ICT Premium and Discount Zone
content:
## Fibonacci Settings for ICT Premium and Discount Zone

Use the following inputs in the Fibonacci retracement tool for identification of ICT Premium and Discount zones:

1| Start  
---|---  
0.5| 50% Retracement  
0| End  
  
The 50% level is the midline. Anything above 50% is the Premium Zone. Anything below 50% is the Discount Zone. The two extreme zones (above 79% and below 21%) are the deepest premium and discount, respectively — the highest-probability entry areas.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: What is the ICT Premium Zone?
content:
## What is the ICT Premium Zone?

As discussed earlier, traders use the Premium Zone to sell. So the ICT Premium Zone is utilised in a bearish trend mostly.

To identify the ICT Premium Zone in a bearish trend, draw the Fibonacci retracement tool from [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/> "ICT Swing High") to [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "ICT Swing Low").

The area above the 50% Fib retracement level is the Premium Zone, where you will look for sell trade execution after a confirmation like an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift").

![ICT Premium Zone example: Fibonacci drawn from Swing High to Swing Low in a bearish trend with the area above 50% marked as the premium zone for sell entries](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ict-premium-zone.png)

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: What is the ICT Discount Zone?
content:
## What is the ICT Discount Zone?

Traders use the Discount Zone to buy. So the ICT Discount Zone is used in a bullish trend primarily.

To identify the ICT Discount Zone in a bullish trend, draw the Fibonacci retracement tool from Swing Low to Swing High.

The area below the 50% Fib retracement level is the Discount Zone, where you will look for buy trade execution after a confirmation like an ICT Market Structure Shift.

![ICT Discount Zone example: Fibonacci drawn from Swing Low to Swing High in a bullish trend with the area below 50% marked as the discount zone for buy entries](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ict-discount-zone.png)

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: How to Trade ICT Premium and Discount Zones — Step by Step
content:
## How to Trade ICT Premium and Discount Zones — Step by Step

The unified trade flow:

  1. **Confirm the higher-timeframe trend.** Bullish for buys, bearish for sells.
  2. **Identify the relevant swing high and swing low** on your bias timeframe.
  3. **Draw the Fibonacci tool** — high to low for a bearish trend, low to high for a bullish trend.
  4. **Mark the zones.** Above 50% = Premium. Below 50% = Discount.
  5. **Wait for price to retrace into the relevant zone** — Premium Zone for sells, Discount Zone for buys.
  6. **Drop to a lower timeframe** and look for an ICT Market Structure Shift in your trade direction as confirmation.
  7. **Enter on the close of the MSS candle** or on a clean retest. Stop loss beyond the swing extreme that produced the zone.
  8. **Target the opposite side of the range** or the next opposing PD Array.

**Pro Tip** — The deepest part of either zone (above 79% in premium, below 21% in discount) usually offers the highest-probability entries. When a higher-timeframe [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array") like an order block, fair value gap, or breaker block sits inside the deep zone, the confluence is what makes the reaction sharp. Skip entries in the middle of the range — that is no-man’s-land where neither buyers nor sellers have an edge.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Bonus Tip: Pairing Premium and Discount With PD Arrays
content:
## Bonus Tip: Pairing Premium and Discount With PD Arrays

Premium and Discount zones tell you _which half of the range_ to take entries from. PD Arrays tell you _which exact level_ inside that half to enter at. Combined, they narrow your entry from a general zone to a precise institutional level.

For longs in a bullish trend: find a Discount Zone, then look for an order block, fair value gap, or breaker block inside it. Take entry at the PD Array level after MSS confirmation.

For shorts in a bearish trend: find a Premium Zone, then look for a PD Array inside it. Same flow, opposite direction.

For a deeper walk through the PD Array hierarchy, see the [ICT PD Array Matrix](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array Matrix").

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I trade solely using ICT Premium and Discount zones?

No. You cannot trade solely using Premium and Discount zones. Premium and Discount zones are part of the ICT trading strategy, so you should use them along with other ICT concepts while keeping the current market structure in view.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Does the Premium and Discount Zone change after a break of structure?
content:
### Does the Premium and Discount Zone change after a break of structure?

Yes. After every break of structure, you have to mark a new Premium and Discount zone. In a bearish trend, when price breaks the low and marks a new low, identify the new Premium Zone by drawing Fibonacci from the latest swing high to swing low for fresh sell entries. In a bullish trend, when price breaks the high and makes a higher high, look for a fresh Discount Zone by drawing Fibonacci from the fresh low to fresh high for fresh buy entries.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Which markets do ICT Premium and Discount zones work in?
content:
### Which markets do ICT Premium and Discount zones work in?

ICT Premium and Discount zones work in every market where price is delivered live on a price chart — crypto, Forex, indices, and stocks. The Fibonacci-based logic does not depend on the asset class.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: What is the difference between Premium and Discount?
content:
### What is the difference between Premium and Discount?

Premium is any price above the 50% midline of the range — the half of the range where you look for sell entries. Discount is any price below the 50% midline — the half where you look for buy entries. The midline is the fair value reference point.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: What confirmation do I need before entering a Premium or Discount Zone trade?
content:
### What confirmation do I need before entering a Premium or Discount Zone trade?

An ICT Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe in the direction of your bias. Without that confirmation, the zone is just an area of interest — not a trade.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Where do I place stop loss on a Premium and Discount Zone trade?
content:
### Where do I place stop loss on a Premium and Discount Zone trade?

Beyond the swing extreme that produced the zone — above the swing high for a Premium Zone short, below the swing low for a Discount Zone long. The swing extreme is your invalidation: if price closes through it, the trade thesis has failed.

title: ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification
section: Can I use Premium and Discount zones on every timeframe?
content:
### Can I use Premium and Discount zones on every timeframe?

Yes, but the deeper the timeframe, the more reliable the zone. Daily and 4-hour zones are most reliable for swing trades. For intraday entries, mark zones on the 1-hour or 15-minute, and use 5-minute charts for execution after the MSS confirmation.

content:

section: What is an ICT Propulsion Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Propulsion Block?

The word “propulsion” means to push something. In trading it is a single candlestick that pushes price away from itself.

The ICT propulsion block is the single candlestick which traded into an [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "Order Block") — and price then moved away from it.

When price tests the propulsion candle, it delivers a quick reaction in the form of a sudden price move. That is why the propulsion candle is used as an entry zone — the reaction is fast, the stop is small, and the reward-to-risk is excellent when it works.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Bullish ICT Propulsion Block
content:
#### Bullish ICT Propulsion Block

A bullish ICT propulsion block is the last bearish candlestick that traded into a bullish order block — and from which price then moved up.

![ICT Bullish Propulsion Block diagram — last bearish candle that traded into the bullish order block and propelled price upward](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ICT-bullish-propulsion-block.png)

The next time price retraces it will take support at the propulsion candlestick and move quickly to the upside.

**How to Trade a Bullish ICT Propulsion Block**

To trade a bullish ICT propulsion block you have to identify the mean threshold (50% retracement level) of the propulsion candlestick by applying the Fibonacci from the high to the low of the propulsion candlestick.

A good propulsion block will not let price go down below the mean threshold.

Now wait for price to retrace back and retest the propulsion candlestick.

You can execute the buy trade when price approaches the body of the propulsion candlestick above the mean threshold level.

![Bullish ICT Propulsion Block trade example — price retraces into the propulsion candle, holds above the mean threshold and propels back up](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/bullish-ICT-propulsion-block.png)

In this case your stop loss will be 10 pips below the low of the propulsion candlestick.

For take profit you can target the next buy-side liquidity level or you can use the [ICT fib levels](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-fibonacci-levels/>) to set your take profit.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Bearish ICT Propulsion Block
content:
#### Bearish ICT Propulsion Block

A bearish ICT propulsion block is the last bullish candlestick that traded into a bearish order block — and from which price then moved down.

![ICT Bearish Propulsion Block diagram — last bullish candle that traded into the bearish order block and propelled price downward](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/bearish-ICT-propulsion-block.png)

The next time price retraces it will face resistance at the propulsion candlestick and move quickly to the downside.

**How to Trade a Bearish ICT Propulsion Block**

To trade a bearish ICT propulsion block you have to identify the mean threshold (50% retracement level) of the propulsion candlestick by applying the Fibonacci from the low to the high of the propulsion candlestick.

A good propulsion block will not let price go up above the mean threshold.

Now wait for price to retrace back and retest the propulsion candlestick.

You can execute the sell trade when price approaches the body of the propulsion candlestick below the mean threshold level.

![Bearish ICT Propulsion Block trade example — price retraces into the propulsion candle, holds below the mean threshold and propels back down](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ICT-bearish-Propulsion-block.png)

In this case your stop loss will be 10 pips above the high of the propulsion candlestick.

For take profit you can target the next sell-side liquidity level or you can use the [ICT fib levels](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-fibonacci-levels/>) to set your take profit.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Step-by-Step ICT Propulsion Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT Propulsion Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a propulsion block.

  1. **Identify a valid order block.** Bullish OB on a higher-timeframe bullish trend, or bearish OB on a higher-timeframe bearish trend.
  2. **Spot the propulsion candle.** The single candle whose body or wick traded into the order block — and from which price then moved sharply away.
  3. **Mark the mean threshold.** 50% of the propulsion candle’s range. Use the Fibonacci tool: high-to-low for bullish, low-to-high for bearish.
  4. **Wait for the retest.** Price must trade back to the propulsion candle on a later leg.
  5. **Confirm the mean-threshold rule.** A valid propulsion block does NOT let price close beyond the mean threshold on the retest. If it does, the propulsion has failed and the trade is invalid.
  6. **Enter on the body retest.** Buy at the body of the propulsion candle above the mean threshold (bullish), or sell at the body below the mean threshold (bearish).
  7. **Set the stop.** 10 pips below the low of the propulsion candle (bullish) or 10 pips above the high (bearish).
  8. **Take profit at the next liquidity.** Buy-side liquidity for longs, sell-side liquidity for shorts. Alternative: stage exits using the ICT fib extension levels.

section: Best Markets for the ICT Propulsion Block
content:
#### Best Markets for the ICT Propulsion Block

The propulsion block works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to.

  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — fast 1-minute and 5-minute price action makes propulsion-block reactions very precise on US indices.
  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — propulsion candles inside London-killzone order blocks deliver clean retest entries during NY-AM.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — large-body propulsion candles around US 08:30 ET news produce textbook retest setups.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, NQ and ES are the most natural fit for the propulsion block. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) often produces the propulsion candle whose retest delivers an intraday entry inside the same session — making the setup especially time-efficient.

section: Is the ICT Propulsion Block Reliable for Trading?
content:
#### Is the ICT Propulsion Block Reliable for Trading?

Yes — the ICT propulsion block is reliable for trading because of its accuracy and a small stop loss, resulting in a high reward-to-risk ratio.

The reliability is highest when the propulsion candle sits inside a clearly defined order block and the higher-timeframe bias agrees with the propulsion direction.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Can I Trade Using a Propulsion Block Alone?
content:
#### Can I Trade Using a Propulsion Block Alone?

Yes — you can trade using a propulsion block alone. The propulsion block helps you execute a precise entry, but you should have a correct daily bias to trade accurately.

In practice I prefer the propulsion block as a continuation entry inside an existing higher-timeframe bias, rather than as a standalone signal in choppy conditions.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Can I Use the Propulsion Block for Scalping?
content:
#### Can I Use the Propulsion Block for Scalping?

Yes — you may use it for scalping, day trading or swing trading as you wish.

The only difference is the timeframe used for identifying the propulsion block.

  * **Scalping** — M1, M3 or M5 propulsion candles inside lower-timeframe order blocks.
  * **Day trading** — M30, 1H or 4H propulsion candles inside intraday order blocks.
  * **Swing trading** — daily and weekly propulsion candles inside higher-timeframe order blocks.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: Common Mistakes Trading the Propulsion Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the Propulsion Block

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading propulsion blocks.

  1. **Trading propulsion blocks outside an order block.** The propulsion block is defined as a candle that traded into an order block. Without the OB context, the candle is just a single bar — not a propulsion block.
  2. **Ignoring the mean-threshold rule.** A valid propulsion block does NOT close beyond the mean threshold on the retest. If price closes through the 50% level, the trade is invalid.
  3. **Stop too tight.** The 10-pip buffer below the low (bullish) or above the high (bearish) is the minimum. On gold or indices, scale this to ticks of equivalent dollar value.
  4. **Trading against the daily bias.** A bullish propulsion block in a bearish daily bias often fails on the retest. Always reference the higher-timeframe bias first.
  5. **Wrong Fibonacci direction.** For bullish, draw fib from high to low (so 50% sits at the bullish midpoint). For bearish, draw from low to high. Reversing the direction inverts the mean threshold.
  6. **Confusing propulsion with the order block.** The order block is the broader zone (the bearish candle before a bullish impulse, or the bullish candle before a bearish impulse). The propulsion block is the single candle that traded into the OB after it formed and gave the second push.

title: ict-propulsion-block
section: FAQs about the ICT Propulsion Block
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Propulsion Block

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the propulsion block.

**What is an ICT propulsion block?**

A single candlestick that traded into an order block and pushed price away from it. When price retests the propulsion candle on a later leg, the algorithm typically delivers a sharp reaction — making it a high-probability entry zone.

**How is the propulsion block different from an order block?**

The order block is the broader zone (the last opposite-coloured candle before a strong impulse). The propulsion block is the single candle that traded into the order block after it formed and produced the second push.

**What is the mean threshold of a propulsion block?**

The 50% retracement level of the propulsion candle’s range. Found by applying the Fibonacci tool from the high to the low (for bullish) or low to the high (for bearish) of the propulsion candle.

**Where do I enter a bullish propulsion block trade?**

At the body of the propulsion candlestick above the mean threshold (50%) on the retest, with bias-aligned higher-timeframe context.

**Where do I enter a bearish propulsion block trade?**

At the body of the propulsion candlestick below the mean threshold (50%) on the retest, with bias-aligned higher-timeframe context.

**Where is the stop loss?**

10 pips below the low of the propulsion candle (bullish) or 10 pips above the high (bearish).

**Where is the take profit?**

The next buy-side liquidity level for longs and the next sell-side liquidity level for shorts. Alternatively, stage exits using the ICT fib extensions (-1, -2, -2.5).

**Is the propulsion block reliable?**

Yes — it is one of the more reliable ICT entries because the stop is small and the reward-to-risk is high. Reliability improves further when the propulsion candle sits inside a higher-timeframe order block and the daily bias agrees.

**Can I use the propulsion block for scalping?**

Yes — on M1, M3 or M5. The setup mechanic is timeframe-agnostic; only the timeframe of identification changes.

**What if price closes through the mean threshold?**

The propulsion block has failed. The trade is invalid. Look for the next setup — do not chase price below the mean threshold on a bullish propulsion (or above it on a bearish propulsion).

**Does the propulsion block work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce textbook propulsion-block retests, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

# ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap: The Institutional Entry Hidden Behind the Breaker Block

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap/)

![ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap diagram showing the IFVG sitting deeper inside the dealing range, just before the Breaker Block, as the true institutional entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/REAPER-IFVG.png)

The ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap is an [Inversion Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>) that forms immediately before a [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) and serves as the true institutional entry point — the level price reaches after traders who entered at the Breaker have already been punished.

Rather than focusing only on the Breaker Block, the Reaper IFVG teaches you to look deeper into the dealing range, to the area where smart money is actually likely to become active. It is the hidden entry behind the obvious one.

This guide is the complete explainer for the ICT Reaper IFVG — what it is, why it carries that name, how it differs from the Breaker, the step-by-step trade flow I run for both the bullish and bearish version, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the questions I get asked most often. Used correctly, it improves your entries, reduces drawdown, and delivers a much stronger risk-to-reward than entering at the Breaker.

section: What is Fair Value Gap?
content:
#### What is Fair Value Gap?

An [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>) is a three-candle structure showing a gap between the high and the low of the first and third candles. The gap is created because price moved with such force that it did not retrace into that area, leaving an imbalance open on the chart.

Price tends to return to that imbalance later to rebalance it, which is why the Fair Value Gap is one of the most reliable entry arrays in the entire ICT method.

For the complete study of the Fair Value Gap, read the full [ICT Fair Value Gap guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap \(FVG\) Explained"). An example is shown below:

![ICT Fair Value Gap example — three-candle imbalance with an unfilled gap between the high and low of the first and third candles](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/FVG.png)

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: What is ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap?
content:
#### What is ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap?

The ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap is a failed Fair Value Gap — one that price did not respect. An IFVG forms when price closes beyond a Fair Value Gap, breaking it in the direction opposite to its original delivery. The level that once acted as support then flips to resistance, or resistance flips to support.

For the complete study of the Inversion Fair Value Gap, read the full [ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap guide](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/> "ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap \(IFVG\) Explained"). An example is shown below:

![ICT Inversion Fair Value Gap example — a fair value gap broken by a close in the opposite direction, flipping support to resistance](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-Inverse-Fair-Value-Gap.png)

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: What is ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap?
content:
#### What is ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap?

A Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap is an Inversion Fair Value Gap that sits immediately before a Breaker Block and serves as a refined institutional entry array. Think of it as the hidden entry behind the obvious entry. Most traders focus on the Breaker. Institutions often focus on the Reaper IFVG.

One of the biggest mistakes I see ICT traders make is assuming that every Breaker Block will immediately produce a continuation move. You identify a bullish Breaker, wait for price to retrace into it, enter long — and then the market continues lower. Before long your stop loss is hit, only for price to reverse from a deeper level and rally exactly as you originally anticipated. If that scenario sounds familiar, you are not alone.

This is precisely the problem the Reaper IFVG solves. It usually sits deeper within the dealing range and offers better pricing for institutional participation, which is why price frequently trades through the Breaker before finding support or resistance inside the Reaper IFVG.

The Reaper IFVG is an advanced ICT concept that explains why price so often trades beyond a Breaker Block before continuing in the intended direction. It shows you where institutions truly want to accumulate or distribute, and why many traders who enter directly at the Breaker simply become the liquidity for the next move. Understanding it can improve your entries, reduce your drawdown, and give you superior risk-to-reward. An illustration is shown below:

![ICT Reaper IFVG illustration — price trades through the Breaker Block into discount and finds support at the deeper Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ICT-Reaper-IFVG.png)

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Why Is It Called a Reaper IFVG?
content:
#### Why Is It Called a Reaper IFVG?

The name “Reaper” comes from what the market does before it reaches the Inversion Fair Value Gap. Most traders identify a Breaker Block and enter immediately, expecting price to continue in the anticipated direction.

Institutions, however, seek better pricing. Instead of respecting the Breaker right away, the market frequently trades beyond it — creating drawdown, triggering stop losses, and collecting liquidity from early participants. In a bullish setup, price may trade below the Breaker into discount before finding support at the Reaper IFVG. In a bearish setup, price may trade above the Breaker into premium before finding resistance at the Reaper IFVG.

The market effectively “reaps” the traders who entered too early at the Breaker before it ever reaches the true institutional entry zone. This is why many ICT traders prefer the Reaper IFVG over the Breaker itself — the Breaker attracts the crowd, while the Reaper IFVG is where institutions find the pricing they were looking for.

The Breaker attracts the crowd. The Reaper collects the crowd. Then the real move begins.

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Reaper IFVG vs Breaker Block
content:
#### Reaper IFVG vs Breaker Block

The Reaper IFVG and the Breaker Block sit at almost the same place on the chart, but they are traded very differently. The Breaker Block is the obvious, crowded level — the first place retail enters. The Reaper IFVG is the deeper imbalance inside the same price leg, where institutions actually find their fill.

In practice, the Breaker is the bait and the Reaper is the trap. When price taps the Breaker and keeps running against you, it is usually on its way to the Reaper IFVG. Treating the Breaker as your alert and the Reaper IFVG as your entry is the entire shift this concept asks you to make. For the standalone level, see the full [ICT Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) guide.

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: How to Trade the ICT Reaper IFVG?
content:
#### How to Trade the ICT Reaper IFVG?

The Reaper IFVG should never be traded in isolation. The highest-probability setups occur when it aligns with higher-timeframe bias, market structure, liquidity, and [premium and discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) concepts. Run the steps below in order for each direction.

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Trading a Bullish Reaper IFVG
content:
#### Trading a Bullish Reaper IFVG

  1. **Establish a bullish bias.** Start with the higher timeframe and confirm the market is bullish using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). Look for bullish market structure and draw a dealing range to identify discount pricing.
  2. **Identify the bullish Breaker.** Find a bearish [Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>) that has been violated to the upside and transformed into a Bullish Breaker Block.
  3. **Locate the Reaper IFVG.** Mark the Inversion Fair Value Gap immediately before the Bullish Breaker. This is your area of interest.
  4. **Wait for price to reach discount.** Rather than buying directly from the Breaker, allow price to retrace deeper into discount and reach the Reaper IFVG.
  5. **Look for confirmation.** As price enters the Reaper IFVG, look for signs that buyers are returning to the market: 
     * A lower-timeframe [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>)
     * Displacement to the upside
     * Rejection candles
     * A liquidity sweep followed by bullish displacement
  6. **Execute the trade.** Enter long after confirmation. Place the stop loss below the Reaper IFVG or below the recent swing low. Target previous highs, buy-side liquidity, equal highs, and higher-timeframe liquidity objectives.

A bullish Reaper IFVG trade setup is shown below:

![Bullish ICT Reaper IFVG trade setup — price sweeps below the Bullish Breaker into discount, finds support at the Reaper IFVG, MSS to the upside, long entry targeting previous highs](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ICT-BULLISH-REAPER-IFVG.png)

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Trading a Bearish Reaper IFVG
content:
#### Trading a Bearish Reaper IFVG

  1. **Establish a bearish bias.** Begin with higher-timeframe analysis and confirm the market is bearish. Identify premium pricing within the dealing range.
  2. **Identify the bearish Breaker.** Find a bullish Order Block that has been violated to the downside and transformed into a Bearish Breaker Block.
  3. **Locate the Reaper IFVG.** Mark the Inversion Fair Value Gap immediately before the Bearish Breaker.
  4. **Wait for price to reach premium.** Instead of selling directly from the Breaker, allow price to rally into premium and reach the Reaper IFVG.
  5. **Look for confirmation.** As price enters the Reaper IFVG, look for evidence that sellers are returning: 
     * A lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift (MSS)
     * Displacement to the downside
     * Rejection candles
     * A liquidity sweep followed by bearish displacement
  6. **Execute the trade.** Enter short after confirmation. Place the stop loss above the Reaper IFVG or above the recent swing high. Target previous lows, sell-side liquidity, equal lows, and higher-timeframe liquidity objectives.

A bearish Reaper IFVG trade setup is shown below:

![Bearish ICT Reaper IFVG trade setup — price sweeps above the Bearish Breaker into premium, finds resistance at the Reaper IFVG, MSS to the downside, short entry targeting previous lows](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ICT-BEARISH-REAPER-IFVG.png)

content:

The Reaper IFVG works best when the higher-timeframe context is clean. title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Reaper IFVG
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Reaper IFVG

A handful of repeatable errors account for most of the failed Reaper IFVG trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the setup converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Entering at the Breaker instead of waiting for the Reaper.** This is the whole reason the concept exists. If you enter at the obvious Breaker level, you are the liquidity the Reaper is built to collect. Treat the Breaker as the alert, not the entry.
  2. **Marking an IFVG that is not inside the Breaker price leg.** A valid Reaper IFVG lives within the Breaker leg and in the correct premium or discount zone. Any other inversion gap on the chart is not a Reaper, no matter how clean it looks.
  3. **Trading without higher-timeframe bias.** The Reaper IFVG is a refinement tool, not a standalone signal. Counter-bias setups fail far more often. Confirm the daily bias before you act.
  4. **Entering before confirmation.** Reaching the IFVG is not a buy or sell signal by itself. Wait for the Market Structure Shift, displacement, or rejection that proves participation has returned.
  5. **Placing the stop inside the IFVG.** A stop loss set too tight, inside the gap, gets tagged on the normal re-test wick. Place it below the Reaper IFVG or the recent swing low for longs, and above for shorts.

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: The Golden Rule
content:
#### The Golden Rule

A Reaper IFVG is always the Fair Value Gap found within the Breaker price leg. In a bullish market, the Reaper IFVG should sit in the discount area. In a bearish market, it should sit in the premium area.

Simply put: if the Fair Value Gap is not inside the Breaker price leg and not in the correct premium or discount zone, it is not a valid Reaper IFVG.

content:

The Reaper IFVG is the difference between entering where the crowd enters and entering where institutions enter. Once you stop trading the obvious Breaker and start waiting for the deeper inversion gap inside its price leg, your entries tighten, your stops shrink, and your risk-to-reward improves. Build it on top of the [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) and [Inversion Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>) foundations, and it becomes one of the highest-precision entries in the ICT method.

title: ict-reaper-inversion-fair-value-gap
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
#### Frequently Asked Questions

**What is an ICT Reaper Inversion Fair Value Gap?**

A Reaper IFVG is an Inversion Fair Value Gap that sits immediately before a Breaker Block, inside the Breaker price leg. It is the deeper, refined institutional entry that price often reaches after sweeping through the obvious Breaker level and collecting early traders’ stop losses.

**Why is it called a Reaper?**

Because the market “reaps” the traders who entered too early at the Breaker. Price trades beyond the Breaker, triggers their stops, and collects that liquidity before reversing from the true institutional entry — the Reaper IFVG.

**How is the Reaper IFVG different from the Breaker Block?**

The Breaker Block is the obvious, crowded level where retail enters. The Reaper IFVG is the deeper inversion gap inside the same price leg, where institutions find their fill. The Breaker is the bait; the Reaper is the entry.

**How do I identify a valid Reaper IFVG?**

It must be an Inversion Fair Value Gap located inside the Breaker price leg, and in the correct zone — discount for a bullish setup, premium for a bearish setup. If it is not inside the Breaker leg and in the right premium or discount area, it is not a valid Reaper IFVG.

**Where do I place my stop loss on a Reaper IFVG trade?**

Below the Reaper IFVG or the recent swing low for a long, and above the Reaper IFVG or the recent swing high for a short. Avoid placing the stop inside the gap, where a normal re-test wick will tag it.

**Should I enter as soon as price reaches the Reaper IFVG?**

No. Reaching the gap is the alert, not the entry. Wait for confirmation — a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift, displacement, a rejection candle, or a liquidity sweep followed by displacement — before executing.

**Which instruments work best for the Reaper IFVG?**

Before diving deep into the ICT reclaimed order block, you should be familiar with the [ICT Market Maker Buy Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-buy-model/> "ICT Market Maker Buy Model") and the [ICT Market Maker Sell Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-sell-model/> "ICT Market Maker Sell Model"). The reclaimed OB sits inside that broader framework.

This guide is part of the ICT Order Block family on this site. The parent [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>) guide covers the framework. The bullish and bearish sub-pillars are [Bullish OB](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bullish-order-block/>) and [Bearish OB](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bearish-order-block/>). Other OB-derivatives include the [propulsion block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-propulsion-block/>), [breaker block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>), [mitigation block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-mitigation-block-explained/>) and [rejection block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-rejection-block/>).

title: ict-reclaimed-order-block
section: What is an ICT Reclaimed Order Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Reclaimed Order Block?

Reclaimed order blocks are the areas where institutional traders accumulate their positions by hedging, and the market shows a minor displacement at that area.

Later on, these blocks are reclaimed and act as support or resistance to push price up or down.

As you know, the market moves like a curve and it has two sides.

**(I)** Buy side of the curve.

**(II)** Sell side of the curve.

In the case of the [Market Maker Buy Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-buy-model/> "Market Maker Buy Model"), the reclaimed order blocks are found on the sell side of the curve — where smart money accumulates buy positions before the market moves higher.

In the case of the [Market Maker Sell Model](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-maker-sell-model/> "Market Maker Sell Model"), reclaimed order blocks are found on the buy side of the curve — where institutional traders accumulate sell positions before the market moves down.

title: ict-reclaimed-order-block
section: Bullish Reclaimed Order Block
content:
#### Bullish Reclaimed Order Block

A bullish reclaimed order block is a candlestick that was previously used to buy price, and a short-term bounce confirms the minor displacement.

![Bullish ICT Reclaimed Order Block diagram — candlestick previously used to buy followed by a short-term bounce that confirms the minor displacement on the sell side of the curve](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/recliamed-order-block.png)

Bullish reclaimed order blocks are identifiable in the Market Maker Buy Model — when the market is in a bullish trend and, before moving higher, it moves down to sweep liquidity and approach a higher-timeframe [PD array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "PD Array").

In this scenario, when the market moves down before approaching the higher-timeframe PD array, smart money starts to accumulate buy positions.

Because they have deep pockets and large orders that cannot be fulfilled in a single transaction, they accumulate their positions by hedging on the sell side of the curve.

A **bullish reclaimed order block** is the last down-closed candle before the minor displacement, followed by an upward move on the sell side of the curve.

![ICT Bullish Reclaimed Order Block real chart example — price moves higher after shifting momentum to the buy side and reclaims the old block created on the sell side of the curve](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ict-reclaimed-order-block.png)

In the picture above you can see when price moves higher after shifting its momentum to the buy side, it reclaims the old block created on the sell side of the curve.

These blocks support price to move higher.

In fact, smart money uses these blocks again to enter the market and add to their long positions.

title: ict-reclaimed-order-block
section: Bearish Reclaimed Order Block
content:
#### Bearish Reclaimed Order Block

A bearish reclaimed order block is a candlestick that was previously used to sell price, and a short-term decline confirms the minor displacement.

![Bearish ICT Reclaimed Order Block diagram — candlestick previously used to sell followed by a short-term decline that confirms the minor displacement on the buy side of the curve](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-reclaimed-order-block.png)

These are identifiable in the Market Maker Sell Model. Before moving down, price moves up to approach a higher-timeframe PD array, which is called the buy side of the curve.

During the buy side of the curve, institutional traders (with deep pockets and large orders) start to accumulate their short orders, which create a short decline with minor displacement.

A **bearish reclaimed order block** is the last up-closed candlestick before the minor displacement, followed by a decline on the buy side of the curve.

Smart money uses these blocks during the sell side of the curve to add to their short positions.

![ICT Bearish Reclaimed Order Block real chart example — old blocks acting as resistance and pushing price downward during the sell side of the curve](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-bearish-reclaimed-order-block.png)

In the picture above you can see the old blocks acting as resistance and pushing price downward.

section: Step-by-Step Reclaimed Order Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Reclaimed Order Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a reclaimed order block.

  1. **Confirm the Market Maker model.** Bullish setup — Market Maker Buy Model. Bearish setup — Market Maker Sell Model.
  2. **Identify the curve direction.** Buy-side curve (price approaching the higher-timeframe PD array on the way up) or sell-side curve (price approaching the PD array on the way down).
  3. **Mark the higher-timeframe PD array.** Order block, FVG or breaker on the daily or H4.
  4. **Watch for accumulation candles.** Multiple small-bodied candles with minor displacement — institutional hedging in progress.
  5. **Identify the reclaimed OB candle.** Bullish — the last down-closed candle before the minor displacement on the sell-side curve. Bearish — the last up-closed candle before the minor displacement on the buy-side curve.
  6. **Wait for the reclaim.** Price must shift momentum and return to the reclaimed OB candle on the opposite-side curve.
  7. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry trigger and confirmation.
  8. **Enter on the retest.** Buy at the reclaimed OB on a bullish setup; sell at the reclaimed OB on a bearish setup.
  9. **Set the stop.** Below the low of the reclaimed OB (bullish) or above the high (bearish), with a small buffer.
  10. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high/low, relative equal level or higher-timeframe FVG.

The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) often delivers the reclaim of an earlier-session OB inside the Market Maker model — making the setup especially time-efficient on US-session trading.

#### Does Every ICT Reclaimed Order Block Work?

Not every ICT reclaimed order block is tradeable. Before taking any trade based on a reclaimed order block, look for extra confirmations on the lower timeframe — typically a Market Structure Shift, an SMT divergence on a correlated pair, or a fair value gap formed during the reclaim move.

Never risk more than 1% of your capital on a single trade setup.

title: ict-reclaimed-order-block
section: Common Mistakes Trading the Reclaimed Order Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the Reclaimed Order Block

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading reclaimed OBs.

  1. **Trading reclaimed OBs without the Market Maker model.** The reclaimed OB is defined inside the Market Maker Buy/Sell Model curve. Without that broader context, the candle is just an order block — the “reclaim” classification has no meaning.
  2. **Wrong side of the curve.** Bullish reclaimed OBs sit on the sell side of the curve. Bearish reclaimed OBs sit on the buy side. Reversing the side inverts the entire setup.
  3. **No lower-timeframe confirmation.** The reclaim retest alone is not the entry. A 5-minute or 1-minute MSS at the reclaimed OB is the trigger.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked at the body high/low of the reclaimed OB get hunted on the wick. Leave a small buffer.
  5. **Trading every old order block.** Most order blocks do not get reclaimed in the technical Market-Maker-model sense. The reclaimed OB requires the explicit hedging-and-displacement footprint, not every retraced OB.
  6. **Risking more than 1%.** Even high-conviction reclaimed OBs fail occasionally. The 1% per trade rule keeps you in the game through the inevitable losing streaks.

section: FAQs about the ICT Reclaimed Order Block
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Reclaimed Order Block

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the reclaimed OB.

**What is a reclaimed order block?**

A reclaimed order block is a candle or zone where institutional traders accumulated positions by hedging, with a minor displacement marking the accumulation. When price returns to the zone on a later leg, the block is “reclaimed” and acts as support (bullish) or resistance (bearish) for the next directional move.

**How is the reclaimed OB different from a regular order block?**

A regular order block is the last opposite-coloured candle before a strong impulse. A reclaimed order block is specifically tied to the Market Maker Buy/Sell Model — it sits on the opposite side of the curve from where the actual move is taken, and the “reclaim” happens when price returns to it during the directional leg.

**What is the bullish reclaimed order block?**

The bullish reclaimed OB is the last down-closed candle before a minor displacement on the sell side of the curve in a Market Maker Buy Model. Smart money accumulates long positions at this candle and price reclaims it on the way up.

**What is the bearish reclaimed order block?**

The bearish reclaimed OB is the last up-closed candle before a minor displacement on the buy side of the curve in a Market Maker Sell Model. Smart money accumulates short positions at this candle and price reclaims it on the way down.

**Where do I enter a reclaimed OB trade?**

At the body of the reclaimed OB candle on the retest, ideally with a lower-timeframe MSS confirmation on the 5-minute or 1-minute chart.

**Where is the stop loss?**

Below the low of the reclaimed OB (bullish) or above the high (bearish), with a small buffer.

**Where is the take profit?**

The next draw-on-liquidity in the trade direction — typically a relative equal high/low, the prior session high/low or an unfilled higher-timeframe FVG.

**Does every reclaimed OB work?**

No — not every reclaimed OB is tradeable. Always wait for lower-timeframe confirmation (MSS, SMT or FVG) before taking the entry, and never risk more than 1% per trade.

**What is the difference between reclaimed OB and breaker block?**

A breaker block is a failed order block that has been broken and now acts as the opposite zone (a flipped role). A reclaimed OB is a successful accumulation zone that gets reclaimed on the way to the directional target — it is not a flipped role; it remains support/resistance in the same direction.

**Does the reclaimed OB work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce textbook reclaimed OB setups inside Market Maker Buy/Sell Model patterns, especially during the New York AM session.

**How does the curve concept work?**

The market moves like a curve with two sides. The buy side is the upward leg of the curve, the sell side is the downward leg. In a Market Maker Buy Model, smart money accumulates buy positions on the sell side of the curve before pushing price up. The reclaim happens when price moves through the buy side and revisits the candles where the accumulation occurred.

content:
#### RDRB vs Fair Value Gap

The RDRB looks superficially similar to an FVG but the mechanic is different.

  * **Fair Value Gap (FVG)** — a 3-candle imbalance where the wicks of the 1st and 3rd candle do NOT overlap. The gap is visible on the chart.
  * **RDRB price range** — a 2-candle delivery-and-redelivery pattern where price moves, retraces leaving a wick, then redelivers in the same direction. The “range” is marked between the wicks of the surrounding candles, not between the RDRB candles themselves. The price-range area is “hidden” inside what looks like an efficient delivery.

Both work as PD arrays — support in a bullish setup, resistance in a bearish setup. The RDRB is the rarer and less-recognised variant.

#### FAQs about the ICT Redelivered Rebalanced Price Range

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the RDRB.

**What is the ICT Redelivered Rebalanced Price Range?**

The RDRB (also called RRPR) is a hidden PD array formed by two consecutive candlesticks where price delivers, retraces leaving a wick, then redelivers in the same direction. The price range is marked between the wicks of the candles immediately before and after the RDRB pair, and acts as support (bullish) or resistance (bearish).

**What does RDRB stand for in ICT?**

RDRB stands for Redelivered Rebalanced. The term refers to price that delivers in one direction, pulls back to rebalance, and then redelivers in the same direction.

**How is the RDRB different from a fair value gap?**

A fair value gap is a 3-candle wick-to-wick imbalance — there is a visible gap between the 1st and 3rd candle wicks. An RDRB is a 2-candle delivery-and-redelivery pattern with no visible gap. The RDRB is the “hidden” PD array; the FVG is the visible one.

**How do I identify an RDRB on the chart?**

Look for two consecutive candles where the first delivers in one direction and closes with a pull-back wick, and the second opens and continues in the same direction without a gap. Then mark the wicks of the candles immediately before and after this pair — the area between those wicks is the RDRB price range.

**Where is the RDRB price range marked?**

Between the wicks of the candle immediately before the RDRB pair and the candle immediately after the pair. NOT between the two RDRB candles themselves.

**How do I trade a bullish RDRB?**

After price retraces back into the bullish RDRB range, wait for a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift to the upside, then enter long. Stop below the opposite edge of the RDRB range, target the next draw on liquidity above.

**How do I trade a bearish RDRB?**

After price retraces back into the bearish RDRB range, wait for a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift to the downside, then enter short. Stop above the opposite edge of the RDRB range, target the next draw on liquidity below.

**Does the RDRB always work?**

No — like any PD array, the RDRB has a hit rate, not a guarantee. Bias-aligned RDRBs with a lower-timeframe MSS confirmation deliver the highest reliability. Counter-trend RDRBs often fail.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the opposite edge of the RDRB range, with a small buffer. For a bullish RDRB, below the lowest wick of the marked range. For a bearish RDRB, above the highest wick of the marked range.

**Where is the take profit?**

The next draw-on-liquidity in the trade direction — typically a relative equal high/low, the prior session high/low or an unfilled higher-timeframe FVG.

**Does the RDRB work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce RDRBs during clean directional legs, especially during the New York AM session.

# ICT Rejection Block — Wick Rejection Reversal Setup (Free PDF)

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-rejection-block/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-rejection-block/)

![ICT Rejection Block diagram showing the wick rejection at a swept extreme acting as a reversal zone](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Rejction-block-ict.png)

![ICT Rejection Block detailed example — long-tailed wick reversal at swept high or low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/ICT-rejection-Block-1024x539.png)

An ICT Rejection Block is the wick of a long-tailed candle that swept liquidity at a swing extreme, where the rejection itself becomes the reversal zone. It is one of the three “block trio” PD Arrays in the ICT toolkit, alongside the Breaker Block and the Mitigation Block, and it has a distinct role: the Rejection focuses on the wick, not the body.

The Rejection Block is what I look for after a clean wick rejection at a swept high or swept low. The candle body did not close past the extreme, but the wick speared into liquidity and reversed sharply. That wick — and the unfilled portion of it — is the entry zone for the reversal.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT Rejection Block — what it is, the bullish and bearish variants, the trade flow, the difference from a regular order block and from the other block types, the common mistakes, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: ict-rejection-block
section: What is an ICT Rejection Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Rejection Block?

An ICT Rejection Block is a wick rejection at a swing extreme. The candle reaches into liquidity above an old high or below an old low, the wick gets rejected, and the candle closes back inside the prior range. The wick — specifically the area between the candle’s open/close range and the extreme of the wick — becomes the Rejection Block.

The mechanism is simple: smart money used the wick to trigger retail stops sitting beyond the extreme, then snapped price back. The wick is the footprint of that liquidity raid. When price returns to the wick zone later, the same institutional level is in play, and the reversal often plays out a second time.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: (I) Bullish ICT Rejection Block
content:
#### (I) Bullish ICT Rejection Block

A bullish ICT Rejection Block forms at a swing low after a long-tailed bearish wick has swept liquidity below the low and reversed back inside the prior range.

The wick — the area between the body close of that candle and the low of the wick — is the Rejection Block. When price returns to that zone later, I expect a bullish reaction.

![Bullish ICT Rejection Block example — long bearish wick sweeps swing low, body closes back inside range, wick zone becomes bullish entry](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bullish-rejection-block.png)

**How to Trade the Bullish Rejection Block**

To trade a bullish Rejection Block, I follow this sequence:

  1. **Set a bullish daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-trick/>). Rejection Block trades only work in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  2. **Identify the swing low** that has been swept by a long-tailed bearish candle. The wick must extend clearly below the prior swing low and the candle must close back inside the range.
  3. **Mark the Rejection Block zone** — the wick area between the candle close and the candle low.
  4. **Wait for price to retrace** back to the wick zone. Do not chase the initial reversal leg.
  5. **Drop to a lower timeframe** (5-minute or 3-minute) at the wick tap and watch for a Market Structure Shift to the upside.
  6. **Execute the buy trade** on the wick tap with stop loss below the candle low (the deepest point of the wick), with a small buffer.
  7. **Take profit** at the next significant draw on liquidity — typically the recent swing high or the next old high.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: (II) Bearish ICT Rejection Block
content:
#### (II) Bearish ICT Rejection Block

A bearish ICT Rejection Block forms at a swing high after a long-tailed bullish wick has swept liquidity above the high and reversed back inside the prior range.

The wick — the area between the body close of that candle and the high of the wick — is the Rejection Block. When price returns to that zone later, I expect a bearish reaction.

![Bearish ICT Rejection Block example — long bullish wick sweeps swing high, body closes back inside range, wick zone becomes bearish entry](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/bearish-rejection-block.png)

**How to Trade the Bearish Rejection Block**

The flow mirrors the bullish version:

  1. **Set a bearish daily bias.**
  2. **Identify the swing high** that has been swept by a long-tailed bullish candle. Wick clearly above the prior high, body closes back inside.
  3. **Mark the Rejection Block zone** — the wick area between the candle close and the candle high.
  4. **Wait for price to retrace** back to the wick zone.
  5. **Drop to a lower timeframe** at the wick tap and watch for a Market Structure Shift to the downside.
  6. **Execute the sell trade** on the wick tap with stop loss above the candle high.
  7. **Take profit** at the next significant draw on liquidity — recent swing low or the next old low.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: ICT Rejection Block vs Order Block
content:
#### ICT Rejection Block vs Order Block

The Rejection Block and the Order Block are related but distinct PD Arrays.

A regular [Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>) is the body range of a candle that preceded a strong displacement leg. The trade is on the body of the OB candle.

A Rejection Block is the wick range of a candle that swept liquidity and reversed. The trade is on the wick, not the body.

Both are reversal-zone tools, but the Rejection Block is sharper because the wick gives a tighter, more precise entry zone than the OB body.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Rejection Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Rejection Block

Five mistakes show up in nearly every Rejection Block comment thread.

  1. **Trading every long-tailed wick as a Rejection Block.** Not every wick is a Rejection. The wick must sweep a clear swing extreme — not just any random spike. Without the swept extreme, the Rejection has no institutional context.
  2. **Stop loss too tight inside the wick.** The stop must sit beyond the deepest point of the wick (the candle high for bearish, the candle low for bullish), with a small buffer. Stops inside the wick get tagged routinely.
  3. **Trading Rejections against the daily bias.** Rejection Block trades work in the direction of the daily bias. Counter-bias Rejections fail far more often than aligned ones.
  4. **Confusing the Rejection with the Breaker.** A Rejection is a wick reversal — the body did not break the OB. A Breaker is a failed OB — the body closed past the extreme. They look similar at a glance but represent opposite trade ideas.
  5. **Forcing the trade in low-volatility windows.** Rejection setups in Asia lunch or NY lunch produce weaker reactions than in London open or NY AM. Pair the Rejection with a kill-zone time for the cleanest entries.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: Is the ICT Rejection Block Reliable for Trading?
content:
#### Is the ICT Rejection Block Reliable for Trading?

The Rejection Block is one of the most reliable single-candle reversal tools in the ICT method when used inside a clear daily bias and at a swept higher-timeframe extreme. The win rate I see on strict execution sits in the 55-65% range with a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-to-reward target.

The reliability degrades sharply outside those conditions: against the daily bias, on random wicks that did not sweep a real extreme, or in low-volatility sessions. The setup is high quality in the right context and a coin flip outside it.

title: ict-rejection-block
section: FAQs About the ICT Rejection Block
content:
#### FAQs About the ICT Rejection Block

**What is an ICT Rejection Block?**

An ICT Rejection Block is the wick of a long-tailed candle that swept liquidity at a swing extreme, where the wick zone becomes the entry on the retracement. The trade is on the wick, not the body.

**What is a bullish Rejection Block?**

A bullish Rejection Block forms at a swing low after a long bearish wick sweeps liquidity below the low and reverses back inside the prior range. The wick zone becomes the buy entry on the retrace.

**What is a bearish Rejection Block?**

A bearish Rejection Block forms at a swing high after a long bullish wick sweeps liquidity above the high and reverses back inside the prior range. The wick zone becomes the sell entry on the retrace.

**How is the Rejection Block different from an Order Block?**

An Order Block is the body range of a candle that preceded displacement. A Rejection Block is the wick range of a candle that swept liquidity and reversed. Same idea (reversal zone), different reference area (body vs wick).

**How is the Rejection Block different from the Breaker Block?**

A Rejection is a wick reversal — the body did not break the prior structure. A Breaker is a failed order block — the body closed past the extreme. Different mechanics, opposite trade direction.

**Where do I place stop loss on a Rejection Block trade?**

Beyond the deepest point of the wick — the candle high for a bearish Rejection, the candle low for a bullish Rejection — with a small buffer to absorb wick re-tests.

**What timeframe works best for the Rejection Block?**

1-hour and 4-hour for identification when validated against a daily extreme. The 5-minute or 3-minute for entry timing on the retrace.

**Is the ICT Rejection Block reliable?**

Yes, when used inside a clear daily bias and at a swept higher-timeframe extreme. Win rate on strict execution sits around 55–65% with a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-to-reward. Outside those conditions reliability drops sharply.
