# How to Trade ICT Seek and Destroy Friday – ICT Trading Strategy

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-seek-and-destroy-friday/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-seek-and-destroy-friday/)

![ICT Seek and Destroy Friday weekly profile chart showing Monday to Thursday consolidation and Friday two-sided liquidity sweep](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/seek-and-destroy.png)

I lost three NFP Fridays in a row before I learned to spot a Seek and Destroy week. The market would chop sideways Monday to Thursday, I’d convince myself a setup was forming, take an early entry, and watch price knife through both my stop loss and the next obvious one before continuing in the direction I had originally bet on. Painful lessons.

**ICT Seek and Destroy Friday** is the weekly profile where price consolidates from Monday to Thursday in front of a high-impact economic event — usually NFP or FOMC — and then on Friday the market sweeps both sides of that consolidation range to clear liquidity from longs and shorts before the real move. It is a neutral to low-probability profile and the cardinal rule is simple: you do not trade before the news release.

After the news, price hunts the stops on one side, displaces hard, then continues in the direction of the weekly order flow toward whatever higher-timeframe draw on liquidity is sitting above or below. That post-news move is the trade.

In this guide, I’ll show you what the Seek and Destroy profile actually looks like on a chart, how to recognize a Seek and Destroy week before Friday arrives, how to handle it in bullish vs bearish markets, and the exact steps to take an entry once the news has done its work.

Don’t worry — you don’t need to predict the news. You just need to wait for the sweep, then enter on confirmation.

Ready? Let’s break it down.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: What is ICT Seek and Destroy Friday?
content:
## What is ICT Seek and Destroy Friday?

ICT Seek and Destroy Friday is a weekly profile where price consolidates Monday through Thursday and then aggressively sweeps both sides of that consolidation range on Friday in front of — or right at the moment of — a high-impact economic event.

It is part of the family of [ICT weekly profiles](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-profiles/> "ICT Weekly Range Profiles"). Most weeks have a directional bias from the open. This one doesn’t. On Seek and Destroy weeks, Smart Money is engineering liquidity above the range high (where stops from short sellers sit) and below the range low (where stops from buyers sit), so when the news drops, both pools can be cleared and the real move can continue without retail traders along for the ride.

In ICT terminology, Friday becomes a manipulation day. The accumulation has already happened during the Mon-Thu consolidation. The distribution comes after the sweep, in the direction of the higher-timeframe weekly order flow.

Many traders fall into the trap of overtrading during the Mon-Thu chop, only to get stopped out when Friday arrives and price runs both directions. Recognizing the profile early is half the battle.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Why It Forms (The High-Impact News Setup)
content:
## Why It Forms (The High-Impact News Setup)

Seek and Destroy weeks form when the market is waiting for an event big enough to reset positioning. The two main triggers:

  * **NFP (Non-Farm Payroll)** — first Friday of every month, 8:30 AM New York time. Moves USD pairs and indices.
  * **FOMC** — eight times a year, Wednesday 2:00 PM New York time. The Wednesday FOMC creates a similar sweep dynamic earlier in the week.

Other catalysts that can produce a Seek and Destroy week: CPI, central bank rate decisions, major political events. The common factor is **uncertainty large enough that institutional desks don’t want to position before the print** , so they let price coil while engineering liquidity at the extremes of the range.

This is the engineered-liquidity phase. The high of the Mon-Thu range becomes a buy-side liquidity pool. The low becomes a sell-side liquidity pool. Friday’s job is to take both before the actual directional move begins.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: How to Spot a Seek and Destroy Week
content:
## How to Spot a Seek and Destroy Week

You can identify a Seek and Destroy week by Wednesday or Thursday — well before Friday’s news. Three confirming signs:

  1. **A high-impact event is on the calendar for Friday.** Check Forex Factory or your broker’s economic calendar for red-flagged events.
  2. **Monday-Thursday price action is sideways or shows irregular swings** — higher highs paired with lower lows, or low-range candles back and forth — instead of a clean directional drive.
  3. **Higher-timeframe weekly order flow has a clear bias** but the daily candles aren’t honoring it. That divergence (clear weekly direction + range-bound daily action) is the tell.

If all three are true, treat the rest of the week as Seek and Destroy. Do not take counter-trend entries. Do not chase mid-range fakeouts. Wait for Friday.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: ICT Seek and Destroy Friday in Bullish and Bearish Markets
content:
## ICT Seek and Destroy Friday in Bullish and Bearish Markets

The setup is symmetric. Same mechanic, opposite direction.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: (I) Bullish Market
content:
### (I) Bullish Market

In a typical bullish market, prices form higher highs and higher lows. During a Seek and Destroy week, that pattern stalls — the market either consolidates Mon-Thu or shows an irregular pattern of higher highs paired with lower lows as Smart Money positions for the news.

On Friday, after the news drops, price sweeps **sell-side liquidity** below the consolidation low first (clearing the stops of buyers) and then **displaces aggressively to the upside** in line with the weekly bullish bias.

How to trade it:

  1. **Avoid trading before the news release.** No exceptions.
  2. **Wait for the sell-side[liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/> "ICT Liquidity Sweep")** — price taking out the Mon-Thu range low after the news.
  3. **Watch for price to trade back into the range.** This is the institutional fingerprint.
  4. **Drop to a lower timeframe** (5m or 15m) and look for a [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") or a [Change in State of Delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/> "ICT CISD") to the upside.
  5. **Enter long** on the close of the MSS / CISD candle or a clean retest. Stop loss below the swept low.
  6. **Target the next higher-timeframe draw on liquidity** — the most recent significant high, the previous week’s high, or the daily / weekly bullish order flow target.

![ICT Seek and Destroy Friday bullish example: price sweeps sell-side liquidity below the Mon-Thu range low after news release, then displaces upward in line with weekly bullish order flow](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/seek-and-destroy-friday-in-bullish-market-1024x442.png)

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: (II) Bearish Market
content:
### (II) Bearish Market

In a typical bearish market, prices form lower highs and lower lows. During a Seek and Destroy week, that pattern stalls — the market either consolidates Mon-Thu or shows an irregular pattern of lower lows paired with higher highs.

On Friday, after the news drops, price sweeps **buy-side liquidity** above the consolidation high first (clearing the stops of sellers) and then **displaces aggressively to the downside** in line with the weekly bearish bias.

How to trade it:

  1. **Avoid trading before the news release.**
  2. **Wait for the buy-side liquidity sweep** — price taking out the Mon-Thu range high after the news.
  3. **Watch for price to trade back into the range.**
  4. **Drop to a lower timeframe** and look for an MSS or CISD to the downside.
  5. **Enter short** on the close of the MSS / CISD candle or a clean retest. Stop loss above the swept high.
  6. **Target the next higher-timeframe sell-side draw** — the most recent significant low, the previous week’s low, or the daily / weekly bearish order flow target.

![ICT Seek and Destroy Friday bearish example: price sweeps buy-side liquidity above the Mon-Thu range high after news release, then displaces downward in line with weekly bearish order flow](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ICT-seek-and-Destroy-Friday-1-1024x436.png)

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: How to Trade Seek and Destroy Friday — Step by Step
content:
## How to Trade Seek and Destroy Friday — Step by Step

The unified trading flow, regardless of bias direction:

  1. **Confirm the profile by Thursday.** High-impact news on Friday + range-bound Mon-Thu action + clear higher-timeframe weekly bias.
  2. **Mark the Mon-Thu range high and low.** These are your liquidity pools.
  3. **Stand aside until the news release.** Do not pre-position. Do not “scalp the chop”.
  4. **Watch which side gets swept first after the news.** The opposite side is your entry direction.
  5. **Wait for price to return to the range** — the sweep needs to be followed by a retracement back toward the middle.
  6. **Drop to a 5m or 15m chart** and look for an MSS or CISD in the direction opposite the sweep.
  7. **Enter on confirmation.** Stop just beyond the swept extreme. Target the next higher-timeframe draw on liquidity.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest Seek and Destroy trades happen when the post-sweep [displacement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/> "ICT Displacement") leaves a clean Fair Value Gap or breaker block on the way back into the range. If price comes back to fill that imbalance before continuing, you get a second entry with even better risk-to-reward. Skip Seek and Destroy weeks where the higher-timeframe weekly order flow is unclear — without a known directional target, you have no reason to take the trade.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Bonus Tip: Pairing With Weekly Profiles and Daily Bias
content:
## Bonus Tip: Pairing With Weekly Profiles and Daily Bias

Seek and Destroy Friday is one of several [ICT weekly profiles](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-profiles/> "ICT Weekly Range Profiles"). The profile you’re in changes everything about which day you take the trade and which direction you expect the run.

Before you commit to a Seek and Destroy week, run through your higher-timeframe checklist:

  * **What is the weekly bias?** If unclear, sit out — no directional target means no trade.
  * **What is the[daily bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/> "ICT Daily Bias") heading into Friday?** It should align with the post-sweep direction you expect.
  * **Which side is the obvious liquidity?** Smart Money will go for the largest pool first.

The Seek and Destroy entry is just the [Power of 3](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/> "ICT Power of 3") compressed into one Friday session — accumulation Mon-Thu, manipulation at the news, distribution after. Reading it through that frame makes the setup obvious.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the ICT Seek and Destroy Friday profile?

ICT Seek and Destroy Friday is a weekly profile where price consolidates from Monday through Thursday in front of a high-impact economic event (like NFP or FOMC), then on Friday sweeps both sides of the consolidation range to clear liquidity before continuing in the direction of weekly order flow.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: When does Seek and Destroy Friday usually happen?
content:
### When does Seek and Destroy Friday usually happen?

Most often on the first Friday of the month (NFP) or in weeks containing FOMC, CPI, central bank rate decisions, or other red-flagged news events. Always check the economic calendar to identify candidate weeks.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Should I trade before the news release on a Seek and Destroy Friday?
content:
### Should I trade before the news release on a Seek and Destroy Friday?

No. The cardinal rule of the profile is that you stand aside until the news has dropped and the liquidity sweep has happened. Pre-news entries get caught in the engineered moves on both sides of the range.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: How do I know which side will sweep first?
content:
### How do I know which side will sweep first?

The side opposite to your expected post-news direction. If the higher-timeframe weekly order flow is bullish, expect the sell-side (low of the range) to be swept first. If bearish, expect the buy-side (high of the range) to be swept first.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: What confirmation do I use for entry after the sweep?
content:
### What confirmation do I use for entry after the sweep?

A Market Structure Shift or a Change in State of Delivery on a lower timeframe (5-minute or 15-minute), in the direction opposite the sweep. Do not enter on the sweep candle itself — wait for the structural confirmation that price has rejected the swept extreme.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Is Seek and Destroy Friday the same as a stop hunt?
content:
### Is Seek and Destroy Friday the same as a stop hunt?

Stop hunting is the mechanism — the engineered liquidity grab. Seek and Destroy Friday is the weekly profile in which Smart Money does it twice (once on each side of the Mon-Thu range) before delivering the actual move. So a Seek and Destroy Friday contains stop hunts, but a stop hunt by itself doesn’t necessarily mean you’re in a Seek and Destroy week.

title: ict-seek-and-destroy-friday
section: Wrapping Up
content:
## Wrapping Up

We hope this guide helped you understand the ICT Seek and Destroy Friday profile and how to trade it without getting caught in the chop.

The profile shows up roughly once a month around NFP, plus FOMC weeks and other major events. The discipline that separates traders who profit from these weeks from traders who blow accounts is simple: you wait. You wait through the consolidation. You wait for the news. You wait for the sweep. Then — and only then — you take the entry.

Pull up your chart this Sunday and check the calendar for Friday. If there’s a red-flagged event, watch how Mon-Thu plays out. By Thursday close you’ll know whether you’re in a Seek and Destroy week.

Like most ICT concepts, the Silver Bullet strategy is a time-based algorithmic trading model built on liquidity and fair value gaps. It is designed to capture short-term liquidity in a single one-hour window, which makes it the cleanest scalping setup in the ICT toolkit.

The Silver Bullet happens three times every trading day:

London Session Open Silver Bullet — 03:00 AM to 04:00 AM (New York local time).

New York AM Session — 10:00 AM to 11:00 AM (New York local time).

New York PM Session — 02:00 PM to 03:00 PM (New York local time).

You do not need to sit at the screen all day to trade this model. You only need to be at the chart during the one-hour window of whichever session fits your schedule. Each window is designed to deliver a 20–30 pip move on a clean setup.

section: What is the ICT Silver Bullet Strategy?
content:
#### What is the ICT Silver Bullet Strategy?

The ICT Silver Bullet strategy is a time-based algorithmic trading model built on [Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>) and the [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>). It runs three times a day in a one-hour window each session.

As Michael Huddleston, the founder of ICT, put it: “To quit your job, you need something that repeats every day and yields five handles.” The Silver Bullet is what he was talking about — it repeats every session, every day, and a single clean setup can deliver 20–30 pips.

**How the ICT Silver Bullet Strategy Works**

Price moves for two reasons: to balance an imbalance in delivery, or to take liquidity. The Silver Bullet is built on both of those mechanics.

Before the Silver Bullet window opens, I mark the nearest buy-side and sell-side liquidity on the 15-minute chart. Those two levels become the reference for the session.

If price has already [swept the liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) on one side, it tends to rotate to the other side to grab the opposite liquidity. If price has run beyond a level instead of sweeping it, it tends to continue in that direction toward the next pool.

When the Silver Bullet window opens, I drop to a 1-minute or 3-minute chart and watch for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) in the direction of the next draw on liquidity.

After the MSS, I mark the fair value gap left behind during the displacement leg. I use the [premium and discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) framework to confirm the FVG is in the right zone relative to the recent swing.

When price retraces back to that fair value gap, I execute the scalp.

This is how a clean Silver Bullet looks on the chart.

![ICT Silver Bullet trade example — liquidity sweep, market structure shift, and FVG entry inside the one-hour window](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ICT-Silver-Bullet-Trading-Strategy.png)

#### Step-by-Step Silver Bullet Checklist

This is the exact checklist I run before every Silver Bullet session. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Mark the buy-side and sell-side liquidity** on the 15-minute chart before the window opens.
  2. **Wait for the Silver Bullet window to open** — 03:00 AM, 10:00 AM, or 02:00 PM New York local time. Do not pre-position.
  3. **Drop to 1-minute or 3-minute** for execution. The 5-minute can be used for the parent read.
  4. **Watch for a Market Structure Shift** in the direction of the next draw on liquidity.
  5. **Confirm displacement** on the MSS leg — the breaking candle should close decisively and leave a fair value gap behind.
  6. **Mark the fair value gap** created during the displacement leg.
  7. **Validate the FVG sits in the correct premium or discount zone** relative to the most recent swing.
  8. **Wait for price to retrace into the FVG**. Do not chase the displacement leg.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the FVG tap, with stop loss beyond the candle that created the FVG and a take profit at the next liquidity pool — typically a 1:3 risk-reward target.
  10. **Close the trade or trail the stop** within the same session. The Silver Bullet is a scalp, not a swing.

**(I)** Previous day high / low draw on liquidity.

**(II)** Previous session high / low draw on liquidity.

**(III)** Established high / low on the 15-minute chart.

**(VI)** Expansion away from the current or old week opening gap.

**(VII)** Relative equal highs or lows.

The first three are the strongest references because they cluster the most resting orders. The lower four are intraday refinements.

content:
#### Win Rate and Realistic Expectations

The Silver Bullet is not a magic strategy. The win rate I see on a strict execution of the checklist is in the 55–65% range, with a 1:3 average risk-reward target — which is enough to be profitable as long as the rules are honoured.

Two factors degrade the win rate fast: (a) trading outside the one-hour window, and (b) entering before the market structure shift confirms. Both account for the majority of losing setups in the comments I get on this strategy.

Beginners should expect six to twelve months of demo work before risking real capital on the Silver Bullet. A hundred logged setups on the 5-minute chart is a reasonable benchmark before going live.

section: How Daylight Saving Time Affects the ICT Silver Bullet Times
content:
#### How Daylight Saving Time Affects the ICT Silver Bullet Times

Daylight Saving Time (DST) is the US practice of moving clocks forward one hour in spring and back one hour in autumn. The clocks “spring forward” on the second Sunday of March and “fall back” on the first Sunday of November, both at 02:00 AM local.

If your country does not follow DST, the Silver Bullet times in your local time zone shift by one hour twice a year — once in March and once in November.

If your country does follow DST, no adjustment is needed. The session times in NY local stay the same.

The cleanest fix is the one Huddleston himself recommends: regardless of where you live, follow New York local time as the base time. The Silver Bullet windows do not move in NY local time — only the time-zone label changes from EST (Eastern Standard Time) to EDT (Eastern Daylight Time) twice a year.

content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Silver Bullet

Five mistakes show up in nearly every Silver Bullet comment thread on the site. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading outside the one-hour window.** The Silver Bullet is a time-based model. Setups outside the window are not Silver Bullet setups, even when the chart pattern looks identical. The clock matters more than the pattern.
  2. **Entering before the market structure shift confirms.** A liquidity raid alone is not a signal. Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS and the displacement candle close before acting. A wick poke into the FVG without an MSS first is a setup that fails far more often than it works.
  3. **Stop loss too tight on the FVG candle.** Place the stop beyond the wick of the candle that created the fair value gap, with a small buffer. Stops sitting one pip beyond the FVG are routinely tagged before the trade resolves.
  4. **Trading the wrong session for your instrument.** US index futures trade cleanest on the New York AM Silver Bullet. Forex majors trade well on London open and NY AM. Picking the wrong session for the instrument shows up as a low-quality setup.
  5. **Exiting before the trade plays out.** The Silver Bullet setup forms inside the window but can take longer than the window to deliver. Honour the original stop and target — do not close the trade early just because the clock has rolled past the window.

# ICT SMT Divergence Explained — Smart Money Technique with Examples + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-smt-divergence-smart-money-technique/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-smt-divergence-smart-money-technique/)

![ICT SMT Divergence diagram showing two correlated assets exhibiting opposing structure as a reversal signal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-SMT-divergence.png)

ICT SMT divergence is a market condition where two correlated assets — viewed on the same timeframe — exhibit opposing price structure. It is one of the cleanest reversal-confirmation tools in the ICT toolkit because it reads order flow across two instruments instead of one.

In two positively correlated assets, SMT shows up as one asset forming a higher low while the other forms a lower low instead of the higher low (GBP/USD vs EUR/USD).

In two negatively correlated assets, SMT shows up as one asset forming a higher low while the other forms a lower high instead of the expected higher high (GBP/USD vs USDX).

ICT SMT divergence helps me identify key reversal points using two correlated instruments. When one fails to follow the other, smart money is positioning ahead of the reversal — that is the inflection.

This guide is the full breakdown of ICT SMT divergence — what it is, how positive and negative correlation work, the bullish and bearish variants, the trade flow, the best timeframes and pairs, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-smt-divergence-smart-money-technique
section: What is ICT SMT Divergence?
content:
#### What is ICT SMT Divergence?

ICT SMT — also known as Smart Money Technique — is a market condition where two correlated assets, viewed on the same timeframe, exhibit opposing structure.

Most of the time, financial markets move symmetrically: when two assets are positively correlated and one prints a higher high, the other typically prints a higher high too.

But sometimes the correlated assets diverge from each other. If one prints a higher high and the second one fails to print a higher high, that mismatch is SMT divergence.

![SMT divergence example showing two correlated assets diverging — one prints higher high, the other fails to follow](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SMT-DIvergence-2.png)

**How I Use ICT SMT**

I use SMT divergence as the primary reversal signal between two correlated assets.

When two positively correlated assets are moving higher and one prints a higher high while the other fails to do so, the higher high in the first asset is most likely a deceptive move. The overall market condition is weak, and the divergence is signalling the turning point.

I use SMT divergence between two correlated assets as a confirmation of trade entry whenever they tap a higher-timeframe [ICT PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>). The PD Array marks the price; the SMT marks the timing.

A real chart example is shown below.

![Real chart example of ICT SMT divergence between two correlated assets at higher-timeframe PD Array tap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SMT-DIvergence-1.png)

section: Types of ICT SMT Divergence
content:
#### Types of ICT SMT Divergence

By market direction, SMT divergence splits into two clean types.

**(I) Bullish SMT Divergence**

In two positively correlated assets, bullish SMT divergence prints when both are moving lower but one asset makes a lower low while the other makes a higher low.

In two negatively correlated assets, bullish SMT divergence prints when one asset makes a lower high while the other makes a lower low instead of the expected higher low.

The asset making the lower low instead of the higher low is the manipulating leg. The SMT divergence in this case signals a bullish reversal.

![Bullish SMT divergence chart example — one asset prints lower low, correlated asset prints higher low, signalling bullish reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Bullish-SMT.png)

**(II) Bearish SMT Divergence**

In two positively correlated assets, bearish SMT divergence prints when both are moving higher but one asset makes a higher high while the other makes a lower high.

![Bearish SMT divergence chart example — one asset prints higher high, correlated asset prints lower high, signalling bearish reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Bearish-SMT-divergence.png)

In two negatively correlated assets, bearish SMT divergence prints when one asset makes a higher low while the other makes a lower high instead of the expected higher high.

The asset making the lower high instead of the higher high is the manipulating leg. The SMT divergence in this case signals a bearish reversal.

#### Step-by-Step SMT Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when I want to use SMT as a trade trigger. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Identify the correlated pair** for the instrument you are trading — EUR/USD vs GBP/USD, ES vs NQ, BTC vs ETH, or the negative-correlation equivalents.
  2. **Pull both charts side by side** on the same timeframe (preferably 15-minute or lower for execution).
  3. **Mark the higher-timeframe PD Array** on the asset you intend to trade — daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour.
  4. **Wait for both assets to approach a swing high or swing low** at the PD Array tap.
  5. **Compare the two assets** at that swing — one prints a new extreme, the other fails to.
  6. **Confirm the divergence** by reading the structure on both charts simultaneously. The non-confirming leg is the SMT signal.
  7. **Execute the trade** in the direction the divergence suggests, with stop loss beyond the swept extreme of the asset you are trading.
  8. **Take profit** at the next significant liquidity pool or the opposing extreme of the higher-timeframe PD Array.

Five mistakes show up in nearly every SMT comment thread on the site. Avoid these and the signal converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Reading SMT without a higher-timeframe PD Array.** SMT in isolation is just two charts looking different. Inside a tap of a daily or 4-hour PD Array, that same divergence becomes a high-probability reversal trigger. The PD Array is the context.

**What is the best timeframe for SMT divergence?**

15-minute or lower for execution. Higher timeframes take too long to print the divergence, and the entry window typically closes before the signal completes.

SMT alone is just structure on two charts. It is far more reliable when paired with a higher-timeframe PD Array tap, the daily bias, and ideally a confirming Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe.

# ICT STL ITL & LTL – Advance Market Structure

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/)

![ICT advanced market structure showing STL, ITL, and LTL hierarchy of lows on a price chart](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ICT-STL-ITL-LTL.png)

I spent the first year of my ICT trading labelling every swing low the same way. Every reaction looked equally important. Every dip looked like the bottom. Then I read about the ICT hierarchy of lows — Short Term, Intermediate Term, Long Term — and the chart finally made sense. Some lows are noise. Some lows are turning points. Knowing which is which is the entire game.

In ICT, **STL stands for Short Term Low, ITL stands for Intermediate Term Low, and LTL stands for Long Term Low.** These three labels rank every swing low on your chart by importance. The highest rank — LTL — marks the levels that decide whether a market is still bearish or has lost its trend.

In this guide, I will show you exactly how each of these lows is identified, the hierarchy that connects them, the rule I use for reading bearish market structure, and how to use the three labels in actual trading.

If you also want the highs side of advanced market structure (STH, ITH, LTH), see our companion post on the [ICT Advance Market Structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/> "ICT Advance Market Structure").

Do not worry — once you have seen the three-candle pattern a few times, identifying STLs, ITLs, and LTLs becomes mechanical.

Ready? Let us break it down.

Table of Contents

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: What Are STL, ITL, and LTL in ICT?
content:
## What Are STL, ITL, and LTL in ICT?

In ICT trading, every swing low on your chart belongs to one of three tiers:

  * **STL — Short Term Low.** A basic three-candle swing low.
  * **ITL — Intermediate Term Low.** An STL with a higher STL on each side.
  * **LTL — Long Term Low.** An ITL with a higher ITL on each side, usually at a higher-timeframe PD Array.

Each tier is a stricter version of the one before it. An STL is just a local dip. An ITL is a meaningful low because the dips around it were shallower. An LTL is a structural low because the meaningful lows around it were shallower still. The deeper you go in the hierarchy, the more weight that low carries for the larger trend.

The [market structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/market-structure-in-trading/> "Market Structure in Trading") on a chart is, at heart, the combination of highs and lows. But not every high or low matters equally. STL, ITL, and LTL give you the language to tell the noise from the structure.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: Why These Lows Matter (The Hierarchy of Market Structure)
content:
## Why These Lows Matter (The Hierarchy of Market Structure)

Every retail trader can mark a low. The hard part is knowing which low matters.

When price prints a fresh local dip, you do not yet know if it is a Short Term Low that will be broken five candles later, an Intermediate Term Low that defines the current pullback, or a Long Term Low that holds a trend together. The hierarchy gives you a procedural answer: wait for the swing-low neighbours on each side, then label accordingly.

This matters in two practical situations:

  * **Identifying the trend.** A bearish market is one printing lower LTLs and lower LTHs. A bullish market is the inverse. Without LTL labelling, you are guessing whether a pullback is healthy or whether the trend has changed.
  * **Anticipating reversals.** LTLs that form after a reaction at a higher-timeframe PD Array are high-probability turning points. Knowing one has formed lets you watch for confirmation rather than guessing the bottom.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: (I) ICT Short Term Low (STL)
content:
## (I) ICT Short Term Low (STL)

ICT STL — Short Term Low — is basically a [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "ICT Swing Low") being a three-candle formation in such a way that the low (wick) of the 2nd (middle) candle is lower than the low of both candles — the 1st on the left and the 3rd on the right of it.

So the low of the 2nd (middle) candle is termed as the Short Term Low (STL).

![ICT Short Term Low \(STL\) example: a three-candle swing low with the middle candle wick lower than the left and right candles](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/short-term-low-STL.png)

Every dip on a chart that meets this three-candle test is an STL. They are common, they are everywhere, and they are the building block of the next two tiers.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: (II) ICT Intermediate Term Low (ITL)
content:
## (II) ICT Intermediate Term Low (ITL)

The word “intermediate” refers to something that is in the middle, or between two stages. So the ICT Intermediate Term Low (ITL) is basically a Short Term Low — but with a **higher Short Term Low on the left and right side of it**.

It is in the middle of two short term lows, and it is lower than both the left and right short term lows.

![ICT Intermediate Term Low \(ITL\) example: a Short Term Low flanked by two higher Short Term Lows on each side](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Intermediate-TERM-LOW-ITL.png)

ITLs are less common than STLs. Each ITL marks a deeper dip that the surrounding STLs failed to match — a sign that the move into that low had real momentum.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: (III) ICT Long Term Low (LTL)
content:
## (III) ICT Long Term Low (LTL)

An ICT Long Term Low (LTL) is also an Intermediate Term Low by nature, but it is mostly formed at a higher-timeframe [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array") after a reaction of price.

A Long Term Low (LTL) is indicated by an Intermediate Term Low in the middle of two Intermediate Term Lows. It is the lowest Intermediate Term Low, having a higher Intermediate Term Low on the left and right side of it.

![ICT Long Term Low \(LTL\) example: an Intermediate Term Low flanked by two higher Intermediate Term Lows, formed at a higher-timeframe PD Array](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Long-term-low-LTL.png)

LTLs are the most weighted lows on your chart. Each one is a structural anchor — until it is broken, the larger trend it belongs to remains intact.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: Reading Bearish Market Structure With LTLs and LTHs
content:
## Reading Bearish Market Structure With LTLs and LTHs

In bearish market structure, price will make lower Long Term Lows and lower long-term highs.

If price is supposed to go lower, it should not violate the recent lower long-term high.

This is the rule that decides whether a bearish trend is still alive. As long as each new long-term high prints below the previous long-term high, and each new long-term low prints below the previous long-term low, the bearish structure is intact. The moment price closes above a recent long-term high, the structure has changed and the bias must be re-evaluated.

The same rule mirrors for bullish markets — higher LTLs and higher long-term highs, and the structure stays bullish as long as price does not violate the most recent long-term low.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: How to Use STL, ITL, and LTL in Your Trading
content:
## How to Use STL, ITL, and LTL in Your Trading

The hierarchy is a labelling system, not an entry signal on its own. Here is how it integrates into a trade:

  1. **Mark the LTLs first.** Identify the highest-tier lows on your bias timeframe. These define the trend.
  2. **Mark the ITLs.** These define the active swing structure inside the trend.
  3. **Mark the STLs.** These give you reaction levels for shorter-term entries.
  4. **Watch the most recent long-term high.** As long as it holds (in a bearish trend), you can keep selling pullbacks. If it breaks, the bias has shifted.
  5. **Use LTLs as targets.** A bullish trade looking for room runs to the next opposing level — often a recent LTH. Same logic mirrored for shorts.
  6. **Use ITLs and STLs as entry zones.** When price retraces back into an ITL or STL during a continuation move, that is your refined entry area.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest LTL trades happen when the LTL forms inside a higher-timeframe PD Array — a [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap"), [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block"), or [breaker block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block"). The PD Array is the institutional level. The LTL is the structural confirmation. When both line up, the level holds with conviction.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: Bonus Tip: Pair STL, ITL, LTL With STH, ITH, LTH
content:
## Bonus Tip: Pair STL, ITL, LTL With STH, ITH, LTH

The lows side is only half of advanced market structure. The highs side — STH (Short Term High), ITH (Intermediate Term High), and LTH (Long Term High) — uses the same three-candle hierarchy in reverse.

Read the lows for support structure, read the highs for resistance structure, and the chart tells you exactly where the trend is and what it has to break to change direction. For the full highs walkthrough, see [ICT Advance Market Structure — STH, ITH & LTH](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/> "ICT Advance Market Structure - STH ITH LTH").

For the underlying market-structure framework that ties highs and lows together, see [Market Structure in Trading](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/market-structure-in-trading/> "Market Structure in Trading").

content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What does ITL mean in trading?

ITL stands for Intermediate Term Low. It is an ICT market structure label for a Short Term Low that has a higher Short Term Low on each side of it — making it the lowest STL in a sequence of three.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: What is the full form of STL, ITL, and LTL?
content:
### What is the full form of STL, ITL, and LTL?

STL is Short Term Low, ITL is Intermediate Term Low, and LTL is Long Term Low. All three are ICT labels for swing lows ranked by structural importance.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: How is an LTL different from an ITL?
content:
### How is an LTL different from an ITL?

An LTL is an ITL with a higher ITL on each side of it — making it the lowest ITL in a sequence of three. An LTL is also typically formed at a higher-timeframe PD Array. The hierarchy is STL → ITL → LTL, with each tier requiring two same-tier neighbours that are higher.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: How is an STL identified on a chart?
content:
### How is an STL identified on a chart?

An STL is a three-candle swing low. The low of the middle candle must be lower than the low of both the candle to its left and the candle to its right. The middle candle is then marked as the STL.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: What is the difference between an STL and a regular swing low?
content:
### What is the difference between an STL and a regular swing low?

In ICT, STL is the specific name for the standard three-candle swing low. A swing low and an STL are the same thing in ICT terminology — the abbreviation is just the labelling system used to rank lows by tier.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: How does a bearish market behave with these lows?
content:
### How does a bearish market behave with these lows?

In a bearish market, price will print lower LTLs and lower long-term highs. The trend is intact as long as the most recent long-term high is not violated. The moment price closes above that high, the bearish structure has shifted.

title: ict-stl-itl-ltl
section: Which timeframe should I use to mark STL, ITL, and LTL?
content:
### Which timeframe should I use to mark STL, ITL, and LTL?

Mark LTLs on your bias timeframe (Daily or 4-hour for swing trading; 1-hour for intraday). ITLs sit on the same timeframe but are less frequent. STLs can be marked on the bias timeframe or one timeframe lower for refined entries.

# ICT Suspension Block (2025) — New PD Array Suspended Between Volume Imbalances + Examples

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-suspension-block/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-suspension-block/)

![ICT Suspension Block — single candlestick suspended between two volume imbalances \(one above, one below\) with the body fully overlapped by the prior candle's wick](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Suspension-Block-ICT.png)

In September 2025, Michael Huddleston (the ICT) introduced a brand-new [PD array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "PD Array") named the ICT Suspension Block.

This PD array is named the suspension block because it is suspended between two volume imbalances — one on the upside and the other on the downside.

It is fundamentally a candlestick that has a wick overlapping its body on the left side, so there is no chance of a [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "FVG") formation. But it has a volume imbalance on the top and a volume imbalance on the bottom — and that combination acts like an FVG would as a support or resistance level.

In this guide I walk you through the suspension block — the volume-imbalance prerequisite, the bullish and bearish setups, the entry sequence with MSS confirmation, the common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can continue reading the whole article or jump to the section you are most interested in.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: ict-suspension-block
section: What is an ICT Volume Imbalance?
content:
#### What is an ICT Volume Imbalance?

An ICT Volume Imbalance is a price inefficiency that occurs when buy and sell orders fail to match efficiently, creating a body-to-body gap between consecutive candles.

**Bullish Volume Imbalance:**

The second candle opens above the prior candle’s close, forming a body gap.

**Bearish Volume Imbalance:**

The second candle opens below the prior candle’s close, forming a body gap.

Wick overlap is acceptable — what defines the imbalance is the body separation.

These zones highlight areas of inefficient price delivery, which the market often revisits to restore balance.

You can see the example of ICT Volume Imbalance in the picture below.

![ICT Volume Imbalance diagram — body-to-body gap between consecutive candles, with wick overlap allowed and the body separation defining the imbalance](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Volume-Imbalance.png)

title: ict-suspension-block
section: What is the ICT Suspension Block?
content:
#### What is the ICT Suspension Block?

The ICT Suspension Block is a single candlestick that has a volume imbalance at the top and a volume imbalance at the bottom — so it is suspended between two volume imbalances.

Its body should be completely overlapped by a wick on the left side, so there is no chance of a Fair Value Gap formation.

This candlestick’s body along with the two volume imbalances will act just like the FVG — as support or resistance for the price.

You can see the example of the ICT Suspension Block in the picture below.

![ICT Suspension Block diagram — single candlestick with wick fully overlapping the body on the left and a volume imbalance both above and below the body](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ICT-Suspension-block.png)

title: ict-suspension-block
section: How to Trade the ICT Suspension Block
content:
#### How to Trade the ICT Suspension Block

The suspension block can be used as a [PD array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "PD Array") to look for trade entries or execute orders.

It acts as a level of support or resistance just like other ICT PD arrays.

To understand the trading strategy of the ICT Suspension Block, I will divide it into two types.

title: ict-suspension-block
section: (I) Bullish Suspension Block
content:
#### (I) Bullish Suspension Block

A bullish suspension block is a bullish candlestick that has a volume imbalance at the top and another volume imbalance at the bottom, but its body is completely overlapped by the wick on the left side.

A bullish suspension block can be traded in a bullish market when price taps the discount area of the higher timeframe and you see a confirmation such as a [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "MSS").

After the MSS, wait for price to retrace back to the suspension block and take support at it.

You can execute a buy trade at the bullish suspension block with a stop loss below the suspension block candle — or below the recent low, depending on your risk management.

You can see the example of a bullish suspension block in the picture below.

![ICT Bullish Suspension Block trade example — price taps higher-timeframe discount, MSS confirms reversal and the bullish suspension block delivers a long entry on the retest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ICT-Bullish-Suspension-Block.png)

title: ict-suspension-block
section: (II) Bearish Suspension Block
content:
#### (II) Bearish Suspension Block

A bearish suspension block is identified by a bearish candlestick that has a volume imbalance at the top and another volume imbalance at the bottom, while its body is completely overlapped by the wick of the candle on its left side.

A bearish suspension block can be traded in a bearish market when price reaches the premium area of a higher timeframe and you observe a confirmation such as an [MSS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "MSS").

After the MSS, wait for price to retrace back to the bearish suspension block and find resistance at that level.

You can execute a sell trade at the bearish suspension block, placing your stop loss above the suspension block candle — or above the recent swing high, depending on your risk management approach.

You can see an example of a bearish suspension block in the image below.

![ICT Bearish Suspension Block trade example — price taps higher-timeframe premium, MSS confirms reversal and the bearish suspension block delivers a short entry on the retest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ICT-Bearish-Suspension-Block.png)

title: ict-suspension-block
section: Step-by-Step ICT Suspension Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT Suspension Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a suspension block.

  1. **Set the higher-timeframe bias.** Daily and H4 — bullish or bearish.
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe premium and discount zones.** 50% level of the swing.
  3. **Wait for price to tap the bias-aligned zone.** Bullish bias — price taps discount. Bearish bias — price taps premium.
  4. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 5-minute or 1-minute for the trigger.
  5. **Wait for the MSS.** A clean Market Structure Shift in the bias direction at the higher-timeframe zone.
  6. **Identify the suspension block candle.** A candle whose body is fully overlapped by the prior candle’s wick on the left, with a volume imbalance above and below the body.
  7. **Verify the volume imbalances.** Body-to-body gap between the suspension candle and the candles immediately before and after it (wick overlap is acceptable; body separation is required).
  8. **Wait for the retest.** Price must retrace back to the suspension block candle on the next leg.
  9. **Enter at the suspension block.** Buy at a bullish suspension block, sell at a bearish suspension block.
  10. **Set the stop.** Below the low of the suspension block candle (or the recent low) for longs; above the high (or the recent swing high) for shorts.
  11. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high/low, relative equal level or higher-timeframe FVG.

title: ict-suspension-block
section: Best Markets for the ICT Suspension Block
content:
#### Best Markets for the ICT Suspension Block

The suspension block works on every market that the ICT methodology is applied to.

  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — fast 1-minute and 5-minute price action makes the body-to-body volume imbalances very visible on US indices.
  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — major forex pairs deliver clean suspension-block setups on London-killzone retracements into NY-AM premium and discount zones.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — large-body gold candles around US 08:30 ET news routinely produce suspension blocks with two clear volume imbalances.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, NQ and ES on the 1-minute and 5-minute charts are the most natural fit for suspension-block setups. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) often produces the suspension candle whose retest delivers an intraday entry inside the same session — making the setup especially time-efficient.

title: ict-suspension-block
section: Common Mistakes Trading the Suspension Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the Suspension Block

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading suspension blocks.

  1. **Confusing volume imbalance with FVG.** A volume imbalance is body-to-body (wicks can overlap). An FVG is wick-to-wick (a clean gap between the wicks of the 1st and 3rd candle). The suspension block requires volume imbalances, not FVGs.
  2. **Trading suspension blocks without the wick-overlap condition.** The suspension block specifically requires the body to be fully overlapped by the prior candle’s wick on the left. Without this, the setup is just a candle with two adjacent volume imbalances — not a true suspension block.
  3. **No MSS confirmation.** The suspension-block retest alone is not the entry. The lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift in the bias direction is the trigger.
  4. **Ignoring premium/discount context.** Bullish suspension blocks are traded only when price has tapped the higher-timeframe discount. Bearish suspension blocks only when price has tapped the higher-timeframe premium.
  5. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked at the body of the suspension block can get hunted on the wick. Either use the candle low/high with a buffer, or use the recent swing low/high for additional safety.
  6. **Treating every body-overlapped candle as a suspension block.** The candle must have BOTH a volume imbalance above AND a volume imbalance below. Without both, it is not a suspension block — it is just a wick-overlapped candle.

title: ict-suspension-block
section: FAQs about the ICT Suspension Block
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Suspension Block

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the suspension block.

**What is the ICT suspension block?**

The ICT suspension block is a single candlestick suspended between two volume imbalances — one above the body and one below the body — with the candle’s body fully overlapped by the prior candle’s wick on the left side. It was introduced by Michael Huddleston in September 2025 as a new PD array.

**Why is it called a suspension block?**

Because the candle is “suspended” between two volume imbalances — one above and one below. The combination acts as a support or resistance zone, similar to a fair value gap.

**What is the difference between a suspension block and an FVG?**

A fair value gap is a wick-to-wick gap between the 1st and 3rd candle of a 3-candle formation. A suspension block is a candle with body-to-body volume imbalances above and below — but no wick gap. The wick of the prior candle fully overlaps the suspension candle’s body on the left.

**What is a volume imbalance?**

A volume imbalance is a body-to-body gap between two consecutive candles — the second candle opens above (bullish VI) or below (bearish VI) the prior candle’s close. Wicks can overlap; the body separation is what defines the imbalance.

**How do I identify a bullish suspension block?**

Look for a bullish candle whose body is fully overlapped by the prior candle’s wick on the left, with a volume imbalance above the body and another volume imbalance below the body.

**How do I identify a bearish suspension block?**

Look for a bearish candle whose body is fully overlapped by the prior candle’s wick on the left, with a volume imbalance above the body and another volume imbalance below the body.

**Where do I enter a suspension block trade?**

After price taps the higher-timeframe premium (bearish) or discount (bullish), wait for an MSS on a lower timeframe, then enter on the retest of the suspension block candle.

**Where is the stop loss?**

Below the low of the suspension block candle (or the recent low) for longs. Above the high (or the recent swing high) for shorts.

**Where is the take profit?**

The next draw-on-liquidity in the trade direction — typically a relative equal high/low, the prior session high/low or an unfilled higher-timeframe FVG.

**When was the suspension block introduced?**

Michael Huddleston introduced the ICT Suspension Block in September 2025 as a brand-new PD array inside the broader ICT methodology.

**Does the suspension block work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce textbook suspension-block setups, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: ict-swing-high-explained

# ICT Swing High Explained in 3 Steps

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/)

![ICT Swing High three-candle formation marked on a price chart with the middle candle highest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ict-swing-high-1.png)

Before I knew what an ICT Swing High actually was, I would draw a horizontal line at every wick I thought looked important. Half my “resistance” was noise. The day someone showed me the simple three-candle test for a swing high, my charts cleaned up overnight. Three candles. Middle one highest. That is the entire rule.

An **ICT Swing High** is basically a turning point in the market after price makes a peak. The turn can be a short-term retracement or a full reversal of the trend, but the structural definition is the same in either case — a three-candle formation where the middle candle prints the highest high.

To understand the ICT swing high properly, you should also be familiar with the basic anatomy of a [Candlestick](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/all-candlestick-patterns-explained-with-visuals/> "Candlestick patterns"). The opposite of an ICT Swing High is the [ICT Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "ICT Swing Low").

In this guide, I will show you the formation rule, a three-step identification flow, how to use swing highs to read trend, what causes them to form, and how the swing high you mark today becomes the building block for the advanced ICT highs hierarchy.

Do not worry — the test is mechanical. Once you know it, you will not unknow it.

Ready? Let us break it down.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: What is an ICT Swing High?
content:
## What is an ICT Swing High?

The word “swing” means to revolve around a fixed point. In trading, when price moves up and then down around a particular level, making a peak, that peak is called a swing high.

Swing highs can be seen in any market and on any timeframe. Traders use the swing high in technical analysis to read the trend of the market — higher swing highs over time indicate an uptrend, lower swing highs indicate a downtrend.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: Swing High Formation
content:
## Swing High Formation

An ICT swing high is basically a three-candle formation. Three candles are aligned in such a way that the high of the 2nd candle (also the mid candle) is highest than the highs of the 1st and 3rd candles.

![ICT Swing High formation diagram showing three candles with the middle candle's high higher than the left and right candles](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/sing-high-formation.png)

The high of the 2nd candle is termed as the swing high — because price takes a swing from there and moves down after making a peak.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: Swing High Identification — Step by Step
content:
## Swing High Identification — Step by Step

To identify a swing high on a live chart, follow these simple steps:

  1. **Mark the high of a candlestick** — probably the highest in the local area you are scanning.
  2. **Check the high of the candlestick on the left** — it should be lower.
  3. **Check the high of the candlestick on the right** — it should be lower too.

If the highs of the candlesticks on the left and right are both lower than the high of the candlestick in the middle, you have a swing high.

![ICT Swing High real market example: a three-candle formation marked on a live price chart with the middle wick the highest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-swing-high.png)

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: How to Use Swing Highs in Trading
content:
## How to Use Swing Highs in Trading

The swing high is a useful tool for two things — reading trend direction and reading trend strength.

  * **Higher swing highs over time indicate an uptrend.**
  * **Lower swing highs indicate a downtrend.**
  * **The distance between swing highs shows the strength of the trend** — wider distance = stronger trend.
  * **A swing high can also mark the turning point of the market** after a shift in momentum.

For an entry-level setup, mark the most recent swing high on your bias timeframe. If the trend is bearish, that swing high becomes a sell zone if price retraces back to it.

![ICT Swing High used in trading: marking a recent swing high as resistance after a bearish shift in momentum](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Swing-High.png)

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: Why a Swing High is Formed
content:
## Why a Swing High is Formed

A swing high is formed mostly at a resistance area where price faces rejection due to sellers entering the market.

What happens after a swing high prints depends on the broader trend:

  * **In a bullish trend** , the swing high often produces a short bearish retracement before price continues higher.
  * **In a bearish trend** , a swing high typically marks the top of a counter-trend bounce — and price continues lower into the next leg of the downtrend.

**Pro Tip** — Not every swing high carries equal weight. The most reliable swing highs form at higher-timeframe [PD Arrays](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array") — order blocks, fair value gaps, breaker blocks. A swing high that prints inside a higher-timeframe institutional level holds far better than a swing high that prints in the middle of nowhere. Use the three-candle test to find swing highs, then filter for the ones that overlap with PD Arrays.

section: Bonus Tip: From Swing Highs to the STH, ITH, LTH Hierarchy
content:
## Bonus Tip: From Swing Highs to the STH, ITH, LTH Hierarchy

The ICT Swing High is the foundation for the more advanced ICT highs hierarchy — Short Term High (STH), Intermediate Term High (ITH), and Long Term High (LTH). Every STH is a swing high. Every ITH is a swing high with a lower swing high on each side. Every LTH is an ITH with a lower ITH on each side.

Once you can mark a swing high using the three-candle test, ranking them up the hierarchy is the next step. For the full walkthrough, see the [ICT Advance Market Structure — STH, ITH & LTH](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-advance-market-structure/> "ICT Advance Market Structure - STH ITH LTH") guide.

For the lows side of the same hierarchy, see the companion [ICT STL, ITL & LTL](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-stl-itl-ltl/> "ICT STL ITL LTL").

section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does the type of candlestick matter for swing high formation?

No. The candlestick type does not matter for swing high formation. You just need to look for the highest wick of three candles — whether the middle candle is bullish or bearish does not change the validity of the swing high.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: What is a swing high in trading?
content:
### What is a swing high in trading?

A swing high is a peak in price formed by a three-candle pattern where the middle candle has the highest high of the three. It marks a turning point — either a short-term retracement or a full trend reversal — and it is one of the basic building blocks of market-structure analysis.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: How do I identify a swing high on a chart?
content:
### How do I identify a swing high on a chart?

Three steps: mark the candle whose high looks highest in the local area, then verify that the candle to its left has a lower high, then verify that the candle to its right also has a lower high. If both neighbours are lower, the middle candle is the swing high.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: What is the difference between a swing high and a swing low?
content:
### What is the difference between a swing high and a swing low?

A swing high is a peak — the middle candle of a three-candle formation has the highest high. A swing low is a trough — the middle candle has the lowest low. Both use the same three-candle test, just inverted. See the companion [ICT Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/> "ICT Swing Low") guide.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: What does it mean when the market makes a higher swing high?
content:
### What does it mean when the market makes a higher swing high?

A higher swing high (a new swing high above the previous one) signals that the market is in an uptrend. As long as price keeps printing higher swing highs and higher swing lows, the bullish trend is intact.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: Can a swing high be used as a resistance level?
content:
### Can a swing high be used as a resistance level?

Yes. Swing highs are the most direct way to mark resistance because they show the exact price points where buyers were rejected and sellers stepped in. The most recent swing high in a bearish trend is the cleanest resistance for sell setups.

title: ict-swing-high-explained
section: What timeframe should I use to mark swing highs?
content:
### What timeframe should I use to mark swing highs?

Match the swing-high timeframe to your trade horizon. For swing trading, mark swing highs on the Daily or 4-hour. For intraday, the 1-hour or 15-minute. The three-candle test works the same way at every timeframe.

# ICT TGIF Setup — Friday Profit-Taking Trade Like a Pro + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro/)

![ICT TGIF Setup — Friday profit-taking trade after the week high or low forms, with Judas Swing, MSS confirmation and Fibonacci take-profit retracement back into the weekly range](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ICT-TGIF-SETUP.png)

The ICT TGIF setup — short for “Thank God It Is Friday” — is a day-based algorithmic ICT trading model. It is also called the Friday profit-taking trade because, on a trendy week, price typically creates the weekly high or low on Friday and then retraces back into the weekly trading range during the same session.

This guide walks you through the ICT TGIF setup — the meaning, the Fibonacci inputs, the timing windows, the Judas Swing + MSS identification, the bullish and bearish entries, the take-profit zones, common mistakes and the free PDF download.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro
section: What is the ICT TGIF Setup?
content:
#### What is the ICT TGIF Setup?

TGIF is the abbreviation of “Thank God It Is Friday”. In the ICT framework it is a day-based algorithmic trading model that works on every asset.

Day-based means it appears one day per week — Friday.

On Friday, in a trendy market, after creating the week’s high or low, prices mostly retrace back to the weekly trading range.

The ICT TGIF setup helps to catch and trade that retracement back into the weekly range on Friday.

The concept behind the TGIF setup is straightforward: you survived the work week, now you can party and rest on the weekend — and the algorithm takes profits before the close.

title: ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro
section: Fibonacci Inputs for the ICT TGIF Setup
content:
#### Fibonacci Inputs for the ICT TGIF Setup

To trade using the ICT TGIF setup you should set your Fibonacci inputs as recommended by ICT himself.

1| Start  
---|---  
0| End  
0.20| 1st profit target  
0.30| 2nd profit target  
  
These inputs allow you to map both the entry zone (after the week high or low forms) and the take-profit retracement back into the weekly range.

title: ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro
section: Timings for the ICT TGIF Setup
content:
#### Timings for the ICT TGIF Setup

The week high or low is mostly formed on Friday between the morning and afternoon session, according to New York local time.

If you do not see it forming in the morning session, you can look for it in the afternoon session — between 01:30 PM and 02:00 PM New York local time.

That afternoon window — 01:30 to 02:00 PM ET — is the most reliable secondary opportunity for the TGIF setup. It coincides with the post-NY-lunch period when the algorithm reactivates after midday consolidation.

title: ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro
section: How to Identify the ICT TGIF Setup
content:
#### How to Identify the ICT TGIF Setup

To identify the ICT TGIF setup you should first know about the [ICT Judas Swing](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-judas-swing-complete-guide/> "ICT Judas Swing"), the [ICT Power of 3](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/> "ICT Power of 3") and the [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift").

On Friday in the morning-to-afternoon session, wait for the ICT Judas Swing formation to confirm the high or low of the week.

After the Judas Swing forms, wait for price to shift its structure on the 15-minute timeframe.

**In a bullish market,** after the formation of the Judas Swing and the Market Structure Shift, the high of the week is most probably confirmed.

You can then execute a sell trade in any fair value gap or order block above the Market Structure Shift point.

A real market example is shown below.

![ICT TGIF bullish-week setup — Judas Swing forming the Friday high, 15-minute MSS to the downside and short entry from the FVG/OB above the MSS point](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ICT-TGIF-bullish-2.png)

![ICT TGIF bullish-week setup retest — price retraces back into the weekly range and delivers to the 20-30% Fibonacci profit target](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ICT-TGIF-bullish.png)

For the profit target, plot the Fibonacci from the week low to the week high and mark the 20% and 30% retracement levels (i.e., where price retraces 20% and 30% of the weekly range from the high back toward the low).

**In a bearish market,** after the formation of the Judas Swing and the Market Structure Shift, the low of the week is most probably confirmed.

You can then execute a buy trade in any fair value gap or order block below the Market Structure Shift point.

A real market example is shown below.

![ICT TGIF bearish-week setup — Judas Swing forming the Friday low, 15-minute MSS to the upside and long entry from the FVG/OB below the MSS point](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ICT-TGIF.png)

![ICT TGIF bearish-week setup retest — price retraces back into the weekly range and delivers to the 20-30% Fibonacci profit target](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/TGIF-ICT.png)

For the profit target, plot the Fibonacci from the week high to the week low and mark the 20% and 30% retracement levels (i.e., where price retraces 20% and 30% of the weekly range from the low back toward the high).

section: Step-by-Step ICT TGIF Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT TGIF Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on Friday to trade the TGIF setup.

  1. **Map the weekly range.** Mark the week’s high and low on Sunday/Monday so you can reference them on Friday.
  2. **Confirm the trend.** Bullish week — expect the high of week on Friday. Bearish week — expect the low of week on Friday.
  3. **Sit at the screen Friday morning.** The week high or low typically forms in the morning to afternoon NY-local session.
  4. **Watch for the Judas Swing.** A failed move toward the prior week’s extreme — that is your high-of-week or low-of-week candidate.
  5. **If morning is quiet, wait for 01:30 to 02:00 PM ET.** The afternoon window is the secondary setup window.
  6. **Wait for the 15-minute MSS.** A clean Market Structure Shift in the opposite direction confirms the week extreme is in.
  7. **Mark the FVG and OB above (bullish week) / below (bearish week) the MSS.** These are the entry zones.
  8. **Enter on the retracement.** Sell into the FVG or OB above the MSS (bullish week) or buy into the FVG or OB below the MSS (bearish week).
  9. **Set the stop.** Above the week high (shorts) or below the week low (longs) — the structural extreme.
  10. **Take profit at 20% and 30%.** Plot the Fibonacci from low-to-high (bullish week) or high-to-low (bearish week) and target the 20% and 30% retracements back into the range.
  11. **Close before the weekly close.** The TGIF setup is designed to be closed before the Friday weekly close — that is the entire point of “Thank God It Is Friday”.

content:
#### Best Markets for the ICT TGIF Setup

The TGIF setup works on every asset that the ICT methodology is applied to.

  * **NQ (NASDAQ futures)** and **ES (S &P 500 futures)** — US indices print clean Friday profit-taking patterns when the week is trendy.
  * **GBP/USD** and **EUR/USD** — major forex pairs deliver textbook Friday-afternoon retracements after the London-NY overlap.
  * **XAU/USD (Gold)** — gold’s Friday-afternoon retracement after a trendy week is one of the most reliable TGIF setups on the chart.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the TGIF setup is most natural on NQ and ES futures (CME Group). The 01:30 to 02:00 PM ET afternoon window aligns with US-trader lunch return and the post-NY-lunch reactivation, making it especially time-efficient for US-based readers.

title: ict-tgif-setup-trade-like-a-pro
section: Common Mistakes Trading the ICT TGIF Setup
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the ICT TGIF Setup

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the TGIF setup.

  1. **Trading TGIF on a non-trendy week.** The setup requires a clear directional weekly bias. A choppy or range-bound week does not produce a clean Friday extreme.
  2. **Pre-positioning before the Judas Swing.** The Judas Swing is the catalyst that confirms the week extreme. Entering before it forms front-runs the setup.
  3. **Skipping the 15-minute MSS.** Without the lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift, the Judas Swing alone is just a wick. The MSS is the trigger.
  4. **Ignoring the afternoon window.** If morning is quiet, the 01:30 to 02:00 PM ET window is the secondary setup. Skipping it means missing the back-up trade of the day.
  5. **Holding through the weekly close.** The TGIF setup is designed to be closed before the weekly close. Holding into Sunday open exposes the position to weekend gap risk.
  6. **Stop too tight.** The stop must sit beyond the week extreme — not at the MSS pivot. A tight stop gets hunted on the second test of the high/low.

#### Final Thoughts

While using the ICT TGIF setup in trading, keep in mind that no strategy is foolproof — you should not risk all your capital on this strategy.

To mitigate your risks, always trade with a stop loss in place to keep your equity safe. Standard 1% per trade applies here as much as anywhere else.

The TGIF setup is at its strongest when the broader weekly bias is clear and the Friday session is the natural exit point for institutional flow built up earlier in the week — that is the algorithmic logic the model leverages.

section: FAQs about the ICT TGIF Setup
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT TGIF Setup

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the TGIF setup.

**What is the ICT TGIF setup?**

The ICT TGIF setup is a Friday-only algorithmic trading model. After a trendy week creates the weekly high or low on Friday morning or afternoon, the setup catches the retracement back into the weekly range using a Judas Swing, a 15-minute MSS and an FVG or order block entry.

**What does TGIF mean in trading?**

In ICT trading, TGIF stands for “Thank God It Is Friday”. It is the day-based algorithmic model used to trade the Friday retracement back into the weekly range — also called the Friday profit-taking trade.

**What time does the TGIF setup occur?**

The week high or low typically forms on Friday between the morning and afternoon NY-local session. If the morning is quiet, the secondary window is 01:30 PM to 02:00 PM NY local time.

**How do I identify a TGIF setup?**

Wait for a Judas Swing forming the week’s high (in a bullish week) or low (in a bearish week). After the Judas Swing, wait for a 15-minute Market Structure Shift in the opposite direction to confirm the week extreme.

**Where do I enter the TGIF trade?**

In any fair value gap or order block above the MSS point (bullish week / sell trade) or below the MSS point (bearish week / buy trade).

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Above the week high (for shorts) or below the week low (for longs) — the structural extreme of the week.

**Where do I take profit?**

Plot the Fibonacci from week low to week high (bullish week) or week high to week low (bearish week) and target the 20% and 30% retracement levels back into the weekly range.

**Why is the TGIF setup called Friday profit-taking?**

Because the algorithm typically takes profits on Friday afternoon — closing positions built up earlier in the week before the weekend. The retracement back into the weekly range reflects this profit-taking flow.

**What is the difference between TGIF and Seek-and-Destroy Friday?**

TGIF is the standard Friday profit-taking model where the week extreme is set in the morning and price retraces during the afternoon. [Seek-and-Destroy Friday](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-seek-and-destroy-friday/>) describes a different Friday pattern where price hunts both the weekly high and low before settling — typically associated with consolidation weeks.

**Which prerequisite concepts should I learn first?**

Learn the [ICT Judas Swing](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-judas-swing-complete-guide/>), [ICT Power of 3](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/>) and [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) before attempting the TGIF setup. Without those three foundations, the model is hard to apply consistently.

**Does TGIF work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD produce textbook TGIF retracements during Friday afternoon, especially after a trendy bullish or bearish week.

# ICT Top Down Analysis for High-Probability Trade Setups

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-top-down-analysis/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-top-down-analysis/)

![ICT Top Down Analysis diagram showing the Daily, H4, H1 and M15 timeframes stacked from bias down to entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ICT-TOP-DOWN-ANALYSIS.png)

One of the biggest mistakes I see traders make is opening a chart on a lower timeframe and taking trades without understanding the bigger picture. That usually ends with buying straight into higher timeframe premium, or selling into higher timeframe discount, which is the worst price to enter at.

The whole point of ICT top down analysis is to understand what the higher timeframes are doing first, and only then drop to the lower timeframes to find a precise entry. You stop guessing and start trading with a roadmap.

This guide walks through the full process, what top down analysis actually is, the step by step bullish read from the Daily down to the M15, the bearish version, the common mistakes that wreck the approach, and the questions I get asked most often. If you are new to the building blocks, read the [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) and [premium and discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) guides first, then come back here to tie them together.
