title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: What is ICT Top Down Analysis?
content:
#### What is ICT Top Down Analysis?

ICT top down analysis is a trading approach that starts from the higher timeframes and gradually works down to the lower timeframes to build a complete market picture. Instead of making decisions from a single chart, you read the Daily, H4, H1 and M15 together to find the overall direction, the key premium and discount zones, and the high probability entries.

Done properly, top down analysis keeps you aligned with higher timeframe market structure, stops you trading against the dominant trend, and sharpens your entries by using the lower timeframes only for confirmation. Think of each timeframe as having a job:

  * **Daily chart** gives the overall market direction and bias
  * **H4 chart** gives the medium term direction
  * **H1 chart** gives the short term direction
  * **M15 chart** is the entry timeframe where trades are executed

The rule never changes. You always start from the highest timeframe and work your way down, never the other way around.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Bullish Top-Down Analysis
content:
#### Bullish Top-Down Analysis

Let us walk through a complete bullish scenario from top to bottom.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Step 1: Analyze the Daily Chart
content:
#### Step 1: Analyze the Daily Chart

The Daily chart is responsible for your overall bias. The first thing to look for is the most recent [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>). If the Daily has recently shifted to the upside, your overall bias becomes bullish. That does not mean you buy immediately. You first have to know whether price is currently trading in premium or in discount.

**What if price is already in premium?**

If price is already in a premium area, buying is risky because the market has already moved higher. Instead of chasing, you wait patiently for a retracement.

**What if price is in discount?**

This is where you become interested in buying. A discount area gives you a far better risk to reward because you are buying at relatively lower prices. At this point your job becomes finding lower timeframe confirmation to buy. The Daily chart example is shown below:

![ICT top down analysis Daily chart example, recent bullish MSS sets the bias and price trading into the discount area below 50 percent of the range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Top-Down-analysis-1D.png)

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Step 2: Move to the H4 Chart
content:
#### Step 2: Move to the H4 Chart

Now look at what the H4 chart is doing.

**Scenario A: H4 is also bullish**

This is the ideal situation. The Daily is bullish, the H4 is bullish, and both timeframes agree. The market is moving the same way on both higher timeframes, so the plan is simple:

  * Focus only on buying
  * Ignore sell setups
  * Keep looking for buying opportunities

The Daily and H4 bullish alignment is shown below:

![ICT top down analysis with Daily and H4 both bullish, the ideal aligned scenario where only buy setups are taken](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/top-down-analysis-d1-h4-same.png)

**Scenario B: Daily is bullish but H4 is bearish**

This means the H4 is currently pulling back against the Daily trend. Treat it as a temporary correction. In this situation:

  * Short term selling opportunities may exist
  * The sell is not meant to start a new downtrend
  * The only objective is for price to reach the Daily discount area

Once price reaches Daily discount, you stop looking for sells, begin searching for buy setups in the Daily discount, and prepare to trade in the direction of the Daily bullish trend. The contradicting Daily and H4 example is shown below:

![ICT top down analysis with bullish Daily and bearish H4, the H4 pullback used as a sell only until price reaches Daily discount](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/top-down-analysis-d1-h4-contradict.png)

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Step 3: Compare H1 with H4
content:
#### Step 3: Compare H1 with H4

Now drop to the H1 chart. The purpose of the H1 is to give you more detail about what the H4 is doing.

**H4 bullish and H1 bullish**

This is a strong bullish alignment. The Daily is bullish, the H4 is bullish, and the H1 is bullish, so all the major timeframes agree. This is where many of the highest probability trades happen. Your plan:

  * Look for buy entries
  * Hold buys toward higher timeframe objectives
  * Ignore bearish setups

The H1 and H4 bullish alignment is shown below:

![ICT top down analysis with H4 and H1 both bullish, strong alignment for buy entries toward higher timeframe targets](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/h1-h4-bullish.png)

**H4 bullish and H1 bearish**

This tells you the H1 is making a temporary pullback against the H4 uptrend. In this case a small sell may be possible, and the target of that sell is the H4 discount area. Once price reaches H4 discount, you stop selling, wait for a bullish confirmation, and look to buy with the H4 trend. The bullish H4 and bearish H1 example is shown below:

![ICT top down analysis with bullish H4 and bearish H1, the H1 pullback sold only down to the H4 discount before buying resumes](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/TOP-DOWN-ANALYSIS-H1-H4-Contradict.png)

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Step 4: Compare M15 with H1
content:
#### Step 4: Compare M15 with H1

The M15 chart is used for execution. This is where trades are actually entered.

**H1 bullish and M15 bullish**

This is exactly what you want to see. The H1 and M15 are moving in the same direction. Your plan:

  * Look for an M15 bullish confirmation, such as an MSS or a [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>)
  * Enter the buy
  * Target H4 premium or Daily premium levels

**H1 bullish and M15 bearish**

This tells you the M15 is pulling back inside an H1 uptrend. A very short term sell may be possible, with the target being the H1 discount area. That move is often around 100 to 200 points depending on the market. Once H1 discount is reached, you stop looking for sells, wait for an M15 bullish confirmation, and enter buys in the direction of the H1 trend.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Bearish Top-Down Analysis
content:
#### Bearish Top-Down Analysis

The bearish read is the exact mirror of the bullish one, so once you understand the steps above you already know this. Start on the Daily and look for a recent bearish Market Structure Shift to set a bearish bias. Then check whether price is in premium or discount. You only want to sell from premium, never from discount, because selling into discount is chasing.

Work down the same way. If the H4 agrees and is bearish, focus only on selling and ignore buys. If the H4 is pulling back bullish against a bearish Daily, treat that bullish move as a temporary buy that runs only up to the Daily premium, then look to sell again. Repeat the same logic between H1 and H4, and finally between M15 and H1. Your sells get executed on the M15 once it aligns bearish with the H1, targeting H4 discount or Daily discount. Same cascade, opposite direction.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make with Top-Down Analysis
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make with Top-Down Analysis

A handful of repeatable errors quietly ruin top down analysis for most traders. Avoid these and the approach gets a lot more reliable.

  1. **Starting on the M15 instead of the Daily.** If you open the entry timeframe first and form an opinion, you will force the higher timeframes to fit that bias. Always start at the top and let the Daily decide the direction.
  2. **Buying in premium or selling in discount.** This is the single most common way traders enter at the worst possible price. Buy from [discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>), sell from premium, on every timeframe you read.
  3. **Trading the pullback as if it were the new trend.** A lower timeframe move against the higher timeframe is a correction, not a reversal. Trade it only to the higher timeframe premium or discount, then get back in line with the dominant trend.
  4. **Skipping the premium and discount check.** Bias alone is not enough. A bullish Daily still does not mean buy now if price is sitting in premium. The zone tells you whether the entry is at a good price.
  5. **Forcing alignment that is not there.** When the timeframes genuinely disagree and there is no clean read, the correct move is to wait. Not every session offers a clean top down setup.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: The Golden Rule
content:
#### The Golden Rule

Always trade in the direction of the highest timeframe available. The Daily controls the H4, the H4 controls the H1, and the H1 controls the M15. Lower timeframes can move against the higher ones for a while, but they eventually fall back in line with the larger trend.

This is exactly why I start from the Daily and work downward instead of starting on the M15 and guessing where price will go. When you combine market structure shifts with premium and discount zones across several timeframes, you end up with a clear roadmap of where price is likely to move and where the high probability trades actually sit.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: USA Trading Note
content:
#### USA Trading Note

The same Daily to M15 cascade works on the US index futures, the NASDAQ 100 (NQ) and the E-mini S&P 500 (ES). Index futures tend to respect higher timeframe premium and discount very cleanly, so the top down read on ES and NQ is often sharper than on low volume forex pairs. The major USD pairs and Gold (XAU/USD) follow the same logic.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Final Thoughts
content:
#### Final Thoughts

Top down analysis is the framework that holds every other ICT concept together. Market structure shifts, premium and discount, order blocks and fair value gaps all become far more useful once you know which timeframe is in charge. Get into the habit of reading the Daily first and only entering on the M15, and most of the random, against the trend losses simply stop happening. For the foundations, revisit the [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>), [premium and discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>), and [Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>) guides.

title: ict-top-down-analysis
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
#### Frequently Asked Questions

**What is ICT top down analysis?**

It is a method of reading the market from the higher timeframes down to the lower ones. You use the Daily for bias, the H4 and H1 for direction, and the M15 for the actual entry, so every trade aligns with what the larger timeframes are doing.

**Which timeframes are used in ICT top down analysis?**

The common set is the Daily, H4, H1 and M15. The Daily sets the overall direction and bias, the H4 and H1 refine that direction, and the M15 is the execution timeframe where you enter the trade.

**Which timeframe should I start with?**

Always start with the highest timeframe, the Daily, and work downward. Starting on the M15 leads you to force a bias and trade against the larger trend, which is the most common mistake in the whole approach.

**What do I do when the timeframes disagree?**

A lower timeframe moving against a higher one is a pullback, not a reversal. Trade that pullback only as far as the higher timeframe premium or discount, then get back in the direction of the higher timeframe trend. If there is no clean read at all, wait.

**How does premium and discount fit into top down analysis?**

Bias tells you the direction, premium and discount tell you the price. In a bullish bias you only buy from discount, and in a bearish bias you only sell from premium. Checking the zone on each timeframe keeps you from entering at a poor price.

**Is top down analysis only for forex?**

No. The same cascade works on the US index futures like ES and NQ, on Gold, and on the major USD pairs. The timeframes and the premium and discount logic stay identical across markets.

# ICT Turtle Soup Trading Strategy — Complete Step-by-Step Guide + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-turtle-soup-pattern/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-turtle-soup-pattern/)

![ICT Turtle Soup pattern diagram showing a false breakout above a swing high reversing back inside the range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-Turtle-soup-pattern.png)

The ICT Turtle Soup trading strategy was developed by Michael Huddleston as a stop-hunt and false-breakout setup. It trades the failed breakout — the moment price spikes through a swing high or low to clear stops, fails to follow through, and snaps back inside the range. That snap-back is the trade.

Used correctly, the Turtle Soup pattern keeps me one step ahead of the breakout traders. While they are entering the move that just broke out, the Turtle Soup tells me to wait for the failure and trade the reversal instead.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT Turtle Soup strategy — what it is, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the win rate and realistic expectations, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

Use the table of contents to jump to any section.

title: ict-turtle-soup-pattern
section: What is the ICT Turtle Soup Pattern?
content:
#### What is the ICT Turtle Soup Pattern?

The ICT Turtle Soup pattern is built on hunting the stop orders sitting above a key resistance level or below a key support level. The setup is most effective in ranging markets, where price oscillates between an established high and an established low, repeatedly tagging both extremes.

The Turtle Soup focuses on [Liquidity Sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) and false-breakout mechanics. Price briefly runs past the support or resistance level, takes the stops sitting beyond it, then reverses sharply back inside the range.

Most traders read that breakout as the start of a new trend. ICT reads it as a stop-hunt — a run on the stops of traders who positioned long at support and short at resistance, engineered specifically to provide liquidity for the reversal.

Price moves for two reasons:

**(I)** To rebalance an imbalance.

**(II)** To take liquidity.

After the Turtle Soup hunts liquidity on one side of the range, price reverses to either rebalance an imbalance left behind or to target the liquidity sitting on the opposite side.

The illustration below shows a clean Turtle Soup pattern.

![ICT Turtle Soup trading example — false breakout above range high, sharp reversal, target on the opposite side of the range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-Turtle-Soup-Trading.png)

title: ict-turtle-soup-pattern
section: Logic Behind the Name “Turtle Soup”
content:
#### Logic Behind the Name “Turtle Soup”

Back in the 1980s, Richard Dennis and William Eckhardt taught a famous breakout strategy called “Turtle Trading” to a group of novice traders. The strategy bought every clean breakout in the direction of the trend — and worked well in trending markets.

The ICT Turtle Soup strategy is named humorously after that original Turtle Trading method. Where the original Turtle traders bought every breakout, the Turtle Soup capitalises on the breakouts that fail. ICT is “cooking soup from turtles” — turning the unsuccessful breakouts of the original Turtle Trader system into profitable counter-trade entries.

title: ict-turtle-soup-pattern
section: Bullish ICT Turtle Soup
content:
#### Bullish ICT Turtle Soup

A bullish Turtle Soup forms at a swing low after a false breakdown. Price briefly trades below a recent support level, takes the sell-side liquidity sitting below it, and reverses sharply back inside the range.

The trade is buy. The stop loss sits below the false-breakdown low, with a small buffer. The take profit targets the buy-side liquidity at the opposite end of the range.

Confirmation: a Market Structure Shift to the upside on the lower timeframe immediately after the sweep, and ideally a fair value gap left behind on the displacement leg.

title: ict-turtle-soup-pattern
section: Bearish ICT Turtle Soup
content:
#### Bearish ICT Turtle Soup

A bearish Turtle Soup forms at a swing high after a false breakout. Price briefly trades above a recent resistance level, takes the buy-side liquidity sitting above it, and reverses sharply back inside the range.

The trade is sell. The stop loss sits above the false-breakout high, with a small buffer. The take profit targets the sell-side liquidity at the opposite end of the range.

Confirmation: a Market Structure Shift to the downside on the lower timeframe immediately after the sweep, and ideally a fair value gap left behind on the displacement leg.

title: ict-turtle-soup-pattern
section: Step-by-Step Turtle Soup Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Turtle Soup Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every Turtle Soup setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe order flow** on the daily and 4-hour charts. The Turtle Soup works best in ranging markets — confirm the higher timeframe is consolidating, not trending strongly.
  2. **Identify the higher-timeframe draw on liquidity** — the next significant pool of stops above current price (old highs, equal highs) and below (old lows, equal lows).
  3. **Drop to the 15-minute chart** and mark the recent [Internal Range Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-internal-external-liquidity/>) levels — the swings inside the higher-timeframe range that traders use as support and resistance.
  4. **Wait for price to raid the internal range liquidity** — a sharp spike through the support or resistance level. The wick alone is not enough; the spike should clear the level decisively.
  5. **Confirm the failure** — price must return back inside the range after the sweep. If price closes past the level instead of snapping back, the breakout is real and the Turtle Soup is invalidated.
  6. **Drop to the 1-minute or 3-minute chart** for execution.
  7. **Watch for a Market Structure Shift** on the lower timeframe in the direction opposite to the sweep — confirms the false breakout.
  8. **Mark the displacement candle** that broke structure on the lower timeframe. The fair value gap or order block created by that candle is the entry zone.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the retrace into the entry zone, with stop loss beyond the wick of the swept extreme.
  10. **Take profit** at the opposite end of the higher-timeframe range, or at the next significant draw on liquidity in the trade direction.

**What is Turtle Soup in trading?**

The ICT Turtle Soup is a stop-hunt and false-breakout trading strategy. It trades the failed breakout — when price spikes through a key support or resistance level, fails to follow through, and reverses back inside the range. The reversal is the trade.

**What is a bullish Turtle Soup?**

A bullish Turtle Soup forms at a swing low after a false breakdown. Price spikes below a support level, sweeps the sell-side stops, then reverses sharply upward. The trade is buy, with stop below the swept low and target at the opposite end of the range.

**What is a bearish Turtle Soup?**

A bearish Turtle Soup forms at a swing high after a false breakout. Price spikes above a resistance level, sweeps the buy-side stops, then reverses sharply downward. The trade is sell, with stop above the swept high and target at the opposite end of the range.

**How do I confirm a valid Turtle Soup setup?**

Three conditions: alignment with higher-timeframe order flow, a clean liquidity sweep that fails to hold past the level, and a Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe in the opposite direction of the sweep.

**What is the win rate of the ICT Turtle Soup?**

On a strict execution of the checklist, the win rate sits in the 60–70% range with a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-to-reward target. The win rate drops sharply outside the conditions where the model performs best — trending markets, low-volatility sessions, and setups taken without MSS confirmation.

**What is the best timeframe for the Turtle Soup?**

15-minute for the parent chart and the internal range liquidity. 5-minute, 3-minute, or 1-minute for execution and confirmation. The 15-minute is the most reliable level-marking timeframe.

**What are the best pairs for the Turtle Soup?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) are the cleanest. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect the same mechanics.

**What risks does the Turtle Soup carry?**

The main risks are misidentifying a real breakout as a Turtle Soup, trading the setup in a strong trend, and stop loss placement that is too tight. Strict adherence to the checklist and proper risk management are non-negotiable.

**Can the Turtle Soup work in trending markets?**

It can, but the win rate drops significantly. The setup is most effective in ranging markets where price oscillates between established highs and lows. In a strong trend, prefer continuation tools like the Mitigation Block or OTE.

**Where do I place stop loss on a Turtle Soup trade?**

Beyond the wick of the swept extreme — above the high for a bearish setup, below the low for a bullish setup — with a small buffer. Stops one pip past the level get tagged routinely on the spike that often follows the initial sweep.

# ICT Unicorn Model — Breaker Block & Fair Value Gap Overlap Setup + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-unicorn-model/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-unicorn-model/)

![ICT Unicorn Model diagram showing the overlap zone between a breaker block and a fair value gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-unicorn-pattern.png)

The ICT Unicorn Model is a high-precision trade-execution tool used to maximise the probability of a clean entry. It is the area of overlap between an ICT Breaker Block and an ICT Fair Value Gap — two reliable PD Arrays that, when stacked at the same price level, produce one of the strongest reversal triggers in the ICT toolkit.

The Unicorn is one of the institutional [PD Arrays](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>) in the ICT method, and it earns the “unicorn” name because the precise overlap between a Breaker Block and a Fair Value Gap is rare. When you spot one, the win rate on the entry is meaningfully higher than either tool used alone.

The fastest way to identify a Unicorn on the chart: mark every Breaker Block first, then check whether any of those Breaker Blocks have a Fair Value Gap overlapping them. The shaded overlap zone is the Unicorn entry area.

This guide is the full breakdown of the ICT Unicorn Model — what it is, how to identify it, the bullish and bearish variants, the step-by-step trade flow, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: ict-unicorn-model
section: What is the ICT Unicorn Model?
content:
#### What is the ICT Unicorn Model?

The ICT Unicorn Model is the area of overlap between an ICT Fair Value Gap and an ICT Breaker Block. By stacking two independent PD Arrays at the same price level, the Unicorn produces a uniquely reliable trade-entry signal that neither tool delivers on its own.

The Breaker Block contributes the directional confirmation — a failed order block flipping into reversal support or resistance after a liquidity sweep. The Fair Value Gap contributes the price-imbalance magnet — a three-candle gap that price returns to rebalance.

Together, the Unicorn marks a future area of support or resistance with both structural and imbalance backing. The model signals an early shift in the direction of price delivery and often precedes a meaningful trend reversal.

title: ict-unicorn-model
section: How to Identify the ICT Unicorn Model
content:
#### How to Identify the ICT Unicorn Model

The Unicorn is built from two underlying ICT concepts. Before working with it, make sure both the Breaker Block and the Fair Value Gap are familiar.

**Breaker Block**

A Breaker Block is a failed order block formed after a shift in price structure and a liquidity sweep. The original order block is broken, and that broken zone now acts as support or resistance from the opposite side.

![ICT Breaker Block example showing a failed bearish order block flipping into a bullish breaker after liquidity sweep](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ICT-breaker-Block-1.png)

For the full breakdown of the Breaker Block — bullish, bearish, and the four-condition validation — see my dedicated [ICT Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) guide.

**Fair Value Gap (FVG)**

A Fair Value Gap is a three-candle price imbalance — the gap between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3 (or inverse for bearish), where buy-side and sell-side delivery were not balanced. Price tends to return to rebalance the gap before continuing in the original direction.

![Bullish Fair Value Gap example — three-candle pattern with unfilled gap between candle 1 high and candle 3 low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Bullish-fair-value-gap.png)

For the full FVG breakdown — strength tiers, identification rules, and trade flow — see my [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>) guide.

**Unicorn Model — Validation Checklist**

To validate an ICT Unicorn Model, three conditions must be true:

  1. A break of a swing high or swing low (the structural shift).
  2. A Breaker Block forming at the broken swing.
  3. A Fair Value Gap overlapping that Breaker Block.

The shaded overlap area between the Breaker Block and the Fair Value Gap is the Unicorn entry zone.

content:
#### Step-by-Step Unicorn Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every Unicorn setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Set the daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). Unicorn trades work best in the direction of the higher-timeframe bias.
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe[PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>)** on the daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour chart — the level where institutions are likely to be positioning.
  3. **Wait for price to approach** the higher-timeframe PD Array in the premium or discount zone.
  4. **Drop to the 15-minute or 5-minute chart** and watch for a Market Structure Shift in the direction of your bias.
  5. **Mark the Breaker Block** created by the structural shift — the failed order block at the swing extreme.
  6. **Check for a Fair Value Gap** overlapping the Breaker Block. No FVG = no Unicorn. Pass on the trade and wait for a different setup.
  7. **Confirm the overlap zone** — the area where the Breaker Block body and the Fair Value Gap intersect. That is the Unicorn entry zone.
  8. **Wait for price to retrace** back to the Unicorn zone. Do not chase the displacement leg.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the retest, with stop loss 10–20 pips beyond the candle that created the FVG.
  10. **Take profit** at the next draw on liquidity in the trade direction.

section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Unicorn Model
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on the Unicorn Model

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed Unicorn trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the model converts at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading the Breaker Block alone without the Fair Value Gap overlap.** The whole point of the Unicorn is the overlap of two PD Arrays. A Breaker Block by itself is a valid trade — but it is not a Unicorn. If there is no FVG overlapping the Breaker, do not call it a Unicorn and do not size up as if it were.
  2. **Using a stale Fair Value Gap.** The FVG must be the one created during the recent structural shift, not a random older FVG that happens to sit at the same price. The Unicorn is built on a fresh, in-context overlap.
  3. **Trading Unicorns against the daily bias.** Counter-bias Unicorns fail far more often than aligned Unicorns. Filter every setup through the daily bias before acting.
  4. **Stop loss too tight on the FVG candle.** Place the stop 10–20 pips beyond the wick of the FVG candle, with a small buffer. Stops one pip past the FVG are routinely tagged before the retracement plays out.
  5. **Confusing the Unicorn with a regular order block retest.** If price retraces to a normal order block and there is no Breaker-FVG overlap, that is an OB trade, not a Unicorn. The two have different probability profiles and should not be sized identically.

It is named “vacuum” because of the vacuum of liquidity left behind, and price typically returns to fill or partially reprice the gap on a later leg.

title: ict-vacuum-block-opening-gaps
section: What is an ICT Vacuum Block?
content:
#### What is an ICT Vacuum Block?

The ICT vacuum block is a gap created in price action because of a high-volatility event like FOMC, NFP, or a geopolitical event such as war.

It can also be created because of a week, day or session opening.

It is called a vacuum block because of the vacuum of liquidity inside the gap.

When price opens up or down from the previous market price leaving a gap behind, that gap is the ICT vacuum block. There has been no trading activity inside the gap because no trader was able to execute a trade during the high-volatility event.

Price tends to return to fill these gaps and then continue its move in the direction of the gap.

title: ict-vacuum-block-opening-gaps
section: (I) Bullish ICT Vacuum Block
content:
#### (I) Bullish ICT Vacuum Block

A bullish ICT vacuum block is created when price opens above the previous market price, leaving a gap behind. The gap may be due to a high-volatility event or a geopolitical event.

Economic and geopolitical events affect the price of assets — so price can increase heavily because of these events.

section: Step-by-Step ICT Vacuum Block Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT Vacuum Block Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a vacuum block.

  1. **Identify the catalyst.** FOMC, NFP, CPI, geopolitical news or a session/week opening — the event that created the gap.
  2. **Mark the vacuum block on the chart.** The full gap range from the prior close to the new open.
  3. **Mark the consequent encroachment.** The 50% midpoint of the vacuum block — the most reactive level inside the gap.
  4. **Assess the catalyst’s longevity.** If the event has long-term impact (FOMC rate change, structural geopolitical shift), price is more likely to respect the vacuum block on the retest. Short-lived catalysts produce less reliable retests.
  5. **Wait for the retracement.** Price must trade back into the vacuum block.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry trigger.
  7. **Wait for the LTF MSS.** A clean Market Structure Shift at or near the consequent encroachment confirms the reaction.
  8. **Enter on confirmation.** Buy at a bullish vacuum block; sell at a bearish vacuum block.
  9. **Set the stop.** Below the low of the vacuum block (bullish) or above the high (bearish).
  10. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Use ICT fib extensions or the next external liquidity pool.

section: Common Mistakes Trading the Vacuum Block
content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the Vacuum Block

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading vacuum blocks.

  1. **Treating every gap as a vacuum block.** Small intraday gaps without a clear high-volatility catalyst are not vacuum blocks. The setup specifically requires a news, geopolitical or session-open catalyst.
  2. **Ignoring the catalyst longevity.** A vacuum block created by a temporary event (a single news headline that fades) often does not get respected on the retest. Long-term catalysts deliver more reliable setups.
  3. **Skipping the LTF MSS.** The retest of the consequent encroachment alone is not the entry. A lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift is the trigger.
  4. **Stop too tight.** Stops parked at the body of the vacuum block can get hunted on the wick. Use the full vacuum-block edge with a small buffer.
  5. **Holding past the next draw on liquidity.** Vacuum-block trades have a clear first target. Holding past it without a structural reason often gives the move back.
  6. **Confusing vacuum block with NWOG.** The [New Week Opening Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-week-opening-gap-nwog/>) is a specific weekly-open vacuum block. The general vacuum block can occur on any high-volatility event — not just weekends.

content:
#### Does Price Always Fill the Gap?

No — it is not certain that price will fill the gap, and it is not necessary.

title: ict-vacuum-block-opening-gaps

content:
#### Does Price Fill the Gap Completely?

If price fills a gap completely, that is a perfect price delivery. But it is not the case in most circumstances.

Price may just tap the gap and move away — or it may fill the gap completely. Statistically, the consequent encroachment (50%) is the most reactive level, and most reactions occur there rather than at the full-fill point.

content:
#### Does the Vacuum Block Fail to Hold Price?

Yes — the vacuum block can fail to hold price if it was created as a result of a temporary volatile event whose impact does not last long.

This is why understanding the catalyst’s longevity is the critical filter for vacuum-block trades. A long-term catalyst (FOMC rate change, structural news) produces a vacuum block that holds. A short-lived headline produces a vacuum block that often fails on the retest.

section: FAQs about the ICT Vacuum Block
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Vacuum Block

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the vacuum block.

**What is the ICT vacuum block?**

The ICT vacuum block is a gap created in price action by a high-volatility event (FOMC, NFP, geopolitical news or a session/week opening) where no trading activity occurred inside the gap. The gap is named “vacuum” because of the vacuum of liquidity, and price typically returns to fill or reprice the gap on a later leg.

**What creates a vacuum block?**

A high-volatility event such as FOMC, NFP, CPI, war or a major political event — or a normal session/week opening — that causes price to open at a different level from the prior close, leaving a gap with no trading activity inside it.

**How is a vacuum block different from a fair value gap?**

A fair value gap is a 3-candle wick-to-wick imbalance during normal trading. A vacuum block is created by a price-discontinuity (a true gap with no trading inside) caused by a high-volatility event or session open. The vacuum block is a specific subset of “opening gap” patterns, often containing FVGs inside it.

**Where do I enter a vacuum block trade?**

At or near the consequent encroachment (50% midpoint) of the vacuum block on the retest, after a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift confirms the reaction.

**Where is the stop loss?**

Below the low of the vacuum block (bullish) or above the high of the vacuum block (bearish), with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw-on-liquidity in the direction of the original gap, or use the ICT fib extensions to stage exits.

**Will price always fill a vacuum block?**

No — fills are not guaranteed. Long-term catalysts (FOMC rate change, structural news) produce vacuum blocks that are more likely to hold and be respected on the retest. Short-lived catalysts can fail.

**Does the vacuum block work on indices, gold and forex?**

Yes — NQ, ES, XAU/USD and major forex pairs all produce vacuum blocks around scheduled news (FOMC, NFP, CPI) and weekend opens.

**What is the difference between vacuum block and NWOG?**

The [New Week Opening Gap (NWOG)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-new-week-opening-gap-nwog/>) is a specific subtype of vacuum block formed only at the weekly open. The vacuum block is the general category — it can occur at any session/week open or on any high-volatility event.

**How do I know if the catalyst will hold?**

Long-term structural catalysts (rate decisions, sustained policy shifts, major geopolitical events) produce vacuum blocks that hold on the retest. Single-headline events that fade within a session produce vacuum blocks that often fail. Use the size and persistence of the move after the gap as a guide.

**What timeframe is best for vacuum-block setups?**

The daily and H4 are best for marking the vacuum block. The 5-minute and 1-minute are used for the LTF MSS entry trigger at the consequent encroachment retest.

# ICT Venom Trading Model 2025 — 90-Minute Liquidity Sweep Strategy with Examples

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-venom-trading-model-2025/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-venom-trading-model-2025/)

![ICT Venom Trading Model 2025 — 90-minute liquidity-sweep strategy on US index futures \(US100/US30/US500\) where price poisons retail stops at 09:30 AM and reverses sharply](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/ICT-Venom-model.png)

The ICT Venom trading model is the latest trading strategy introduced by Michael Huddleston in April 2025.

This trading model is specifically designed for the US stock index futures — US100, US30 and US500.

The Venom model is an intraday trading strategy based on the [liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) plus the time and price theory of ICT, and it may target 50 to 80 ticks per day.

In this guide I walk you through the ICT Venom trading model — the meaning of the name, the 90-minute window mechanic, the bullish and bearish setups, the BPR confirmation, the alternate session windows and the common mistakes traders make.

section: What is the ICT Venom Trading Model?
content:
#### What is the ICT Venom Trading Model?

The ICT Venom Trading Model gets its name from how price action “poisons” retail traders by triggering their stop orders, only to sharply reverse direction.

The ICT Venom model is a complete intraday trading model using a 90-minute window, and it acts the same way as the [ICT AMD](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-power-of-3/> "ICT AMD") (Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution) pattern. This guide focuses primarily on the New York opening Venom model.

While the regular stock market officially opens at 09:30 AM NY time, electronic trading begins at 08:00 AM.

The 90-minute window from 08:00 AM to 09:30 AM creates a defined range of early price action.

Once the market opens at 09:30 AM, price often targets and sweeps the high or low of this initial range, collecting liquidity.

After this sweep, the market typically reverses and resumes movement in line with the prevailing trend.

You can see the visual representation of the ICT Venom model in the picture below.

![ICT Venom Trading Model diagram — 08:00-09:30 AM NY 90-minute range, liquidity sweep at 09:30 open, FVG-and-BPR formation, then sharp reversal back into the range](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/ICT-Venom-Trading-Model.png)

section: (I) Bullish ICT Venom Trading Model
content:
#### (I) Bullish ICT Venom Trading Model

On a bullish day when regular trading begins at 09:30 AM, price typically sweeps the low of the 90-minute trading range and then reverses to the buy-side.

To trade the ICT Venom trading model in a bullish market, follow these steps.

**Identify the Initial Range:**

Monitor the price action from 08:00 AM to 09:30 AM (New York time) — the electronic trading session.

Mark the highest high and lowest low of this 90-minute range.

**Wait for the Regular Market Open:**

The official US stock market opens at 09:30 AM NY time.

Hold off on taking trades until this session begins.

**Watch for a Liquidity Sweep:**

After the market opens, look for price to dip below the low of the 90-minute range.

This move is intended to trigger stop losses and gather sell-side liquidity.

**Look for Imbalance (Fair Value Gap):**

As price moves down to sweep the low, it should create an inefficiency or [fair value gap (FVG)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>).

**Expect a Sharp Reversal (BPR):**

Once the liquidity is taken and the FVG is formed, price often makes an aggressive, imbalanced move to the upside.

Price forms a fair value gap in this sharp reversal which is against the previous FVG, thus making an [ICT BPR](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/> "ICT BPR").

This strong reversal is what gives the model its name — it strikes like a venomous mamba, quickly attacking and then retreating.

**Look for the MSS or CISD:**

In the reversal price move look for the [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) or [Change in the State of Delivery](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>).

After the CISD or MSS to the upside you can execute a buy trade on retracement back to any [PD array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>).

**Stop Loss:**

Your stop loss in this case will be 10 to 20 ticks lower than the low marked at the liquidity sweep.

**Take Profit:**

Your initial profit target will be the high of the 90-minute trading range, and the next target can be the high of the previous day or week or any equal highs.

You can see the example of the ICT Venom trading strategy in the picture below.

![Bullish ICT Venom Trading Model real chart example — sweep below the 90-minute range low, FVG formation, BPR sharp reversal upward and long entry on retracement](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Bullish-ICT-Venom-Trading-Model.png)

section: (II) Bearish ICT Venom Trading Model
content:
#### (II) Bearish ICT Venom Trading Model

On a bearish day, when the regular trading session begins at 09:30 AM (New York time), price typically sweeps the high of the 90-minute trading range and then reverses to the sell-side.

To apply the ICT Venom strategy in a bearish scenario, follow these steps.

**Identify the Initial Range:**

Monitor the price action during the electronic trading session from 08:00 AM to 09:30 AM (New York time).

Mark the highest high and lowest low of this 90-minute range.

**Wait for the Regular Market Open:**

The official US stock market opens at 09:30 AM NY time.

Avoid entering any trades before this time.

**Watch for a Liquidity Sweep:**

After 09:30 AM, observe if price moves above the high of the 90-minute range.

This sweep is designed to trigger buy-side stop losses, collecting liquidity from trapped retail buyers.

**Look for Imbalance (Fair Value Gap):**

As price moves up to sweep the high, it should leave behind an inefficiency, such as a fair value gap (FVG). Read the full [ICT Fair Value Gap Explained Step by Step](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap Explained Step by Step") guide for the FVG basics.

**Expect a Sharp Reversal (BPR):**

Once the buy-side liquidity is collected and the FVG is formed, price often reverses aggressively to the downside.

Price forms a fair value gap in this sharp reversal which is against the previous FVG, thus making an [ICT BPR](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/> "ICT BPR").

This sharp drop mimics the venomous strike of a mamba — quick, deceptive and deadly.

**Look for MSS or CISD:**

During the bearish reversal, watch for an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") or a [Change in the State of Delivery](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/> "Change in the State of Delivery").

Once confirmed, you can enter a sell trade on the retracement to a PD array.

**Stop Loss:**

Your stop loss should be set 10 to 20 ticks above the high created during the liquidity sweep.

**Take Profit:**

The initial target is the low of the 90-minute range.

Further targets can include the previous day’s low, the weekly low or any equal lows below.

content:

This is the exact sequence I run when trading the ICT Venom model around the 09:30 NY open.

  1. **Be at the screen by 08:00 AM NY.** The 90-minute window starts at 08:00 and ends at 09:30.
  2. **Mark the high and low of the 90-minute range.** The boundaries set by 08:00 to 09:30 NY price action.
  3. **Set the directional bias.** Bullish day — expect a sweep of the range low. Bearish day — expect a sweep of the range high.

  5. **Watch for the liquidity sweep.** Below the range low (bullish day) or above the range high (bearish day).
  6. **Verify the FVG formation.** The sweep move should leave a fair value gap behind.
  7. **Wait for the sharp reversal and BPR.** Price reverses aggressively, forming a fair value gap in the opposite direction — together with the prior FVG this creates a Balanced Price Range.
  8. **Wait for MSS or CISD.** Confirmation of structural reversal on the lower timeframe.
  9. **Enter on the retracement to a PD array.** Buy at the PD array on a bullish setup; sell at the PD array on a bearish setup.
  10. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 ticks beyond the swept low (bullish) or swept high (bearish).
  11. **Take profit at the 90-minute range opposite extreme.** First target — then extend to prior day high/low, weekly extremes or equal levels.

content:
#### Common Mistakes Trading the ICT Venom Model

section: FAQs about the ICT Venom Trading Model
content:
#### FAQs about the ICT Venom Trading Model

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the Venom model.

**What is the ICT Venom trading model?**

The ICT Venom trading model is a 2025 intraday trading strategy by Michael Huddleston designed for US index futures. It uses a 90-minute window (08:00 to 09:30 AM NY local) and trades the liquidity sweep at the 09:30 NY open with FVG-and-BPR confirmation followed by an MSS or CISD entry.

**Why is it called Venom?**

Because price action “poisons” retail traders — it sweeps their stop orders below the range low (or above the range high) and then reverses sharply, like the strike of a venomous mamba.

**What is the 90-minute window?**

The primary 90-minute window is 08:00 AM to 09:30 AM New York local time — the electronic-trading session before the regular NYSE open. Two alternate windows are 01:30 AM to 03:00 AM and 12:00 PM to 01:30 PM NY local.

**What instruments does the Venom model work on?**

US stock index futures — US100 (NQ), US30 (YM) and US500 (ES). The model is specifically designed for these instruments because the 09:30 NYSE open is the critical catalyst.

**How many ticks does the Venom model target?**

50 to 80 ticks per day on US index futures.

**Where do I enter a Venom trade?**

After the 09:30 sweep + FVG + BPR sequence and an MSS or CISD confirmation, enter on the retracement back to a PD array (order block, fair value gap or breaker block).

**Where is the stop loss on a Venom trade?**

10 to 20 ticks below the sweep low (bullish setup) or above the sweep high (bearish setup).

**Where is the take profit?**

The opposite extreme of the 90-minute range as the initial target. Extended targets include the previous day’s high or low, the weekly extremes, or any equal highs/lows.

**Can I trade the Venom on the BPR alone?**

You can, with a smaller stop and better risk-reward, but the BPR can fail. Most traders prefer to wait for the CISD or MSS confirmation before entering.

**Is the Venom related to Power of 3?**

Yes — the Venom model acts like the ICT Power of 3 (Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution). The 90-minute window is the accumulation, the sweep is the manipulation, and the reversal is the distribution.

**Can I use the Venom outside the US session?**

Yes — the 01:30 to 03:00 AM and 12:00 to 01:30 PM NY-local windows are alternate Venom windows. The 90-minute window is fundamental to the model; the 09:30 NY open is just the most reliable trigger.

# ICT Weekly Range Expansion — Tuesday Open Entry, 3 PD Arrays & Thursday Hold Model

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-expansion/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-expansion/)

![ICT Weekly Range Expansion — short-term trading model based on weekly direction, Tuesday range expansion entry and 3 PD arrays \(FVG, old high/low, liquidity pool\)](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/ICT-Weekly-Range-Expansion.png)

ICT Weekly Range Expansion is a short-term trading model from ICT charter content — built on the expanding weekly candle (bullish or bearish) and just three PD arrays. Reading this guide and dedicating yourself to real market practice will enable you to identify and trade ICT weekly range expansion like a pro.

The model is based on the expanding week — either bullish or bearish — and focuses on three [ICT PD Arrays](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>):

(I) [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>)

(II) Old Low / High

(III) [Liquidity Pool](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-pool/>)

In this guide I walk you through the weekly range expansion model — the three-stage framework (stage, setup, pattern), the bullish and bearish execution, the Tuesday open entry, the Thursday hold rule, the 50-pip stop, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: What is ICT Weekly Range Expansion Model?
content:
#### What is ICT Weekly Range Expansion Model?

It is a short-term trading model in an expanding week — bullish or bearish — using only the three ICT PD arrays listed above.

The model is based on 3 steps.

**(I) STAGE** — Weekly direction.

**(II) SETUP** — Range expansion.

**(III) PATTERN** — Execution.

First, you need the stage — the weekly direction or bias for the weekly candle. You find it by looking at the weekly chart and asking whether price is going to take the liquidity or fill the fair value gap.

The setup is the range expansion. The pattern is based on the PD-array matrix — looking for opposing PD arrays.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: How to Trade Bullish Week Range Expansion
content:
#### How to Trade Bullish Week Range Expansion

First of all you should have a correct weekly bias that confirms the next week’s bullish price move.

You can find this by looking at the weekly chart — has it taken any sell-side liquidity, or is it inside the [Discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) PD array?

If yes, it is going to target buy-side liquidity or any [Premium](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/>) PD array.

For extra confirmation you may look for a daily-timeframe [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) to the buy-side.

After having a correct bullish weekly bias, wait for the new week opening — you may use Sunday opening or Monday opening, it does not matter.

But for execution of the trade, we will wait until Monday opening — because mostly Monday creates the low of the week and an expansion as well.

You will be buying on Tuesday at the opening of the 04:00 AM (NY local time) candlestick — at the opening price or below the opening price of the Tuesday candlestick.

![Bullish ICT weekly range expansion example — Monday creates the low of the week, Tuesday 4 AM NY open is the buy entry, Tuesday-to-Thursday range expansion higher](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Bullish-week-expansion.png)

Hold this trade for at least Thursday New York opening — Tuesday to Thursday mostly sees range expansion.

Your stop loss in this model will be only 50 pips below the buying price.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: How to Trade Bearish Week Range Expansion
content:
#### How to Trade Bearish Week Range Expansion

First, ensure you have a correct weekly bias that confirms the next week’s bearish price move.

You can determine this by examining the weekly chart — has it taken any buy-side liquidity, or is it inside the Premium PD array?

If yes, it is going to target sell-side liquidity or any Discount PD array.

For additional confirmation, you may look for a daily-timeframe Market Structure Shift to the sell-side.

After establishing a correct bearish weekly bias, wait for the new week opening — you may use Sunday opening or Monday opening, it does not matter.

For executing the trade, wait until Tuesday opening — because Tuesday often creates the high of the week and an expansion as well.

You will be selling on Tuesday at the opening of the 04:00 AM (NY local time) candlestick — at the opening price or above the opening price of the Tuesday candlestick.

![Bearish ICT weekly range expansion example — Monday creates the high of the week, Tuesday 4 AM NY open is the sell entry, Tuesday-to-Thursday range expansion lower](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Bearish-Week-expansion.png)

Hold this trade at least until Thursday New York opening — Tuesday to Thursday mostly sees range expansion.

Your stop loss in this model will be only 50 pips above the selling price.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: Step-by-Step Weekly Range Expansion Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Weekly Range Expansion Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for the weekly range expansion model.

  1. **Set the weekly bias.** Examine the weekly chart — has the previous candle taken sell-side liquidity (bullish bias) or buy-side liquidity (bearish bias)? Is the candle inside the discount PD array (bullish) or premium PD array (bearish)?
  2. **Confirm the bias with daily MSS.** A daily MSS in the bias direction is extra confirmation.
  3. **Identify the three PD arrays.** FVG, old high or low, and the liquidity pool — these are the targets of the expansion.
  4. **Wait for the new week to open.** Sunday or Monday — does not matter for the bias, but Monday typically creates the weekly low (bullish) or weekly high (bearish).
  5. **Wait for the Tuesday 04:00 AM NY open.** This is the execution window for the model.
  6. **Enter at the Tuesday open.** Bullish — buy at or below the Tuesday open. Bearish — sell at or above the Tuesday open.
  7. **Set the stop.** 50 pips below the entry (bullish) or 50 pips above the entry (bearish).
  8. **Hold to Thursday NY open.** Tuesday to Thursday is the range-expansion window.
  9. **Target the bias-aligned PD arrays.** Buy-side liquidity, premium PD array (bullish) or sell-side liquidity, discount PD array (bearish).

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: Best Pairs for Weekly Range Expansion
content:
#### Best Pairs for Weekly Range Expansion

The model works on every major instrument that respects the weekly delivery cycle — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, USD/JPY, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the weekly range expansion framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The Tuesday 09:30 NY cash open is a particularly strong execution window for indices.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: Common Mistakes Around Weekly Range Expansion
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Weekly Range Expansion

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the weekly range expansion.

  1. **Entering on Monday instead of Tuesday.** Monday typically creates the weekly extreme (low for bullish, high for bearish) — entering on Monday gets stopped out by the same expansion the model is built to capture.
  2. **Wrong timezone.** The 04:00 AM Tuesday entry is in New York local time. Using broker-server time or your local time produces a different execution window.
  3. **Holding past Thursday.** The range-expansion window is Tuesday to Thursday. Holding into Friday exposes the trade to the weekly close and reversal risk.
  4. **50-pip stop too wide for small instruments.** The 50-pip stop is calibrated for major forex pairs. For lower-volatility instruments, scale the stop to the same percentage of weekly range.
  5. **Trading without a weekly bias.** The model demands a CORRECT weekly bias — bullish or bearish. Without one, the Tuesday open is just noise.
  6. **Trading every week.** The model only works on expanding weeks. Inside-week or consolidation weeks do not produce the Tuesday-to-Thursday expansion the entry depends on.

title: ict-weekly-range-expansion
section: FAQs about ICT Weekly Range Expansion
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Weekly Range Expansion

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the weekly range expansion model.

**What is ICT Weekly Range Expansion?**

A short-term trading model in an expanding week (bullish or bearish) that uses three PD arrays — FVG, old high or low, and liquidity pool — and executes on the Tuesday 04:00 AM NY open.

**What are the three PD arrays in the model?**

(1) Fair Value Gap, (2) Old Low or Old High, and (3) Liquidity Pool. These are the targets that drive the weekly expansion.

**What are the three stages?**

(1) STAGE — weekly direction. (2) SETUP — range expansion. (3) PATTERN — execution on the Tuesday open.

**When do I enter the trade?**

At the Tuesday 04:00 AM New York local time candle open. Bullish — buy at or below the open. Bearish — sell at or above the open.

**Why Tuesday?**

Because Monday typically creates the weekly extreme (low for bullish, high for bearish), and Tuesday begins the range-expansion phase that runs into Thursday.

**How long do I hold the trade?**

At least until Thursday New York opening — Tuesday to Thursday is the range-expansion window. Beyond Thursday, the trade is exposed to weekly close volatility.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

50 pips below the entry for buy trades, 50 pips above the entry for sell trades.

**Where do I take profit?**

The bias-aligned PD arrays — buy-side liquidity and premium PD array (bullish) or sell-side liquidity and discount PD array (bearish).

**How do I confirm the weekly bias?**

Bullish — weekly candle has taken sell-side liquidity or is in the discount PD array. Bearish — weekly candle has taken buy-side liquidity or is in the premium PD array. Optional daily MSS confirms.

**Does the model work every week?**

No — only on expanding weeks. Inside-week or consolidation weeks do not produce the Tuesday-to-Thursday expansion the entry depends on.

**Does weekly range expansion work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all respect the weekly delivery cycle, especially during weeks with high-impact economic events.

**What timezone are the times in?**

All times are New York local time. The 04:00 AM Tuesday entry is NY time, not broker-server or local time.

# ICT Weekly Profiles — 12 Patterns to Identify the Weekly High & Low + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-profiles/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-weekly-range-profiles/)

![ICT Weekly Profiles diagram showing the 12 typical weekly patterns of price delivery from Monday to Friday](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/ICT-Weekly-Range-Profiles.png)

ICT Weekly Profiles are conceptual frameworks Michael Huddleston taught for reading the typical day-by-day delivery of price across a single trading week. There are 12 distinct weekly profiles, and each one describes a different pattern of how the high and low of the week are likely to form — Tuesday low, Wednesday high, Thursday consolidation reversal, midweek expansion, and so on.

I use the Weekly Profiles to anticipate where the high and low of the week will likely print BEFORE the week unfolds. That changes how I plan trades on Monday and Tuesday — instead of reacting to each day, I am positioning for the weekly extreme that the dominant profile suggests.

The profiles are not fixed predictions. They are tendencies — frameworks to read price against. Combined with a clear higher-timeframe bias and the right premium / discount context, they sharpen weekly setups significantly.

This guide is the full breakdown of all 12 ICT Weekly Profiles — what each one looks like, when to anticipate it, the higher-timeframe filters that signal which profile is in play, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

Table of Contents
