title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: What is a Pin Bar Candlestick?
content:
#### What is a Pin Bar Candlestick?

It is a single candlestick pattern that has a long tail (known as shadow or wick) and a small real body as compared to the tail.

Due to the long pin-shaped wick and small bar-shaped body, it is called a Pin Bar candlestick.

The long wick of a pin bar candlestick shows a strong price rejection and signals the reversal of price from a certain price level.

Pin bar candlestick is of two types.

**(I) Bullish Pin Bar** has a long shadow at the bottom and a small body at the top — so it looks like a hammer.

**(II) Bearish Pin Bar** has a long shadow at the top and a small body at the bottom — also known as a [shooting star candlestick](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/shooting-star-candlestick/>).

Below is the illustration explaining the bullish and bearish pin bars.

![Bullish pin bar candlestick example — long lower wick \(rejection from below\) with small body near the top, similar in shape to a hammer pattern](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Bullish-pin-bar.png)

![Bearish pin bar candlestick example — long upper wick \(rejection from above\) with small body near the bottom, also known as a shooting star pattern](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/bearish-pin-bar.png)

Pin bars are highly reliable on higher timeframes like the week, day or 4-hour.

title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: What is Pin Bar Trading Strategy?
content:
#### What is Pin Bar Trading Strategy?

Pin Bar Trading Strategy is a combination of the pin bar candlestick pattern and support / resistance strategy.

**Bullish Pin Bar** is mostly traded in a bullish trend, when price moves higher making higher highs and higher lows.

In a bullish trend, mark the strong support zone and wait for price to test that zone.

When price approaches the support zone, wait for the closing of the candlestick and the formation of a Bullish Pin Bar candlestick.

After the formation of a bullish pin bar at the support zone, you may execute a buy trade directly — or wait for price to retrace at least 50% of the pin bar and then execute a buy trade.

In the picture below you can see the XAU/USD daily-timeframe chart where price approached a strong support zone and a pin bar formed there. After the formation of the pin bar, you can see the boom in prices and a successful buy trade.

![Bullish pin bar trade example on XAU/USD daily — price tests strong support, a bullish pin bar prints with long lower wick, buy entry with stop below the pin bar low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/PIN-BAR-TRADING.png)

While trading a bullish pin bar, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the low of the pin bar or below the support zone, whichever is lower.

For profit target, you may mark the next resistance as your take profit.

**Bearish Pin Bar** is reliable in a bearish trend, where prices tend to fall making lower highs and lower lows.

Mark the resistance zones in a bearish trend and wait for price to test the resistance.

When price tests the resistance zone, wait until the close of the candlestick and the formation of a bearish pin bar.

Formation of a pin bar at the resistance zone represents strong rejection and a continuation of the selling trend.

You can execute a sell trade immediately after the formation of the bearish pin bar — or wait for price to retrace at least 50% of the pin bar to execute the sell trade.

In the picture below you can see a XAG/USD daily-timeframe chart where price approached the resistance and made a bearish pin bar signaling a drop in price. You can see the results — a successful sell trade.

![Bearish pin bar trade example on XAG/USD daily — price tests strong resistance, a bearish pin bar prints with long upper wick, sell entry with stop above the pin bar high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/bearish-pin-bar-trading-strategy.png)

In this case, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the high of the bearish pin bar or above the resistance zone, whichever is higher.

For take profit, you may target the next support level.

title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: Pin Bar Quality — How to Pick the Best Ones
content:
#### Pin Bar Quality — How to Pick the Best Ones

Not every pin bar is worth trading. The highest-quality pin bars share these characteristics.

**(1) Long wick relative to body.** The wick should be at least 2x the body, ideally 3x or more. The longer the rejection, the stronger the signal.

**(2) Forms at a higher-timeframe key level.** Daily and 4-hour support / resistance — not 5-minute noise.

**(3) Aligned with the higher-timeframe trend.** Bullish pin bar in an uptrend; bearish pin bar in a downtrend.

**(4) Closes near the opposite end of the wick.** A bullish pin bar should close near its high, with the wick stretching down. A bearish pin bar should close near its low, with the wick stretching up.

**(5) Volume confirmation.** Higher volume on the pin bar candle adds conviction.

title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: Pin Bar in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Pin Bar in the ICT Framework

The pin bar maps onto the ICT framework as the candle-level signature of an [inducement sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) at a higher-timeframe PD array.

The long wick is the sweep — price grabs the liquidity below support (bullish pin bar) or above resistance (bearish pin bar). The small body and close near the opposite end is the candle-level [change in state of delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>).

In ICT terms, the pin bar is a single-candle CISD at the inducement sweep — which makes it one of the cleanest reversal triggers on the chart.

title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: Step-by-Step Pin Bar Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Pin Bar Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for a pin bar trade.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Bullish (HH/HL) for bullish pin bar setups, bearish (LH/LL) for bearish pin bar setups.
  2. **Mark the bias-aligned level.** Strong support for a bullish pin bar; strong resistance for a bearish pin bar.
  3. **Wait for price to reach the level.** Patience is mandatory.
  4. **Watch for the pin bar to form.** Long wick (≥ 2x the body) on the rejection side, small body on the opposite end.
  5. **Wait for the candle to close.** Mid-candle action is meaningless — only the closed candle counts.
  6. **Verify quality.** Wick-to-body ratio, alignment with trend, close near opposite end, volume.
  7. **Enter the trade.** Immediately on the pin bar close — or wait for a 50% retracement into the pin bar for a tighter entry.
  8. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips below the pin bar low (buy) or above the pin bar high (sell) — whichever is the more extreme level.
  9. **Set the target.** Next resistance (buy) or next support (sell). For extended targets, project to the next higher-timeframe PD array.
  10. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1, trail the runner to the full target.

section: Best Pairs for Pin Bar Trading

section: Common Mistakes Around Pin Bar Trading
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Pin Bar Trading

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading pin bars.

  1. **Trading every pin bar.** Pin bars are common — but only the ones at higher-timeframe key levels are tradeable. The rest are noise.
  2. **Pin bars on the wrong timeframe.** Daily and 4-hour pin bars are reliable. 5-minute pin bars produce many fakes.
  3. **Trading pin bars against the trend.** Counter-trend pin bars have a much lower hit rate. Stick to bias-aligned pin bars in uptrends and downtrends respectively.
  4. **Tight stops at the pin bar extreme.** The 10–20 pip buffer is mandatory — wicks often spike just past the level on the second test.
  5. **Entering mid-candle.** Pin bars are only valid AFTER the close. Mid-candle reads change before the close completes.
  6. **Ignoring the wick-to-body ratio.** A pin bar with a 1:1 wick-to-body is not a pin bar. Require at least 2:1.

title: pin-bar-trading-strategy
section: FAQs about Pin Bar Trading Strategy
content:
#### FAQs about Pin Bar Trading Strategy

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about pin bar trading.

**What is a pin bar?**

A single candlestick with a long wick (shadow) and a small real body. The long wick shows strong price rejection from a level, and the small body indicates the close occurred near the opposite end of the wick.

**What is the difference between a bullish and bearish pin bar?**

Bullish pin bar — long lower wick with small body near the top (looks like a hammer). Bearish pin bar — long upper wick with small body near the bottom (also called a shooting star).

**What ratio should the wick have to the body?**

The wick should be at least 2x the body, ideally 3x or more. The longer the wick, the stronger the rejection signal.

**What timeframes work best for pin bars?**

Higher timeframes — daily, weekly, and 4-hour — produce the most reliable pin bars. Lower timeframes generate many false pin bars.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

Two options — (1) immediately on the pin bar candle close, or (2) wait for price to retrace 50% into the pin bar for a tighter entry. Option 2 has a lower hit rate but higher reward.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips below the low of a bullish pin bar (or below support) for buy trades — 10 to 20 pips above the high of a bearish pin bar (or above resistance) for sell trades, whichever is the more extreme level.

**Where do I take profit?**

Next resistance for a buy trade, next support for a sell trade. For extended targets, the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**Can I trade pin bars without support and resistance?**

The hit rate drops significantly. Pin bars are reliable BECAUSE they form at S&R — without that context, they are just random rejection candles.

**How does the pin bar fit in the ICT framework?**

It is a single-candle signature of an inducement sweep plus CISD at a higher-timeframe PD array. The long wick is the sweep, the small body and close are the CISD.

**What is the difference between a pin bar and a doji?**

A doji has a very small body with wicks of similar length on both sides — signaling indecision. A pin bar has ONE long wick (the rejection side) and a small body on the OPPOSITE end — signaling directional rejection.

**Does the pin bar work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook pin bars at higher-timeframe support and resistance, especially during the New York AM session.

**What is the success rate of pin bar trading?**

Pin bars at higher-timeframe key levels in a confirmed trend historically deliver a 60–70% hit rate. Random pin bars without level context have a much lower success rate.

# Powerful ICT Reversal Patterns — IFVG/BPR, CISD & MSS Three-Stage Sequence

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/powerful-ict-reversal-patterns/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/powerful-ict-reversal-patterns/)

![Powerful ICT Reversal Patterns — three sequential reversal confirmations using IFVG/BPR, CISD and MSS to identify trend changes at their earliest stages](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/ict-reversal-patterns.png)

Powerful ICT Reversal Patterns are the three sequential confirmations that let you identify a trend reversal at its earliest stages — IFVG/BPR for the first weakness signal, CISD for the second confirmation, and MSS for the final structural break. Mastering these three in order means you catch reversals before retail traders have spotted the change.

These ICT reversal patterns can also be used as trade entry confirmation on a lower timeframe when price is standing at a higher-timeframe [ICT PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/>).

In this guide I walk you through the three reversal patterns — the IFVG/BPR weakness signal, the CISD candle-level confirmation, the MSS structural break, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

title: powerful-ict-reversal-patterns
section: (I) ICT IFVG / BPR Reversal
content:
#### (I) ICT IFVG / BPR Reversal

ICT [IFVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-inversion-fair-value-gap/>) is the 1st and initial indication of reversal in the direction of price.

When price moves in a trend, it tends to respect the fair value gaps and gets rejected from the FVGs. But if price starts breaking the FVGs, it indicates the weakness of the trend and can lead to the reversal of the trend.

If price breaks an FVG, it becomes the inverse fair value gap (IFVG) — which is a weak confirmation of reversal.

But while breaking an FVG, if price forms ANOTHER FVG against the previous FVG, that is a strong confirmation of reversal — called the [ICT Balanced Price Range (BPR)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-balanced-price-range-bpr/>).

ICT BPR signals the weakness of the previous trend and the strength of the new direction.

When price, after forming a BPR, retraces back to the BPR, you can execute the trade in the direction of the BPR.

You can see the examples of ICT IFVG/BPR reversals in the pictures given below.

![ICT BPR reversal example — overlapping bullish and bearish FVGs forming the Balanced Price Range with price reversing strongly from the BPR retest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/BPR-300x234.png)

![ICT IFVG reversal example — original FVG broken in the opposite direction, flipping polarity into the Inversion Fair Value Gap as the first weakness signal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/IFVG-300x220.png)

title: powerful-ict-reversal-patterns
section: (II) ICT CISD Reversal
content:
#### (II) ICT CISD Reversal

[ICT CISD](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>) stands for the Change in State of Delivery.

When price is delivering in one direction, it is indicated by consecutive candles of that side — for example, bullish price delivery is indicated by consecutive bullish candles.

When price breaks below the start of bullish price delivery, it is called the change in state of delivery to the sell side.

The start of bullish price delivery is marked by the closing price (the low of the body) of the last bearish candlestick before the consecutive bullish candlesticks.

The start of bearish price delivery is marked by the closing price (the high of the body) of the last bullish candlestick before the consecutive bearish candlesticks.

ICT CISD is the 2nd initial confirmation of price reversing its direction.

After the CISD, wait for price to retrace back to the [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/>) or any BPR, FVG and IFVG formed during the CISD. Then you can execute your trade in the direction of CISD.

You can see the example of ICT CISD reversals in the picture given below.

![ICT CISD reversal example — bullish price delivery ends when price breaks below the low of the last bearish candle before the consecutive bullish candles, signaling a bearish CISD](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CISD.png)

title: powerful-ict-reversal-patterns
section: (III) ICT MSS Reversal
content:
#### (III) ICT MSS Reversal

[ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) is indicated by the break above the [ICT Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>) or break below the [ICT Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>).

ICT MSS is the 3rd and almost final confirmation of price reversing its direction.

When the market is moving bullish, it marks higher swing highs — meaning it breaks the previous swing high and forms a new swing high while forming higher swing lows.

If price starts moving down and breaks the latest higher swing low, it is marked as the bearish market structure shift.

When the market is trending bearish, price keeps creating lower swing highs — meaning every new high fails to reach the level of the previous one — and lower swing lows, showing continuous weakness.

But the moment price pushes upward and breaks the most recent lower swing high, that is your signal of a bullish market structure shift. It tells you that sellers are losing control and buyers are stepping in with strength.

After the MSS, wait for price to retrace back to any breaker block, IFVG or BPR formed while shifting the structure — then execute your trade in the direction of the MSS.

You can see the example of ICT MSS reversal in the picture given below.

![ICT MSS reversal example on XAU/USD — bearish swing low broken upward signaling the bullish market structure shift, with price retracing to the breaker block for the buy entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/XAUUSD_2025-12-01_23-03-12.png)

title: powerful-ict-reversal-patterns
section: The Three-Pattern Sequence
content:
#### The Three-Pattern Sequence

The strongest reversal trades happen when all three patterns appear in sequence — IFVG/BPR first, then CISD, then MSS.

**Stage 1 — IFVG/BPR:** The first sign of weakness. Worth watching, not trading.

**Stage 2 — CISD:** The second confirmation. You can take an aggressive entry here at the breaker block or post-CISD PD array.

**Stage 3 — MSS:** The structural confirmation. The highest-conviction entry — on the retest of the post-MSS PD array.

When all three line up at a higher-timeframe PD array (FVG, order block, or premium/discount zone), the reversal trade is at its highest probability.

title: powerful-ict-reversal-patterns
section: Step-by-Step Reversal Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Reversal Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading an ICT reversal.

  1. **Identify the higher-timeframe PD array.** Where price is expected to react — daily/4-hour FVG, OB, or premium/discount zone.
  2. **Wait for price to reach the PD array.** Confirmation that the algorithm is delivering toward the level.
  3. **Watch for Stage 1 — IFVG/BPR.** Price breaks the most recent FVG against the trend, and ideally forms a BPR.
  4. **Watch for Stage 2 — CISD.** Price closes below the start of bullish delivery (or above the start of bearish delivery).
  5. **Watch for Stage 3 — MSS.** Price breaks the most recent swing low (bullish trend ending) or swing high (bearish trend ending).
  6. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to the breaker block, BPR, IFVG or FVG formed during the structure shift.
  7. **Enter on the retest.** In the new direction at the post-MSS PD array.
  8. **Set the stop.** Beyond the MSS swing extreme, with a small buffer.
  9. **Take profit at the opposite extreme.** The other side of the prior range / leg.

section: Common Mistakes Around ICT Reversal Patterns
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around ICT Reversal Patterns

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using the three reversal patterns.

  1. **Trading the IFVG alone.** The IFVG is Stage 1 — the first weakness signal. Trading on it without CISD or MSS confirmation produces frequent counter-trend losses.
  2. **Confusing IFVG with BPR.** An IFVG is a single FVG broken in the opposite direction. A BPR is two overlapping opposite-direction FVGs. BPR is the stronger signal.
  3. **Mis-marking the CISD level.** The CISD is the start of the delivery — the body of the last opposing candle before the directional run. Not the wick, not the open of the first directional candle.
  4. **Treating every swing break as MSS.** The MSS only counts when it breaks the most recent counter-trend swing point. Random swing breaks are noise.
  5. **Skipping the retest.** Entering at the MSS candle is aggressive and gets stopped out often. Wait for the retest of the post-MSS PD array.
  6. **Trading reversals without a higher-timeframe PD array.** A three-stage reversal in the middle of nowhere has a low hit rate. Anchor every reversal trade to a higher-timeframe level.

section: FAQs about ICT Reversal Patterns
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Reversal Patterns

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about ICT reversal patterns.

**What are the three powerful ICT reversal patterns?**

(1) IFVG/BPR — the initial weakness signal. (2) CISD — the candle-level change-of-delivery confirmation. (3) MSS — the structural break confirmation. The three appear in sequence at every clean reversal.

**What is the IFVG reversal pattern?**

When a fair value gap gets broken in the opposite direction, it becomes an Inversion FVG. This break signals the weakness of the prevailing trend — the first reversal hint.

**What is the BPR reversal pattern?**

When price breaks an FVG and simultaneously forms a new FVG in the opposite direction, the overlap of the two is called the Balanced Price Range. BPR is a stronger reversal signal than IFVG alone.

**What is the CISD reversal pattern?**

Change in State of Delivery — when price breaks the start of the prior directional run (the body of the last opposing candle before the consecutive directional candles). It is the second-stage reversal confirmation.

**What is the MSS reversal pattern?**

Market Structure Shift — the break of the most recent counter-trend swing point. The third and almost-final reversal confirmation. Bullish MSS breaks the most recent lower swing high; bearish MSS breaks the most recent higher swing low.

**In what order do the three patterns appear?**

IFVG/BPR first (Stage 1 weakness), then CISD (Stage 2 candle confirmation), then MSS (Stage 3 structural break). The highest-conviction reversal has all three in sequence.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After the MSS, wait for the retest of the post-MSS PD array (breaker block, BPR, IFVG or FVG formed during the shift). Enter at the retest with the new directional bias.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the MSS swing extreme — below the structural low for buy trades, above the structural high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

The opposite extreme of the prior leg — the start of the prior trend, plus relative equal highs/lows and higher-timeframe FVGs along the way.

**What timeframe works best?**

The three patterns scale to any timeframe. For day trading use 15-minute and 1-hour for the patterns and 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry. For swing trading use 4-hour and daily.

**Do these reversal patterns work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook IFVG/BPR/CISD/MSS sequences, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**What if I see CISD but no MSS yet?**

You can take an aggressive entry at the post-CISD PD array (breaker block, BPR, FVG, IFVG). The hit rate is lower than waiting for the MSS, but the reward is higher because you catch the reversal earlier.

**How is the three-pattern sequence different from a single reversal signal?**

A single signal (just IFVG, just CISD, or just MSS) can fail. The three-pattern sequence stacks the confirmations — by the time all three have triggered, the reversal probability is much higher than any single pattern alone.

During the Asian session (20:00–00:00 NY), price sweeps short-term highs or lows formed in the late NY session. After the sweep, a 1-minute MSS or rejection candle confirms the entry, with 20-pip stop and 20-pip target.

**How does the New York session setup work?**

During NY (07:00–10:00 NY), if London has already posted the daily high or low, NY retraces. Short-term highs or lows formed after the NY open get swept, then 1-minute MSS confirms the entry.

**What is the risk-reward ratio?**

5-minute for identifying the short-term liquidity. 1-minute for the MSS entry trigger.

20 pips is the realistic daily minimum from short-term liquidity raids on major forex pairs. It is small enough to fit inside a single session, and large enough to compound meaningfully when traded consistently.

**Does the model work every day?**

No — almost every day. Some days have multiple opportunities; some have none. Read the market environment first (consolidation, reversal, expansion) and skip days with no setup.

**What if price never sweeps the short-term level?**

Skip the trade. Without the liquidity raid, the model’s core trigger is missing.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

20 pips from the entry. Stricter scalpers use the swept short-term extreme plus a small buffer — but never wider than 20 pips.

**Does the strategy work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook short-term liquidity raids during the Asian and NY sessions. Adjust the pip equivalent for the instrument’s tick size.

**What is the difference between 20 Pips a Day and ICT Scalping Strategy?**

The [ICT Scalping Strategy](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/simple-ict-scalping-strategy/>) targets 30 to 50 pips using OTE entries on the 3rd daily candle. 20 Pips a Day targets a strict 20 pips using session-based short-term liquidity raids. Smaller target, faster execution.

# QML (Quasimodo) Chart Pattern — Bullish/Bearish Reversal Setup, QML Zone & MSS Confirmation

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/qml-chart-pattern/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/qml-chart-pattern/)

![QML Quasimodo chart pattern — reversal pattern with higher high and lower low at the end of a bullish trend, marked as the QML zone between the two highs](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/ICT-Liquidity-Sweep-and-Liquidity-Run_20240811_150951_0000.png)

QML — Quasimodo — is a reversal chart pattern that, when formed at a higher-timeframe support or resistance level, signals the change of trend. It is the structural cousin of the Change of Character (CHOCH) and one of the cleanest pre-CHOCH reversal signals on the chart.

In this guide I walk you through the QML pattern — the meaning, the bullish and bearish variants, the QML zone identification, the step-by-step trade flow, the QML vs CHOCH comparison, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: What is the QML (Quasimodo) Chart Pattern?
content:
#### What is the QML (Quasimodo) Chart Pattern?

QML (Quasimodo) is a reversal chart pattern widely used by day traders to anticipate price reversals from a key level — a higher-timeframe supply or demand zone, or a support or resistance level.

It is indicated by the **higher high and lower low** at the end of a bullish trend, or **lower low and higher high** at the end of a bearish trend.

On the basis of the trend, the QML pattern has two types — bullish and bearish.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: (I) Bullish QML (Quasimodo) Pattern
content:
#### (I) Bullish QML (Quasimodo) Pattern

Bullish QML is formed at the end of a bearish trend at a key level.

In a bearish trend price makes lower lows and lower highs. But when price reaches a key support level and makes a higher high that violates the previous lower high, a structure with a lower low and a higher high is formed — that is the bullish QML pattern.

![Bullish QML pattern example — bearish trend reaches a key support level, prints a new lower low, and then breaks the previous lower high to confirm a higher high reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/bullish-QM.png)

It indicates the reversal of price from bearish trend to bullish.

**How to Trade a Bullish QML Pattern**

**(I)** Identify the second-to-last low and the last low before the formation of QML.

**(II)** Mark the area between these two lows (the QML area).

**(III)** Look for imbalances, demand zones, or FTR (failed-to-return) levels in this area.

**(IV)** Execute a bullish trade when price taps this area, or wait for a confirmation like a [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on a lower timeframe.

**(V)** Place the stop-loss below the last low (QML low) and target the last high (QML high) for take profit.

![Bullish QML trade example — QML zone between the second-to-last and last low, demand zone refinement, MSS confirmation, buy entry with stop below QML low and target at QML high](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Untitled1.png)

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: (II) Bearish QML (Quasimodo) Pattern
content:
#### (II) Bearish QML (Quasimodo) Pattern

In a bullish trend price makes higher highs and higher lows. However, when price reaches a key resistance level and then makes a lower low, breaking the previous higher low, it forms a structure known as a bearish QML pattern.

![Bearish QML pattern example — bullish trend reaches a key resistance level, prints a new higher high, and then breaks the previous higher low to confirm a lower low reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/bearsih-QM-pattern.png)

This pattern indicates a potential reversal from a bullish trend to a bearish trend.

**How to Trade a Bearish QML Pattern**

**(I)** Identify the second-to-last high and the last high before the formation of QML.

**(II)** Mark the area between these two highs (the QML area).

**(III)** Look for imbalances, supply zones, or FTR levels in this area.

**(IV)** Execute a bearish trade when price taps this area, or wait for a confirmation like a Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe.

**(V)** Place the stop-loss above the last high (QML high) and target the last low (QML low) for take profit.

![Bearish QML trade example — QML zone between the second-to-last and last high, supply zone refinement, MSS confirmation, sell entry with stop above QML high and target at QML low](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Untitled3.png)

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: Basis of the QML Pattern
content:
#### Basis of the QML Pattern

QML is basically based on the concept of [Change of Character (CHOCH)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>) — when price changes its trend and breaks the lower high or higher low in a bullish or bearish trend, that is called a change of character, which is a smart money concept.

Sometimes the QML may indicate the reversal of price BEFORE the CHOCH happens — because every high or low is not a structural high or low, and the QML may form without breaking the structural high or low.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: QML vs CHOCH — How They Relate
content:
#### QML vs CHOCH — How They Relate

QML and CHOCH are closely related but they are not the same level.

CHOCH is the break of the most recent structural higher low (in a bullish trend) or lower high (in a bearish trend) — the structural reversal confirmation.

QML can form earlier — at any non-structural higher low or lower high — and gives an earlier reversal signal that may or may not become a full CHOCH.

In practice, every CHOCH is a QML, but not every QML is a CHOCH. The QML zone is the entry zone; the CHOCH is the bias confirmation.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: Step-by-Step QML Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step QML Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading a QML pattern.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour charts — identify the trend and the key support / resistance level price is approaching.
  2. **Wait for price to reach the key level.** Bullish QML — at higher-timeframe support or demand. Bearish QML — at higher-timeframe resistance or supply.
  3. **Watch for the QML structure.** Bullish — lower low followed by a higher high that violates the previous lower high. Bearish — higher high followed by a lower low that breaks the previous higher low.
  4. **Mark the QML zone.** Bullish — between the second-to-last low and the last low. Bearish — between the second-to-last high and the last high.
  5. **Refine inside the QML zone.** Look for an imbalance, demand / supply zone, or FTR level inside the zone for the entry.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe (5-minute or 15-minute).** For the entry trigger.
  7. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS.** A clean break of the most recent counter-trend swing point in the new direction.
  8. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the refinement level inside the QML zone.
  9. **Set the stop.** Below the QML low (bullish) or above the QML high (bearish), with a small buffer.
  10. **Take profit at the QML opposite extreme.** Bullish — target the last high (QML high). Bearish — target the last low (QML low).

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: Best Pairs for QML Trading
content:
#### Best Pairs for QML Trading

QML works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD. The cleanest QML prints come from instruments that produce strong reversals at key higher-timeframe levels.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the QML framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for QML reversals.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: Common Mistakes Around the QML Pattern
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around the QML Pattern

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading the QML pattern.

  1. **Marking QML without a key level.** A QML structure in the middle of a range is meaningless. The QML only works when it forms at a higher-timeframe support or resistance level.
  2. **Entering blindly at the QML zone.** The QML is the zone — wait for the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation before entering. Blind entries at the zone get hunted regularly.
  3. **Confusing QML with a regular pullback.** A pullback continues the trend. A QML reverses it. The structural difference is the violated higher low / lower high.
  4. **Tight stops at the QML extreme.** Stops parked exactly at the QML low or high get hunted on the second test. Place the stop with a buffer.
  5. **Ignoring the higher-timeframe trend at the entry.** A bullish QML against the daily bearish trend has a much lower hit rate than one aligned with a daily bullish bias.
  6. **Trading every higher-high or lower-low as a QML.** The structure must include both the violated swing AND the new reversal extreme. One leg alone is not a QML.

title: qml-chart-pattern
section: FAQs about the QML Pattern
content:
#### FAQs about the QML Pattern

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the QML pattern.

**What is the QML chart pattern?**

QML (Quasimodo) is a reversal chart pattern indicated by a higher high and lower low (at the end of a bullish trend) or a lower low and higher high (at the end of a bearish trend) at a higher-timeframe support or resistance level.

**Why is the QML pattern significant in trading?**

The QML pattern is significant because it helps traders identify potential trend reversals at key levels, allowing them to enter trades with a higher probability of success.

**Can the QML pattern be used on any timeframe?**

Yes — the QML pattern can be used on any timeframe. However, it is most effective when identified on higher-timeframe support or resistance levels.

**How is the QML pattern used by traders?**

Day traders use the QML pattern to anticipate price reversals from key levels such as higher-timeframe supply or demand zones, and support or resistance levels. It helps in identifying potential turning points in the market.

**What is the difference between QML and CHOCH?**

CHOCH is the break of the most recent structural higher low (bullish trend) or lower high (bearish trend). QML can form earlier — at any non-structural higher low or lower high — giving an earlier reversal signal. Every CHOCH is a QML, but not every QML is a CHOCH.

**Where do I place the stop loss on a QML trade?**

Below the QML low (bullish QML) or above the QML high (bearish QML), with a small buffer. Not at the level itself.

**Where do I take profit?**

The QML opposite extreme — bullish QML targets the last high (QML high); bearish QML targets the last low (QML low). For an extended target, use the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What confirmation do I wait for before entering?**

A lower-timeframe MSS, fair value gap or order block formed inside the QML zone after price taps it. Do not enter on the touch alone.

**What is the FTR level inside the QML zone?**

FTR (failed-to-return) is a smart-money concept zone where price failed to return after the structural break. It is one of the refinement levels inside the QML zone for the entry.

**Does the QML pattern work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook QML reversals at higher-timeframe key levels, especially during the New York AM session.

**How is QML different from a head-and-shoulders pattern?**

A QML is structurally the inverse of a head-and-shoulders — same three-extreme structure but the entry rules and zone definitions are different. Both signal reversals; QML emphasizes the violation of the previous lower high or higher low as the trigger.

# Rally Base Rally (RBR) — Bullish Continuation Pattern with 70:30 / 25:75 Body-Wick Rules

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/rally-base-rally/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/rally-base-rally/)

![Rally Base Rally — supply and demand bullish continuation pattern showing initial rally, consolidation base, and second rally after breakout](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Rally-base-rally-strategy.png)

Rally Base Rally (RBR) is a powerful bullish continuation pattern from the supply and demand framework — an initial rally, a consolidation base, and a second rally after the base breaks. It is one of the cleanest continuation setups inside an established bullish trend, and once you can identify the body-to-wick ratio rules, the pattern becomes very visible on the chart.

Rally Base Rally is one of the various strategies used in technical analysis to predict the future move of any asset — forex currency pairs, commodities, crypto, stocks or indices. This strategy originates from smart money concepts, and its foundation lies in [Supply and Demand](<https://www.innercircletrader.net/tutorials/supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading/>).

In this guide I walk you through Rally Base Rally — the definition, the three-component identification, the candle body-to-wick rules, the trade execution, the confirmation filters, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: rally-base-rally
section: What is Rally Base Rally?
content:
#### What is Rally Base Rally?

Rally Base Rally is a powerful bullish continuation concept from the supply and demand trading strategy. The RBR concept states that prices move in a series of rallies and consolidations — these rallies and consolidations create a pattern that can be identified and traded easily.

![Rally Base Rally illustration — initial bullish rally, sideways base consolidation, then a second bullish rally extending the trend higher](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Rally-base-rally.png)

The rally phase occurs when prices move sharply on the buy side, indicating strong demand. The base phase is marked by consolidation of prices in a range as the market digests the previous sharp move. The 2nd rally phase starts after the breakout of the previous consolidation range and prices again move sharply to the buy side.

title: rally-base-rally
section: How to Identify Rally Base Rally
content:
#### How to Identify Rally Base Rally

To trade a Rally Base Rally pattern, it is essential to identify and mark it correctly on the price chart.

Rally Base Rally pattern consists of 3 main components:

**(I)** Initial Rally

**(II)** The Base

**(III)** Subsequent Rally

The initial rally is a sharp move toward the buy side, followed by a period of consolidation in the base phase, and finally a second rally after the breakout of the base — showing continuation of the previous bullish move.

![Rally Base Rally three-component breakdown — sharp initial rally, narrow horizontal base, breakout above the base followed by the second rally continuation](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/rally-base-rally-2.png)

title: rally-base-rally
section: Body-to-Wick Ratio of Candles for Rally Base Rally
content:
#### Body-to-Wick Ratio of Candles for Rally Base Rally

To confirm an initial rally, look for two or more consecutive bullish candles with a body-to-wick ratio of 70:30 or more — meaning the body should cover at least 70% of the total candlestick and the wick should not be more than 30% of the total candlestick.

The base is characterized by a single or more candlesticks that show a temporary pause in the bullish momentum. The body-to-wick ratio of base candles should be 25:75 or less — meaning the body should cover 25% or less of the total candlestick while the wick should cover 75% or more.

This body-to-wick filter is what separates a real RBR from a noisy retracement — the rally candles are decisive, the base candles are indecisive, and the directional change is structurally visible.

title: rally-base-rally
section: How to Trade Rally Base Rally
content:
#### How to Trade Rally Base Rally

To trade a Rally Base Rally pattern, you should wait for the formation of the initial rally and the base. After the formation and identification of the initial rally and the base, you should wait for price to break the base.

A candle closing above the price range of the base area is considered the breakout of the base.

After the breakout of the base, you can take a buy trade immediately if price retests the base area. If it does not retest the base area immediately, you can wait for price to retest the base area and execute a buy trade at this retest.

![Rally Base Rally trade execution example — base breakout candle above the consolidation range, retest of the base, then buy entry with stop below the base low](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/RBR-trade-1.png)

While trading a Rally Base Rally pattern, your stop loss will be below the low of the base, and for take profit you can target a 1:2 risk-reward or the next resistance zone.

title: rally-base-rally
section: Other Confirmations to Execute a Trade
content:
#### Other Confirmations to Execute a Trade

To execute a buy trade after breakout and retest of the base, look for extra confirmations.

**Bullish Candlestick Pattern Confirmation** can be very useful while trading Rally Base Rally. Any bullish candlestick pattern like a hammer, morning star or engulfing will increase the probability of winning.

**Volume Confirmation** is also essential while trading Rally Base Rally. A strong breakout from the base phase accompanied by high volume signals a high-probability trade entry.

**Lower-Timeframe MSS Confirmation** — ICT traders can drop to the 5-minute or 15-minute and wait for a [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) at the retest of the base for the tightest entry trigger.

title: rally-base-rally
section: Rally Base Rally in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Rally Base Rally in the ICT Framework

RBR maps cleanly onto ICT concepts. The initial rally is the displacement leg that produced a [break of structure](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>). The base is the demand zone — specifically the consolidation that smart money uses for accumulation. The base low is often the [inducement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-inducement-in-forex/>) level, and the breakout-and-retest entry pairs naturally with the post-inducement-sweep MSS trigger.

If you trade ICT, treat RBR as a visual shortcut for the bullish BOS-plus-demand setup, and use the body-to-wick ratio as a quick filter for whether the leg is high-conviction.

title: rally-base-rally
section: Step-by-Step Rally Base Rally Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Rally Base Rally Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading Rally Base Rally.

  1. **Confirm bullish trend.** Higher-timeframe structure must be bullish.
  2. **Identify the initial rally.** Two or more consecutive bullish candles with body-to-wick ratio of 70:30 or more.
  3. **Mark the base.** One or more consolidation candles with body-to-wick ratio of 25:75 or less.
  4. **Wait for the breakout.** A candle closes above the high of the base.
  5. **Wait for the retest of the base.** Price retraces back to the base area.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** Bullish candlestick pattern, volume spike, or lower-timeframe MSS at the base retest.
  7. **Enter the buy.** On the confirmation candle close.
  8. **Set the stop.** Below the low of the base, with a small buffer.
  9. **Set the target.** 1:2 risk-reward, or the next resistance / liquidity zone.
  10. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1, trail to the full target.

section: Best Pairs for Rally Base Rally
content:
#### Best Pairs for Rally Base Rally

Rally Base Rally works on every major instrument that produces trending moves — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD, and indices like NQ and ES.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the RBR framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for RBR breakouts.

title: rally-base-rally
section: Common Mistakes Around Rally Base Rally
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Rally Base Rally

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading Rally Base Rally.

  1. **Ignoring the body-to-wick ratio.** Without the 70:30 rally and 25:75 base filter, every pullback looks like an RBR. The ratio is the structural filter.
  2. **Trading RBR against the trend.** The pattern is a bullish CONTINUATION setup. In a bearish trend, the inverse pattern (Drop Base Drop) applies — not RBR.
  3. **Entering at the breakout without retest.** Many breakouts are fakeouts. Wait for the retest of the base, plus a confirmation candle.
  4. **Marking the base too small.** A base needs at least 2 to 3 indecisive candles. A single candle pause is too thin to qualify.
  5. **Tight stops at the base low.** Stops parked exactly at the base low get hunted. Place the stop with a buffer below the base low.
  6. **No risk-reward discipline.** The model targets 1:2 minimum. Holding for less than 1:1 or chasing 1:5+ both break the model statistics.

title: rally-base-rally
section: FAQs about Rally Base Rally
content:
#### FAQs about Rally Base Rally

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about Rally Base Rally.

**What is Rally Base Rally?**

A bullish continuation pattern from the supply and demand framework consisting of three components — an initial rally, a consolidation base, and a second rally after the base breaks.

**How do I identify Rally Base Rally?**

Find a bullish trend, identify the initial rally (2+ candles with 70:30 body-to-wick ratio), mark the consolidation base (candles with 25:75 body-to-wick ratio), and wait for the breakout above the base.

**What is the body-to-wick rule?**

Rally candles need body ≥ 70% of total candle height (wick ≤ 30%). Base candles need body ≤ 25% of total candle height (wick ≥ 75%). This filter separates real rallies from noisy moves.

**What is the difference between Rally Base Rally and Drop Base Drop?**

RBR is the bullish version (rally → base → rally). DBD is the bearish mirror (drop → base → drop). Same structural rules, opposite direction.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After the base breakout, either enter immediately on the retest of the base, or wait for price to retrace back to the base and enter at the retest with a bullish confirmation candle.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Below the low of the base, with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

1:2 risk-reward minimum, or the next resistance / liquidity zone. Some traders trail with the trend for larger targets.

**What timeframe works best for RBR?**

RBR appears on every timeframe. For day trading use 15-minute and 1-hour. For swing trading use 4-hour and daily.

**How does RBR fit in the ICT framework?**

The initial rally is the BOS displacement leg. The base is the demand zone (often containing the order block). The breakout-and-retest is the post-inducement continuation play.

**What confirmations do I add?**

Bullish candlestick patterns (hammer, morning star, engulfing), high-volume breakout, or a lower-timeframe MSS at the base retest.

**Does Rally Base Rally work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook RBR setups, especially during the New York AM session.

**What is the success rate of RBR?**

In a confirmed bullish trend with a clean rally and tight base meeting the body-to-wick rules, RBR historically delivers a 60–75% breakout-success rate when the retest is waited out.

# Shooting Star Candlestick — Bearish Reversal at Resistance with Long Upper Tail

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/shooting-star-candlestick/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/shooting-star-candlestick/)

![Shooting Star Candlestick — bearish reversal pattern with long upper wick and small body at resistance, marking the top of price before a bearish reversal](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/shooting-star-candlestick.png)

Shooting Star Candlestick is one of the cleanest bearish reversal candles in price action — a single candle with a long upper “tail” (wick) and a small body that closes near the open, signaling that buyers pushed price up but were overwhelmed by sellers who drove it right back down. When it prints at strong resistance after an uptrend, it is one of the highest-conviction tops in candlestick analysis.

In this guide I walk you through the shooting star — the definition, what it tells us, the confirmation rule, how to trade it, timeframe selection, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ. For the doji variants see [Gravestone Doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/gravestone-doji-candlestick/>) (no body) and [Dragonfly Doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/dragonfly-doji-candlestick/>) (bullish mirror).

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: What is Shooting Star Candlestick?
content:
#### What is Shooting Star Candlestick?

It is a single candlestick pattern, and it resembles a shooting star because of its long tail and small body.

Shooting star candlestick is a bearish candlestick pattern which marks the top of price before a reversal.

It is formed when a candlestick opens and moves up — but after that price moves down, coming back to the opening price and closing near the opening price, leaving a long wick to the upside called the tail.

![Shooting star candlestick anatomy — small body near the open with a long upper wick \(tail\) showing buyer rejection from the highs and a return to the open](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/shooting-star-candlestick-pattern.png)

Due to its closing near the opening price, it has a small body — either bullish or bearish.

There can be a little wick at the bottom of the shooting star, but a shooting star without a wick at the bottom is more reliable.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: What does Shooting Star Candlestick Tell?
content:
#### What does Shooting Star Candlestick Tell?

A shooting star candlestick shows that at opening, the buyers were strong, leading price to move up significantly.

But the buyers failed to hold price higher, and price came back to the opening price — which shows that the sellers got control and they look strong.

It also indicates that the first bullish move was a trap for retailers, and the real trend is going to be bearish.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Confirmation of Shooting Star Candlestick
content:
#### Confirmation of Shooting Star Candlestick

A shooting star formed at a strong resistance level can be reliable — but if it is forming anywhere else, then you need to confirm the shooting star before trading it.

The follow-up candlestick formed after the shooting star will act as a confirmation of the shooting star candlestick.

If the next candle remains below the high of the shooting star candlestick and closes below the low of the shooting star candlestick, then it is a confirmation of decline in price.

But if the next candle crosses the high of the shooting star or closes above the high of the shooting star, it indicates that the shooting star formed was a false signal and is not reliable.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: How to Trade Using Shooting Star Candlestick
content:
#### How to Trade Using Shooting Star Candlestick

As discussed earlier, the shooting star is a bearish candlestick — so it acts as a confirmation of decline in price at strong resistance levels.

When a shooting star forms at a resistance level, wait for the follow-up candlestick for the confirmation of the shooting star.

After the confirmation of the shooting star, you can place a sell order when price retraces and tests the body of the shooting star candlestick.

In this scenario, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the high of the shooting star candlestick.

![Shooting star trade example — bullish trend tests resistance, shooting star prints, confirmation candle closes below the low, retest of body triggers the sell entry](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/shooting-star-candlestick-trading.png)

For take profit, you may target 1:2 risk-reward — or you can target the next support level as your take profit.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Timeframe to Trade Shooting Star Candlestick
content:
#### Timeframe to Trade Shooting Star Candlestick

The shooting star candlestick pattern can be used on any timeframe, but its effectiveness varies.

On shorter timeframes like 5-minute, it might only lead to small moves of 20, 30 or 50 pips.

However, on higher timeframes like 4-hour or daily, it tends to be more reliable and can result in larger trade setups of 100 pips or more.

It is better to use the shooting star pattern on higher timeframes such as 1-hour, 4-hour or daily.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Shooting Star vs Gravestone Doji
content:
#### Shooting Star vs Gravestone Doji

Both are bearish reversal candles with a long upper wick at resistance. The structural difference is the body size.

**Shooting Star** — has a small real body (either bullish or bearish) near the open.

**[Gravestone Doji](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/gravestone-doji-candlestick/>)** — has virtually no real body (open and close at the same level).

Both signal bearish reversal — the gravestone is the stronger, no-body version; the shooting star is the more common, small-body version. The trade rules are identical: wait for the confirmation candle and enter on the retest of the body.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Shooting Star in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Shooting Star in the ICT Framework

In ICT terms, the shooting star is the single-candle signature of an [inducement sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/>) above resistance followed by strong rejection.

The long upper wick is the sweep — buyers grab the liquidity above resistance. The close back near the open is the candle-level [change in state of delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-change-in-the-state-of-delivery/>) — buyers exhausted, sellers in control.

For the highest-conviction setup, look for shooting star at a higher-timeframe supply zone or bearish PD array, then drop to the 15-minute for the lower-timeframe MSS confirmation before entering.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Step-by-Step Shooting Star Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Shooting Star Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for a shooting star trade.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Bullish — making higher highs and higher lows.
  2. **Mark the resistance zone.** Strong horizontal resistance, ideally aligned with a higher-timeframe PD array.
  3. **Wait for price to test resistance.** Patience is mandatory.
  4. **Watch for the shooting star to print.** Long upper wick, small body near the open. No or minimal lower wick is more reliable.
  5. **Wait for the candle to close.** Only the closed candle counts.
  6. **Wait for the confirmation candle.** Next candle must remain below the shooting star’s high and close below its low.
  7. **Wait for the retest.** Price retraces back to the body of the shooting star.
  8. **Enter the sell.** On the retest, with bearish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.
  9. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips above the high of the shooting star.
  10. **Set the target.** 1:2 risk-reward minimum or the next support level.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Best Pairs for Shooting Star
content:
#### Best Pairs for Shooting Star

Shooting star works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD, and indices like NQ and ES.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the shooting star framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for shooting star reversals.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: Common Mistakes Around Shooting Star
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Shooting Star

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading shooting stars.

  1. **Trading every shooting star.** Without a resistance level above the wick, the shooting star is just noise. The level is mandatory.
  2. **Skipping the confirmation candle.** The follow-up candle must close below the shooting star’s low. Without it, the pattern may fail.
  3. **Trading shooting stars on low timeframes.** 5-minute produces many fakes. 1-hour, 4-hour and daily are far more reliable.
  4. **Stops too tight.** The 10-20 pip buffer above the high is mandatory — wicks often spike just past the shooting star high on the second test.
  5. **Confusing shooting star with gravestone doji.** Shooting star has a small body; gravestone has none. Treat them as related but distinct — the no-body version is structurally stronger.
  6. **Entering before retest.** The clean entry is on the retest of the body, not on the confirmation candle close.

title: shooting-star-candlestick
section: FAQs about Shooting Star Candlestick
content:
#### FAQs about Shooting Star Candlestick

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about the shooting star candlestick.

**What is a shooting star candlestick?**

A single bearish reversal candlestick with a long upper wick (tail) and a small body that closes near the open. It marks the top of price before a reversal — buyers pushed price up but sellers overwhelmed them and drove price back.

**What does shooting star candlestick tell us?**

That buyers were strong at the open and pushed price up, but sellers regained control and forced price back to the open — signaling exhaustion of buyers and the start of a bearish reversal.

**Where does a shooting star form?**

Most reliably at strong horizontal resistance after a bullish trend. Shooting stars in the middle of a range or against the trend have a much lower hit rate.

**How do I confirm a shooting star?**

The follow-up candle must remain below the shooting star’s high AND close below its low. Without that close, the shooting star is unconfirmed.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After the confirmation candle, wait for price to retrace back to the body of the shooting star. Enter on the retest with bearish confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips above the high of the shooting star candlestick.

**Where do I take profit?**

1:2 risk-reward minimum, or the next support level. For extended targets, use the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What timeframe works best for shooting star?**

1-hour, 4-hour and daily produce the most reliable shooting stars. 5-minute and 15-minute generate many false signals.

**What is the difference between a shooting star and gravestone doji?**

Both have a long upper wick at resistance. Shooting star has a small real body; gravestone doji has virtually no body (open and close at the same level). Gravestone is the stronger no-body version of the same pattern.

**What is the difference between a shooting star and an inverted hammer?**

Same shape — but context differs. Shooting star forms at the top of an uptrend (bearish reversal). Inverted hammer forms at the bottom of a downtrend (bullish reversal hint). The level it forms at decides the meaning.

**Can a shooting star fail?**

Yes — if the next candle crosses or closes above the shooting star’s high, the pattern is invalidated. Always wait for the confirmation candle before committing.

**How does shooting star fit in the ICT framework?**

It is a single-candle signature of an inducement sweep above resistance with a candle-level CISD. The strongest setup is shooting star at a higher-timeframe supply zone with lower-timeframe MSS confirmation.

**Does shooting star work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook shooting stars at higher-timeframe resistance and supply zones, especially during the New York AM session.

# ICT SIBI and BISI Explained — Sell-Side & Buy-Side Imbalance FVGs + Free PDF

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts/)

![ICT SIBI and BISI diagram showing sell-side imbalance buy-side inefficiency and buy-side imbalance sell-side inefficiency fair value gaps](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/ICT-SIBI-and-BISI.png)

SIBI and BISI are two of the most important ICT concepts every trader should master. They are the directional types of [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap") — SIBI for the bearish version, BISI for the bullish — and understanding them clarifies how price imbalance actually works on the chart.

SIBI stands for Sell-side Imbalance Buy-side Inefficiency. BISI stands for Buy-side Imbalance Sell-side Inefficiency. Both are 3-candle imbalance patterns; the difference is direction. Once I understand which is which, I know whether the FVG I am looking at signals strong selling pressure (SIBI) or strong buying pressure (BISI), and I can position accordingly.

This guide is the full breakdown of ICT SIBI and BISI — what each one means, how they form, the bullish and bearish setups, the step-by-step trade flow, the common mistakes I see traders make, and the answers to the questions I get most often.

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: What is SIBI?
content:
#### What is SIBI?

SIBI is the abbreviation for **Sell-side Imbalance Buy-side Inefficiency**.

It is a bearish fair value gap formed by an impulsive downward price movement driven primarily by sellers, with minimal buying activity to counter the move. Three large bearish candles with short wicks print in sequence, and the gap between the low of the first candle and the high of the third candle becomes the SIBI zone.

The “imbalance” is on the sell side — sellers dominated. The “inefficiency” is on the buy side — buyers were absent enough that the price levels between candle 1’s low and candle 3’s high were never traded with overlap. Hence the full name: Sell-side Imbalance, Buy-side Inefficiency.

![ICT SIBI example chart — three large bearish candles with short wicks creating a sell-side imbalance fair value gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SIBI.png)

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: How to Use SIBI in Trading
content:
#### How to Use SIBI in Trading

Relying solely on SIBI for trade entries is not advisable. To use SIBI effectively, align it with other ICT concepts — particularly the [ICT PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array") framework, the daily bias, and lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift confirmation.

A SIBI performs three main functions in trading:

**(I) Trade Execution.** The SIBI zone is the entry area for sell trades after a confirming Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe. Wait for the MSS, then enter on the retest of the SIBI.

**(II) Resistance.** The SIBI acts as resistance — it prevents price from moving back above the imbalance. Price returning to a SIBI typically gets rejected, which is why it makes a good short entry zone.

**(III) Stop Loss Placement.** Stop loss on a SIBI sell trade is typically placed above the high of the first candle (the topmost candle of the 3-candle SIBI sequence), with a small buffer.

![SIBI trading example showing entry inside the imbalance zone, stop loss above the first candle's high, and target at the next sell-side liquidity](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/sibi-Trading.png)

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: What is BISI?
content:
#### What is BISI?

BISI is the abbreviation for **Buy-side Imbalance Sell-side Inefficiency**.

It is the bullish counterpart of SIBI — a fair value gap formed by an impulsive upward price movement driven predominantly by buyers, with minimal selling activity to counter it. Three large bullish candles with short wicks print in sequence, and the gap between the high of the first candle and the low of the third candle becomes the BISI zone.

The “imbalance” is on the buy side — buyers dominated. The “inefficiency” is on the sell side — sellers were absent enough that the price levels between candle 1’s high and candle 3’s low were never traded with overlap. Hence the full name: Buy-side Imbalance, Sell-side Inefficiency.

![ICT BISI example chart — three large bullish candles with short wicks creating a buy-side imbalance fair value gap](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BISI.png)

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: How to Use BISI in Trading
content:
#### How to Use BISI in Trading

BISI alone is not enough — pair it with other ICT concepts (PD Array, daily bias, MSS) for the cleanest setups.

A BISI performs three main functions in trading:

**(I) Trade Execution.** The BISI zone is the entry area for buy trades after a confirming Market Structure Shift on the lower timeframe. Wait for the MSS, then enter on the retest of the BISI.

**(II) Support.** The BISI acts as support — it prevents price from falling back below the imbalance. Price returning to a BISI typically gets rejected upward, which is why it makes a good long entry zone.

**(III) Stop Loss Placement.** Stop loss on a BISI buy trade is typically placed below the low of the first candle (the bottommost candle of the 3-candle BISI sequence), with a small buffer.

![BISI trading example showing entry inside the imbalance zone, stop loss below the first candle's low, and target at the next buy-side liquidity](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/BISI-trading-strategy.png)

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: Step-by-Step SIBI/BISI Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step SIBI/BISI Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run on every SIBI or BISI setup. Save it, print it, do not skip a step.

  1. **Set the daily bias** using [ICT Daily Bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/>). Trade SIBI for sells when the bias is bearish; trade BISI for buys when the bias is bullish.
  2. **Mark the higher-timeframe PD Array** on the daily, 4-hour, or 1-hour chart — the level where price delivery is expected to begin.
  3. **Wait for price to approach** the higher-timeframe PD Array.
  4. **Drop to the 5-minute or 3-minute chart** at the moment of the tap.
  5. **Watch for the displacement leg** in the direction of the daily bias — three large candles with short wicks creating the SIBI (bearish) or BISI (bullish) imbalance.
  6. **Confirm with a Market Structure Shift** on the lower timeframe. Without the MSS, the SIBI/BISI is a continuation pattern, not a high-probability entry.
  7. **Mark the SIBI or BISI zone** precisely — the gap between candle 1 and candle 3.
  8. **Wait for the retest** back into the imbalance. Do not chase the displacement leg.
  9. **Execute the trade** on the retest, with stop loss above the high of candle 1 (for SIBI sells) or below the low of candle 1 (for BISI buys), with a small buffer.
  10. **Take profit** at the next significant draw on liquidity in the trade direction.

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: SIBI vs BISI — Quick Comparison
content:
#### SIBI vs BISI — Quick Comparison

The two patterns are mirrors of each other. The fastest way to remember which is which:

**SIBI** — three bearish candles, sell-side dominates, buy-side inefficient, gap between candle 1 LOW and candle 3 HIGH. Used as resistance for short entries. Stop above candle 1 high.

**BISI** — three bullish candles, buy-side dominates, sell-side inefficient, gap between candle 1 HIGH and candle 3 LOW. Used as support for long entries. Stop below candle 1 low.

Same 3-candle imbalance pattern. Opposite direction. Opposite trade.

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on SIBI and BISI
content:
#### Common Mistakes I See Traders Make on SIBI and BISI

Five mistakes account for the majority of failed SIBI/BISI trades I see in the comments. Avoid these and the patterns convert at a much higher rate.

  1. **Trading every SIBI and BISI on the chart.** Not every imbalance is tradable. The reliable ones print at higher-timeframe PD Array taps with confirming Market Structure Shifts. Random SIBI/BISIs in the middle of trending price without context are coin flips.
  2. **Trading SIBI in a bullish market or BISI in a bearish market.** SIBI is a sell-direction tool; BISI is a buy-direction tool. Counter-bias entries fail far more often than aligned ones. Filter every setup through the daily bias.
  3. **Confusing SIBI and BISI.** SIBI = bearish; BISI = bullish. Mixing them up inverts your trade direction. The mnemonic: S(IBI) starts with S like Sell; B(ISI) starts with B like Buy.
  4. **Stop loss inside the imbalance zone.** Place the stop beyond the high of candle 1 (SIBI) or the low of candle 1 (BISI), with a small buffer. Stops inside the SIBI/BISI body get tagged on the typical re-test spike.
  5. **Skipping the Market Structure Shift confirmation.** A SIBI or BISI without an MSS in the trade direction is a weaker signal. Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS before pulling the trigger.

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: Final Thoughts on SIBI and BISI
content:
#### Final Thoughts on SIBI and BISI

Not every SIBI and BISI on the chart is tradable. To trade them effectively, use them in conjunction with other ICT tools — daily bias, higher-timeframe PD Array, lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift, and the premium / discount framework. At those filtered levels, SIBI and BISI become reliable entries. Used in isolation, they are just two coincidental candle shapes. Always trade with a stop loss in place — no strategy is foolproof.

title: sibi-and-bisi-the-ict-concepts
section: FAQs About ICT SIBI and BISI
content:
#### FAQs About ICT SIBI and BISI

**What does SIBI stand for?**

SIBI stands for Sell-side Imbalance Buy-side Inefficiency. It is the bearish version of an ICT fair value gap — a 3-candle pattern where sellers dominate and buyers are inefficient, leaving an unfilled gap between candle 1’s low and candle 3’s high.

**What does BISI stand for?**

BISI stands for Buy-side Imbalance Sell-side Inefficiency. It is the bullish version of an ICT fair value gap — a 3-candle pattern where buyers dominate and sellers are inefficient, leaving an unfilled gap between candle 1’s high and candle 3’s low.

**What is the difference between SIBI and BISI?**

SIBI is bearish — used for sell trades, acts as resistance, stop above candle 1’s high. BISI is bullish — used for buy trades, acts as support, stop below candle 1’s low. Same imbalance mechanic, opposite direction.

**How do I trade a SIBI?**

Wait for a higher-timeframe PD Array tap, drop to the 5-minute, watch for a Market Structure Shift to the downside, mark the SIBI imbalance, wait for price to retrace into it, then short with stop above the SIBI high.

**How do I trade a BISI?**

Wait for a higher-timeframe PD Array tap, drop to the 5-minute, watch for a Market Structure Shift to the upside, mark the BISI imbalance, wait for price to retrace into it, then buy with stop below the BISI low.

**Are SIBI and BISI the same as fair value gaps?**

Yes — SIBI and BISI are directional names for fair value gaps. SIBI is the bearish FVG; BISI is the bullish FVG. The mechanics are identical to a regular FVG; the labels just specify the direction.

**Where do I place stop loss on a SIBI or BISI trade?**

SIBI: above the high of candle 1 (the topmost candle of the 3-candle sequence), with a small buffer. BISI: below the low of candle 1 (the bottommost candle), with a small buffer. Stops inside the imbalance get tagged routinely.

**Can I trade SIBI and BISI alone?**

You can, but the win rate is much lower. The reliable setups pair SIBI/BISI with the daily bias, a higher-timeframe PD Array tap, and a lower-timeframe Market Structure Shift. Use them in context, not in isolation.

**What instruments work best for SIBI and BISI?**

US index futures (NASDAQ 100 / NQ and E-mini S&P 500 / ES) produce the cleanest SIBI/BISI imbalances. Major forex pairs (GBP/USD, EUR/USD) and Gold (XAU/USD) also respect the same mechanics.
