# ICT Scalping Strategy — 30 to 50 Pips a Day with Daily Bias, OTE & Killzone Timing

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/simple-ict-scalping-strategy/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/simple-ict-scalping-strategy/)

![ICT Scalping Strategy — daily-bias driven scalping model targeting 30 to 50 pips per day using OTE entries on the 3rd daily candle inside London or New York killzones](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/ICT-Scalping-Strategy-2.png)

ICT Scalping Strategy is designed to capitalize on short-term price moves and book 30 to 50 pips a day. If you do not want to sit in front of the screen all day looking for setups, this is the model for you — bias from the daily, entries on the lower timeframe, and execution restricted to the London and New York killzones.

In this guide I walk you through the ICT scalping strategy — the four elements, the daily-bias rule, the swing-high / swing-low setup, the lower-timeframe OTE entry, the killzone time filter, money management, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Elements of ICT Scalping Strategy
content:
#### Elements of ICT Scalping Strategy

**(I)** Directional bias from higher-timeframe institutional sponsorship.

**(II)** Framing high-probability setups for the run on liquidity.

**(III)** Highlighting multiple scalping opportunities.

**(IV)** Determining the highest-probability time of the day.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Implementing the Daily Bias
content:
#### Implementing the Daily Bias

The daily bias can be either bullish or bearish.

For a **Bullish Daily Bias** , wait for a [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>) on the daily timeframe to be broken.

Look for a [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>) to form without breaking the recent swing low.

![Bullish daily bias example for ICT scalping — daily swing high broken, then a new swing low forms without breaking the recent low, anticipating the 3rd daily candle high sweep](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bullish-bias.png)

When the swing low forms, anticipate the 3rd daily candle high to be swept on the following day or the next day.

For a **Bearish Daily Bias** , wait for a [Swing Low](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-low-formation/>) on the daily timeframe to be broken.

Look for a [Swing High](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-swing-high-explained/>) to form without breaking the recent swing high.

![Bearish daily bias example for ICT scalping — daily swing low broken, then a new swing high forms without breaking the recent high, anticipating the 3rd daily candle low sweep](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/bearish-bias.png)

When the swing high forms, anticipate the 3rd daily candle low to be swept on the following day or the next day.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Framing High-Probability Setups for the Run on Liquidity
content:
#### Framing High-Probability Setups for the Run on Liquidity

After finding the daily bias and the formation of a swing low or swing high, drop to lower timeframes like 1-hour and 30-minute and mark the next possible [Draw on Liquidity](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/liquidity-in-forex-trading/>).

Draw on liquidity can be in the form of relative equal highs or lows.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Highlighting Scalping Opportunities
content:
#### Highlighting Scalping Opportunities

After identifying the directional bias and the next possible draw on liquidity, the next step is to frame possible scalping setups on lower timeframes like 30-minute and 15-minute.

In a **bullish directional bias** , scalping opportunities are marked at the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) level of the 3rd daily candlestick of the swing low.

When price retraces back and approaches the [OTE level](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) of the 3rd daily candle, look to buy after confirmation like an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on the lower timeframe.

In a **bearish daily bias** , scalping opportunities are marked at the [ICT Optimal Trade Entry](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-optimal-trade-entry-ote-pattern/>) level of the 3rd daily candlestick of the swing high.

When price retraces up and approaches the OTE level of the 3rd daily candle, look to sell after confirmation like an [ICT Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/>) on the lower timeframe.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Determining the Highest-Probability Time of the Day
content:
#### Determining the Highest-Probability Time of the Day

For ICT scalping strategy you have to pay attention to the time of the day.

ICT mentioned to use [ICT Killzone](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-kill-zones/>) timings — specifically the London and New York killzones.

The high or low of the day is expected to form between these killzones.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Money Management
content:
#### Money Management

Consider risking 1% of your capital per setup, and gradually work your way to 2% if it meets your risk tolerance.

The strategy targets 30 to 50 pips per setup. With a tight stop beyond the OTE swing extreme, that is typically a 1:2 to 1:3 risk-reward ratio.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Step-by-Step ICT Scalping Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step ICT Scalping Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for an ICT scalp trade.

  1. **Set the daily bias.** Bullish — daily swing high broken plus a new swing low without breaking the recent low. Bearish — daily swing low broken plus a new swing high without breaking the recent high.
  2. **Identify the 3rd daily candle.** Bullish — the 3rd daily candle of the new swing low. Bearish — the 3rd daily candle of the new swing high.
  3. **Mark the OTE level on the 3rd daily candle.** 62%–79% Fibonacci retracement of that candle.
  4. **Mark the next draw on liquidity.** Relative equal highs (bullish target) or relative equal lows (bearish target) on the 1-hour or 30-minute.
  5. **Wait for the killzone.** Only execute during London or New York killzones.
  6. **Wait for price to reach the OTE level.** On the 30-minute or 15-minute.
  7. **Drop to the 5-minute or 1-minute for the trigger.**
  8. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS.** A clean break in the bias direction at the OTE.
  9. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the post-MSS PD array.
  10. **Set the stop.** Beyond the OTE swing extreme, with a small buffer.
  11. **Take profit at 30 to 50 pips.** Or at the next draw on liquidity, whichever comes first.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Best Pairs for ICT Scalping
content:
#### Best Pairs for ICT Scalping

ICT scalping works on every major instrument that respects the London and New York sessions — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, USD/JPY, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the ICT scalping framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) and the [10:00–11:00 NY Silver Bullet window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-silver-bullet-strategy/>) are the highest-conviction execution windows.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: Common Mistakes Around ICT Scalping
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around ICT Scalping

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start using ICT scalping.

  1. **Trading outside the killzones.** The model is built around London and NY killzone delivery. Setups outside the killzones have a much lower hit rate.
  2. **Skipping the daily bias.** Without the daily-bias filter, every retracement looks like an OTE setup. The bias is what flips the OTE from random to high-conviction.
  3. **Marking OTE on the wrong candle.** Use the 3rd daily candle of the new swing — not the most recent daily candle.
  4. **Entering at the OTE without lower-timeframe MSS.** The OTE is the zone — the entry is the post-MSS PD array. Touching the OTE is not a trigger.
  5. **Targeting too far.** The model is a scalping model — 30 to 50 pips is the target. Holding for 100+ pips converts the trade into a swing and breaks the model.
  6. **Risking more than 1%–2%.** Because the setup is high-frequency over a month, even small over-risking blows up the account when a few setups fail in a row.

title: simple-ict-scalping-strategy
section: FAQs about ICT Scalping Strategy
content:
#### FAQs about ICT Scalping Strategy

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about ICT scalping.

**Does ICT scalping strategy work on every asset?**

Yes — every ICT concept including the scalping strategy works on every asset class whose price is delivered online on the chart. Test it on a demo account first before going live.

**Does the ICT scalping setup appear every day?**

As ICT himself mentioned, day trading is not every-day trading. So it is not necessary that the ICT scalping setup will appear every day — but you have to watch and wait for it every day.

**What return can I expect from ICT scalping?**

It is a scalping strategy — the target is 30 to 50 pips. It may deliver up to a 1:2 risk-reward ratio.

**Can I be profitable using ICT scalping?**

Before choosing a scalping strategy, analyze yourself — are you a scalp trader, day trader, or swing trader? If this strategy suits your style, yes — you can be profitable using ICT scalping if you learn it properly, apply the concepts, and manage your risk.

**What timeframes do I use?**

Daily for the bias, 1-hour or 30-minute for the next draw on liquidity, 30-minute or 15-minute for the OTE level marking, and 5-minute or 1-minute for the entry trigger.

**What is the OTE level?**

OTE (Optimal Trade Entry) is the 62%–79% Fibonacci retracement zone of the most recent impulsive leg — in this scalping model, the 3rd daily candle of the new swing.

**Why the 3rd daily candle?**

The 3rd daily candle of the new swing is the candle that produces the directional move ICT teaches as the high-probability scalp window. The OTE on that candle is where price retraces back to before continuing.

**What killzones do I trade?**

London killzone (02:00 AM to 05:00 AM NY time) and New York killzone (07:00 AM to 11:00 AM NY time). The high or low of the day usually forms between these.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Beyond the OTE swing extreme — below the 3rd daily candle low for buy trades, above the high for sell trades — with a small buffer.

**Where do I take profit?**

30 to 50 pips, or the next draw on liquidity (relative equal high or low), whichever comes first.

**How much should I risk per setup?**

1% of capital per setup, scaling to 2% only if your risk tolerance allows. Never more than 2% on a single scalping trade.

**Does ICT scalping work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook scalping setups, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

# 3 Step Guide to Single Candle Order Block – SCOB

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/single-candle-order-block-scob/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/single-candle-order-block-scob/)

![ICT Single Candle Order Block \(SCOB\) confirmation pattern marked on a price chart at a point of interest](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/single-candle-order-block-SCOB.png)

The first time I missed a clean SCOB and watched price reverse exactly off the candle I had ignored, I knew I had been overcomplicating my entries. One candle. Three rules to confirm it. Done.

A **Single Candle Order Block (SCOB)** comprises a singular candle that emerges at a significant price level, indicating a confirmed reversal in price direction from that specific area of interest. It is used for confirmation and execution of a trade — and using a SCOB for entry minimizes risk and maximizes reward because you only act after the reversal is structurally confirmed.

In this guide, I will show you exactly what a SCOB is, the 3-candle pattern that confirms one, how the bullish and bearish versions form, and how to enter a trade off it cleanly with stop-loss placement.

If you are brand new to order blocks, start with our full guide on the [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block") and come back here for the single-candle confirmation variant.

Do not worry — once you know the 3-rule check, spotting SCOBs becomes mechanical.

Ready? Let us break it down.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: What is a Single Candle Order Block (SCOB)?
content:
## What is a Single Candle Order Block (SCOB)?

A Single Candle Order Block (SCOB) is a singular candle that emerges at a significant price level, indicating a confirmed reversal in price direction from that specific area of interest.

Mostly, SCOB is used for confirmation and execution of a trade. Instead of buying or selling the moment price reaches a point of interest, you wait for the SCOB to print — and only then do you take the entry. That single-candle rule is what makes the strategy mechanical and what minimizes the risk of entering before the reversal has actually happened.

A point of interest, in this context, is any high-probability area where institutional orders are likely to defend price — such as a [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap"), an [Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block"), or a [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block"). The SCOB is the reversal signal that fires inside one of those areas.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Why SCOB Works as a Confirmation
content:
## Why SCOB Works as a Confirmation

Most retail entries fail because the trader sees price reach a point of interest, gets impatient, and clicks buy or sell before the move has actually turned. The SCOB rule fixes that.

By requiring three specific candle relationships before you mark the middle candle as a SCOB, the pattern forces you to wait for the reversal to be visible on the chart. The displacement on the third candle is your evidence that institutional participants stepped in. Without the third-candle confirmation, you do not have a SCOB — you have a hopeful guess.

That is why traders who use SCOB for entry typically see better win rates than those who buy or sell directly at a point of interest.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: How to Identify a SCOB
content:
## How to Identify a SCOB

For better understanding, we will study the Single Candle Order Block in two parts — bullish and bearish.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: (I) Bullish Single Candle Order Block
content:
### (I) Bullish Single Candle Order Block

A Bullish SCOB is formed at bullish points of interest like fair value gaps, order blocks, and breaker blocks.

It is a single candle formation, but to identify a bullish SCOB you have to look for a sequence of three candles that meet these conditions:

  1. **First candle** closes at a bullish point of interest with a short or long wick.
  2. **Second candle** sweeps the low of the previous (first) candle and closes above the low of the previous candle.
  3. **Third candle** closes above the high of the second candle.

Once those three conditions are satisfied, the bullish SCOB is confirmed and you mark the **middle (second) candle as the bullish Single Candle Order Block**.

![Bullish Single Candle Order Block \(SCOB\) example: 3-candle pattern at a bullish point of interest with the middle candle marked as SCOB](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Bullish-single-candle-order-block.png)

To trade using a bullish SCOB, you wait for price to come back down and test the SCOB. When price tests the SCOB, you can directly execute a buy trade — or for a more precise entry, wait for a [Market Structure Shift](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") on a lower timeframe before entering.

![Bullish SCOB trade example: price retraces back to test the marked Single Candle Order Block and reverses to the upside](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/TRADING-scob.png)

While buying at a Single Candle Order Block, your stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the low of the SCOB.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: (II) Bearish Single Candle Order Block
content:
### (II) Bearish Single Candle Order Block

A Bearish Single Candle Order Block (SCOB) occurs at bearish points of interest such as fair value gaps, order blocks, and breaker blocks.

Although it is a single candle formation, identifying a bearish SCOB requires observing a sequence of three candles:

  1. **First candle** concludes at a bearish point of interest with either a short or long wick.
  2. **Second candle** surpasses the high of the preceding (first) candle and closes below its high.
  3. **Third candle** closes below the low of the second candle.

With the bearish SCOB confirmed, you identify the **middle (second) candle as the bearish Single Candle Order Block**.

![Bearish Single Candle Order Block \(SCOB\) example: 3-candle pattern at a bearish point of interest with the middle candle marked as SCOB](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/bearish-SCOB.png)

To trade using the bearish SCOB, you wait for price to retrace upward and test the SCOB. Once price tests the SCOB, you have two options:

  * **Execute a sell trade directly.**
  * **Wait for a Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe** for a more precise entry.

![Bearish SCOB trade example: price retraces back to test the marked Single Candle Order Block and reverses to the downside](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/trading-bearish-SCOB.png)

Stop loss for a bearish SCOB sell sits 10 to 20 pips above the high of the SCOB.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: How to Trade a SCOB — Step by Step
content:
## How to Trade a SCOB — Step by Step

The unified flow for either direction:

  1. **Identify your point of interest** on a higher timeframe — a fair value gap, order block, or breaker block.
  2. **Wait for price to reach that area** and watch the next 3 candles closely.
  3. **Check the 3-candle SCOB conditions** match (bullish or bearish per the rules above).
  4. **Mark the middle (second) candle** as the SCOB once confirmed.
  5. **Wait for price to retrace and test the SCOB.** Do not enter immediately on confirmation — let price come back to the zone.
  6. **Choose your entry style** — direct entry on test, or drop to a lower timeframe and wait for a Market Structure Shift for tighter precision.
  7. **Place your stop loss** 10–20 pips beyond the SCOB extreme (below for buys, above for sells).
  8. **Set your target** at the next opposing point of interest, the next significant liquidity pool, or a fixed risk-reward like 1:3.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest SCOBs form at confluence zones — where a [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT FVG"), [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block"), or [breaker block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block") all stack at the same price level. When the SCOB prints inside that kind of confluence, the reaction is more violent and the win rate jumps. Skip SCOBs that form in the middle of a range with no clean point of interest behind them — they are often just noise.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Bonus Tip: SCOB vs Mitigation Block
content:
## Bonus Tip: SCOB vs Mitigation Block

A SCOB and a [Mitigation Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-mitigation-block-explained/> "ICT Mitigation Block") can look similar at first glance — both involve a single candle reacting at a level. The key difference is the role each plays:

  * **SCOB** is a _confirmation_ pattern at an active point of interest. The level is still acting as support or resistance, and the SCOB confirms the reversal.
  * **Mitigation Block** is a _failed_ order block that has been broken and reclaimed — the level flipped role.

If you see a single-candle reaction at a level you have recently watched price break, you are likely looking at a mitigation block, not a SCOB. Confirm which one you have before assuming the trade direction.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a SCOB in trading?

SCOB stands for Single Candle Order Block. It is an ICT trading concept where one candle at a significant price level confirms a reversal — used for trade entry at points of interest like fair value gaps, order blocks, and breaker blocks.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: What does SCOB mean?
content:
### What does SCOB mean?

In ICT trading, SCOB is the abbreviation for Single Candle Order Block. It is a one-candle confirmation pattern that signals a reversal at a high-probability point of interest.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: What is the full form of SCOB?
content:
### What is the full form of SCOB?

The full form of SCOB is **Single Candle Order Block**.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: How do you identify a SCOB on a chart?
content:
### How do you identify a SCOB on a chart?

A SCOB is identified through a 3-candle sequence at a point of interest. For a bullish SCOB: the 2nd candle sweeps the low of the 1st and closes above it, and the 3rd candle closes above the high of the 2nd. The 2nd (middle) candle is the SCOB. The bearish version is the mirror.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: What is the difference between a SCOB and a regular order block?
content:
### What is the difference between a SCOB and a regular order block?

A regular [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block") is the last opposing candle before a strong move — defined on its own. A SCOB is a single-candle confirmation pattern that prints _inside_ an existing point of interest (like a fair value gap or order block) to confirm the reversal is happening. SCOB is a confirmation tool; an order block is a level.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Where do I place my stop loss on a SCOB trade?
content:
### Where do I place my stop loss on a SCOB trade?

10 to 20 pips below the low of the SCOB for a buy trade, or 10 to 20 pips above the high of the SCOB for a sell trade.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Is SCOB an SMC concept too?
content:
### Is SCOB an SMC concept too?

The Single Candle Order Block originates in ICT but the same 3-candle confirmation idea appears in Smart Money Concepts (SMC) trading literature, often under similar or slightly different names. The mechanics — single candle at a point of interest, 3-candle confirmation — are the same.

title: single-candle-order-block-scob
section: Wrapping Up
content:
## Wrapping Up

We hope this guide helped you understand the Single Candle Order Block and how to use it as a clean entry confirmation.

The biggest practical edge of the SCOB is patience. Price reaching a point of interest is not the trade. The 3-candle confirmation is the trade. If you can wait for those three candles to line up before clicking, you will be ahead of most retail traders who enter the moment price taps a level.

Pull up your favorite pair this week, find a fresh fair value gap or order block, and watch how price interacts with it. Mark every SCOB you see. Once you train your eye on the pattern, you will spot it everywhere.

# Supply and Demand in Forex Trading — Zone Identification, BOS/CHOCH Context & SMC Trade Setup

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading/)

![Supply and Demand in Forex Trading — supply zone above price and demand zone below price marked with break of structure and change of character](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Supply-and-Demand-trading-strategy.png)

Supply and Demand in Forex Trading is the foundational SMC framework that explains every reversal, continuation and balance area on the chart — supply is the area where institutional sellers stack orders and price drops, demand is the area where institutional buyers stack orders and price rises. Once you can identify these zones, every BOS, CHOCH and PD-array entry becomes a refinement of supply or demand.

Price of any asset depends on the supply and demand of that asset in the market.

Supply means availability of the asset against demand. When the supply of an asset is more than the demand, prices may fall.

Demand means willingness of buyers to buy an asset at the market price. When the demand of an asset is more than the supply, prices may rise.

In trading, a supply zone is an area on the price chart where many sell orders are placed — due to which the supply of the asset increases and the price falls. A demand zone is an area on the price chart where many buy orders are placed — due to which the demand increases and the price rises.

In this guide I walk you through the supply and demand trading strategy — the meaning, the BOS / CHOCH context, the supply and demand zone identification, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

You can jump to the section you are most interested in from below or continue reading the full article for a complete view.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Purpose of Supply and Demand Zones
content:
#### Purpose of Supply and Demand Zones

Supply and demand zones are key areas on the price chart that traders pay attention to in order to execute a buy or sell trade. Supply and demand zones can also help capture reversal trades as well as continuation trades in a trending market.

These areas are important because the market often reacts quickly from them — in Smart Money Concepts it is believed that institutional traders enter in this area with huge volume, leading to high supply or demand.

That is why retail traders wait for the market to test these supply or demand zones to execute their sell or buy trades and follow the footprints of institutional traders.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: How to Identify a Supply and Demand Zone
content:
#### How to Identify a Supply and Demand Zone

To identify supply and demand zones in the market, we first have to understand basic market structure.

**(I)[Break of Structure (BOS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/break-of-structure-bos/>)**

When the market is in a trend, it breaks the previous structure in the direction of the trend and continues — which is called break of structure (BOS).

In a bullish trend the market breaks the previous high and makes a higher high. In a bearish trend the market breaks the previous low and makes a lower low. An illustration is shown below.

![Break of Structure example — bullish trend producing a higher high above the previous swing high to confirm continuation](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/break-of-structure.png)

**(II)[Change of Character (CHOCH)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/change-of-character-choch-in-trading/>)**

When the market changes trend it breaks structure in the opposite direction and starts a new trend — which is called reversal or change of character (CHOCH).

When the market reverses from bearish to bullish, it breaks the previous lower high and makes a new higher high. When it reverses from bullish to bearish, it breaks the previous higher low and makes a new lower low. An illustration is shown below.

![Change of Character example — bullish trend ending with a break below the previous higher low confirming the bearish reversal](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/change-of-character.png)

Once you have understood the structural context, the supply and demand zones can be marked.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Supply Zone Identification
content:
#### Supply Zone Identification

A supply zone is the area in the market from which prices fall quickly — so a supply zone is found and is useful in a bearish trend.

Before a change of character from bullish to bearish, and before a break of structure in a bearish trend, a retracement after which prices fall quickly and strongly is called a supply zone. The retracement can be a single bullish candle or a number of bullish candles.

![Supply zone identification example — bullish retracement candle at the top of the leg before a strong bearish move marked as the supply zone](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Supply-zone.png)

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Demand Zone Identification
content:
#### Demand Zone Identification

A demand zone is the area in the market from which prices rise quickly — so a demand zone is found and is useful in a bullish trend.

Before a change of character from bearish to bullish, and before a break of structure in a bullish trend, a retracement after which prices rise quickly and strongly is called a demand zone. The retracement can be a single bearish candle or a number of bearish candles.

![Demand zone identification example — bearish retracement candle at the bottom of the leg before a strong bullish move marked as the demand zone](https://www.innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Demand-zone.png)

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: How to Trade Using Supply and Demand Strategy
content:
#### How to Trade Using Supply and Demand Strategy

To trade using supply and demand zones we need to identify the market trend first.

In a bullish trend, after a bullish CHOCH or BOS, we have to identify the demand zone. When the market retraces back and approaches the demand zone, we can buy at that test.

If the demand zone is a large area, we should wait for the market to test at least 50% of the demand zone — in conjunction with other confirmations like a market structure shift on a lower timeframe.

When executing a buy trade at the demand zone, the stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips below the low of the demand zone.

In a bearish trend, after a bearish CHOCH or BOS, we have to identify the supply zone. When the market retraces back and approaches the supply zone, we can sell at that test.

If the supply zone is a large area, we should wait for the market to test at least 50% of the supply zone — in conjunction with other confirmations like a market structure shift on a lower timeframe.

When executing a sell trade at the supply zone, the stop loss will be 10 to 20 pips above the high of the supply zone.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Supply and Demand vs ICT Order Block
content:
#### Supply and Demand vs ICT Order Block

Supply and demand zones and the [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>) overlap heavily but they are not the same thing.

The order block is the SPECIFIC last opposing candle before the displacement that produced the structural break — a refined, single-candle subset of the broader supply or demand zone.

The supply or demand zone is the WIDER area that includes the order block plus any nearby pullback candles.

Trading with the order block gives a tighter stop and higher reward-to-risk. Trading with the broader S&D zone gives a higher hit rate at the cost of stop width. ICT-style traders often layer them — using the supply / demand zone as the area, then refining to the order block inside it for the entry.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Step-by-Step Supply and Demand Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Supply and Demand Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run when trading from a supply or demand zone.

  1. **Read the higher-timeframe context.** 1-day and 4-hour structure — bullish, bearish or neutral.
  2. **Wait for the structural confirmation.** BOS in the trend direction (continuation play) or CHOCH at the higher-timeframe extreme (reversal play).
  3. **Identify the supply or demand zone.** Bullish — the bearish retracement candle (or cluster) before the bullish move that produced the BOS / CHOCH. Bearish — the bullish retracement candle (or cluster) before the bearish move.
  4. **Mark the zone boundary.** High and low of the retracement candles.
  5. **Wait for price to retrace and tap the zone.** If the zone is large, require at least 50% retracement into the zone.
  6. **Drop to the lower timeframe (5-minute or 15-minute).** For the entry trigger.
  7. **Wait for the lower-timeframe MSS at the zone.** A clean break in the bias direction.
  8. **Enter on the post-MSS retest.** At the post-MSS PD array (FVG, OB or breaker).
  9. **Set the stop.** 10 to 20 pips below the demand low (or above the supply high), with a small buffer.
  10. **Take profit at the next draw on liquidity.** Old high or low, relative equal level, or higher-timeframe FVG.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Best Pairs for Supply and Demand Trading
content:
#### Best Pairs for Supply and Demand Trading

Supply and demand works on every major instrument — GBP/USD, EUR/USD, USD/CAD, plus metals such as XAU/USD and XAG/USD.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the supply and demand framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. The 09:50 NY-AM [macro window](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-macro-time-based-strategy/>) is a particularly strong place to watch for supply and demand zone reactions because the algorithmic delivery is most concentrated there.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: Common Mistakes Around Supply and Demand
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Supply and Demand

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading supply and demand.

  1. **Marking S &D zones without structural context.** Every retracement candle is not a zone. Only the retracement BEFORE a BOS or CHOCH qualifies.
  2. **Trading every zone touch as an entry.** The zone is the area — the entry trigger is the lower-timeframe MSS or order block formed inside the zone.
  3. **Tight stops at the zone boundary.** Stops parked at the zone high / low get hunted on the second test. Always use the 10–20 pip buffer.
  4. **Ignoring zone size.** A 5-pip zone is high-conviction; a 50-pip zone needs the 50% rule before entering.
  5. **Trading S &D against the higher-timeframe trend.** Counter-trend zones have a much lower hit rate than bias-aligned zones.
  6. **Confusing supply / demand with order block.** The OB is the refined single-candle subset of the S&D zone. Trade the OB for tighter stops and higher reward; trade the broader S&D for a higher hit rate.

title: supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading
section: FAQs about Supply and Demand in Forex Trading
content:
#### FAQs about Supply and Demand in Forex Trading

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about supply and demand.

**What is supply and demand in forex trading?**

Supply is the availability of an asset against demand — when supply exceeds demand, prices fall. Demand is the willingness of buyers to buy at the market price — when demand exceeds supply, prices rise. Supply and demand zones are price areas where institutional orders create these imbalances.

**What is a supply zone?**

A supply zone is the area on the price chart from which prices fall quickly. It is identified as the bullish retracement candle (or cluster) before the bearish move that produced a BOS or CHOCH.

**What is a demand zone?**

A demand zone is the area on the price chart from which prices rise quickly. It is identified as the bearish retracement candle (or cluster) before the bullish move that produced a BOS or CHOCH.

**How is supply and demand different from ICT order block?**

The ICT order block is the specific last opposing candle before the displacement — a refined, single-candle subset of the broader supply or demand zone. The S&D zone is the wider area; the OB is the refinement inside it.

**How do I trade a demand zone?**

In a bullish trend, after a bullish BOS or CHOCH, mark the demand zone. When price retraces and tests the zone, wait for a lower-timeframe MSS, then buy on the retest. Stop 10–20 pips below the demand low.

**How do I trade a supply zone?**

In a bearish trend, after a bearish BOS or CHOCH, mark the supply zone. When price retraces and tests the zone, wait for a lower-timeframe MSS, then sell on the retest. Stop 10–20 pips above the supply high.

**What if the zone is too large?**

If the zone is a large area, wait for at least 50% of the zone to be tested before considering an entry — combined with a lower-timeframe MSS confirmation.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

10 to 20 pips beyond the zone extreme — below the demand low for buy trades, above the supply high for sell trades.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next draw on liquidity — old high or low, relative equal level, or the next higher-timeframe PD array.

**What timeframe is best for supply and demand?**

Mark the zone on the 1-hour or 4-hour for the higher-timeframe area. Use the 5-minute or 15-minute for the entry trigger.

**Does supply and demand work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all produce textbook supply and demand reactions, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**Is supply and demand the same as support and resistance?**

Related but not identical. Support and resistance are horizontal lines drawn at price extremes. Supply and demand are zones that include the structural context (BOS or CHOCH) of why those areas matter. S&D adds the institutional-volume layer to traditional S&R.

# Support and Resistance Trading Strategy — Zones, Four Pillars & Bullish/Bearish Setups

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/support-resistance-trading/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/support-resistance-trading/)

![Support and Resistance Trading Strategy — horizontal support and resistance zones, four pillars \(history, timeframe, freshness, psychology\), bullish and bearish trade execution](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/support-and-resistance-trading-strategy.png)

Support and Resistance Trading Strategy is the foundational price-action framework — support is the historical zone where price has bounced higher, resistance is the zone where price has been rejected lower, and trading at these levels with proper confirmation is one of the most reliable approaches in technical analysis.

Support and resistance are the key elements of price action trading strategy — these are the key areas for price to react (reverse or retrace).

In this guide I walk you through the support and resistance strategy from basic to advanced — the definitions, the four pillars (history, timeframe, freshness, psychology), the identification rules, the bullish and bearish trade execution, the step-by-step trade flow, common mistakes and the FAQ.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: What is Support and Resistance Trading Strategy?
content:
#### What is Support and Resistance Trading Strategy?

It is one of the best price action trading strategies, in which traders use support levels to execute a buy trade and resistance levels to execute a sell trade — with other confirmations too, which are discussed later in this guide.

To have a grip on this strategy, you must know about support and resistance levels first.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: What is a Support Zone?
content:
#### What is a Support Zone?

A support is a horizontal price zone from where traders expect a retracement or reversal of a bearish trend.

It can also be a single price level, but marking a zone of price as support is better.

It is based on **historical price movement** — in the past price had respected this level and bounced back. There can be a single or multiple bounces of price from a single support zone.

**Timeframe** matters — the higher the timeframe, the stronger the support zone.

**Fresh** support levels are more reliable for price reaction.

**Psychology** plays a great role while identifying a support zone — you may prefer a complete number instead of a half / odd number. Price in hundreds and thousands has a psychological connection with support zones (for example, instead of 1999 you may mark 2000 as a support).

**How to Identify a Support Zone**

To identify a support zone, go to a price chart and mark the levels from where price had bounced toward the buy side in the past.

If it is not a single price level, you can mark the complete area as a support zone.

Next time when price tests that zone, you can look for a price reversal or retracement from this area.

In the picture below you can see XAU/USD daily-timeframe chart with a support zone marked from $1805–1815. Price has tested this zone two times and made a support here. When price touches this zone for the third time you can see the result — a boom in price.

![Support zone example on XAU/USD daily — $1805-1815 zone tested twice with bullish reactions, third test produces a strong bullish move higher](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Support-zone.png)

title: support-resistance-trading
section: What is a Resistance Zone?
content:
#### What is a Resistance Zone?

Resistance is a horizontal price area where traders anticipate a potential reversal or retracement of a bullish trend.

It can manifest as a single price level but is often identified as a zone.

This identification is grounded in **historical price behavior** — past instances where price respected this level by reversing or retracing.

Within a resistance zone, there may be multiple instances of price bouncing off.

The significance of a resistance zone can vary with the **timeframe** , typically stronger on higher timeframes.

**New** resistance levels are typically considered more reliable for price reactions.

**Psychology** also plays a crucial role in identifying resistance zones, with traders often favoring whole numbers over half or odd numbers. Round numbers — especially in hundreds and thousands — tend to be associated with resistance zones (preferring to mark 2010 instead of 2008 as a resistance level).

**How to Identify a Resistance Zone**

To identify a resistance zone, examine a price chart and identify levels where price has previously fallen impulsively after touching — either once or multiple times.

If the resistance is not confined to a single price point, you can mark the entire area as a resistance zone.

When price approaches this zone again in the future, you can anticipate a potential reversal or retracement from this area.

In the picture below you can see XAU/USD 4H chart where $1975–1955 is marked as a resistance zone. Price has fallen impulsively from this zone two times, making it a strong resistance zone. When price tested this resistance zone for the third time, you can see the result — a crash.

![Resistance zone example on XAU/USD 4H — $1955-1975 zone tested twice with bearish reactions, third test produces a strong bearish crash lower](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/resistance-zone.png)

title: support-resistance-trading
section: How to Trade Using Support and Resistance Strategy
content:
#### How to Trade Using Support and Resistance Strategy

To trade using this strategy, first identify the trend of the market.

**In a bullish trend** , price makes higher highs and higher lows, resulting in higher prices.

In a bullish trend, support zones tend to be highly regarded as price consistently rises. Price reacts from these support zones because they signify levels where buyers have historically stepped in to drive price higher. In this context, bullish momentum will eventually lead to the breaking of resistance levels.

Mark the support zones and wait for price to test these levels. When price reaches a support zone, wait for bullish confirmations like a candlestick confirmation or chart-pattern confirmation to execute a buy trade.

![Bullish trend support trade example — support zone tested with bullish engulfing candle confirmation, buy entry with stop below support and target at next resistance](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SUPPORT-AND-RESISTANCE-TRADING.png)

In this case your stop loss will be below the support zone, and for profit you may target the next resistance level.

**In a bearish trend** , price makes lower highs and lower lows, resulting in lower prices.

In a bearish trend, mark the resistance areas and wait for price to test these levels. When price touches the resistance zone, you can execute a sell trade after confirmation — like a bearish candlestick or chart-pattern confirmation.

![Bearish trend resistance trade example — resistance zone tested with bearish rejection candle confirmation, sell entry with stop above resistance and target at next support](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/support-and-resistance-tyrading-strategy.png)

In this case your stop loss will be above the resistance level, and for profit target you can mark the next support level.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: Support and Resistance vs Supply and Demand
content:
#### Support and Resistance vs Supply and Demand

Support and resistance are related to but not identical to [supply and demand](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/supply-and-demand-in-forex-trading/>) zones.

Support and resistance are HORIZONTAL price lines or zones drawn at historical reaction points. Supply and demand are DIRECTIONAL zones identified by the candle pattern that produced the reaction (a sharp bullish move from a demand zone, a sharp bearish move from a supply zone).

Every supply zone acts as resistance, and every demand zone acts as support — but not every resistance is a supply zone, and not every support is a demand zone. S&D adds the structural-context layer (BOS or CHOCH) on top of the horizontal-level S&R.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: Support and Resistance in the ICT Framework
content:
#### Support and Resistance in the ICT Framework

ICT traders treat support and resistance as a sanity check on top of the structural framework. The cleanest setups occur when an S&R level aligns with a higher-timeframe PD array — for example, a daily support zone that overlaps a daily [fair value gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/>), a daily [order block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/>), or a 4-hour bullish breaker.

Use S&R for the higher-timeframe price-target zone, then drop to the 15-minute or 5-minute for the lower-timeframe MSS trigger. The combination filters out random S&R touches that have no institutional structure behind them.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: Step-by-Step Support and Resistance Trade Flow
content:
#### Step-by-Step Support and Resistance Trade Flow

This is the exact sequence I run for an S&R trade.

  1. **Identify the trend.** Higher highs and higher lows = bullish. Lower highs and lower lows = bearish.
  2. **Mark the bias-aligned levels.** Bullish — mark support zones below price. Bearish — mark resistance zones above price.
  3. **Filter by the four pillars.** History (multiple bounces), timeframe (higher = stronger), freshness (newer = more reliable), psychology (round numbers).
  4. **Wait for price to reach the level.** Be patient — do not chase.
  5. **Drop to the lower timeframe.** 15-minute or 5-minute for the trigger.
  6. **Wait for confirmation.** Bullish candlestick at support / bearish at resistance, or lower-timeframe MSS in the bias direction.
  7. **Enter on the confirmation candle close.**
  8. **Set the stop.** Below the support zone (buy) or above the resistance zone (sell), with a small buffer.
  9. **Set the target.** Next bias-opposite S&R level — the next resistance for a buy, the next support for a sell.
  10. **Manage the trade.** Book partials at 1:1, trail to the full target.

**For traders in the United States** who follow the CFTC FIFO and no-hedge rules, the S&R framework maps cleanly onto NQ and ES futures (CME Group) plus regulated forex pairs through US-based brokers. title: support-resistance-trading
section: Common Mistakes Around Support and Resistance
content:
#### Common Mistakes Around Support and Resistance

These are the recurring mistakes I see when traders first start trading S&R.

  1. **Marking too many levels.** Every wick is not a level. Only the most-tested zones with clear reactions qualify.
  2. **Trading S &R against the trend.** Buy at support in bullish trend, sell at resistance in bearish trend — counter-trend S&R has a much lower hit rate.
  3. **Entering without confirmation.** S&R is the zone — the entry trigger is the candlestick confirmation or lower-timeframe MSS. Touching the zone alone is not enough.
  4. **Stops parked exactly at the zone.** S&R zones get hunted with wicks. Place the stop with a buffer below support / above resistance.
  5. **Ignoring the timeframe rule.** A daily support is stronger than a 5-minute support. Trade the higher-timeframe zone first.
  6. **Treating broken levels as still valid.** Once price closes through a level, it flips polarity — old support becomes resistance and vice versa. Treat the broken level as opposite-direction support / resistance now.

title: support-resistance-trading
section: FAQs about Support and Resistance Trading
content:
#### FAQs about Support and Resistance Trading

Brief answers to the questions readers ask most often about support and resistance.

**What is support in trading?**

A horizontal price zone where price has historically bounced upward. Traders expect the bearish trend to retrace or reverse from a support zone.

**What is resistance in trading?**

A horizontal price zone where price has historically been rejected downward. Traders expect the bullish trend to retrace or reverse from a resistance zone.

**What are the four pillars of S &R identification?**

(1) Historical price reaction — multiple bounces strengthen the zone. (2) Timeframe — higher timeframes produce stronger zones. (3) Freshness — newer levels are more reliable than older ones. (4) Psychology — round numbers (100s, 1000s) draw more order flow.

**Should I mark S &R as a line or a zone?**

A zone is generally better than a single line. Price rarely reacts at the exact pip — the zone gives room for the reaction to set up.

**How is support and resistance different from supply and demand?**

S&R are horizontal historical-reaction levels. Supply and demand are directional zones identified by the candle pattern that produced the move. Every S&D zone acts as S&R, but not every S&R is a S&D zone.

**Where do I enter the trade?**

After price reaches the S&R zone and a confirmation candle prints (bullish at support, bearish at resistance) — or after a lower-timeframe MSS triggers in the bias direction.

**Where do I place the stop loss?**

Below the support zone for buy trades, above the resistance zone for sell trades, with a small buffer for wick hunts.

**Where do I take profit?**

The next bias-opposite S&R level — the next resistance for a buy trade, the next support for a sell trade.

**What timeframe is best for S &R?**

Higher timeframes (daily, 4-hour) for marking the strongest zones. Lower timeframes (15-minute, 5-minute) for the entry trigger.

**How does S &R fit in the ICT framework?**

S&R is the price-target layer; ICT structure (BOS, CHOCH, MSS) is the entry layer. Use higher-timeframe S&R aligned with a PD array, then take the lower-timeframe MSS trigger.

**What happens when a level breaks?**

It flips polarity — broken support becomes resistance, broken resistance becomes support. Retests of the flipped level are often very tradeable.

**Does S &R work on indices and gold?**

Yes — NQ, ES and XAU/USD all respect horizontal S&R, especially during the New York AM session and around US economic releases.

**Can I trade with S &R alone?**

Yes, but the hit rate improves significantly when paired with trend alignment, candlestick confirmation, or lower-timeframe MSS at the zone.

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/valid-ict-fair-value-gap/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/valid-ict-fair-value-gap/)

![Valid ICT Fair Value Gap explained — three strength tiers of the 3-candle pattern](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/ICT-CISD-vs-ICT-MSS-c.png)

I used to think every fair value gap was the same. Then I lost a string of trades on FVGs that “looked clean” — only to realize months later that I was trading the weak ones and ignoring the strong ones. The chart was telling me everything I needed to know. I just didn’t know what to look for.

A **Valid ICT Fair Value Gap** is a 3-candle pattern that has the strength to hold price when it returns to it. Not every FVG is built the same. Some get blown through on the first retest. Others act like a wall.

In this guide, I’ll show you the 3-candle pattern an FVG forms, exactly what makes one “valid”, and the three strength tiers — Weak, Quietly Strong, and Exceptional — so you can stop wasting trades on FVGs that were never going to hold.

If you’re brand new to the concept, start with our full guide on the [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap") and come back here for the validity layer.

Ready? Let’s break it down.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: What is a Valid ICT Fair Value Gap?
content:
## What is a Valid ICT Fair Value Gap?

A valid ICT Fair Value Gap is a 3-candle pattern strong enough to deliver a real reaction when price retraces back to it.

The basic FVG itself is simple: an unretraced area between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3 (for bullish), or between the low of candle 1 and the high of candle 3 (for bearish). Michael Huddleston introduced it as one of the core PD Arrays in ICT trading.

But here’s the part most traders miss — not every FVG that prints on a chart is worth trading. The strength of an FVG depends on what the surrounding candles look like, especially the relative size of candle 2.

That difference is what separates a valid FVG from a setup that fails on first touch.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: The 3-Candle Pattern (Quick Recap)
content:
## The 3-Candle Pattern (Quick Recap)

Every Fair Value Gap is made from three consecutive candles.

  * **Candle 1:** the candle before the displacement.
  * **Candle 2:** the displacement candle — the big body that creates the imbalance.
  * **Candle 3:** the candle after the displacement, completing the pattern.

For a **bullish FVG** , the gap sits between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3 — a vertical area candle 2 ripped through without filling.

For a **bearish FVG** , the gap sits between the low of candle 1 and the high of candle 3 — same idea, opposite direction.

For a deeper walkthrough of the basic 3-candle structure with both bullish and bearish examples, see our full guide on the [ICT Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap").

Now that you’ve got the pattern down, let’s see what makes one valid.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Why Some FVGs Hold and Others Fail
content:
## Why Some FVGs Hold and Others Fail

Here’s the simple version. An FVG forms when candle 2 displaces price hard enough to leave an imbalance. The further candle 2 displaces past candle 1’s range, the stronger the imbalance — and the stronger the FVG.

If candle 2 barely makes it out of candle 1’s range, the imbalance is weak. Smart money has barely committed. Price has no real reason to respect that area on retest.

If candle 2 blows through candle 1’s range AND candle 3 keeps going, that’s an institutional fingerprint. Price will almost always react when it returns to that zone.

This is the basis of the three tiers below.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: 3 Types of Valid Fair Value Gap (By Strength)
content:
## 3 Types of Valid Fair Value Gap (By Strength)

There are three strength tiers based on how candle 2 and candle 3 behave relative to candle 1.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: (I) Weak Fair Value Gap
content:
### (I) Weak Fair Value Gap

A weak FVG forms entirely **inside the range of a previous large candle**.

The 3-candle pattern is technically there, but the whole structure sits within the body and wicks of a single earlier candle. Candle 2’s displacement isn’t strong enough to break out of that earlier range.

Because price hasn’t actually broken any prior structure, the imbalance is shallow. Higher chance of failure when price retraces — price often blows right through it.

![Weak ICT Fair Value Gap example formed entirely inside the range of a previous large candle](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/ICT-Weak-FVG.png)

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: (II) Quietly Strong Fair Value Gap
content:
### (II) Quietly Strong Fair Value Gap

A quietly strong FVG breaks the range of the previous candle on candle 2 — but candle 3 fails to continue.

For a bullish setup, candle 3 is an inside candle that doesn’t break candle 2’s high. For a bearish setup, candle 3 doesn’t break candle 2’s low.

So the displacement was real, but the follow-through was hesitant. Smart money committed but didn’t push. This FVG can hold — sometimes — but its strength is questioned because the move stalled.

![Quietly Strong ICT Fair Value Gap example with displacement on candle 2 and an inside candle 3 that fails to continue](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Order-Block-Example-1.png)

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: (III) Exceptional Fair Value Gap
content:
### (III) Exceptional Fair Value Gap

An exceptional FVG does both: candle 2 breaks the previous candle’s range, AND candle 3 continues the move beyond candle 2’s high (bullish) or low (bearish).

Three things are true at once: the imbalance is real, the displacement is strong, and the follow-through confirms institutional commitment.

This is the lowest-failure tier. When price returns to an exceptional FVG, the reaction is almost always violent and immediate.

![Exceptional ICT Fair Value Gap example with strong displacement on candle 2 and clear continuation on candle 3](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Exceptional-Fair-Value-Gap.png)

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: How to Use the Strength Filter in Your Trades
content:
## How to Use the Strength Filter in Your Trades

Once you can rank an FVG by strength, your trade plan changes.

  1. **Mark every FVG on your bias timeframe.** Then categorize each one — weak, quietly strong, or exceptional.
  2. **Drop the weak ones.** Don’t trade them. They’re traps.
  3. **Trade quietly strong only with confluence** — a higher-timeframe order block, a liquidity sweep, or a kill-zone window. On its own, the strength is not enough.
  4. **Take exceptional FVGs as primary entries.** Wait for price to retrace, drop to a lower timeframe, and confirm with [CISD or MSS](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-cisd-and-ict-mss/> "ICT CISD vs MSS") before entering.
  5. **Place your stop loss beyond the FVG itself** , not just below the entry candle. The FVG is your invalidation level — if price closes back through it, the trade thesis is broken.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest valid FVGs sit inside a [displacement](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-displacement-move/> "ICT Displacement Move") move that also takes liquidity. When all three are true — exceptional FVG, real displacement, liquidity grabbed — that’s when ICT calls it institutional order flow. The win rate on these setups is significantly higher than trading FVGs in isolation.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Bonus Tip: Confirming a Valid FVG with CISD or MSS
content:
## Bonus Tip: Confirming a Valid FVG with CISD or MSS

The fastest way to know if a valid FVG is going to hold on retest is to wait for confirmation on a lower timeframe.

When price taps a quietly strong or exceptional FVG, drop from your bias timeframe to 5-minute or 15-minute. Watch for one of two things:

  * A [Change in the State of Delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-cisd-and-ict-mss/> "ICT CISD") in your direction.
  * A [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") in your direction.

Either confirms the FVG is being defended by smart money. Without confirmation, even an exceptional FVG can be a trap. With it, your win rate jumps.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the 3-candle pattern of an ICT Fair Value Gap?

An ICT Fair Value Gap is a 3-candle pattern. Candle 2 is the displacement candle that creates an imbalance. The gap is the unretraced area between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3 (for a bullish FVG), or between the low of candle 1 and the high of candle 3 (for a bearish FVG).

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: What is a valid ICT Fair Value Gap?
content:
### What is a valid ICT Fair Value Gap?

A valid ICT Fair Value Gap is a 3-candle pattern strong enough to deliver a real reaction when price retraces back to it. Not every FVG on a chart is valid — only the ones formed by genuine displacement, where candle 2 breaks out of candle 1’s range and candle 3 confirms the move.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: How do I know if an FVG is bullish or bearish?
content:
### How do I know if an FVG is bullish or bearish?

A bullish FVG has the gap between the high of candle 1 and the low of candle 3, with candle 2 closing higher. A bearish FVG has the gap between the low of candle 1 and the high of candle 3, with candle 2 closing lower. The direction of candle 2 sets the bias.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: What’s the difference between a weak FVG and an exceptional FVG?
content:
### What’s the difference between a weak FVG and an exceptional FVG?

A weak FVG forms entirely inside the range of a previous large candle — the displacement isn’t strong enough to break the prior structure. An exceptional FVG breaks the prior candle’s range AND has a candle 3 that continues the move. Weak FVGs fail often. Exceptional FVGs almost always hold.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Should I trade every Fair Value Gap I see?
content:
### Should I trade every Fair Value Gap I see?

No. Only the quietly strong and exceptional ones — and ideally only with lower-timeframe CISD or MSS confirmation. Weak FVGs are traps.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Is a Valid FVG the same as an Inverse FVG?
content:
### Is a Valid FVG the same as an Inverse FVG?

No. A Valid FVG is one strong enough to hold price on retest. An [Inverse FVG](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/inverse-fair-value-gap-ict-ifvg/> "ICT Inverse FVG") is a failed FVG that flips role and acts in the opposite direction — different concept entirely.

title: valid-ict-fair-value-gap
section: Wrapping Up
content:
## Wrapping Up

We hope this guide helped you separate the FVGs worth trading from the ones that look clean but fail on first touch.

Most retail traders skip the validity layer entirely and wonder why their FVG trades miss. Now you know the three tiers — and which one to actually take.

Run through your last 20 charted FVG trades this week. Tag each one as weak, quietly strong, or exceptional. The pattern in your win rate will be obvious.

# What is ICT Hidden Order Block – The Secret PD Array

**Source:** [https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-ict-hidden-order-block/](https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/what-is-ict-hidden-order-block/)

![ICT Hidden Order Block on a Daily chart — the secret PD Array hidden inside overlapping wicks](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/ict-hidden-OB.png)

The first time someone showed me a hidden order block on a Daily chart, I couldn’t believe I had been ignoring this PD Array my entire trading career. It was sitting right there on every higher timeframe — buried inside two overlapping candlestick wicks — and I’d been walking past it like it was nothing.

An **ICT Hidden Order Block** is exactly that — a secret [PD Array](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array Matrix") hidden inside overlapping wicks on a higher timeframe. You can’t see it with the naked eye. But once you drop to a lower timeframe inside that wick overlap, a fully formed order block is sitting there.

That’s why we call it “hidden”. It’s a real order block — just camouflaged by the higher timeframe candles.

In this guide, I’ll show you what a hidden order block is, how to spot it in 3 simple steps, how it differs from a regular order block, and exactly how to trade it with CISD or MSS confirmation.

Don’t worry — you don’t need years of experience to find these. Once you know the pattern, you’ll see hidden order blocks on almost every higher-timeframe chart you open.

Ready? Let’s break it down.

Table of Contents

[Toggle](<#>)

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: What is ICT Hidden Order Block?
content:
## What is ICT Hidden Order Block?

An ICT Hidden Order Block is an order block that does not show up clearly on a higher timeframe.

It forms when two same-colour candles overlap each other’s wicks. Inside that wick overlap — on a lower timeframe — an order block has already formed.

So instead of seeing a clean order block candle, you only see overlapping wicks. The institutional order is still sitting there. It is just hidden in plain sight.

The hidden order block is the price range from one wick extreme to the other. For a bullish setup that’s the wick low of the second candle to the wick high of the first candle. For a bearish setup it’s the inverse.

You can see the example of an ICT Hidden Order Block in the picture below:

![ICT Hidden Order Block zone marked between two consecutive same-colour candles with overlapping wicks](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/hidden-order-block.png)

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Hidden Order Block vs Regular ICT Order Block
content:
## Hidden Order Block vs Regular ICT Order Block

The quick contrast:

  * **Regular[Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block"):** visible on the chart as one candle.
  * **Hidden Order Block:** visible only as overlapping wicks — the actual order block lives on the lower timeframe.

If you’re new to order blocks, read the [ICT Order Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-order-block/> "ICT Order Block") guide first (and the [bullish](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bullish-order-block/> "ICT Bullish Order Block") / [bearish](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-bearish-order-block/> "ICT Bearish Order Block") variants), then come back here. The [Mitigation Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-mitigation-block-explained/> "ICT Mitigation Block") and [Breaker Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block") are different concepts again — covered in their own posts.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: How to Identify an ICT Hidden Order Block
content:
## How to Identify an ICT Hidden Order Block

You can spot a hidden order block in three simple steps.

  1. **Find two consecutive same-colour candles.** Both bullish for a bullish hidden OB. Both bearish for a bearish one.
  2. **Check for wick overlap.** The wick of the first candle and the wick of the second candle must overlap each other.
  3. **Mark the overlap zone.** Draw a box from one wick extreme to the other. That’s your hidden order block.

If you drop to a lower timeframe inside that wick overlap zone, you’ll usually see a clean order block formed there. That’s the institutional footprint the higher timeframe is hiding.

With identification down, here are the two types you’ll find on a chart.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Types of ICT Hidden Order Block
content:
## Types of ICT Hidden Order Block

There are two types based on market direction.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: (I) Bullish Hidden Order Block
content:
### (I) Bullish Hidden Order Block

A bullish hidden OB forms when two consecutive bullish (green) candles overlap their wicks.

The first candle has an upper wick. The second candle has a lower wick that overlaps with the first candle’s upper wick.

Mark the box from the low of the second candle’s wick to the high of the first candle’s wick. That whole range is the bullish hidden order block.

You can see the example of bullish hidden order block in the picture below:

![Bullish ICT Hidden Order Block — first bullish candle’s upper wick overlapping with second bullish candle’s lower wick](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/BULLISH-HIDDEN-OB.png)

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: (II) Bearish Hidden Order Block
content:
### (II) Bearish Hidden Order Block

A bearish hidden OB forms when two consecutive bearish (red) candles overlap their wicks.

The first candle has a lower wick. The second candle has an upper wick that overlaps with the first candle’s lower wick.

Mark the box from the high of the second candle’s wick to the low of the first candle’s wick. That’s your bearish hidden order block.

You can see an example of a bearish hidden order block in the picture below:

![Bearish ICT Hidden Order Block — first bearish candle’s lower wick overlapping with second bearish candle’s upper wick](https://innercircletrader.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/bearish-hidden-order-block.png)

Now that you can spot both types on a chart, let’s look at why hidden order blocks behave the way they do.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Hidden Order Block as a PD Array
content:
## Hidden Order Block as a PD Array

The hidden order block is part of the wider [ICT PD Array Matrix](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-pd-array-key-to-trade-execution/> "ICT PD Array Matrix") — that guide covers the full hierarchy and why price returns to PD Arrays.

For the hidden OB specifically, two things are worth knowing inside this post:

**Proximal and distal lines.** The proximal line is the side of the hidden OB closest to current price. The distal line is the far side. You enter near the proximal line and place your stop beyond the distal line.

**Where it sits in the range.** A bullish hidden OB sitting in [discount](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-premium-and-discount-zone-identification/> "ICT Premium and Discount Zone") is a strong long signal. A bearish one sitting in premium is a strong short.

With the why out of the way, let’s pin down the timeframes.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Best Timeframes for ICT Hidden Order Block
content:
## Best Timeframes for ICT Hidden Order Block

Hidden order blocks form on every timeframe. But they’re most reliable on higher timeframes.

  * **Bias timeframe:** Daily or 4-hour for swing trades. 1-hour for intraday.
  * **Hidden OB timeframe:** the same higher timeframe you use for bias.
  * **Confirmation timeframe:** 5-minute or 15-minute to spot CISD or MSS once price taps the hidden OB.

The bigger the timeframe of the hidden OB, the bigger the move it tends to drive. A Daily hidden OB will usually push price further than a 1-hour one.

Now you know which timeframes to use. Let’s walk through the actual trade.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: How to Trade ICT Hidden Order Block (Step by Step)
content:
## How to Trade ICT Hidden Order Block (Step by Step)

Trading a hidden order block follows the same flow as any PD Array trade. Here’s the exact sequence.

  1. **Set your higher timeframe bias.** Decide if you’re looking for longs or shorts based on [institutional order flow](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-order-flow-explained/> "ICT Institutional Order Flow") and your [daily bias](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-daily-bias-explained/> "ICT Daily Bias").
  2. **Mark your hidden order block.** Find the overlapping wicks on your bias timeframe and draw the box.
  3. **Wait for price to retrace.** Don’t chase. Let price come back to tap the hidden OB.
  4. **Drop to a lower timeframe for confirmation.** Once price enters the hidden OB zone, switch to 5m or 15m.
  5. **Look for CISD or MSS.** A [Change in the State of Delivery (CISD)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-cisd-and-ict-mss/> "ICT CISD vs MSS") or a [Market Structure Shift (MSS)](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-market-structure-shift/> "ICT Market Structure Shift") in your direction confirms the trade.
  6. **Enter the trade.** Take entry on the close of the CISD/MSS candle or on a clean retest of it.
  7. **Place your stop loss.** Below the CISD/MSS swing low for longs. Above the swing high for shorts. For a wider stop, place it just beyond the distal line of the hidden OB itself.
  8. **Set your target.** Aim for the next opposing PD Array, the next liquidity pool, or use a fixed risk-reward like 1:3.

**Pro Tip** — The strongest hidden order blocks are the ones that have a [Fair Value Gap](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/fair-value-gap-trading-strategy/> "ICT Fair Value Gap"), [breaker block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-breaker-block-trading/> "ICT Breaker Block"), or [liquidity void](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/master-ict-liquidity-void/> "ICT Liquidity Void") stacked inside the same zone. Confluence makes the reaction more violent. Skip hidden OBs during low-liquidity sessions like the Asia lunch hour — they often fail.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Bonus Tip: Combine Hidden Order Blocks with Liquidity Sweeps
content:
## Bonus Tip: Combine Hidden Order Blocks with Liquidity Sweeps

The highest-probability hidden OB trades happen right after a [liquidity sweep](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-liquidity-sweep-vs-liquidity-run/> "ICT Liquidity Sweep").

The setup: price sweeps liquidity above a swing high (for shorts) or below a swing low (for longs), then retraces back into the hidden order block. The sweep clears the early entries. The hidden OB delivers the institutional fill. CISD on the lower timeframe gives you the entry trigger.

When all three line up — sweep, hidden OB, lower-timeframe confirmation — the win rate jumps significantly.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Frequently Asked Questions
content:
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a hidden order block in ICT trading?

A hidden order block is an order block that’s not visible on the higher timeframe but is hiding inside the overlapping wicks of two same-colour candles. The actual order block lives on the lower timeframe inside that wick overlap.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: How is a hidden order block different from a regular ICT order block?
content:
### How is a hidden order block different from a regular ICT order block?

A regular order block is a single visible candle. A hidden order block is two candles whose wicks overlap, with the real order block tucked inside that overlap on a lower timeframe.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Which timeframe is best for hidden order blocks?
content:
### Which timeframe is best for hidden order blocks?

Daily and 4-hour are the most reliable for swing trades. For intraday trades, mark hidden OBs on the 1-hour and confirm on 5-minute or 15-minute.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Is a hidden order block a PD array?
content:
### Is a hidden order block a PD array?

Yes. The hidden order block sits inside the PD array family alongside regular order blocks, fair value gaps, breakers, and mitigation blocks.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Where should I place my stop loss on a hidden order block trade?
content:
### Where should I place my stop loss on a hidden order block trade?

The tighter stop is below the CISD or MSS swing low for longs (above the swing high for shorts). The wider stop sits just beyond the distal line of the hidden order block itself.

title: what-is-ict-hidden-order-block
section: Is a hidden order block the same as a suspension block?
content:
### Is a hidden order block the same as a suspension block?

No. A suspension block is a separate PD array introduced by ICT in September 2025. Both are “hidden” PD arrays in the sense that they don’t show up obviously on the chart, but the formation rules are different. See our [ICT Suspension Block](<https://innercircletrader.net/tutorials/ict-suspension-block/> "ICT Suspension Block") guide for the full breakdown.

section: Wrapping Up
content:
## Wrapping Up

We hope this guide helped you understand the ICT Hidden Order Block and how to trade it with confidence.

The hidden order block is one of the most underrated PD Arrays — most retail traders ignore it because they only look at the higher timeframe. Now you know better.

Mark a few hidden OBs on your charts this week. Once you see them, you can’t unsee them.
